item.title: How to Disable Contactless Payment on a Credit Card
item.description: A practical guide to disabling contactless payment on a spare credit card while keeping chip and magnetic-stripe payments available, with safety limits and better alternatives.
item.content:encoded: <p><strong>A contactless card has a separate NFC antenna.</strong> If you keep the card inside a phone case, the antenna triggers card clash or repeated NFC alerts on some phones. A physical break in the antenna loop disables tap to pay while the chip and magnetic stripe remain available on some cards.</p> <p><em>Use a spare card for this project. Treat the modification as permanent, and confirm the result with the card issuer before relying on it.</em></p> <h2 id="why-disable-contactless-payment"> <a href="#why-disable-contactless-payment" title="Why Disable Contactless Payment?">Why Disable Contactless Payment?</a> <a href="#why-disable-contactless-payment" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Why Disable Contactless Payment?">#</a> </h2> <p>Tap to pay is convenient, and modern mobile wallets add another payment token to the same phone. The problem starts when an NFC-enabled physical card sits close to the phone’s NFC reader.</p> <p>Two payment instruments might answer the same reader. Android might also detect the physical card when you open or handle the phone. Removing the card from the case solves the problem, but it adds friction every time you pay.</p> <p>The goal here is narrow: disable the card’s contactless interface while keeping other payment methods available.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Payment method</th> <th>Expected result after an antenna break</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Contactless payment</strong></td> <td>Disabled because the NFC antenna loop no longer couples with a reader</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>EMV chip</strong></td> <td>Often remains available if the chip and its contacts are untouched</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Magnetic stripe</strong></td> <td>Often remains available if the stripe is untouched</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Online card payments</strong></td> <td>Usually unaffected, but the issuer might replace or deactivate the card after damage</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <h2 id="how-the-card-works"> <a href="#how-the-card-works" title="How the Card Works">How the Card Works</a> <a href="#how-the-card-works" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="How the Card Works">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>The NFC antenna is a thin conductive loop inside the plastic.</strong> It usually runs around much of the card perimeter. A contactless reader powers the card through this loop and exchanges data with the embedded NFC chip.</p> <p>The EMV contact chip uses exposed metal contacts on the card face. The magnetic stripe uses a separate strip along the back. These systems share the same card body, but they do not need the same antenna loop.</p> <p>This separation explains the modification. Breaking the loop stops NFC communication. It does not erase the card number, destroy the stripe, or remove the EMV contacts when the cut stays clear of those components.</p> <h2 id="the-lower-risk-options"> <a href="#the-lower-risk-options" title="The Lower-Risk Options">The Lower-Risk Options</a> <a href="#the-lower-risk-options" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="The Lower-Risk Options">#</a> </h2> <p>Physical modification is a last resort. Check these options first:</p> <ul> <li><strong>Ask the issuer for a non-contactless replacement.</strong> Some issuers offer card variants without tap to pay.</li> <li><strong>Store the card away from the phone.</strong> A separate sleeve removes the NFC collision without changing the card.</li> <li><strong>Use a card holder with shielding.</strong> Test the holder with the phone and the card before depending on it for payment.</li> <li><strong>Use a virtual wallet token.</strong> Apple Pay and Google Pay let the phone handle contactless payment while the physical card stays in reserve.</li> <li><strong>Use a different backup card.</strong> Keeping the modified card out of daily service avoids a failure at a merchant.</li> </ul> <p><em>Do not microwave, burn, bend, or puncture the card near the chip. Those methods create unnecessary damage and might expose you to heat, sharp fragments, or a failed backup payment method.</em></p> <h2 id="antenna-modification"> <a href="#antenna-modification" title="Antenna Modification">Antenna Modification</a> <a href="#antenna-modification" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Antenna Modification">#</a> </h2> <p>The method described by the linked examples is simple in concept: locate the antenna loop, then make one small break in the loop with a fine tool. The exact antenna route differs by card design, so do not copy a location from one card to another.</p> <p>A bright flashlight behind the card might reveal the antenna path. Some cards show a visible wire or loop near the perimeter. Keep the break away from the EMV chip, its contacts, the magnetic stripe, embossed numbers, and any visible issuer markings.</p> <p>Work on a stable surface with eye protection. Secure the card before cutting or drilling. Use controlled pressure, stop when the loop is broken, and inspect both sides for cracks. A tiny cut or hole is enough. More damage does not improve the result.</p> <p>The result is permanent. A damaged card falls outside some issuer replacement policies, and a merchant terminal refuses cards with cracked bodies or misaligned contacts. Keep another payment method available before testing it.</p> <h2 id="test-the-result"> <a href="#test-the-result" title="Test the Result">Test the Result</a> <a href="#test-the-result" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Test the Result">#</a> </h2> <p>Test each function separately:</p> <ol> <li>Hold the card away from the phone and try it at a contactless reader. The tap should fail if the antenna loop is broken.</li> <li>Insert the card into a compatible terminal and test the EMV chip with the required PIN.</li> <li>Test the magnetic stripe only where the merchant and issuer still support it.</li> <li>Check the card account or call the issuer to confirm the card remains active.</li> <li>Add the card to the phone wallet only if the issuer supports the wallet token and you still want phone-based contactless payments.</li> </ol> <p>Do not test with an important purchase. Use a low-value transaction, and keep a second card or cash available.</p> <h2 id="video-demonstration"> <a href="#video-demonstration" title="Video Demonstration">Video Demonstration</a> <a href="#video-demonstration" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Video Demonstration">#</a> </h2> <p>The following video shows the physical modification and explains why breaking the antenna loop stops contactless operation:</p> <script> function loadLiteYouTubeScript() { if (document.querySelector('script[src^="/p/jsdelivr/npm/@justinribeiro/lite-youtube@1.5.0/lite-youtube.js"]')) { console.log('Lite YouTube script is already loaded.'); return; } var scriptTag = document.createElement('script'); scriptTag.src = '/p/jsdelivr/npm/@justinribeiro/lite-youtube@1.5.0/lite-youtube.js'; scriptTag.setAttribute('defer', ''); scriptTag.setAttribute('type', 'module'); scriptTag.setAttribute('fetchpriority', 'low'); document.body.appendChild(scriptTag); } document.addEventListener('DOMContentLoaded', function () { if (typeof yieldToMain === 'function') { yieldToMain(loadLiteYouTubeScript, "user-visible"); } else { loadLiteYouTubeScript(); } }); </script> <style scoped> .lite-youtube-fallback { aspect-ratio: 16 / 9; display: flex; justify-content: center; align-items: center; flex-direction: column; gap: 1em; padding: 1em; background-color: #000; color: #fff; text-decoration: none; } .lite-youtube-fallback::before { display: block; content: ''; border: solid transparent; border-width: 2em 0 2em 3em; border-left-color: red; } .lite-youtube-fallback:hover::before { border-left-color: #fff; } .lite-youtube-fallback:focus { outline: 2px solid red; } </style><div itemscope itemtype="http://schema.org/VideoObject http://schema.org/LearningResource" style="position: relative; padding-bottom: 56.25%; height: 0; overflow: hidden;"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Why Does My Credit Card Have a Hole in It?"> <meta itemprop="description" content="YouTube Video"> <meta itemprop="thumbnailUrl" content="https://img.youtube.com/vi/XH_st471JEU/maxresdefault.jpg"> <meta itemprop="contentUrl" content="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XH_st471JEU"> <meta itemprop="learningResourceType" content="Concept Overview"> <meta itemprop="educationalLevel" content="High school (US)"> <lite-youtube videoid="XH_st471JEU" videotitle="Why Does My Credit Card Have a Hole in It?" videoplay="" nocookie posterloading="lazy" loading="lazy" params=""> <noscript> <a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XH_st471JEU" class="lite-youtube-fallback" style="position: absolute; top: 0; left: 0; width: 100%; height: 100%; border:0;" title="Why Does My Credit Card Have a Hole in It?"> <span class="lyt-visually-hidden"></span> </a> </noscript> </lite-youtube> </div> <script type="application/ld+json"> { "@context": "https://schema.org", "@type": ["VideoObject", "LearningResource"], "name": "Why Does My Credit Card Have a Hole in It?", "description": "YouTube Video", "thumbnailUrl": ["https:\/\/img.youtube.com\/vi\/XH_st471JEU\/maxresdefault.jpg"], "contentUrl": "https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XH_st471JEU", "learningResourceType": "Concept Overview", "educationalLevel": "High school (US)" } </script> <p>The video is a demonstration, not a guarantee for every card design. Use it to understand the concept, then inspect your own card before deciding whether the risk is acceptable.</p> <h2 id="what-the-sources-show"> <a href="#what-the-sources-show" title="What the Sources Show">What the Sources Show</a> <a href="#what-the-sources-show" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="What the Sources Show">#</a> </h2> <p>The examples below use two related approaches. Art Chaidarun describes making a small cut in the antenna loop while keeping the chip and stripe functional. The Instructables guide documents a similar physical approach for disabling contactless payment on a debit card. The forum discussion adds a useful warning: break the loop away from the EMV chip rather than drilling beside it.</p> <p>These reports describe individual cards. They do not establish a universal antenna layout or promise issuer approval after modification. Your card issuer’s replacement and deactivation rules control the final outcome.</p> <h2 id="references"> <a href="#references" title="References">References</a> <a href="#references" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="References">#</a> </h2> <ol> <li> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Art Chaidarun, How to Disable Contactless Payment on a Credit Card"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://chaidarun.com/disable-contactless-payment"> <a href="https://chaidarun.com/disable-contactless-payment" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Art Chaidarun, How to Disable Contactless Payment on a Credit Card</a> </span> </li> <li> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Instructables, How to Disable Contactless Payment on Your Debit Card"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://www.instructables.com/How-to-Disable-Contactless-Payment-on-Your-Debit-C/"> <a href="https://www.instructables.com/How-to-Disable-Contactless-Payment-on-Your-Debit-C/" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Instructables, How to Disable Contactless Payment on Your Debit Card</a> </span> </li> <li> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Dangerous Things Forum, Easiest way of disabling NFC in a credit card"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://forum.dangerousthings.com/t/easiest-way-of-disabling-nfc-in-a-credit-card/"> <a href="https://forum.dangerousthings.com/t/easiest-way-of-disabling-nfc-in-a-credit-card/" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Dangerous Things Forum, Easiest way of disabling NFC in a credit card</a> </span> </li> <li> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="DeviantOllam, Why Does My Credit Card Have a Hole in It?"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XH_st471JEU"> <a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XH_st471JEU" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >DeviantOllam, Why Does My Credit Card Have a Hole in It?</a> </span> </li> </ol> <h2 id="next-steps"> <a href="#next-steps" title="Next Steps">Next Steps</a> <a href="#next-steps" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Next Steps">#</a> </h2> <p>If you need a payment card for a phone case, start with an issuer-approved non-contactless card or a separate sleeve. If you modify a spare card, test every remaining payment method before carrying it as your only backup.</p> <p>For related payment-card details, read the <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Privacy.com virtual cards guide"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/articles/privacy-com-virtual-debit-cards-security-privacy/"> <a href="/articles/privacy-com-virtual-debit-cards-security-privacy/" rel="follow me" >Privacy.com virtual cards guide</a> </span> and use the <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="magnetic stripe decoder"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/magnetic-stripe-decoder/"> <a href="/magnetic-stripe-decoder/" rel="follow me" >magnetic stripe decoder</a> </span> to study the data stored on Tracks 1 and 2.</p> Read More at https://simeononsecurity.com/

item.title: Llama 3.1 8B and Qwen3.8 27B GPU Benchmarks on Vast.ai
item.category: "Local AI" , "GPU Benchmarking" , "Self-Hosted AI" , "Cloud Computing" , "Artificial Intelligence" , "AI Economics"
item.description: Measured Ollama benchmarks of Llama 3.1 8B and Qwen3.8 27B across leading Vast.ai GPUs. Compare decode speed, long-context behavior, rental cost, self-hosting tradeoffs, API credits, and subscriptions.
item.content:encoded: <p><strong>The H100 SXM was the fastest card in both Ollama model tests, but it was not the best value.</strong> The RTX PRO 5000 and RTX 6000 Ada delivered a stronger speed-to-rental-cost balance, while the CMP 170HX offered the lowest hourly rate among the completed Qwen3.8 27B runs.</p> <p><em>These results measure one model, one Ollama wrapper, one default quantization, and one serving pattern. Treat them as sizing data for this workload, not as a universal GPU ranking.</em></p> <p>This article compares <strong>Llama 3.1:8b</strong>, an Ollama Q4_K_M build at 8.03B parameters, with <strong>Qwen3.8:27b</strong>, an Ollama Q4_K_M build at roughly 27.3B parameters. Both were tested across GPU instances rented from Vast.ai. The tests focused on decode throughput at actual prompt lengths up to the supported context limit.</p> <h2 id="the-short-answer"> <a href="#the-short-answer" title="The Short Answer">The Short Answer</a> <a href="#the-short-answer" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="The Short Answer">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Rent an RTX PRO 5000 or RTX 6000 Ada for regular single-user work.</strong> The RTX PRO 5000 led the value comparison at short and medium context lengths. The RTX 6000 Ada cost less and kept a useful lead over the A100 cards. Rent an H100 SXM when response speed matters more than hourly cost or when long prompts are part of the workload.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Goal</th> <th>Recommendation</th> <th>Reason</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Lowest test cost</strong></td> <td>CMP 170HX</td> <td>$0.420 per hour and enough VRAM for the tested Q4_K_M models</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Best value under $1.25/hr</strong></td> <td>RTX PRO 5000 or RTX 6000 Ada</td> <td>Strong decode speed without H100 rental cost</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Fastest replies</strong></td> <td>H100 SXM</td> <td>Highest decode speed in both model tests</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Long-context Qwen work</strong></td> <td>H100 SXM or RTX PRO 6000 Max-Q</td> <td>Both completed the approximately 131k-token Qwen run with substantial VRAM headroom</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Popular 8B baseline</strong></td> <td>Llama 3.1:8b</td> <td>A practical 8B comparison with a 128K context limit</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Small recurring workload</strong></td> <td>API credits or a chat subscription</td> <td>No idle GPU charge, maintenance, or deployment work</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Private and frequent workload</strong></td> <td>Owned GPU workstation</td> <td>Hardware cost becomes easier to justify with sustained utilization</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Abliterated or uncensored experiments</strong></td> <td>Rent first, then buy only after sustained use</td> <td>Model behavior, licensing, and operational risk deserve a separate test before hardware spend</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <h2 id="what-was-tested"> <a href="#what-was-tested" title="What Was Tested">What Was Tested</a> <a href="#what-was-tested" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="What Was Tested">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>The benchmark used Ollama with the default Q4_K_M model build.</strong> No special quantization, speculative decoding, custom sampler, or serving stack was added. The goal was a simple, locally reproducible comparison of the GPU instances.</p> <p>Vast.ai describes its service as a GPU cloud marketplace connecting compute providers with users. Its documentation lists on-demand, reserved, interruptible, and serverless options, with search filters for GPU model, memory, price, and availability. The hourly rates below came from the selected instances during this benchmark session, not from a permanent Vast.ai price list.</p> <p>The measured output was <strong>decode throughput</strong>, expressed as generated tokens per second. Prefill throughput is listed separately because it describes prompt processing, not the speed at which the answer appears. A long prompt often takes substantial time to process even when decode speed remains high.</p> <p>The benchmark used two valid trials per context and recorded the median decode result. The completed prompt levels were based on actual <code>prompt_eval_count</code> values:</p> <ul> <li><strong>Approximately 16.4k prompt tokens</strong></li> <li><strong>Approximately 32.8k prompt tokens</strong></li> <li><strong>Approximately 65.5k prompt tokens</strong></li> <li><strong>Approximately 131k prompt tokens</strong></li> </ul> <p>The requested 256k-token run was not completed. The 40 GB A100 cards and several smaller cards were still processing or failed to finish at the target context length.</p> <blockquote> <p><strong>Benchmark limit:</strong> The figures describe two Ollama Q4_K_M workloads under one serving pattern. They do not predict training speed, multi-user throughput, image generation speed, vLLM performance, or another model’s result.</p> </blockquote> <h2 id="llama-31-8b-rerun"> <a href="#llama-31-8b-rerun" title="Llama 3.1 8B Rerun">Llama 3.1 8B Rerun</a> <a href="#llama-31-8b-rerun" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Llama 3.1 8B Rerun">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Llama 3.1:8b provides a useful practical baseline for the same GPU pool.</strong> Ollama lists the model at roughly 120 million downloads, which makes it a reasonable popularity-based choice for a second benchmark. The <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="official Ollama model page"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://ollama.com/library/llama3.1:8b"> <a href="https://ollama.com/library/llama3.1:8b" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >official Ollama model page</a> </span> lists a 4.9 GB Q4_K_M build, 8.03B parameters, and a 128K context window.</p> <p>The rerun used a model-specific benchmark runner and calibrated the prompt generator against Ollama’s tokenizer. The labels below use actual prompt counts rather than requested context settings:</p> <ul> <li><strong>Approximately 32,676 actual prompt tokens</strong> for the 32k target</li> <li><strong>Approximately 65,342 actual prompt tokens</strong> for the 64k target</li> <li><strong>Approximately 130,671 actual prompt tokens</strong> for the 128k target</li> </ul> <p>The 256k level is explicitly unsupported for Llama 3.1 8B because the model’s listed context limit is 128K. The runner added retry handling and status rows, so a timeout remains visible instead of disappearing from the table.</p> <h3 id="llama-31-8b-results"> <a href="#llama-31-8b-results" title="Llama 3.1 8B Results">Llama 3.1 8B Results</a> <a href="#llama-31-8b-results" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Llama 3.1 8B Results">#</a> </h3> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>GPU</th> <th style="text-align: right">~32k decode tok/s</th> <th style="text-align: right">~64k decode tok/s</th> <th style="text-align: right">~128k decode tok/s</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>H100 SXM</strong></td> <td style="text-align: right"><strong>163.5</strong></td> <td style="text-align: right"><strong>124.0</strong></td> <td style="text-align: right"><strong>82.4</strong></td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>H100 SXM</strong></td> <td style="text-align: right"><strong>158.6</strong></td> <td style="text-align: right"><strong>121.2</strong></td> <td style="text-align: right"><strong>80.6</strong></td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>RTX PRO 5000</strong></td> <td style="text-align: right">110.1</td> <td style="text-align: right">79.8</td> <td style="text-align: right">49.9</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>CMP 170HX 64GB</strong></td> <td style="text-align: right">91.9</td> <td style="text-align: right">71.0</td> <td style="text-align: right">50.1</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>RTX 6000 Ada</strong></td> <td style="text-align: right">88.3</td> <td style="text-align: right">53.9</td> <td style="text-align: right">29.3</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>RTX PRO 6000 Max-Q</strong></td> <td style="text-align: right">66.7</td> <td style="text-align: right">53.0</td> <td style="text-align: right">40.3</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>RTX PRO 6000 S</strong></td> <td style="text-align: right">60.3</td> <td style="text-align: right">42.5</td> <td style="text-align: right">33.9</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>A100 SXM4 40GB</strong></td> <td style="text-align: right">2.0</td> <td style="text-align: right">40.6</td> <td style="text-align: right">38.5</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>A100 PCIe 40GB</strong></td> <td style="text-align: right">1.2</td> <td style="text-align: right">20.3</td> <td style="text-align: right">20.3</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>2x RTX 5060 Ti</strong></td> <td style="text-align: right">1.3</td> <td style="text-align: right">26.8</td> <td style="text-align: right">Timeout</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>The two H100 rows came from separate valid instances of the same GPU class. Both were clearly ahead of the other cards. Their 32k results were 44% to 48% faster than the RTX PRO 5000, and their 128k results were about 61% to 65% faster.</p> <p>The A100 and RTX 5060 Ti 32k results are too low to represent comparable GPU execution for this workload. The RTX 5060 Ti host also timed out during the second 128k trial. Treat the host as unsuitable for valid GPU throughput comparisons rather than as a genuine ranking result.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Context target</th> <th>Status</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>32k</strong></td> <td>Completed on all 10 hosts</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>64k</strong></td> <td>Completed on all 10 hosts</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>128k</strong></td> <td>Completed on 9 hosts. The 2x RTX 5060 Ti host timed out during its second trial</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>256k</strong></td> <td>Unsupported for all hosts because Llama 3.1 8B supports up to 128K context</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <h2 id="comparing-the-two-models"> <a href="#comparing-the-two-models" title="Comparing the Two Models">Comparing the Two Models</a> <a href="#comparing-the-two-models" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Comparing the Two Models">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>The smaller Llama model was faster on every comparable GPU, but model size and quality are not interchangeable.</strong> Llama 3.1 8B is useful for a popular, lower-memory baseline. Qwen3.8 27B needs more memory and delivers a different capability profile, so the numbers should guide hardware selection rather than declare one model universally better.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Use case</th> <th>Better benchmark reference</th> <th>Why</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Fast 8B assistant</strong></td> <td>Llama 3.1:8b</td> <td>Higher decode speed and lower model memory demand</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>27B local model sizing</strong></td> <td>Qwen3.8:27b</td> <td>More representative of a larger single-GPU workload</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>128K context ceiling</strong></td> <td>Llama 3.1:8b</td> <td>The model has an explicit 128K limit, so 256k is not a valid target</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Testing VRAM headroom</strong></td> <td>Qwen3.8:27b</td> <td>The larger model exposes memory and long-context limits sooner</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Cross-provider baseline</strong></td> <td>Llama 3.1:8b</td> <td>Popularity and model size make the result easier to reproduce</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>The earlier Qwen rerun also corrected its actual prompt counts to approximately <strong>32,770</strong>, <strong>65,538</strong>, and <strong>131,074</strong> tokens on the supported context levels. Those corrected labels replace requested <code>num_ctx</code> values when comparing Qwen runs.</p> <h2 id="approximately-16k-tokens"> <a href="#approximately-16k-tokens" title="Approximately 16k Tokens">Approximately 16k Tokens</a> <a href="#approximately-16k-tokens" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Approximately 16k Tokens">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>The H100 SXM led the short-context run at 134.4 decode tokens per second.</strong> The RTX PRO 5000 followed at 113.9 tokens per second while costing less than half as much per hour.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th style="text-align: right">Rank</th> <th>GPU</th> <th style="text-align: right">VRAM</th> <th style="text-align: right">Decode tok/s</th> <th style="text-align: right">Prefill tok/s</th> <th style="text-align: right">Rental rate</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td style="text-align: right">1</td> <td><strong>H100 SXM</strong></td> <td style="text-align: right">79.6 GB</td> <td style="text-align: right"><strong>134.4</strong></td> <td style="text-align: right">89,974</td> <td style="text-align: right">$2.693/hr</td> </tr> <tr> <td style="text-align: right">2</td> <td><strong>RTX PRO For interactive use, the extra waiting time often matters more than the lowest token cost.</p> <h2 id="rent-buy-credits-subscribe-or-buy-hardware"> <a href="#rent-buy-credits-subscribe-or-buy-hardware" title="Rent, Buy Credits, Subscribe, or Buy Hardware?">Rent, Buy Credits, Subscribe, or Buy Hardware?</a> <a href="#rent-buy-credits-subscribe-or-buy-hardware" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Rent, Buy Credits, Subscribe, or Buy Hardware?">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>The right option depends on utilization and control requirements.</strong> A GPU rental is a variable compute bill. API credits are a variable model bill. A chat subscription is a fixed access fee with usage limits. Owned hardware is a capital purchase followed by electricity, cooling, maintenance, and depreciation.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Monthly budget and workload</th> <th>Recommended path</th> <th>Why</th> <th>Main compromise</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Under $10</strong></td> <td>Buy API credits or use a free local model</td> <td>Proves the workflow without idle GPU cost</td> <td>Less control over model hosting and rate limits</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>$10 to $30</strong></td> <td>API credits for occasional work, or a chat subscription for daily interactive use</td> <td>A subscription suits human chat, while credits suit scripts and measured calls</td> <td>Neither option gives a private 27B endpoint by default</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>$30 to $100</strong></td> <td>Rent an RTX 6000 Ada or RTX PRO 5000 only during active sessions</td> <td>This budget covers short research bursts and avoids ownership overhead</td> <td>The instance still needs setup, storage, monitoring, and shutdown discipline</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>$100 to $250</strong></td> <td>Rent a fast card for scheduled work, or test an owned workstation plan</td> <td>Sustained monthly usage starts to make utilization visible</td> <td>Rental availability and hourly rates change</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>$250 to $600</strong></td> <td>Compare a month of RTX PRO 5000 rental against a used or new local GPU</td> <td>This is the decision point for frequent private inference</td> <td>Hardware adds power, heat, support, and resale risk</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Above $600</strong></td> <td>Buy hardware only with high utilization, or reserve H100-class rental for burst work</td> <td>A mixed strategy avoids owning peak hardware for occasional demand</td> <td>Capital remains tied up in a single configuration</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>These bands are decision guides, not provider quotes. The benchmark rates show the key break-even issue: an H100 at $2.693 per hour costs about $64.63 for a continuous 24-hour day and about $1,941.00 for 30 days before storage or other charges. The RTX PRO 5000 at $1.005 per hour costs about $24.12 per day and $723.60 for 30 continuous days. A GPU rented only for active sessions has a different total from a GPU left running all month.</p> <h3 id="when-api-credits-win"> <a href="#when-api-credits-win" title="When API Credits Win">When API Credits Win</a> <a href="#when-api-credits-win" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="When API Credits Win">#</a> </h3> <p><strong>API credits win when usage is irregular, automation matters, and the task does not require a specific local model.</strong> Credits avoid GPU provisioning, model downloads, driver problems, and idle time. They also let you compare several hosted models before committing to hardware.</p> <p>API pricing differs by model and provider. OpenRouter’s model catalog is designed for comparing model context sizes, providers, and token pricing. Use the provider’s live calculator before comparing an API bill with this benchmark. A local GPU produces tokens without a per-token provider charge, but its rental hour continues while the instance waits.</p> <h3 id="when-a-subscription-wins"> <a href="#when-a-subscription-wins" title="When a Subscription Wins">When a Subscription Wins</a> <a href="#when-a-subscription-wins" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="When a Subscription Wins">#</a> </h3> <p><strong>A subscription suits a person who uses a hosted assistant every day.</strong> Claude’s current individual plans, for example, separate free, Pro, and Max access levels with different usage limits and features. A subscription is not the same as API access. It often gives a polished interface and bundled tools, while API credits give programmatic control.</p> <p>Choose a subscription when the work is mostly interactive writing, research, coding, or file review. Choose API credits when a script, application, or agent needs a metered endpoint.</p> <h3 id="when-vastai-wins"> <a href="#when-vastai-wins" title="When Vast.ai Wins">When Vast.ai Wins</a> <a href="#when-vastai-wins" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="When Vast.ai Wins">#</a> </h3> <p><strong>Vast.ai wins when you need an open model, private runtime control, or a short burst of high throughput.</strong> You select the GPU, launch an instance, run Ollama, test a model, and shut the instance down when finished. This is a strong path for Qwen3.8 27B, abliterated variants, and other model files unable to fit a consumer laptop.</p> <p>The cost is operational work. You need to confirm the model is using the GPU, watch VRAM, protect the exposed service, preserve any required model files, and stop the instance after the run. A low hourly rate does not fix a forgotten instance.</p> <h3 id="when-buying-a-gpu-wins"> <a href="#when-buying-a-gpu-wins" title="When Buying a GPU Wins">When Buying a GPU Wins</a> <a href="#when-buying-a-gpu-wins" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="When Buying a GPU Wins">#</a> </h3> <p><strong>Buying hardware wins after sustained utilization, stable model requirements, and a need for local control.</strong> The purchase removes rental availability risk and gives you a persistent environment. It also gives you the option to run private data without sending prompts to a hosted provider.</p> <p>The purchase price is only one part of the bill. Add the host system, power supply, storage, cooling, electricity, replacement risk, and the value of your setup time. A high-end card also sits idle during periods when API credits or a subscription would cost less.</p> <p>NVIDIA’s RTX 4090 reference specifications list 24 GB of memory, a 450 W total graphics power rating, and an 850 W minimum system power recommendation. This makes it a useful local-inference reference point, but its 24 GB capacity is below the 27B Q4_K_M configurations tested here. Check actual model memory use rather than assuming a card fits from the parameter count alone.</p> <h2 id="abliterated-and-uncensored-models"> <a href="#abliterated-and-uncensored-models" title="Abliterated and Uncensored Models">Abliterated and Uncensored Models</a> <a href="#abliterated-and-uncensored-models" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Abliterated and Uncensored Models">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Abliterated and uncensored model variants change the buying decision.</strong> Their appeal is often fewer refusal behaviors or fewer built-in restrictions. Their costs include weaker safety behavior, uncertain provenance, inconsistent prompt formatting, higher review needs, and possible license or acceptable-use limits.</p> <p>For these models, rent before buying. A one-day RTX PRO 5000 test at the supplied rate costs about $24.12 before other charges. This is enough to confirm model fit, GPU use, response quality, and operational risk.</p> <p><strong>Do not expose an uncensored model directly to the public internet.</strong> Put authentication, rate limits, logging controls, and network isolation in front of it. Avoid sending personal, confidential, or regulated data to a model source you have not reviewed.</p> <p>If the model becomes a daily tool, compare the monthly rental total with the full cost of an owned workstation. If usage is occasional, the rental remains easier to stop and replace.</p> <h2 id="benchmark-caveats"> <a href="#benchmark-caveats" title="Benchmark Caveats">Benchmark Caveats</a> <a href="#benchmark-caveats" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Benchmark Caveats">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>The missing results are part of the result.</strong> An <code>N/A</code> value means the run did not produce a valid measurement. It does not mean the GPU is slow by the amount implied by another card’s score.</p> <ul> <li><strong>The second H100 instance produced no valid benchmark set</strong> because the model download completed too late.</li> <li><strong>The 2x RTX 5060 Ti instance was excluded</strong> because Ollama loaded the model on the CPU instead of using the GPUs.</li> <li><strong>The Qwen3.8 27B 256k-token prompt was not completed.</strong> Its highest valid level was approximately 131k actual prompt tokens. Llama 3.1 8B marks 256k as unsupported because its context limit is 128K.</li> <li><strong>The requested <code>num_ctx</code> was not used as the ranking label.</strong> The final tables use actual <code>prompt_eval_count</code> values.</li> <li><strong>Two valid trials per context were summarized with the median decode result.</strong> This reduces the effect of one slow run, but it does not replace a larger test set.</li> <li><strong>The wrapper was simple by design.</strong> A tuned vLLM or llama.cpp deployment will produce a different ranking.</li> </ul> <h2 id="final-recommendation"> <a href="#final-recommendation" title="Final Recommendation">Final Recommendation</a> <a href="#final-recommendation" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Final Recommendation">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Start with an RTX 6000 Ada or RTX PRO 5000 rental.</strong> The RTX 6000 Ada is the budget choice when its $0.813 hourly rate is available. The RTX PRO 5000 is the stronger speed choice below H100 pricing. Use the H100 SXM for long prompts, demanding interactive latency, or a short benchmark window where time matters more than rental cost. For an 8B model, the CMP 170HX is worth testing when its lower hourly rate matters more than peak speed.</p> <p><strong>Do not buy a GPU after one successful test.</strong> Rent for a month of real workloads, record active hours, prompt lengths, concurrency, and model changes, then compare the rental total with the complete ownership bill. Buy hardware when the workload is frequent enough to keep the card busy and stable enough to justify the loss of flexibility.</p> <p>For occasional work, API credits or a chat subscription are simpler. For private local inference, open model experimentation, or abliterated model testing, Vast.ai provides a lower-commitment path than buying a workstation immediately. Use Llama 3.1 8B as the lower-memory baseline and Qwen3.8 27B when the larger model is the actual deployment target.</p> <h2 id="references"> <a href="#references" title="References">References</a> <a href="#references" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="References">#</a> </h2> <ol> <li> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Vast.ai GPU cloud marketplace"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://vast.ai/"> <a href="https://vast.ai/" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Vast.ai GPU cloud marketplace</a> </span> </li> <li> <span itemscope item.title: Module 1: Authentication and Credentials
item.description: Why credentials fail, how to choose between a cloud and an offline vault, which second factors stop phishing, and why recovery belongs in the same sitting as setup.
item.content:encoded: <h4 id="-return-to-the-personal-security-course"> <a href="#-return-to-the-personal-security-course" title=" ← Return to the Personal Security Course "> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="← Return to the Personal Security Course"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/personal-security-course-start/"> <a href="/personal-security-course-start/" rel="follow me" >← Return to the Personal Security Course</a> </span> </a> <a href="#-return-to-the-personal-security-course" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title=" ← Return to the Personal Security Course ">#</a> </h4> <p><strong>Authentication is where every other control begins.</strong> An attacker who holds your credentials does not need to defeat your browser hardening, your encrypted disk, or your network segmentation. They log in as you and inherit everything.</p> <p>This module covers how credentials fail, how to choose a vault, which second factors genuinely resist phishing, and why recovery configuration belongs in the same sitting as setup.</p> <p><em>Budget about 45 minutes. The vault decision and the second-factor upgrade are the two highest-yield actions in the entire course.</em></p> <h2 id="what-you-will-learn"> <a href="#what-you-will-learn" title="What You Will Learn">What You Will Learn</a> <a href="#what-you-will-learn" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="What You Will Learn">#</a> </h2> <ul> <li><strong>Explain</strong> how credential stuffing turns one breach into many</li> <li><strong>Distinguish</strong> cloud-synced vaults from offline vaults, including the failure mode of each</li> <li><strong>Rank</strong> second factors by what they resist rather than by convenience</li> <li><strong>Configure</strong> recovery so a lost device does not become a permanent lockout</li> <li><strong>Identify</strong> credentials which should never enter a password manager</li> <li><strong>Produce</strong> an authentication record listing your vault choice, factor per account tier, and recovery location</li> </ul> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Term</th> <th>Meaning</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Credential stuffing</strong></td> <td>Replaying leaked username and password pairs against other services</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Passphrase</strong></td> <td>A password built from several random words, long and easy to recall</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Entropy</strong></td> <td>The unpredictable content of a secret, measured in bits</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Origin binding</strong></td> <td>A credential cryptographically tied to one domain, which defeats lookalike sites</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Recovery key</strong></td> <td>A single-use code which restores access when the second factor is lost</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Vault</strong></td> <td>The encrypted store holding your credentials</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <h2 id="why-credentials-fail"> <a href="#why-credentials-fail" title="Why Credentials Fail">Why Credentials Fail</a> <a href="#why-credentials-fail" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Why Credentials Fail">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Three mechanisms account for most account compromise, and they demand different countermeasures.</strong></p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Attack</th> <th>Mechanism</th> <th>What Stops It</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Credential stuffing</strong></td> <td>Replaying leaked pairs across services</td> <td>Unique passwords per account</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Phishing</strong></td> <td>A lookalike site collecting the password and the code</td> <td>Origin-bound credentials</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Session theft</strong></td> <td>Malware lifts browser cookies and reuses a live session</td> <td>Nothing at the authentication layer, so endpoints matter</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>The third row is the one people miss. <strong>A stolen session cookie bypasses your password and your second factor entirely</strong>, which is why Module 8 exists and why endpoint hygiene is not optional.</p> <p><em>Password reuse is the multiplier. One leaked pair becomes dozens of compromised accounts, automatically and without any further effort from the attacker.</em></p> <h2 id="choosing-a-vault"> <a href="#choosing-a-vault" title="Choosing a Vault">Choosing a Vault</a> <a href="#choosing-a-vault" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Choosing a Vault">#</a> </h2> <p>You need a manager. The only real decision is the architecture.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th></th> <th>Cloud-Synced</th> <th>Offline File-Based</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Examples</strong></td> <td>Bitwarden, 1Password</td> <td>KeePassXC, KeePassDX</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Sync</strong></td> <td>Automatic across devices</td> <td>Manual, or via your own storage</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Recovery</strong></td> <td>Vendor-supported</td> <td>Entirely your responsibility</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Trust</strong></td> <td>The vendor’s encryption and availability</td> <td>Your own backup discipline</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Weakness</strong></td> <td>Vendor outage or breach of the wrapped key</td> <td>Losing the file means losing everything</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Best for</strong></td> <td>Most people, especially multiple devices</td> <td>Users willing to own synchronization</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>Choose cloud-synced unless you have a specific reason not to.</strong> The security gap between a well-run vendor and a self-managed file is small. The gap between either and password reuse is enormous.</p> <p><em>Whichever you pick, the vault is now a single high-value target. The concentration is the trade, and it is a good one because you control the countermeasures.</em></p> <p>Our comparison of the two architectures: <strong> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Best Password Managers 2026: Bitwarden vs KeePassXC"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/articles/bitwarden-and-keepassxc-vs-the-rest/"> <a href="/articles/bitwarden-and-keepassxc-vs-the-rest/" rel="follow me" >Best Password Managers 2026: Bitwarden vs KeePassXC</a> </span> </strong>.</p> <h2 id="the-master-password"> <a href="#the-master-password" title="The Master Password">The Master Password</a> <a href="#the-master-password" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="The Master Password">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Your vault password is now the highest-value secret you own.</strong> Everything else sits behind it.</p> <p>Two rules follow:</p> <ul> <li><strong>Make it long rather than complicated.</strong> A passphrase of five or six random words carries more entropy than a short string of symbols, and you will remember it. Guides to <strong> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Creating Strong Passwords"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/articles/how-to-create-strong-passwords/"> <a href="/articles/how-to-create-strong-passwords/" rel="follow me" >Creating Strong Passwords</a> </span> </strong> cover the arithmetic.</li> <li><strong>Never store it anywhere.</strong> Not in the vault, not in a notes app, not in a browser. If you must write it down during the first week, keep the paper somewhere you control and destroy it once memorized.</li> </ul> <p>If your manager supports it, <strong>enable a second factor on the vault account itself</strong>. This is the one place where a second factor protects the master credential rather than an individual site.</p> <h2 id="second-factors-ranked"> <a href="#second-factors-ranked" title="Second Factors Ranked">Second Factors Ranked</a> <a href="#second-factors-ranked" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Second Factors Ranked">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Second factors are not interchangeable.</strong> They resist different attacks, and the ranking is entirely about what they stop.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Factor</th> <th>Stops Stuffing</th> <th>Stops Phishing</th> <th>Survives Session Theft</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>SMS code</strong></td> <td>Yes</td> <td>Weakly, via SIM swap</td> <td>No</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Email code</strong></td> <td>Yes</td> <td>Weakly, since mail is often already compromised</td> <td>No</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Authenticator app</strong></td> <td>Yes</td> <td>Weakly, via real-time relay</td> <td>No</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Push approval</strong></td> <td>Yes</td> <td>Weakly, via prompt bombing</td> <td>No</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Passkey</strong></td> <td>Yes</td> <td><strong>Yes</strong></td> <td>Yes</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Hardware key (FIDO2)</strong></td> <td>Yes</td> <td><strong>Yes</strong></td> <td>Yes</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>The bottom two rows are the only phishing-resistant options.</strong> The reason is structural. A passkey or hardware key is bound to the domain requesting it, so a lookalike site receives nothing reusable. There is no code for anyone to read aloud.</p> <p>Three failure modes worth naming:</p> <ul> <li><strong>SIM swap</strong> moves your number to an attacker’s device, defeating every SMS factor at once. Set a carrier PIN, covered in Module 7.</li> <li><strong>Prompt bombing</strong> floods you with push requests until you approve one. Number matching helps, and a passkey removes the problem.</li> <li><strong>Real-time relay</strong> puts an attacker between you and the real site, forwarding your code live. Only origin binding defeats it.</li> </ul> <p><em>Upgrade email and finance accounts first. Those two hold the recovery paths for everything else.</em></p> <p>Generate and verify codes locally with the <strong> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="TOTP and HOTP Generator"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/totp-generator/"> <a href="/totp-generator/" rel="follow me" >TOTP and HOTP Generator</a> </span> </strong>, which reads a Base32 secret or an <code>otpauth://</code> URI without sending either anywhere.</p> <h2 id="recovery-belongs-in-the-same-sitting"> <a href="#recovery-belongs-in-the-same-sitting" title="Recovery Belongs in the Same Sitting">Recovery Belongs in the Same Sitting</a> <a href="#recovery-belongs-in-the-same-sitting" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Recovery Belongs in the Same Sitting">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Most lockouts are self-inflicted.</strong> Someone enables a second factor, loses the device, and learns the backup codes were never saved.</p> <p>Do all four steps whenever you enable a factor:</p> <ol> <li><strong>Save the backup codes before closing the setup screen.</strong> Print them or write them down, and store them <strong>separately from your vault</strong>, since one compromise should not yield both.</li> <li><strong>Register a second key or device</strong> where the service allows it.</li> <li><strong>Remove stale recovery details.</strong> An old phone number now belongs to someone else.</li> <li><strong>Confirm which recovery contact is listed</strong>, then update it if it is wrong.</li> </ol> <blockquote> <p><strong>Warning: support teams will not restore access to a properly secured account. Losing your only factor without backup codes frequently means losing the account permanently.</strong></p> </blockquote> <h2 id="what-not-to-store"> <a href="#what-not-to-store" title="What Not to Store">What Not to Store</a> <a href="#what-not-to-store" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="What Not to Store">#</a> </h2> <p>A vault holds credentials. It should not hold everything adjacent to them.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Item</th> <th>Why It Stays Out</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Backup codes</strong></td> <td>Storing both factors together collapses them into one</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Your master password</strong></td> <td>Circular, and any breach of the vault exposes everything</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Full payment card details</strong></td> <td>Use a processor or virtual cards instead, covered in Module 10</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Recovery email credentials</strong></td> <td>Keeping the recovery path separate is the point</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>Also worth reviewing: <strong>password hints and security questions</strong>. Answers about your mother’s maiden name or first car are frequently public record. If a site forces questions, <strong>store invented answers in the vault</strong> rather than real ones.</p> <p>Two more habits deserve a mention because they cut in opposite directions:</p> <ul> <li><strong>Do not let a browser save passwords.</strong> Browser stores are not consistently encrypted and are a primary target for infostealer malware.</li> <li><strong>Do not use your password manager to generate second-factor codes.</strong> It concentrates both factors in one store, which converts a single compromise into a complete one.</li> </ul> <p><em>The counterpoint to the second item is real: a dedicated authenticator adds friction. Take the friction if you hold anything worth protecting.</em></p> <h2 id="the-authentication-record"> <a href="#the-authentication-record" title="The Authentication Record">The Authentication Record</a> <a href="#the-authentication-record" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="The Authentication Record">#</a> </h2> <p>Produce a short record before moving on. It becomes the reference for every later module.</p> <div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" style="color:#f8f8f2;background-color:#272822;-moz-tab-size:4;-o-tab-size:4;tab-size:4;-webkit-text-size-adjust:none;"><code class="language-text" data-lang="text"><span style="display:flex;"><span>AUTHENTICATION RECORD </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Vault: ______________________ (vendor or file location) </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Vault second factor: ______________________ </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Master password: memorized only, not stored </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Account tiers (list your accounts under each): </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> Tier 1 (recovery, email, finance, identity): </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> - ______________________ factor: __________ </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> - ______________________ factor: __________ </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> - ______________________ factor: __________ </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> Tier 2 (work, social, shopping): </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> - ______________________ factor: __________ </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> Tier 3 (low value, no payment method stored): </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> - ______________________ factor: __________ </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Recovery: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> Backup codes stored at: ______________________ </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> Second key registered: yes / no / unavailable </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> Stale details removed: phone / none / unknown </span></span></code></pre></div><p><em>Tier 1 deserves a hardware key or passkey. Tier 3 deserves a unique password and nothing more. Applying Tier 1 effort everywhere is how people abandon the process.</em></p> <script type="application/ld+json"> { "@context": "https://schema.org/", "@type": "ImageObject", "contentUrl": "https:\/\/simeononsecurity.com\/authentication-factor-tiers-and-recovery-path.webp", "caption": "Diagram showing account tiers from recovery and finance accounts down to low-value services, with phishing-resistant factors applied to the top tier and recovery paths stored separately from the vault", "license": "https://simeononsecurity.com/termsandconditions/", "acquireLicensePage": "https://simeononsecurity.com/contactus/", "creditText": "SimeonOnSecurity", "creator": { "@type": "Person", "name": "SimeonOnSecurity" }, "copyrightNotice": "SimeonOnSecurity", "associatedArticle": { "@type": "Person", "name": "SimeonOnSecurity", "url": "https:\/\/simeononsecurity.com\/authors\/simeononsecurity" } } } </script> <center> <figure align="center" style="text-align: center; margin: 0 item.title: Module 10: Personal Finance Security
item.description: Fraud and financial profiling are separate problems. This module covers credit freezes, virtual cards and payment isolation, alias details in commerce, and an honest look at cryptocurrency privacy.
item.content:encoded: <h4 id="-return-to-the-personal-security-course"> <a href="#-return-to-the-personal-security-course" title=" ← Return to the Personal Security Course "> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="← Return to the Personal Security Course"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/personal-security-course-start/"> <a href="/personal-security-course-start/" rel="follow me" >← Return to the Personal Security Course</a> </span> </a> <a href="#-return-to-the-personal-security-course" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title=" ← Return to the Personal Security Course ">#</a> </h4> <p><strong>Two different problems hide under financial security.</strong> One is fraud, where someone spends your money or opens credit in your name. The other is profiling, where your transaction history is analyzed, sold, and used to make decisions about you.</p> <p>They demand different countermeasures, and conflating them produces advice which is good for one and useless for the other.</p> <p><em>Budget about 25 minutes. The credit freeze is the strongest single action and it costs nothing.</em></p> <h2 id="what-you-will-learn"> <a href="#what-you-will-learn" title="What You Will Learn">What You Will Learn</a> <a href="#what-you-will-learn" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="What You Will Learn">#</a> </h2> <ul> <li><strong>Distinguish</strong> fraud prevention from financial profiling</li> <li><strong>Apply</strong> a credit freeze and understand when to lift it</li> <li><strong>Limit</strong> card exposure with virtual and single-use numbers</li> <li><strong>Separate</strong> your identity from your transactions where it matters</li> <li><strong>Evaluate</strong> cryptocurrency privacy claims against how public ledgers behave</li> <li><strong>Produce</strong> a finance record listing frozen bureaus, card controls, and alert subscriptions</li> </ul> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Term</th> <th>Meaning</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Credit freeze</strong></td> <td>Blocking lenders from accessing your file, which prevents new accounts in your name</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Fraud alert</strong></td> <td>A notice asking lenders to verify identity before extending credit</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Virtual card</strong></td> <td>A card number issued for one merchant or one transaction</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Card tokenization</strong></td> <td>Replacing a real number with a device-specific token</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>On-chain analysis</strong></td> <td>Linking blockchain transactions to identities through public ledger data</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <h2 id="two-different-problems"> <a href="#two-different-problems" title="Two Different Problems">Two Different Problems</a> <a href="#two-different-problems" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Two Different Problems">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Fraud is expensive and recoverable. Profiling is cheap and permanent.</strong></p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th></th> <th>Fraud</th> <th>Profiling</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>What is at risk</strong></td> <td>Money and credit standing</td> <td>Behavioral and purchasing record</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Who acts</strong></td> <td>Criminals</td> <td>Processors, brokers, and advertisers</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Countermeasure</strong></td> <td>Freezes, alerts, and card controls</td> <td>Cash, virtual numbers, and alias details</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Recovery</strong></td> <td>Usually possible, with effort</td> <td>Effectively impossible</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Detection</strong></td> <td>Statements and credit monitoring</td> <td>Rarely noticed at all</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>Credit cards are good for fraud and poor for privacy.</strong> Processors analyze transaction data at scale to detect fraud, and some of the data is sold onward. Card controls protect your money. They do not protect your habits.</p> <p><em>Debit cards are worse than credit cards for fraud, because the money leaves your account and recovery takes longer. Use credit where you have the discipline to pay it off.</em></p> <h2 id="the-credit-freeze"> <a href="#the-credit-freeze" title="The Credit Freeze">The Credit Freeze</a> <a href="#the-credit-freeze" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="The Credit Freeze">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>This is the strongest available defense against new-account identity theft, and it is free in the United States.</strong></p> <p>A freeze blocks lenders from pulling your credit file, which prevents accounts from being opened in your name. Unfreezing for a legitimate application is temporary and reversible.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Step</th> <th>Detail</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>1. Freeze at all three bureaus</strong></td> <td>Each holds a separate file, so freezing one leaves two open</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>2. Store the unfreeze PINs</strong></td> <td>These belong in your password manager, not on paper</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>3. Unfreeze temporarily when applying</strong></td> <td>Then re-freeze, since an unfrozen file is an open door</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>4. Consider a fraud alert as well</strong></td> <td>A fraud alert adds verification requests on top of the freeze</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>Do this before you need it.</strong> Learning the unfreeze process while disputing fraudulent accounts is the worst possible time.</p> <p><em>A freeze also serves as a monitoring mechanism of sorts. A lender rejecting an application because the file is frozen is a signal someone tried.</em></p> <p><strong>Also worth doing:</strong> subscribe to fraud alerts through your card issuers, and confirm the alert channel is not an email address you rarely check.</p> <h2 id="limit-what-a-merchant-holds"> <a href="#limit-what-a-merchant-holds" title="Limit What a Merchant Holds">Limit What a Merchant Holds</a> <a href="#limit-what-a-merchant-holds" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Limit What a Merchant Holds">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>A stored card number is a liability you did not choose.</strong> The fewer places holding your real number, the fewer breach notifications matter to you.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Approach</th> <th>Protection</th> <th>Note</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Virtual cards</strong></td> <td>Per-merchant numbers you disable individually</td> <td>The strongest practical option for online shopping</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Single-use numbers</strong></td> <td>A number valid for one transaction</td> <td>Ideal for trials and unfamiliar merchants</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Device tokenization</strong></td> <td>A device-specific token instead of the real number</td> <td>What mobile wallets do, and worth preferring</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Your real number</strong></td> <td>None beyond issuer controls</td> <td>Reserve for merchants you genuinely trust</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>Prefer a mobile wallet over a physical card for in-person payments</strong> where it is accepted. Tokenization means the merchant never receives your real number.</p> <p>Our dedicated guide: <strong> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Enhance Security and Privacy with Privacy.com Virtual Cards"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/articles/privacy-com-virtual-debit-cards-security-privacy/"> <a href="/articles/privacy-com-virtual-debit-cards-security-privacy/" rel="follow me" >Enhance Security and Privacy with Privacy.com Virtual Cards</a> </span> </strong>.</p> <h2 id="separating-identity-from-commerce"> <a href="#separating-identity-from-commerce" title="Separating Identity From Commerce">Separating Identity From Commerce</a> <a href="#separating-identity-from-commerce" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Separating Identity From Commerce">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Your name and address are data points which link purchases into a profile.</strong> Separating them reduces what any single merchant or broker holds.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Practice</th> <th>What It Reduces</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Alias email per merchant</strong></td> <td>Links a purchase to a mailbox rather than to you</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Alternate delivery address</strong></td> <td>A parcel locker or collection point rather than your home</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Alias name where permitted</strong></td> <td>Breaks the link between a purchase and your identity record</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Cash for local purchases</strong></td> <td>Removes the transaction from card networks entirely</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Virtual number for delivery contact</strong></td> <td>Prevents a courier number becoming an identity anchor</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>Cash remains the only payment method with no third-party record.</strong> This is its entire privacy advantage, and it applies only to local, in-person purchases.</p> <p><em>Alias details are most valuable for one-off purchases. For merchants you use regularly, a virtual card plus an alias mailbox captures most of the benefit at a fraction of the friction.</em></p> <h2 id="cryptocurrency-read-the-ledger"> <a href="#cryptocurrency-read-the-ledger" title="Cryptocurrency: Read the Ledger">Cryptocurrency: Read the Ledger</a> <a href="#cryptocurrency-read-the-ledger" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Cryptocurrency: Read the Ledger">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Most cryptocurrency is public by design</strong>, which makes privacy claims worth examining closely.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Claim</th> <th>Reality</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>“Anonymous”</strong></td> <td>Bitcoin and similar chains are pseudonymous. The ledger is public and permanent</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>“Untraceable”</strong></td> <td>Chain analysis links addresses to identities through exchanges, timing, and amounts</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>“Private by default”</strong></td> <td>Only a small number of assets have privacy as a default property</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>“Outside the system”</strong></td> <td>Most purchases and sales route through exchanges which perform identity verification</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>Three practical points for readers who hold crypto:</p> <ul> <li><strong>Self-custody removes exchange risk</strong> and moves the entire burden of key management to you. Hardware wallets exist for this reason, and seed phrase storage is the critical detail.</li> <li><strong>The largest exposure is the on-ramp and off-ramp.</strong> A verified exchange links your identity to addresses, which links to everything downstream.</li> <li><strong>Transaction graph analysis is mature.</strong> Sending coins between your own addresses does not break the link, it documents it.</li> </ul> <blockquote> <p><strong>Warning: treat any promise of anonymity from a cryptocurrency as a claim to verify rather than a property to rely on. Public ledgers are permanent, and analysis improves over time.</strong></p> </blockquote> <p><em>Our own <strong> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Pearl (PRL) mining analysis"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/articles/pearl-prl-mining-guide-2026/"> <a href="/articles/pearl-prl-mining-guide-2026/" rel="follow me" >Pearl (PRL) mining analysis</a> </span> </strong> covers a useful lesson in this space: a public ledger and thin market liquidity combine to make positions visible, and the privacy properties of most chains are weaker than their marketing implies.</em></p> <script type="application/ld+json"> { "@context": "https://schema.org/", "@type": "ImageObject", "contentUrl": "https:\/\/simeononsecurity.com\/personal-finance-fraud-versus-profiling-countermeasures.webp", "caption": "Diagram separating fraud prevention from financial profiling, showing credit freezes and virtual cards addressing fraud while cash, aliases, and alternate delivery addresses address profiling", "license": "https://simeononsecurity.com/termsandconditions/", "acquireLicensePage": "https://simeononsecurity.com/contactus/", "creditText": "SimeonOnSecurity", "creator": { "@type": "Person", "name": "SimeonOnSecurity" }, "copyrightNotice": "SimeonOnSecurity", "associatedArticle": {
