item.title: Module 11: The Human Aspect
item.description: Social engineering targets decisions rather than systems. This module covers why pretexts work, verification patterns which survive pressure, phishing recognition, and reducing what public records reveal.
item.content:encoded: <h4 id="-return-to-the-personal-security-course"> <a href="#-return-to-the-personal-security-course" title=" ← Return to the Personal Security Course "> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="← Return to the Personal Security Course"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/personal-security-course-start/"> <a href="/personal-security-course-start/" rel="follow me" >← Return to the Personal Security Course</a> </span> </a> <a href="#-return-to-the-personal-security-course" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title=" ← Return to the Personal Security Course ">#</a> </h4> <p><strong>Every technical control in this course assumes somebody makes a good decision at the moment it matters.</strong> Social engineering targets the decision directly, which is why it survives every improvement to the layers beneath it.</p> <p>Software did not stop these attacks because the software worked as designed. Someone authorized the action.</p> <p><em>Budget about 30 minutes. One habit, calling back on a number you already had, prevents more loss than any tool in this course.</em></p> <h2 id="what-you-will-learn"> <a href="#what-you-will-learn" title="What You Will Learn">What You Will Learn</a> <a href="#what-you-will-learn" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="What You Will Learn">#</a> </h2> <ul> <li><strong>Explain</strong> why urgency, authority, and familiarity are the three levers in a pretext</li> <li><strong>Apply</strong> verification which works under pressure rather than only in calm conditions</li> <li><strong>Recognize</strong> phishing across email, messaging, calls, and search results</li> <li><strong>Assess</strong> voice cloning and video manipulation as a change to what a familiar voice proves</li> <li><strong>Reduce</strong> what public records and data brokers expose about you</li> <li><strong>Produce</strong> a verified contact list and an agreement with people who might be impersonated</li> </ul> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Term</th> <th>Meaning</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Pretext</strong></td> <td>A fabricated situation which justifies the request being made</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Vishing</strong></td> <td>Voice phishing, where the attacker calls you rather than messaging</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Callback verification</strong></td> <td>Confirming a request by calling back on a number you already had</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Data broker</strong></td> <td>A company which aggregates and sells personal information</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Prompt bombing</strong></td> <td>Flooding approval requests until one is accepted</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <h2 id="why-pretexts-work"> <a href="#why-pretexts-work" title="Why Pretexts Work">Why Pretexts Work</a> <a href="#why-pretexts-work" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Why Pretexts Work">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Attacks succeed by manipulating decisions, and the levers are consistent.</strong></p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Lever</th> <th>How It Appears</th> <th>Countermeasure</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Urgency</strong></td> <td>An account closing, a payment due, a limited window</td> <td>Treat speed pressure as the signal itself</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Authority</strong></td> <td>A bank, an employer, a government agency, or IT support</td> <td>Verify independently before acting</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Familiarity</strong></td> <td>A known name, a real colleague, a matching voice</td> <td>Confirm out of band rather than in the same channel</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Fear of consequence</strong></td> <td>Legal action, account loss, disciplinary outcome</td> <td>Slow down deliberately</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Helpfulness</strong></td> <td>A reasonable-sounding request for small assistance</td> <td>Notice you are being recruited, not attacked</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>The most counterintuitive point: these attacks often do not feel like attacks.</strong> A request which arrives from a known name, with plausible context, and a reasonable ask produces no alarm, which is precisely the design.</p> <p><em>Notice the emotion rather than the content. Urgency, obligation, and embarrassment are the outputs a pretext engineer aims for, and recognizing the feeling is faster than analyzing the message.</em></p> <h2 id="verification-which-survives-pressure"> <a href="#verification-which-survives-pressure" title="Verification Which Survives Pressure">Verification Which Survives Pressure</a> <a href="#verification-which-survives-pressure" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Verification Which Survives Pressure">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Verification you devise in the moment is unreliable.</strong> Decide in advance.</p> <h3 id="the-callback-rule"> <a href="#the-callback-rule" title="The Callback Rule">The Callback Rule</a> <a href="#the-callback-rule" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="The Callback Rule">#</a> </h3> <p><strong>Hang up and call back on a number you already had</strong>, from a card, a statement, or a saved contact. Never use a number supplied by the caller, even if it appears to match.</p> <p>This single habit defeats vishing, bank impersonation, and many business email compromise attempts.</p> <h3 id="agreed-verification-with-people-you-know"> <a href="#agreed-verification-with-people-you-know" title="Agreed Verification With People You Know">Agreed Verification With People You Know</a> <a href="#agreed-verification-with-people-you-know" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Agreed Verification With People You Know">#</a> </h3> <p><strong>Arrange a signal with family members and close contacts before it is needed.</strong> Options include a phrase, a question with an answer only you both know, or an agreed second channel.</p> <p><em>This is worth doing with anyone who might plausibly be impersonated to you, particularly parents, adult children, and anyone with access to shared finances.</em></p> <h3 id="out-of-band-confirmation-for-money"> <a href="#out-of-band-confirmation-for-money" title="Out-of-Band Confirmation for Money">Out-of-Band Confirmation for Money</a> <a href="#out-of-band-confirmation-for-money" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Out-of-Band Confirmation for Money">#</a> </h3> <p><strong>Any payment instruction which arrives by message requires confirmation through a separate channel.</strong> This applies to requests from colleagues, contractors, and family.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Situation</th> <th>What to Do</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>New bank details from a supplier</strong></td> <td>Call the supplier on a previously known number</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Urgent payment from an executive</strong></td> <td>Confirm through a known internal channel, not a reply</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Family emergency request</strong></td> <td>Call the family member directly on a stored number</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Crypto or gift card request</strong></td> <td>Treat as fraud until proven otherwise. Both are irreversible and favored by attackers</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <blockquote> <p><strong>Warning: a request to pay by gift card, cryptocurrency, or wire transfer under time pressure is the signature of a scam. Legitimate organizations do not operate this way. Stop and verify.</strong></p> </blockquote> <h2 id="recognizing-phishing"> <a href="#recognizing-phishing" title="Recognizing Phishing">Recognizing Phishing</a> <a href="#recognizing-phishing" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Recognizing Phishing">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Phishing has moved past badly spelled email</strong>, so the old tells are less useful than the structural ones.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Structural Signal</th> <th>Why It Matters</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Domain differs from the real one</strong></td> <td><code>paypa1.com</code> and <code>paypal-secure.net</code> are attacker-owned. Read the domain right to left, before the first slash</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Unexpected attachment or link</strong></td> <td>Even from a known contact, since accounts get compromised</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Request for credentials or a code</strong></td> <td>No legitimate organization asks for a one-time code</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Channel escalation</strong></td> <td>Someone moves the conversation to messaging to avoid email controls</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Payment detail change</strong></td> <td>A classic business email compromise step</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Lookalike page after a redirect</strong></td> <td>The padlock does not indicate authenticity, as Module 2 established</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>Two habits which reduce exposure:</p> <ul> <li><strong>Enter addresses manually</strong> or use a bookmark for anything involving credentials</li> <li><strong>Treat unsolicited pop-ups as hostile</strong>, including ones warning about viruses or offering support. A legitimate warning arrives from your operating system, not a web page</li> </ul> <p><em>Pop-ups which claim to be system alerts are a reliable sign of a scam. Close the window or the browser entirely rather than clicking anything in it.</em></p> <h2 id="what-a-familiar-voice-proves"> <a href="#what-a-familiar-voice-proves" title="What a Familiar Voice Proves">What a Familiar Voice Proves</a> <a href="#what-a-familiar-voice-proves" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="What a Familiar Voice Proves">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Voice cloning changed the threat model for verification by recognition.</strong></p> <p>A short sample of public audio is enough to produce a convincing replica. Combined with a video call using a manipulated face, the old advice to confirm the caller sounds right no longer holds.</p> <p><strong>The practical consequence: identity confirmation by voice is no longer sufficient for anything consequential.</strong> Replace it with out-of-band verification, which does not depend on recognition at all.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Old Assumption</th> <th>Current Reality</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td>“I recognize their voice”</td> <td>A clone from a few seconds of audio passes</td> </tr> <tr> <td>“Their face was on the video call”</td> <td>Real-time face manipulation exists and is improving</td> </tr> <tr> <td>“They knew our internal details”</td> <td>Those details are often public or leaked</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><em>This does not mean refusing every request. It means confirming consequential ones through a channel the attacker does not control, which is the callback rule applied to people as well as institutions.</em></p> <h2 id="reducing-your-public-exposure"> <a href="#reducing-your-public-exposure" title="Reducing Your Public Exposure">Reducing Your Public Exposure</a> <a href="#reducing-your-public-exposure" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Reducing Your Public Exposure">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Social engineering begins with research</strong>, and a great deal of it is from public sources. Reducing what is available shortens the attacker’s starting material.</p> <h3 id="data-brokers"> <a href="#data-brokers" title="Data Brokers">Data Brokers</a> <a href="#data-brokers" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Data Brokers">#</a> </h3> <ul> <li><strong>Submit opt-out requests</strong> to the major people-search sites, and expect to repeat the process periodically</li> <li><strong>Never provide additional personal information when opting out.</strong> An opt-out form asking for more detail than the listing contained is a collection mechanism</li> <li><strong>Track what you have submitted</strong>, since re-listings are common</li> </ul> <h3 id="domain-registration"> <a href="#domain-registration" title="Domain Registration">Domain Registration</a> <a href="#domain-registration" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Domain Registration">#</a> </h3> <p><strong>Whois privacy protection hides your name, address, and phone from public registration records.</strong> Most registrars offer it at no cost, and it matters most if you registered a personal domain.</p> <p><em>This connects to Module 3. A domain used for email aliasing holds your identity in its registration record unless privacy protection is enabled.</em></p> <h3 id="address-and-identity-separation"> <a href="#address-and-identity-separation" title="Address and Identity Separation">Address and Identity Separation</a> <a href="#address-and-identity-separation" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Address and Identity Separation">#</a> </h3> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Practice</th> <th>Benefit</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Forwarding address or parcel locker</strong></td> <td>Keeps your home address out of commercial databases</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Opt out of marketing lists</strong></td> <td>Reduces the volume of data sold onward</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Review social media privacy on a schedule</strong></td> <td>Terms change, and settings revert with updates</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><em>Our <strong> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Phishing Awareness Checklist"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/checklists/phishing-awareness-checklist/"> <a href="/checklists/phishing-awareness-checklist/" rel="follow me" >Phishing Awareness Checklist</a> </span> </strong> covers the organizational training version of this module.</em></p> <script payment details received by message alone </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> [ ] Never pay by gift card, crypto, or wire under time pressure </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> [ ] Always call back on a number I already had </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> [ ] Confirm any executive request through a known internal channel / no / n/a </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> Broker opt-outs filed: ______________________ </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> Forwarding address: yes / no employer IT today</li> <li><strong>Agree a verification signal</strong> with the two people most likely to be impersonated to you</li> <li><strong>Enable Whois privacy</strong> if you own a personal domain</li> <li><strong>File opt-outs</strong> with the major data brokers, and diarize a repeat in six months</li> <li><strong>Read the organizational counterpart</strong>: <strong> <span itemscope item.title: Module 12: Physical Security
item.description: Every digital control assumes the device stays in your hands. This module covers device seizure and theft, document disposal, observation and skimming, and why a PIN sometimes beats biometrics.
item.content:encoded: <h4 id="-return-to-the-personal-security-course"> <a href="#-return-to-the-personal-security-course" title=" ← Return to the Personal Security Course "> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="← Return to the Personal Security Course"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/personal-security-course-start/"> <a href="/personal-security-course-start/" rel="follow me" >← Return to the Personal Security Course</a> </span> </a> <a href="#-return-to-the-personal-security-course" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title=" ← Return to the Personal Security Course ">#</a> </h4> <p><strong>Every control in the previous eleven modules assumes the device stays in your hands.</strong> Physical access invalidates a great deal of it. An unlocked laptop is a complete account compromise, a stolen phone is a second-factor loss, and a seized device is a question about whether your encryption holds.</p> <p>This final module covers device control, document disposal, observation, and the biometric question which depends on your legal situation rather than your preferences.</p> <p><em>Budget about 25 minutes. The device and biometric decisions are the ones with lasting consequences.</em></p> <h2 id="what-you-will-learn"> <a href="#what-you-will-learn" title="What You Will Learn">What You Will Learn</a> <a href="#what-you-will-learn" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="What You Will Learn">#</a> </h2> <ul> <li><strong>Assess</strong> the difference between theft risk and seizure risk</li> <li><strong>Apply</strong> physical controls proportionate to where you carry devices</li> <li><strong>Dispose</strong> of documents and media without leaving recoverable data</li> <li><strong>Recognize</strong> observation techniques including shoulder surfing and card skimming</li> <li><strong>Evaluate</strong> biometrics against a PIN for your own legal circumstances</li> <li><strong>Produce</strong> a physical security record and a completed course summary</li> </ul> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Term</th> <th>Meaning</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Seizure</strong></td> <td>Lawful or unlawful taking of a device by another party</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Shoulder surfing</strong></td> <td>Reading a screen or keypad from a position you did not notice</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Skimmer</strong></td> <td>A device attached to a card reader to capture card data</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Coercion</strong></td> <td>Compelling a device unlock rather than defeating encryption</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Perimeter</strong></td> <td>The physical boundary around a space containing assets</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <h2 id="theft-and-seizure-are-different-problems"> <a href="#theft-and-seizure-are-different-problems" title="Theft and Seizure Are Different Problems">Theft and Seizure Are Different Problems</a> <a href="#theft-and-seizure-are-different-problems" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Theft and Seizure Are Different Problems">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>They overlap, and they drive opposite design decisions.</strong></p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th></th> <th>Theft</th> <th>Seizure</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Who acts</strong></td> <td>Opportunistic criminal</td> <td>Authority or a known party</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Primary loss</strong></td> <td>The hardware and the data on it</td> <td>The data and its contents</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Best control</strong></td> <td>Encryption plus remote wipe</td> <td>Encryption plus what you chose not to store</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>What helps</strong></td> <td>Not leaving devices visible, cable locks</td> <td>Device power state, and knowing your rights</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>Shutting down rather than suspending matters here.</strong> A device in standby often holds decryption keys in memory, while a powered-off device requires the passphrase to reach the data. The distinction is the practical reason Module 8 recommended full power-off over standby.</p> <p><em>The most effective seizure control is deciding in advance what does not belong on the device. Data you never stored is data nobody recovers.</em></p> <h2 id="devices-in-the-physical-world"> <a href="#devices-in-the-physical-world" title="Devices in the Physical World">Devices in the Physical World</a> <a href="#devices-in-the-physical-world" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Devices in the Physical World">#</a> </h2> <ul> <li><strong>Use cable locks</strong> where a device is left in a semi-public place, such as an office or a library</li> <li><strong>Keep devices out of sight</strong> in vehicles, and treat a charging cable on a seat as a signal something is under it</li> <li><strong>Carry a privacy screen</strong> in transit, which defeats most shoulder surfing</li> <li><strong>Enable remote wipe</strong> and confirm it works before you need it</li> <li><strong>Do not charge from unknown USB ports</strong>, as Module 7 covered. Prefer your own adapter</li> </ul> <p><strong>A short idle lock timeout is the highest-yield setting in this section.</strong> Most physical compromises of a device happen while it is unattended and unlocked, not while it is encrypted and powered off.</p> <h2 id="documents-and-disposal"> <a href="#documents-and-disposal" title="Documents and Disposal">Documents and Disposal</a> <a href="#documents-and-disposal" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Documents and Disposal">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Physical documents carry data which no encryption protects.</strong></p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Item</th> <th>Disposal Approach</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Financial statements</strong></td> <td>Shred, cross-cut rather than strip-cut</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Identity documents</strong></td> <td>Shred, and treat replacement as the better option where available</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Medical records</strong></td> <td>Shred, since they frequently carry identity numbers</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Old storage media</strong></td> <td>Destroy physically. Overwriting is not reliable on all media, and a failed drive often still holds data</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Delivery labels</strong></td> <td>Remove or obscure before discarding packaging</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>Watermark documents you share</strong>, with the recipient and date. It costs nothing, and it traces a leak to a specific copy if one appears somewhere unexpected.</p> <p><em>Cross-cut shredding matters. Strip-cut shredders produce strips which are straightforward to reassemble.</em></p> <h2 id="observation-and-the-biometric-question"> <a href="#observation-and-the-biometric-question" title="Observation, and the Biometric Question">Observation, and the Biometric Question</a> <a href="#observation-and-the-biometric-question" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Observation, and the Biometric Question">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Being observed is subtle, and the countermeasures are simple.</strong></p> <ul> <li><strong>Shield the keypad</strong> when entering a PIN, and clean the screen afterwards on touch devices where smudges reveal digits</li> <li><strong>Inspect card readers and ATMs</strong> for attached skimming hardware, and prefer readers which look untouched</li> <li><strong>Notice who is positioned to see your screen</strong>, and reposition rather than assuming nobody is looking</li> </ul> <p><strong>The biometric decision depends on your legal exposure, not your convenience.</strong></p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Method</th> <th>Strength</th> <th>Consideration</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Biometric</strong></td> <td>Convenient, and difficult to guess</td> <td>In some jurisdictions, compelling a finger or face carries different protections than compelling a passphrase</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>PIN or passphrase</strong></td> <td>Knowledge you hold</td> <td>Slower, and vulnerable to observation</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>If compelled disclosure is a realistic concern, use a PIN or passphrase rather than biometrics.</strong> The reasoning is jurisdictional rather than technical, so it is a decision to make with awareness of where you live and work. Some devices allow biometrics to be disabled temporarily through a specific key combination, which is worth knowing in advance.</p> <p><em>A related note on biometrics: your face is already photographed in public, which is the argument against treating facial recognition as a secret. A passphrase is not in any photograph.</em></p> <h2 id="reducing-ongoing-exposure"> <a href="#reducing-ongoing-exposure" title="Reducing Ongoing Exposure">Reducing Ongoing Exposure</a> <a href="#reducing-ongoing-exposure" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Reducing Ongoing Exposure">#</a> </h2> <p>Two items deserve attention because they persist without your involvement.</p> <p><strong>Crowdsourced and commercial image collection continues regardless of your participation.</strong> Cameras capture your movements, and privacy options are limited. Practical reductions include choosing less-monitored routes where it matters to you, and recognizing a friend’s public post reveals your location even if you post nothing.</p> <p><strong>CCTV and facial recognition are expanding in many cities.</strong> Awareness of where coverage is dense around your home and workplace is more useful than attempting to defeat it.</p> <p><em>Our sibling project mapping ALPR camera locations illustrates how much surveillance infrastructure is publicly inferable: <strong> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Flock Finder"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/sibling-sites/"> <a href="/sibling-sites/" rel="follow me" >Flock Finder</a> </span> </strong>. Knowing the density near you is a starting point for planning, not a complete solution.</em></p> <script type="application/ld+json"> { "@context": "https://schema.org/", "@type": "ImageObject", "contentUrl": "https:\/\/simeononsecurity.com\/physical-security-device-documents-observation.webp", "caption": "Diagram grouping physical security controls into devices, documents, and observation, showing encryption and remote wipe for devices, shredding and watermarking for documents, and observation countermeasures", "license": "https://simeononsecurity.com/termsandconditions/", m=\u002b337.310499498", "author": { "@type": "Person", "name": "SimeonOnSecurity", "url": "https:\/\/simeononsecurity.com\/authors\/simeononsecurity" } } } </script> <center> <figure align="center" remote wipe for devices, shredding and watermarking for documents, and observation countermeasures"loading="lazy" fetchpriority="low" itemprop="contentUrl" /> </figure> </center> <h2 id="the-physical-record"> <a href="#the-physical-record" title="The Physical Record">The Physical Record</a> <a href="#the-physical-record" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="The Physical Record">#</a> </h2> <div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" style="color:#f8f8f2;background-color:#272822;-moz-tab-size:4;-o-tab-size:4;tab-size:4;-webkit-text-size-adjust:none;"><code class="language-text" data-lang="text"><span style="display:flex;"><span>PHYSICAL SECURITY RECORD </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Devices: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> Idle lock timeout: ______________________ </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> Remote wipe tested: yes / no </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> Cable lock in use: yes / no / n/a </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> Privacy screen: yes / no </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> Full power-off habit: yes / no </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Documents: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> Shredder type: cross-cut / strip-cut / none </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> Documents watermarked: yes / no </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> Media destruction plan: ______________________ </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Observation: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> Lock method: PIN (length __) / passphrase / biometric </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> Biometrics disabled when needed: how? __________ </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> ATM and reader checks: habit / sometimes / never </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Exposure: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> CCTV awareness near home/work: reviewed / not reviewed </span></span></code></pre></div><h2 id="course-summary-all-twelve-modules"> <a href="#course-summary-all-twelve-modules" title="Course Summary: All Twelve Modules">Course Summary: All Twelve Modules</a> <a href="#course-summary-all-twelve-modules" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Course Summary: All Twelve Modules">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>You have now covered the full sequence.</strong> This table is the compressed version of the course.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Module</th> <th>The one action which matters most</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>1. Authentication</strong></td> <td>Move email and finance accounts to a passkey or hardware key</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>2. Web Browsing</strong></td> <td>Block third-party cookies and install one content blocker</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>3. Email</strong></td> <td>Turn off automatic remote content loading</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>4. Messaging</strong></td> <td>Enable contact verification and disappearing messages</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>5. Social Media</strong></td> <td>Remove birthday, school, and employer from your profile</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>6. Networks</strong></td> <td>Change the router admin password and disable WPS and UPnP</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>7. Mobile Devices</strong></td> <td>Set a carrier PIN and port freeze</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>8. Personal Computers</strong></td> <td>Confirm disk encryption and restore one file from backup</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>9. Smart Home</strong></td> <td>Move IoT devices to a separate network segment</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>10. Personal Finance</strong></td> <td>Freeze credit at all three bureaus</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>11. Human Aspect</strong></td> <td>Save verified contact numbers and agree a signal with family</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>12. Physical Security</strong></td> <td>Shorten the idle lock timeout and shut devices down fully</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <h2 id="next-steps"> <a href="#next-steps" title="Next Steps">Next Steps</a> <a href="#next-steps" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Next Steps">#</a> </h2> <ol> <li><strong>Return to the course hub</strong> and review your completed records: <strong> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Personal Security Course"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/personal-security-course-start/"> <a href="/personal-security-course-start/" rel="follow me" >Personal Security Course</a> </span> </strong></li> <li><strong>Read the four-tier summary</strong> for the whole course on one page: <strong> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Prioritized Personal Security Checklist"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/articles/personal-security-checklist-prioritized-2026/"> <a href="/articles/personal-security-checklist-prioritized-2026/" rel="follow me" >Prioritized Personal Security Checklist</a> </span> </strong></li> <li><strong>Go deeper with a community checklist</strong> if you want several hundred items: <strong> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Personal Security Checklist by Alicia Sykes"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://github.com/Lissy93/personal-security-checklist"> <a href="https://github.com/Lissy93/personal-security-checklist" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Personal Security Checklist by Alicia Sykes</a> </span> </strong></li> <li><strong>Apply the organizational checklists</strong> if you also manage systems: <strong> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Every Checklist"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/checklists/"> <a href="/checklists/" rel="follow me" >Every Checklist</a> </span> </strong></li> <li><strong>Use the local tools</strong> for anything involving a secret: <strong> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="All Client-Side Tools"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/tools/"> <a href="/tools/" rel="follow me" >All Client-Side Tools</a> </span> </strong></li> <li><strong>Revisit your threat model</strong> annually, since circumstances and adversaries change: <strong> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="How to Form Your Own Personal Threat Model"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/articles/how-to-form-your-own-personal-threat-model-safeguard-online-security/"> <a href="/articles/how-to-form-your-own-personal-threat-model-safeguard-online-security/" rel="follow me" >How to Form Your Own Personal Threat Model</a> </span> </strong></li> </ol> Read More at https://simeononsecurity.com/

item.title: Module 2: Web Browsing and Tracking
item.description: How stateful and stateless tracking differ, which browser changes reduce collection, why fingerprint tweaks are lower yield than they appear, and what incognito does not protect against.
item.content:encoded: <h4 id="-return-to-the-personal-security-course"> <a href="#-return-to-the-personal-security-course" title=" ← Return to the Personal Security Course "> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="← Return to the Personal Security Course"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/personal-security-course-start/"> <a href="/personal-security-course-start/" rel="follow me" >← Return to the Personal Security Course</a> </span> </a> <a href="#-return-to-the-personal-security-course" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title=" ← Return to the Personal Security Course ">#</a> </h4> <p><strong>The browser is where most of your personal data exposure happens.</strong> It holds your authenticated sessions, reports a detailed description of your device to every site you visit, and executes code written by parties you never chose to trust.</p> <p>This module covers the two distinct tracking mechanisms, the changes which reduce collection, and an honest accounting of which popular advice is lower yield than it appears.</p> <p><em>Budget about 30 minutes. Two settings and one extension produce most of the benefit.</em></p> <h2 id="what-you-will-learn"> <a href="#what-you-will-learn" title="What You Will Learn">What You Will Learn</a> <a href="#what-you-will-learn" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="What You Will Learn">#</a> </h2> <ul> <li><strong>Distinguish</strong> stateful tracking, which depends on stored identifiers, from stateless tracking, which does not</li> <li><strong>Explain</strong> why the HTTPS padlock proves confidentiality rather than trustworthiness</li> <li><strong>Configure</strong> a privacy-respecting browser with tracker and cookie controls</li> <li><strong>Evaluate</strong> a browser extension’s access before installing it</li> <li><strong>Identify</strong> which fingerprint countermeasures are worth the effort and which are not</li> <li><strong>Produce</strong> a browser record listing your browser, search engine, and installed extensions</li> </ul> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Term</th> <th>Meaning</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Stateful tracking</strong></td> <td>Identifying you through something stored, such as a cookie or a local storage entry</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Stateless tracking</strong></td> <td>Identifying you from characteristics of the request itself, with nothing stored</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>First-party cookie</strong></td> <td>Set by the site you are visiting, and generally needed for it to function</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Third-party cookie</strong></td> <td>Set by another domain embedded in the page, and the main cross-site tracking mechanism</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Fingerprint</strong></td> <td>The combination of attributes which distinguishes your browser from others</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Container</strong></td> <td>An isolated browser profile with its own cookies and storage</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <h2 id="two-kinds-of-tracking-two-kinds-of-countermeasure"> <a href="#two-kinds-of-tracking-two-kinds-of-countermeasure" title="Two Kinds of Tracking, Two Kinds of Countermeasure">Two Kinds of Tracking, Two Kinds of Countermeasure</a> <a href="#two-kinds-of-tracking-two-kinds-of-countermeasure" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Two Kinds of Tracking, Two Kinds of Countermeasure">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Confusing these two mechanisms is why browser privacy advice often contradicts itself.</strong></p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th></th> <th>Stateful</th> <th>Stateless</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Mechanism</strong></td> <td>Cookies, local storage, cached identifiers</td> <td>Screen size, fonts, timezone, GPU strings, canvas rendering</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Persistence</strong></td> <td>Survives until cleared or expired</td> <td>Recomputed on every request</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Countermeasure</strong></td> <td>Block, isolate, or clear the store</td> <td>Make yourself less distinctive</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Difficulty</strong></td> <td>Straightforward</td> <td>Hard, and it breaks sites</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Yield</strong></td> <td><strong>High</strong></td> <td>Moderate at best</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>The practical consequence.</strong> Blocking third-party cookies and trackers is high-yield and low-cost, so it belongs at the top of the list. Fingerprint randomization is a partial measure against a moving target, so it belongs near the bottom.</p> <p><em>Anyone who spoofs their canvas signature before installing a content blocker has the ordering inverted.</em></p> <h2 id="step-1-choose-the-browser"> <a href="#step-1-choose-the-browser" title="Step 1: Choose the Browser">Step 1: Choose the Browser</a> <a href="#step-1-choose-the-browser" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Step 1: Choose the Browser">#</a> </h2> <p>Your browser sees everything you do, which makes this the highest-leverage single choice in the module.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Browser</th> <th>Strength</th> <th>Cost</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Firefox</strong></td> <td>Configurable, independent engine, strong container support</td> <td>Needs tuning to reach its potential</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Brave</strong></td> <td>Blocks trackers by default, no setup required</td> <td>Chromium-based, and its own features deserve review</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>LibreWolf</strong></td> <td>Hardened Firefox defaults</td> <td>Fewer conveniences, and some sites break</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Tor Browser</strong></td> <td>Anonymity against network observers, not only sites</td> <td>Slower, and many sites block it</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Chrome, Edge, Safari</strong></td> <td>Convenience and integration</td> <td>Collect telemetry and offer weaker isolation by default</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>If you change nothing else, move off Chrome.</strong> Its business model depends on data about your browsing, and the alternative browsers cost nothing.</p> <p>See the full comparison in <strong> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Best Privacy Browsers 2026: LibreWolf vs Brave vs Tor"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/articles/best-privacy-browsers-librewolf-brave-firefox-tor/"> <a href="/articles/best-privacy-browsers-librewolf-brave-firefox-tor/" rel="follow me" >Best Privacy Browsers 2026: LibreWolf vs Brave vs Tor</a> </span> </strong>.</p> <h2 id="step-2-block-the-collection-layer"> <a href="#step-2-block-the-collection-layer" title="Step 2: Block the Collection Layer">Step 2: Block the Collection Layer</a> <a href="#step-2-block-the-collection-layer" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Step 2: Block the Collection Layer">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Ads and trackers are the primary collection mechanism on the web</strong>, and they are also a substantial attack surface. Two changes cover most of the ground.</p> <h3 id="content-and-tracker-blocking"> <a href="#content-and-tracker-blocking" title="Content and Tracker Blocking">Content and Tracker Blocking</a> <a href="#content-and-tracker-blocking" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Content and Tracker Blocking">#</a> </h3> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Tool</th> <th>What It Blocks</th> <th>Note</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>uBlock Origin</strong></td> <td>Ads, trackers, and known malicious domains</td> <td>The default recommendation for Firefox</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Tracker blockers</strong></td> <td>Analytics and cross-site beacons</td> <td>Use one, not several</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Brave Shields</strong></td> <td>Built in, no extension needed</td> <td>Suitable if you prefer zero configuration</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>Use exactly one.</strong> Stacking blockers causes conflicts, slows the browser, and makes breakage harder to diagnose.</p> <h3 id="cookie-and-storage-controls"> <a href="#cookie-and-storage-controls" title="Cookie and Storage Controls">Cookie and Storage Controls</a> <a href="#cookie-and-storage-controls" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Cookie and Storage Controls">#</a> </h3> <ul> <li><strong>Block third-party cookies.</strong> This is the single highest-yield browser setting available.</li> <li><strong>Clear cookies regularly</strong>, or scope them to a container so they never reach other sites.</li> <li><strong>Review site permissions</strong> for location, camera, microphone, and notifications, which are granted per origin and persist silently.</li> </ul> <h3 id="compartmentalization"> <a href="#compartmentalization" title="Compartmentalization">Compartmentalization</a> <a href="#compartmentalization" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Compartmentalization">#</a> </h3> <p><strong>Isolating contexts prevents one identity from being linked to another.</strong> Firefox containers are the cleanest implementation, giving each profile its own cookie jar. The practical setup is one container per purpose: work, shopping, social, and personal. Sites in different containers never observe each other’s storage.</p> <p><em>This is high value and often skipped, because it requires a small amount of ongoing discipline rather than a one-time toggle.</em></p> <h2 id="step-3-reduce-the-fingerprint"> <a href="#step-3-reduce-the-fingerprint" title="Step 3: Reduce the Fingerprint">Step 3: Reduce the Fingerprint</a> <a href="#step-3-reduce-the-fingerprint" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Step 3: Reduce the Fingerprint">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Fingerprinting identifies you by what your browser reports</strong>, including screen dimensions, installed fonts, timezone, language settings, and the exact output of canvas rendering. It does not require storing anything.</p> <p>A useful property: <strong>a distinctive fingerprint is worse than a common one.</strong> The goal is not uniqueness, it is blending in.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Measure</th> <th>Yield</th> <th>Trade-off</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Use a popular browser default configuration</strong></td> <td>Good</td> <td>You lose some convenience settings</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Disable WebRTC where unused</strong></td> <td>Moderate</td> <td>Breaks video calling in the browser</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Spoof canvas output</strong></td> <td>Moderate</td> <td>Breaks some image-heavy sites</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Rotate user agent</strong></td> <td>Low</td> <td>Marginal benefit, and it makes you more distinctive</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Send Do Not Track</strong></td> <td><strong>None</strong></td> <td>Most sites ignore it, and it adds a distinguishing signal</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <blockquote> <p><strong>Common Mistake: treating fingerprint randomization as a primary control.</strong> It is a partial measure against a technique which is designed to survive partial measures. Do the cookie and tracker work first.</p> </blockquote> <h2 id="where-incognito-helps-and-where-it-does-not"> <a href="#where-incognito-helps-and-where-it-does-not" title="Where Incognito Helps and Where It Does Not">Where Incognito Helps and Where It Does Not</a> <a href="#where-incognito-helps-and-where-it-does-not" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Where Incognito Helps and Where It Does Not">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Incognito prevents local storage, not remote observation.</strong> It stops your browser from recording history and cookies on your own device. It does nothing about what the network operator, the site, or your employer observes.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Incognito Protects</th> <th>Incognito Does Not Protect</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td>Local history and cookies</td> <td>Your IP address</td> </tr> <tr> <td>Saved form data in the session</td> <td>Network-level observation</td> </tr> <tr> <td>Session persistence on a shared machine</td> <td>The site’s own server logs</td> </tr> <tr> <td></td> <td>Fingerprinting</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>Use it on other people’s machines</strong>, which is its genuine strength. Do not treat it as anonymity.</p> <h2 id="site-legitimacy-and-the-padlock-myth"> <a href="#site-legitimacy-and-the-padlock-myth" title="Site Legitimacy and the Padlock Myth">Site Legitimacy and the Padlock Myth</a> <a href="#site-legitimacy-and-the-padlock-myth" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Site Legitimacy and the Padlock Myth">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>The padlock indicates encryption, not honesty.</strong> Certificates are free and automated, so almost every phishing site has one. Confidentiality and trustworthiness are separate properties.</p> <p>Signs worth checking:</p> <ul> <li><strong>Verify the domain letter by letter</strong>, especially for login pages and anything involving payment</li> <li><strong>Prefer bookmarks over links</strong> for sites you use often</li> <li><strong>Treat unexpected redirects as a warning</strong>, and check where a short link resolves before following it</li> <li><strong>Trust browser warnings</strong>, which reflect observed malicious behavior rather than configuration</li> </ul> <p>Browser malware produces its own signals: a changed homepage or search engine, unfamiliar toolbars or extensions, a jump in ad volume, and pages loading far slower than before. Any of those justifies an extension audit.</p> <h2 id="the-browser-record"> <a href="#the-browser-record" title="The Browser Record">The Browser Record</a> <a href="#the-browser-record" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="The Browser Record">#</a> </h2> <div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" style="color:#f8f8f2;background-color:#272822;-moz-tab-size:4;-o-tab-size:4;tab-size:4;-webkit-text-size-adjust:none;"><code class="language-text" data-lang="text"><span style="display:flex;"><span>BROWSER RECORD </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Browser: ______________________ </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Search engine: ______________________ </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Content blocker: ______________________ (exactly one) </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Third-party cookies: blocked / allowed / partial </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Container profiles: ______________________ </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Extensions installed: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> - ______________________ why kept: __________ </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> - ______________________ why kept: __________ </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Permissions revoked: camera / microphone / location / notifications </span></span></code></pre></div><p><em>Review the extension list quarterly. An extension you installed once and forgot still reads every page you visit.</em></p> <script type="application/ld+json"> { "@context": "https://schema.org/", "@type": "ImageObject", "contentUrl": "https:\/\/simeononsecurity.com\/browser-tracking-stateful-vs-stateless.webp", "caption": "Diagram contrasting stateful tracking through cookies and local storage with stateless tracking through browser fingerprint attributes, showing which countermeasure applies to each", "license": "https://simeononsecurity.com/termsandconditions/", "acquireLicensePage": "https://simeononsecurity.com/contactus/", "creditText": "SimeonOnSecurity", "creator": { "@type": "Person", "name": "SimeonOnSecurity" }, "copyrightNotice": "SimeonOnSecurity", "associatedArticle": { "@type": "NewsArticle", "headline": "simeononsecurity", "url": "https:\/\/simeononsecurity.com\/", "datePublished": "2026-10-02 21:20:37.589620333 \u002b0000 UTC m=\u002b337.314346079", "author": { "@type": "Person", "name": "SimeonOnSecurity", "url": "https:\/\/simeononsecurity.com\/authors\/simeononsecurity" } } } </script> <center> <figure align="center" style="text-align: center; margin: 0 auto;" itemscope itemtype="http://schema.org/ImageObject"> <meta property="article:published_time" content="2026-10-02 21:20:37.589620333 +0000 UTC m=+337.314346079"> <meta property="article:author" content="SimeonOnSecurity"> <meta property="article:author:url" content="https://simeononsecurity.com/authors/simeononsecurity"> <meta property="og:license" content="https://simeononsecurity.com/termsandconditions/"> <meta property="og:see_also" content="https://simeononsecurity.com/contactus/"> <meta property="og:copyright" content="SimeonOnSecurity"> <img align="center" style="text-align: center; margin: 0 auto; max-width: 80%; max-height: 600px; min-width: 100px; min-height: 100px; height: auto; width: auto;" src="https://simeononsecurity.com/browser-tracking-stateful-vs-stateless.webp" alt="Diagram contrasting stateful tracking through cookies and local storage with stateless tracking through browser fingerprint attributes, showing which countermeasure applies to each"loading="lazy" fetchpriority="low" itemprop="contentUrl" /> </figure> </center> <h2 id="next-steps"> <a href="#next-steps" title="Next Steps">Next Steps</a> <a href="#next-steps" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Next Steps">#</a> </h2> <ol> <li><strong>Continue to Module 3</strong> and secure the account which unlocks everything else: <strong> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Email Security"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/personal-security-course/email/"> <a href="/personal-security-course/email/" rel="follow me" >Email Security</a> </span> </strong></li> <li><strong>Compare browsers properly</strong> before switching: <strong> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="LibreWolf vs Brave vs Tor"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/articles/best-privacy-browsers-librewolf-brave-firefox-tor/"> <a href="/articles/best-privacy-browsers-librewolf-brave-firefox-tor/" rel="follow me" >LibreWolf vs Brave vs Tor</a> </span> </strong></li> <li><strong>Inspect what a site exposes</strong> with the local <strong> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="EXIF Viewer"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/exif-viewer/"> <a href="/exif-viewer/" rel="follow me" >EXIF Viewer</a> </span> </strong> before sharing media</li> <li><strong>Check your deployment’s security headers</strong> if you also run a website: <strong> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Security Headers Check"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/securityheaders/"> <a href="/securityheaders/" rel="follow me" >Security Headers Check</a> </span> </strong></li> <li><strong>Read the organizational counterpart</strong> if you manage item.title: Module 3: Email Security
item.description: Email is the recovery path for every other account. This module covers address strategy, remote content and tracking pixels, provider selection, third-party access, and what self-hosting genuinely requires.
item.content:encoded: <h4 id="-return-to-the-personal-security-course"> <a href="#-return-to-the-personal-security-course" title=" ← Return to the Personal Security Course "> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="← Return to the Personal Security Course"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/personal-security-course-start/"> <a href="/personal-security-course-start/" rel="follow me" >← Return to the Personal Security Course</a> </span> </a> <a href="#-return-to-the-personal-security-course" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title=" ← Return to the Personal Security Course ">#</a> </h4> <p><strong>Your email account is the recovery path for everything else.</strong> A password reset goes there. A second-factor fallback goes there. An account takeover notification goes there. Anyone who controls your inbox does not need to break into your other accounts, because they reset their way in.</p> <p>This module covers address strategy, the tracking mechanisms built into mail itself, provider selection, and an honest assessment of self-hosting.</p> <p><em>Budget about 25 minutes. The address strategy decision is the one which compounds over years.</em></p> <h2 id="what-you-will-learn"> <a href="#what-you-will-learn" title="What You Will Learn">What You Will Learn</a> <a href="#what-you-will-learn" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="What You Will Learn">#</a> </h2> <ul> <li><strong>Explain</strong> why mailbox compromise grants access to unrelated accounts</li> <li><strong>Distinguish</strong> aliasing, subaddressing, and separate accounts as three different strategies</li> <li><strong>Disable</strong> remote content loading, which is the main tracking mechanism in mail</li> <li><strong>Evaluate</strong> a provider on encryption, jurisdiction, and recovery policy rather than marketing</li> <li><strong>Audit</strong> third-party applications with mailbox access</li> <li><strong>Produce</strong> an email record listing your address strategy, provider, and connected applications</li> </ul> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Term</th> <th>Meaning</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Alias</strong></td> <td>A distinct address which forwards to your real mailbox, and which you disable individually</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Subaddress</strong></td> <td>A variant of your real address using a <code>+</code> suffix, which reveals the original</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Catch-all</strong></td> <td>A domain configuration accepting mail to any address at the domain</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Tracking pixel</strong></td> <td>A remotely loaded image which reports when a message was opened</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Third-party access</strong></td> <td>An application granted OAuth or IMAP permission to read your mailbox</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <h2 id="why-the-mailbox-is-the-master-key"> <a href="#why-the-mailbox-is-the-master-key" title="Why the Mailbox Is the Master Key">Why the Mailbox Is the Master Key</a> <a href="#why-the-mailbox-is-the-master-key" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Why the Mailbox Is the Master Key">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Account recovery almost always routes through email.</strong> This single fact makes the inbox more valuable than any individual account it protects.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Attack</th> <th>What It Achieves</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Mailbox takeover</strong></td> <td>Password resets for every connected account</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Read-only mailbox access</strong></td> <td>Silent reconnaissance, including which services you use</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Mail rule insertion</strong></td> <td>Automatic forwarding or deletion of security notifications</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Recovery address change</strong></td> <td>Permanent access even after the victim resets passwords</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>Check your mail rules and forwarding settings today.</strong> A hidden rule which forwards security alerts to an attacker is a common persistence mechanism, and it survives a password change.</p> <p><em>Everything in Module 1 assumes the recovery path is intact. If the inbox falls, the vault is one reset away from being useless.</em></p> <h2 id="address-strategy"> <a href="#address-strategy" title="Address Strategy">Address Strategy</a> <a href="#address-strategy" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Address Strategy">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>One address for everything is the default, and it is the weakest option.</strong> Three strategies improve on it, and they differ in what they reveal.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Strategy</th> <th>Hides Your Real Address</th> <th>Tracks Who Leaked It</th> <th>Cost</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Separate accounts</strong></td> <td>Yes, for the service</td> <td>Partially</td> <td>Multiple inboxes to check</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Aliasing</strong></td> <td><strong>Yes</strong></td> <td><strong>Yes</strong></td> <td>A provider or your own domain</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Subaddressing</strong> (<code>you+service@</code>)</td> <td><strong>No</strong></td> <td>Yes</td> <td>None</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>Aliasing is the strongest option.</strong> A unique address per service means spam identifies the source, a single alias is disabled without touching your inbox, and no two services correlate you by address.</p> <p>A related benefit: <strong>mail arriving at an alias you retired is obviously fraudulent</strong>, which turns your own address strategy into a phishing detector.</p> <p><em>If you own a domain, a catch-all gives you unlimited aliases at no cost, and it lets you change providers without changing your address. The portability is the strongest argument for owning the domain.</em></p> <h2 id="remote-content-and-tracking-pixels"> <a href="#remote-content-and-tracking-pixels" title="Remote Content and Tracking Pixels">Remote Content and Tracking Pixels</a> <a href="#remote-content-and-tracking-pixels" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Remote Content and Tracking Pixels">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>A single remotely loaded image reports the message was opened</strong>, along with your IP address, client, and timestamp. Marketers use this to build engagement profiles, and so does anyone else with access to the same technique.</p> <p><strong>Disable automatic remote content loading in your mail client.</strong> This is one setting, it breaks nothing important, and it removes the mechanism entirely.</p> <p>Two related practices:</p> <ul> <li><strong>View mail as plaintext where practical.</strong> HTML mail carries the same tracking plus additional parser attack surface.</li> <li><strong>Do not treat email as confidential.</strong> Transport encryption protects the message in transit, not the copy sitting in a provider’s mailbox or in a mis-sent thread.</li> </ul> <h2 id="provider-selection"> <a href="#provider-selection" title="Provider Selection">Provider Selection</a> <a href="#provider-selection" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Provider Selection">#</a> </h2> <p>Evaluate against these rather than marketing claims:</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Criterion</th> <th>Why It Matters</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Encryption at rest</strong></td> <td>Whether the provider holds keys to your mailbox</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Jurisdiction</strong></td> <td>Which legal orders the provider responds to</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Recovery policy</strong></td> <td>Whether support will restore access, and under what proof</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Data retention</strong></td> <td>How long deleted mail persists in backups</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Third-party access control</strong></td> <td>Whether you control which apps read your mailbox</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>Mainstream providers are not equivalent.</strong> Some scan message content to build advertising profiles, and some have granted broad third-party access to mailbox contents. Choosing a provider which sells no advertising removes the incentive entirely.</p> <h2 id="third-party-access-and-template-leakage"> <a href="#third-party-access-and-template-leakage" title="Third-Party Access and Template Leakage">Third-Party Access and Template Leakage</a> <a href="#third-party-access-and-template-leakage" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Third-Party Access and Template Leakage">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>An application with mailbox access reads everything, not only the messages it needs.</strong> Sign-in prompts offering to connect a tool to your mail grant the tool full read scope in most implementations.</p> <p>Audit this in two places:</p> <ol> <li><strong>Your mail provider’s connected applications list</strong>, where OAuth grants accumulate and are rarely reviewed.</li> <li><strong>Your mail client’s add-ins</strong>, which run with the client’s own privileges.</li> </ol> <p>Two leakage channels which get far less attention:</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Channel</th> <th>What It Leaks</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Auto-reply messages</strong></td> <td>Travel dates, absence from a property, temporary contact details, and job responsibilities</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Mail signatures</strong></td> <td>Job title, direct number, employer structure, and internal project names</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><em>An out-of-office reply is a public statement your home is empty and you are not checking messages. Keep it to dates and an alternative contact.</em></p> <h2 id="self-hosting-an-honest-assessment"> <a href="#self-hosting-an-honest-assessment" title="Self-Hosting: An Honest Assessment">Self-Hosting: An Honest Assessment</a> <a href="#self-hosting-an-honest-assessment" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Self-Hosting: An Honest Assessment">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Running your own mail server is harder than it looks, and the difficulty is not the software.</strong></p> <p>The technical setup is achievable. The operational burden is the problem:</p> <ul> <li><strong>Deliverability depends on reputation</strong>, which requires correct SPF, DKIM, and DMARC records and a sending history which receivers trust.</li> <li><strong>Availability is on you.</strong> If your server is down, mail is not queued politely, it is refused.</li> <li><strong>Abuse handling is on you</strong>, including bot attempts to relay through your server.</li> <li><strong>Redundancy requires planning</strong>, typically at least two MX records with a documented priority order.</li> </ul> <p>Two reliability items belong in any self-hosted deployment:</p> <div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" style="color:#f8f8f2;background-color:#272822;-moz-tab-size:4;-o-tab-size:4;tab-size:4;-webkit-text-size-adjust:none;"><code class="language-text" data-lang="text"><span style="display:flex;"><span># Check your mail authentication records before sending anything </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>dig +short TXT example.com # SPF </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>dig +short TXT _dmarc.example.com # DMARC policy </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>dig +short MX example.com # at least two, ordered by preference </span></span></code></pre></div><p><strong>If you are not prepared to maintain this, use a reputable provider and put the effort into aliasing instead.</strong> A managed provider with a good privacy posture and unique aliases beats a misconfigured self-hosted server on every axis which matters here.</p> <p><em>If you do not self-host, the portability argument returns: owning the domain means you change providers without changing your address, which is the part which matters over a decade.</em></p> <h2 id="the-email-record"> <a href="#the-email-record" title="The Email Record">The Email Record</a> <a href="#the-email-record" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="The Email Record">#</a> </h2> <div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" style="color:#f8f8f2;background-color:#272822;-moz-tab-size:4;-o-tab-size:4;tab-size:4;-webkit-text-size-adjust:none;"><code class="language-text" data-lang="text"><span style="display:flex;"><span>EMAIL RECORD </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Primary provider: ______________________ </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Address strategy: separate / alias / subaddress / single </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Alias provider or domain: ______________________ </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Retired aliases disabled: ______________________ </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Security settings: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> Remote content loading: OFF </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> View as plaintext: yes / no </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> Recovery address: ______________________ </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> Recovery phone: current / stale / none </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Third-party access (review and revoke): </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> - ______________________ revoked? ______ </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> - ______________________ revoked? ______ </span></span></code></pre></div> <script type="application/ld+json"> { "@context": "https://schema.org/", "@type": "ImageObject", "contentUrl": "https:\/\/simeononsecurity.com\/email-aliasing-versus-subaddressing-comparison.webp", "caption": "Diagram comparing a single email address, subaddressing, and per-service aliases, showing which strategies hide the real address and which reveal who leaked it", "license": "https://simeononsecurity.com/termsandconditions/", "acquireLicensePage": "https://simeononsecurity.com/contactus/", "creditText": "SimeonOnSecurity", "creator": { "@type": "Person", "name": "SimeonOnSecurity" }, "copyrightNotice": "SimeonOnSecurity", "associatedArticle": { "@type": "NewsArticle", "headline": "simeononsecurity", "url": "https:\/\/simeononsecurity.com\/", "datePublished": "2026-10-02 21:20:37.59241331 \u002b0000 UTC m=\u002b337.317139055", "author": { "@type": "Person", "name": "SimeonOnSecurity", "url": "https:\/\/simeononsecurity.com\/authors\/simeononsecurity" } } } </script> <center> <figure align="center" style="text-align: center; margin: 0 auto;" itemscope itemtype="http://schema.org/ImageObject"> <meta property="article:published_time" content="2026-10-02 21:20:37.59241331 +0000 UTC m=+337.317139055"> <meta property="article:author"
