src="https://simeononsecurity.com/email-aliasing-versus-subaddressing-comparison.webp" alt="Diagram comparing a single email address, subaddressing, and per-service aliases, showing which strategies hide the real address and which reveal who leaked it"loading="lazy" fetchpriority="low" itemprop="contentUrl" /> </figure> </center> <h2 id="next-steps"> <a href="#next-steps" title="Next Steps">Next Steps</a> <a href="#next-steps" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Next Steps">#</a> </h2> <ol> <li><strong>Continue to Module 4</strong> and apply the same privacy reasoning to conversation: <strong> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Secure Messaging"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/personal-security-course/messaging/"> <a href="/personal-security-course/messaging/" rel="follow me" >Secure Messaging</a> </span> </strong></li> <li><strong>Disable remote content loading</strong> in your mail client now, which takes about thirty seconds</li> <li><strong>Review connected applications</strong> and revoke anything you no longer use</li> <li><strong>Compare aliasing options</strong> if you want a provider-managed solution rather than a domain</li> <li><strong>Read the module on authentication</strong> if recovery codes are not yet stored: <strong> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Authentication and Credentials"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/personal-security-course/authentication/"> <a href="/personal-security-course/authentication/" rel="follow me" >Authentication and Credentials</a> </span> </strong></li> </ol> Read More at https://simeononsecurity.com/

item.title: Module 4: Secure Messaging
item.description: End-to-end encryption protects content, not metadata. This module covers how to evaluate a messenger, why group chats multiply risk, and what your provider still learns about you.
item.content:encoded: <h4 id="-return-to-the-personal-security-course"> <a href="#-return-to-the-personal-security-course" title=" ← Return to the Personal Security Course "> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="← Return to the Personal Security Course"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/personal-security-course-start/"> <a href="/personal-security-course-start/" rel="follow me" >← Return to the Personal Security Course</a> </span> </a> <a href="#-return-to-the-personal-security-course" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title=" ← Return to the Personal Security Course ">#</a> </h4> <p><strong>End-to-end encryption protects what you say, not who you spoke to.</strong> This distinction defines the whole module. A messenger which encrypts every message perfectly still hands your provider a record of every conversation partner, every timestamp, and every group you belong to.</p> <p>This module covers how to evaluate a messenger on properties rather than reputation, why metadata deserves separate attention, and why group chats raise risk faster than message content ever does.</p> <p><em>Budget about 20 minutes. Messenger choice is a single decision with long-lasting consequences.</em></p> <h2 id="what-you-will-learn"> <a href="#what-you-will-learn" title="What You Will Learn">What You Will Learn</a> <a href="#what-you-will-learn" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="What You Will Learn">#</a> </h2> <ul> <li><strong>Distinguish</strong> transport encryption, encryption at rest, and end-to-end encryption</li> <li><strong>Evaluate</strong> a messenger against open source, maintenance, and default-encryption criteria</li> <li><strong>Explain</strong> what metadata reveals even when message content stays private</li> <li><strong>Assess</strong> why each additional group participant increases exposure</li> <li><strong>Apply</strong> hygiene to shared links and media before sending</li> <li><strong>Produce</strong> a messaging record listing your primary messenger and its security settings</li> </ul> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Term</th> <th>Meaning</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>End-to-end encryption</strong></td> <td>Content encrypted on your device and decrypted only on the recipient’s</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Transport encryption</strong></td> <td>Protection between you and the server, which the server reads past</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Metadata</strong></td> <td>Information about a message rather than its content, including participants and timing</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Forward secrecy</strong></td> <td>A fresh key per message, so a stolen key does not expose earlier traffic</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Ephemeral message</strong></td> <td>Content configured to delete itself after a set period</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Cloud companion</strong></td> <td>A web or desktop client which keeps message history on a server</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <h2 id="the-three-properties-of-a-secure-messenger"> <a href="#the-three-properties-of-a-secure-messenger" title="The Three Properties of a Secure Messenger">The Three Properties of a Secure Messenger</a> <a href="#the-three-properties-of-a-secure-messenger" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="The Three Properties of a Secure Messenger">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>A messenger earns trust through three properties, and a failure in any one of them undermines the other two.</strong></p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Property</th> <th>Why It Matters</th> <th>How to Verify</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>End-to-end encryption by default</strong></td> <td>Opt-in encryption means most conversations are unprotected</td> <td>Check whether the app encrypts without configuration</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Open source</strong></td> <td>Independent review is the only way to find backdoors and flaws</td> <td>Look for a public repository and recent commits</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Actively maintained</strong></td> <td>Unpatched software becomes the vulnerability</td> <td>Check release dates within the last year</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>Default matters more than capability.</strong> A messenger which supports end-to-end encryption but leaves it off for ordinary conversations protects almost nobody, because almost nobody enables it.</p> <p><em>Ask the second question before the first. A platform is sometimes open source and abandoned, which is worse than closed and maintained, because you see the flaws and cannot get them fixed.</em></p> <h2 id="metadata-is-the-unencrypted-part"> <a href="#metadata-is-the-unencrypted-part" title="Metadata Is the Unencrypted Part">Metadata Is the Unencrypted Part</a> <a href="#metadata-is-the-unencrypted-part" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Metadata Is the Unencrypted Part">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Your provider does not need to read your messages to learn a great deal about you.</strong> The delivery record is enough.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Metadata</th> <th>What It Reveals</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Participants</strong></td> <td>Your social graph, including relationships you keep separate</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Timing</strong></td> <td>When you are awake, working, travelling, or asleep</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Frequency</strong></td> <td>Which relationships are active and which have lapsed</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Duration</strong></td> <td>Whether a conversation was a message or a call</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Group membership</strong></td> <td>Associations you have not disclosed elsewhere</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>This is why anonymous platforms matter for some users and not others.</strong> If your threat model includes an adversary able to compel the provider, metadata is the exploitable part, because providers hold it in plaintext to route messages at all.</p> <p><em>A provider cannot route a message without knowing the destination. This is the structural reason metadata survives every encryption improvement.</em></p> <h2 id="evaluating-a-platform"> <a href="#evaluating-a-platform" title="Evaluating a Platform">Evaluating a Platform</a> <a href="#evaluating-a-platform" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Evaluating a Platform">#</a> </h2> <p>Work through this rather than adopting whatever your contacts happen to use.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Criterion</th> <th>Strong Answer</th> <th>Weak Answer</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Encryption</strong></td> <td>On by default, for all conversations</td> <td>Opt-in, or unavailable for groups</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Source</strong></td> <td>Public repository, protocol documented</td> <td>Closed client, unpublished protocol</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Maintenance</strong></td> <td>Releases within months</td> <td>No update in over a year</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>History storage</strong></td> <td>Message content stays on devices</td> <td>Server-side history by design</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Registration</strong></td> <td>No phone number required</td> <td>Mandatory phone number</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Group behaviour</strong></td> <td>Membership changes visible to members</td> <td>Silent participant additions</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Metadata retention</strong></td> <td>Minimized and documented</td> <td>Undisclosed</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>A funded, open protocol maintained by a nonprofit holds the strongest structural position</strong>, because it has no advertising incentive to profile you and no shareholder pressure to monetize metadata.</p> <h2 id="group-chats-multiply-risk"> <a href="#group-chats-multiply-risk" title="Group Chats Multiply Risk">Group Chats Multiply Risk</a> <a href="#group-chats-multiply-risk" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Group Chats Multiply Risk">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Risk scales with participants, and it scales faster than linearly.</strong></p> <p>A two-person conversation requires both parties to be trustworthy. A ten-person group requires all ten, plus everyone who has ever left it, plus everyone who photographed a message before leaving.</p> <p>Practical rules:</p> <ul> <li><strong>Verify membership periodically</strong> and remove inactive participants</li> <li><strong>Prefer smaller groups</strong> over one large channel</li> <li><strong>Assume anything shared in a group is permanent</strong>, regardless of the ephemeral setting</li> <li><strong>Check whether history is shared with new members</strong> when they join</li> </ul> <p><em>Ephemeral messages protect against device seizure. They do not protect against a participant photographing a screen, which is the far more common leak.</em></p> <h2 id="practical-hygiene-before-you-send"> <a href="#practical-hygiene-before-you-send" title="Practical Hygiene Before You Send">Practical Hygiene Before You Send</a> <a href="#practical-hygiene-before-you-send" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Practical Hygiene Before You Send">#</a> </h2> <p>Two habits remove real risk and take seconds:</p> <p><strong>Defang links before sharing them.</strong> A URL shared in a chat is often auto-previewed, which means the service fetches the page on your behalf and associates your account with the visit. Converting <code>https://</code> to <code>hxxps://</code> and dots to <code>[.]</code> prevents the preview while leaving the destination readable to a human.</p> <p><strong>Strip metadata from media.</strong> A photograph carries GPS coordinates, a timestamp, and often a device identifier. This matters most for images taken at home.</p> <p>Both are covered by local tools which never upload the content:</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Task</th> <th>Tool</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Defang a link safely</strong></td> <td><strong> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="IOC Defang, Refang, and Extractor"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/ioc-defang-refang/"> <a href="/ioc-defang-refang/" rel="follow me" >IOC Defang, Refang, and Extractor</a> </span> </strong></td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Check what an image exposes</strong></td> <td><strong> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="EXIF Viewer"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/exif-viewer/"> <a href="/exif-viewer/" rel="follow me" >EXIF Viewer</a> </span> </strong></td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Inspect a link before opening it</strong></td> <td><strong> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="URL Parser and Query Analyzer"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/url-parser/"> <a href="/url-parser/" rel="follow me" >URL Parser and Query Analyzer</a> </span> </strong></td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><em>A preview request is an outbound connection attributable to your account. Defanging prevents it without hiding anything from the recipient.</em></p> <h2 id="the-messaging-record"> <a href="#the-messaging-record" title="The Messaging Record">The Messaging Record</a> <a href="#the-messaging-record" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="The Messaging Record">#</a> </h2> <div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" style="color:#f8f8f2;background-color:#272822;-moz-tab-size:4;-o-tab-size:4;tab-size:4;-webkit-text-size-adjust:none;"><code class="language-text" data-lang="text"><span style="display:flex;"><span>MESSAGING RECORD </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Primary messenger: ______________________ </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Encryption: default / opt-in / none </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Open source: yes / no / partial </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Registration method: phone number / email / none </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Security settings: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> Contact verification: enabled / disabled </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> Read receipts: off / on </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> Typing indicator: off / on </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> Last seen: off / on </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> Disappearing messages: ______ (duration, or off) </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> Cloud companion: enabled / disabled / unavailable </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Groups I belong to (review membership): </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> - ______________________ participants: ______ </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> - ______________________ participants: ______ </span></span></code></pre></div> <script type="application/ld+json"> { "@context": "https://schema.org/", "@type": "ImageObject", "contentUrl": "https:\/\/simeononsecurity.com\/messaging-encryption-content-versus-metadata.webp", "caption": "Diagram separating encrypted message content from unencrypted metadata including participants, timing, and group membership, showing what a provider still retains", "license": "https://simeononsecurity.com/termsandconditions/", "acquireLicensePage": "https://simeononsecurity.com/contactus/", "creditText": "SimeonOnSecurity", "creator": { "@type": "Person", "name": "SimeonOnSecurity" }, "copyrightNotice": "SimeonOnSecurity", "associatedArticle": { "@type": "NewsArticle", "headline": "simeononsecurity", "url": "https:\/\/simeononsecurity.com\/", "datePublished": "2026-10-02 21:20:37.59638933 \u002b0000 UTC m=\u002b337.321115094", "author": { "@type": "Person", "name": "SimeonOnSecurity", "url": "https:\/\/simeononsecurity.com\/authors\/simeononsecurity" } } } </script> <center> <figure align="center" style="text-align: center; margin: 0 auto;" itemscope itemtype="http://schema.org/ImageObject"> <meta property="article:published_time" content="2026-10-02 21:20:37.59638933 +0000 UTC m=+337.321115094"> <meta property="article:author" content="SimeonOnSecurity"> <meta property="article:author:url" content="https://simeononsecurity.com/authors/simeononsecurity"> <meta property="og:license" content="https://simeononsecurity.com/termsandconditions/"> <meta property="og:see_also" content="https://simeononsecurity.com/contactus/"> <meta property="og:copyright" content="SimeonOnSecurity"> <img align="center" style="text-align: center; margin: 0 auto; max-width: 80%; max-height: 600px; min-width: 100px; min-height: 100px; height: auto; width: auto;" src="https://simeononsecurity.com/messaging-encryption-content-versus-metadata.webp" alt="Diagram separating encrypted message content from unencrypted metadata including participants, timing, and group membership, showing what a provider still retains"loading="lazy" fetchpriority="low" itemprop="contentUrl" /> </figure> </center> <h2 id="next-steps"> <a href="#next-steps" title="Next Steps">Next Steps</a> <a href="#next-steps" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Next Steps">#</a> </h2> <ol> <li><strong>Continue to Module 5</strong> and reduce what your public profile reveals: <strong> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Social Media Privacy"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/personal-security-course/social-media/"> <a href="/personal-security-course/social-media/" rel="follow me" >Social Media Privacy</a> </span> </strong></li> <li><strong>Turn on disappearing messages</strong> for conversations which do not need history</li> <li><strong>Verify contacts</strong> in your primary messenger, which is the step most people skip</li> <li><strong>Defang your next shared link</strong> with the <strong> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="IOC Defang tool"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/ioc-defang-refang/"> <a href="/ioc-defang-refang/" rel="follow me" >IOC Defang tool</a> </span> </strong></li> <li><strong>Check photo metadata</strong> before posting with the <strong> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="EXIF Viewer"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/exif-viewer/"> <a href="/exif-viewer/" rel="follow me" >EXIF Viewer</a> </span> </strong></li> <li><strong>Review your group memberships</strong> and remove anyone inactive</li> </ol> Read More at https://simeononsecurity.com/

item.title: Module 5: Social Media Privacy
item.description: Social profiles aggregate into a detailed dossier. This module covers the two assumptions behind every post, upload discipline, permission and integration review, and when leaving is the honest answer.
item.content:encoded: <h4 id="-return-to-the-personal-security-course"> <a href="#-return-to-the-personal-security-course" title=" ← Return to the Personal Security Course "> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="← Return to the Personal Security Course"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/personal-security-course-start/"> <a href="/personal-security-course-start/" rel="follow me" >← Return to the Personal Security Course</a> </span> </a> <a href="#-return-to-the-personal-security-course" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title=" ← Return to the Personal Security Course ">#</a> </h4> <p><strong>A social profile is a dossier you assemble for someone else.</strong> Individually, a birthday, a hometown, a pet’s name, and a photograph of your street are trivial. Aggregated, they answer the security questions protecting your accounts and locate your home.</p> <p>This module covers the two assumptions behind every post, upload discipline, permission and integration review, and when leaving a platform is the honest answer.</p> <p><em>Budget about 25 minutes. Most of the value comes from a settings review and a single privacy decision.</em></p> <h2 id="what-you-will-learn"> <a href="#what-you-will-learn" title="What You Will Learn">What You Will Learn</a> <a href="#what-you-will-learn" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="What You Will Learn">#</a> </h2> <ul> <li><strong>Apply</strong> the two assumptions which should govern every post</li> <li><strong>Explain</strong> how scattered details aggregate into an identity profile</li> <li><strong>Configure</strong> privacy, tagging, and permission settings</li> <li><strong>Remove</strong> location and metadata before uploading media</li> <li><strong>Audit</strong> third-party applications with profile access</li> <li><strong>Produce</strong> a social media record listing your platforms, exposure level, and review date</li> </ul> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Term</th> <th>Meaning</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Digital footprint</strong></td> <td>The accumulated public record of your online activity</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>OSINT</strong></td> <td>Intelligence gathered from public sources, which is what an attacker performs on you</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Geotag</strong></td> <td>Location data embedded in a post or an image file</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Image cloaking</strong></td> <td>Imperceptible alterations which degrade facial recognition against your photos</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Third-party integration</strong></td> <td>An external application granted access to your profile data</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <h2 id="the-two-assumptions"> <a href="#the-two-assumptions" title="The Two Assumptions">The Two Assumptions</a> <a href="#the-two-assumptions" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="The Two Assumptions">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Assume everything is public and permanent, then decide whether to post.</strong></p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Assumption</th> <th>Why It Holds</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Public</strong></td> <td>Platform settings change, connections reshare, and screenshots exist. Private content is frequently visible to someone</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Permanent</strong></td> <td>Archives, caches, and third-party mirrors retain what you delete</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>Deletion is a request, not a guarantee.</strong> Assume anything you post has been copied at least once.</p> <p><em>This is not a reason to avoid social media. It is a reason to ask whether a specific post would embarrass or endanger you if it were the first result for your name.</em></p> <h2 id="securing-the-account"> <a href="#securing-the-account" title="Securing the Account">Securing the Account</a> <a href="#securing-the-account" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Securing the Account">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Social accounts are valuable takeover targets</strong> because they are trusted by your contacts. A compromised account sends convincing messages to people who have no reason to doubt them.</p> <p>Apply Module 1 to these accounts and add two steps specific to social platforms:</p> <ul> <li><strong>Enable login alerts</strong> so an unfamiliar session produces a notification</li> <li><strong>Review active sessions</strong> and sign out anything you do not recognize</li> </ul> <p><em>An account takeover enables social engineering against everyone who trusts you, which is why a compromised profile is a risk to your contacts as much as to you.</em></p> <h2 id="what-your-profile-reveals"> <a href="#what-your-profile-reveals" title="What Your Profile Reveals">What Your Profile Reveals</a> <a href="#what-your-profile-reveals" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="What Your Profile Reveals">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Attackers do not break in. They look you up.</strong> A profile answers questions which would otherwise require effort.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Detail</th> <th>What It Enables</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Full name and birthday</strong></td> <td>Identity verification and impersonation</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Hometown, school, first pet</strong></td> <td>Answers to common security questions</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Employer and role</strong></td> <td>Targeted business email compromise</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Direct email or phone</strong></td> <td>Phishing and SIM swap attempts</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Daily routine and locations</strong></td> <td>Physical risk, and empty property cues</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Family names and relationships</strong></td> <td>Impersonation of people you trust</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>Security questions are the sharpest edge here.</strong> Your mother’s maiden name is often public record, your first car is often in a photograph, and your school is on your profile. Module 1’s answer applies: <strong>store invented answers in your vault</strong> rather than true ones.</p> <p><em>Our <strong> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Prioritized Security Checklist"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/articles/personal-security-checklist-prioritized-2026/"> <a href="/articles/personal-security-checklist-prioritized-2026/" rel="follow me" >Prioritized Security Checklist</a> </span> </strong> places this under Tier 3 in effort but notes it feeds directly into Tier 1 account recovery.</em></p> <h2 id="upload-discipline"> <a href="#upload-discipline" title="Upload Discipline">Upload Discipline</a> <a href="#upload-discipline" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Upload Discipline">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Two details leak from every upload, and both are removable.</strong></p> <h3 id="location"> <a href="#location" title="Location">Location</a> <a href="#location" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Location">#</a> </h3> <p>Publishing a location while still there announces your presence. Publishing it while travelling announces your absence.</p> <ul> <li><strong>Post location-tagged content after you leave</strong>, not during</li> <li><strong>Disable automatic geotagging</strong> in the camera app and the platform</li> <li><strong>Check backgrounds</strong> in photographs, which reveal street signs, house numbers, and landmarks</li> <li><strong>Review check-ins and tagged locations</strong>, including ones your contacts added</li> </ul> <p><em>The absence signal matters more than the presence signal. A tagged holiday photograph tells a reader which property is currently unoccupied.</em></p> <h3 id="metadata"> <a href="#metadata" title="Metadata">Metadata</a> <a href="#metadata" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Metadata">#</a> </h3> <p>Images carry data beyond the visible pixels, including GPS coordinates, timestamps, and device identifiers. Platforms strip some of this and not all of it.</p> <p><strong>Check before uploading</strong> with the local <strong> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="EXIF Viewer"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/exif-viewer/"> <a href="/exif-viewer/" rel="follow me" >EXIF Viewer</a> </span> </strong>, which reads metadata without transmitting the file. Our <strong> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="URL Parser"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/url-parser/"> <a href="/url-parser/" rel="follow me" >URL Parser</a> </span> </strong> does the equivalent for links, exposing tracking parameters appended to a shared address.</p> <h2 id="permissions-and-integrations"> <a href="#permissions-and-integrations" title="Permissions and Integrations">Permissions and Integrations</a> <a href="#permissions-and-integrations" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Permissions and Integrations">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Two review tasks belong in any social media audit.</strong></p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Target</th> <th>What to Check</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>App permissions</strong></td> <td>Contacts, call log, location, photos, and microphone. Revoke what the app does not need</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Third-party integrations</strong></td> <td>Everything connected through social sign-in, which you granted once and never revisited</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>Prefer a dedicated account per service over social sign-in.</strong> A social login links your profiles into one graph and makes a single provider compromise reach every connected service.</p> <p>Our threat model guide covers when this level of separation is justified: <strong> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="How to Form Your Own Personal Threat Model"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/articles/how-to-form-your-own-personal-threat-model-safeguard-online-security/"> <a href="/articles/how-to-form-your-own-personal-threat-model-safeguard-online-security/" rel="follow me" >How to Form Your Own Personal Threat Model</a> </span> </strong>.</p> <h2 id="when-leaving-is-the-answer"> <a href="#when-leaving-is-the-answer" title="When Leaving Is the Answer">When Leaving Is the Answer</a> <a href="#when-leaving-is-the-answer" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="When Leaving Is the Answer">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Some platforms cannot be configured into safety</strong>, because the business model depends on the aggregation you are trying to prevent.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Situation</th> <th>Reasonable Response</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>You post infrequently and mostly read</strong></td> <td>Reduce to a lurking account with minimal profile detail</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Your profile is required for work</strong></td> <td>Separate work and personal identities, and keep the personal one minimal</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>You face harassment, stalking, or a public role</strong></td> <td>Consider leaving, or maintaining a pseudonymous presence with no real details</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>The platform sells behavioral advertising</strong></td> <td>Assume your activity is the product regardless of settings</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>A pseudonymous account is a legitimate middle path</strong> for readers who want the content without the profile. Use a different name, no real contact details, and a separate browser container so no two identities share storage.</p> <p><em>Advanced readers concerned about facial recognition against existing photographs should explore image cloaking tools. The technique degrades recognition rather than preventing it, and it does not remove photographs which are already published.</em></p> <script type="application/ld+json"> { "@context": "https://schema.org/", "@type": "ImageObject", "contentUrl": "https:\/\/simeononsecurity.com\/social-media-profile-aggregation-osint-dossier.webp", "caption": "Diagram showing scattered social media details such as birthday, school, employer, and routine aggregating into a single identity dossier used for impersonation and account recovery attacks", "license": "https://simeononsecurity.com/termsandconditions/", "acquireLicensePage": "https://simeononsecurity.com/contactus/", "creditText": "SimeonOnSecurity", "creator": { "@type": "Person", "name": "SimeonOnSecurity" }, "copyrightNotice": "SimeonOnSecurity", "associatedArticle": { "@type": "NewsArticle", "headline": "simeononsecurity", "url": "https:\/\/simeononsecurity.com\/", "datePublished": "2026-10-02 21:20:37.600654764 \u002b0000 UTC m=\u002b337.325380526", "author": { "@type": "Person", "name": "SimeonOnSecurity", "url": "https:\/\/simeononsecurity.com\/authors\/simeononsecurity" } } } </script> <center> <figure align="center" style="text-align: center; margin: 0 auto;" itemscope itemtype="http://schema.org/ImageObject"> <meta property="article:published_time" content="2026-10-02 21:20:37.600654764 +0000 UTC m=+337.325380526"> <meta property="article:author" content="SimeonOnSecurity"> <meta property="article:author:url" content="https://simeononsecurity.com/authors/simeononsecurity"> <meta property="og:license" content="https://simeononsecurity.com/termsandconditions/"> <meta property="og:see_also" content="https://simeononsecurity.com/contactus/"> <meta property="og:copyright" content="SimeonOnSecurity"> <img align="center" style="text-align: center; margin: 0 auto; max-width: 80%; max-height: 600px; min-width: 100px; min-height: 100px; height: auto; width: auto;" src="https://simeononsecurity.com/social-media-profile-aggregation-osint-dossier.webp" alt="Diagram showing scattered social media details such as birthday, school, employer, and routine aggregating into a single identity dossier used for impersonation and account recovery attacks"loading="lazy" fetchpriority="low" itemprop="contentUrl" /> </figure> </center> <h2 id="the-social-media-record"> <a href="#the-social-media-record" title="The Social Media Record">The Social Media Record</a> <a href="#the-social-media-record" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="The Social Media Record">#</a> </h2> <div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" style="color:#f8f8f2;background-color:#272822;-moz-tab-size:4;-o-tab-size:4;tab-size:4;-webkit-text-size-adjust:none;"><code class="language-text" data-lang="text"><span style="display:flex;"><span>SOCIAL MEDIA RECORD </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Platforms in use: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> - ______________________ profile detail: minimal / full </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> - ______________________ profile detail: minimal / full </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Settings reviewed: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> Profile visibility: public / friends / custom </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> Tagging approval: on / off </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> Location & geotagging: off / on </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> Facial recognition: off / on / unavailable </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Permissions audited: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> Apps with profile access: ______ revoked: ______ </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> Social sign-ins in use: ______________________ </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Details removed from profile: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> birthday / hometown / school / employer / phone / email </span></span></code></pre></div><h2 id="next-steps"> <a href="#next-steps" title="Next Steps">Next Steps</a> <a href="#next-steps" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Next Steps">#</a> </h2> <ol> <li><strong>Continue to Module 6</strong> and secure the network your devices connect through: <strong> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Home Network Security"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/personal-security-course/networks/"> <a href="/personal-security-course/networks/" rel="follow me" >Home Network Security</a> </span> </strong></li> <li><strong>Check what your next upload exposes</strong> with the <strong> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="EXIF Viewer"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/exif-viewer/"> <a href="/exif-viewer/" rel="follow me" >EXIF Viewer</a> </span> </strong></li> <li><strong>Review connected applications</strong> and revoke anything you no longer use</li> <li><strong>Remove security-question answers from your profile</strong> and store invented ones in your vault</li> <li><strong>Read the human aspect module</strong> to see how public details feed social engineering: <strong> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="The Human Aspect"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/personal-security-course/human-aspect/"> <a item.title: Module 6: Home Network Security
item.description: Your router is the boundary between your devices and the internet. This module covers a hardening sequence, what a VPN does and does not change, DNS privacy versus integrity, and how WiFi networks get catalogued.
item.content:encoded: <h4 id="-return-to-the-personal-security-course"> <a href="#-return-to-the-personal-security-course" title=" ← Return to the Personal Security Course "> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="← Return to the Personal Security Course"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/personal-security-course-start/"> <a href="/personal-security-course-start/" rel="follow me" >← Return to the Personal Security Course</a> </span> </a> <a href="#-return-to-the-personal-security-course" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title=" ← Return to the Personal Security Course ">#</a> </h4> <p><strong>The router is the boundary between your devices and the internet.</strong> It decides what reaches your network, what your devices reach, and which of them talk to each other. Everything downstream inherits its configuration.</p> <p>This module covers a hardening sequence in priority order, what a VPN genuinely changes, the two separate problems hiding under “secure DNS”, and how your WiFi network gets catalogued by strangers.</p> <p><em>Budget about 40 minutes. The router work is done once and then mostly forgotten.</em></p> <h2 id="what-you-will-learn"> <a href="#what-you-will-learn" title="What You Will Learn">What You Will Learn</a> <a href="#what-you-will-learn" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="What You Will Learn">#</a> </h2> <ul> <li><strong>Sequence</strong> router hardening by risk rather than by checkbox</li> <li><strong>Explain</strong> which exposures WPS, UPnP, and remote administration each create</li> <li><strong>Distinguish</strong> DNS privacy from DNS integrity</li> <li><strong>Evaluate</strong> a VPN claim against what a VPN protects</li> <li><strong>Describe</strong> how passive WiFi scanning builds public maps of network names and locations</li> <li><strong>Produce</strong> a network record listing router settings, DNS configuration, and open ports</li> </ul> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Term</th> <th>Meaning</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>NAT</strong></td> <td>Address translation which hides internal addresses behind one public address</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>UPnP</strong></td> <td>A protocol letting applications request inbound port mappings automatically</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>WPS</strong></td> <td>A push-button pairing method with a long history of weaknesses</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>DNS leak</strong></td> <td>DNS queries leaving through a different path than your tunnel</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>WiGLE</strong></td> <td>A crowdsourced database of observed WiFi networks and locations</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>MAC address</strong></td> <td>A hardware identifier, and a partial tracking signal on WiFi</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <h2 id="the-router-is-the-boundary"> <a href="#the-router-is-the-boundary" title="The Router Is the Boundary">The Router Is the Boundary</a> <a href="#the-router-is-the-boundary" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="The Router Is the Boundary">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Default configurations favor convenience over safety</strong>, and every convenience feature is an inbound path.</p> <p>Three categories of problem account for nearly all home network compromise:</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Category</th> <th>Examples</th> <th>Consequence</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Credential weakness</strong></td> <td>Default admin password, weak WiFi passphrase</td> <td>Direct access to the network</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Convenience services</strong></td> <td>UPnP, WPS, remote administration, cloud management</td> <td>Attacker-chosen inbound access</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Stale software</strong></td> <td>Unpatched router firmware</td> <td>Exploitation of known vulnerabilities</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><em>The router is the single device on your network which is both permanently internet-facing and rarely updated. The combination is why it belongs in the first hour of work rather than the last.</em></p> <h2 id="a-hardening-sequence"> <a href="#a-hardening-sequence" title="A Hardening Sequence">A Hardening Sequence</a> <a href="#a-hardening-sequence" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="A Hardening Sequence">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Work in this order.</strong> The early steps remove access paths, and the later steps reduce what an attacker learns.</p> <h3 id="1-credentials"> <a href="#1-credentials" title="1. Credentials">1. Credentials</a> <a href="#1-credentials" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="1. Credentials">#</a> </h3> <ul> <li><strong>Change the admin password</strong> before anything else. Default router credentials are published and indexed</li> <li><strong>Use WPA3 where supported</strong>, falling back to WPA2. Both are acceptable, and neither is safe with a weak passphrase</li> <li><strong>Use a long passphrase</strong> rather than a short complex string, following Module 1’s reasoning</li> </ul> <h3 id="2-remove-the-convenience-back-doors"> <a href="#2-remove-the-convenience-back-doors" title="2. Remove the Convenience Back Doors">2. Remove the Convenience Back Doors</a> <a href="#2-remove-the-convenience-back-doors" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="2. Remove the Convenience Back Doors">#</a> </h3> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Feature</th> <th>Risk</th> <th>Action</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>WPS</strong></td> <td>PIN brute force and push-button abuse</td> <td>Disable</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>UPnP</strong></td> <td>Applications open inbound ports without your knowledge</td> <td>Disable unless a specific device requires it</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Remote administration</strong></td> <td>Router admin panel reachable from the internet</td> <td>Disable</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Cloud management</strong></td> <td>Vendor-held control plane over your router</td> <td>Disable if you do not use it</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Telnet and unused services</strong></td> <td>Command-line access with weak or no authentication</td> <td>Disable</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <h3 id="3-firmware"> <a href="#3-firmware" title="3. Firmware">3. Firmware</a> <a href="#3-firmware" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="3. Firmware">#</a> </h3> <p><strong>Enable automatic updates if the vendor offers them.</strong> If not, check quarterly. A router which stopped receiving updates is a decision point: replace it, or place a maintained device in front of it.</p> <h3 id="4-segmentation"> <a href="#4-segmentation" title="4. Segmentation">4. Segmentation</a> <a href="#4-segmentation" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="4. Segmentation">#</a> </h3> <ul> <li><strong>Use a guest network for visitors</strong>, which keeps them off the segment holding your computers and storage</li> <li><strong>Put IoT devices on their own network</strong> where the router supports it, covered further in Module 9</li> <li><strong>Verify nothing important is on the guest segment</strong>, since guest isolation is the point</li> </ul> <h3 id="5-reduce-exposure"> <a href="#5-reduce-exposure" title="5. Reduce Exposure">5. Reduce Exposure</a> <a href="#5-reduce-exposure" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="5. Reduce Exposure">#</a> </h3> <ul> <li><strong>Close forwarded ports</strong> you do not recognize. Every forwarded port is a deliberately opened inbound path</li> <li><strong>Review the port forwarding list</strong> rather than assuming it is empty</li> <li><strong>Change the router’s local address</strong> if you want to defeat scripts which target common defaults, though the benefit is modest</li> <li><strong>Reduce transmit power</strong> if your network reaches further than you need</li> </ul> <h2 id="what-a-vpn-changes"> <a href="#what-a-vpn-changes" title="What a VPN Changes">What a VPN Changes</a> <a href="#what-a-vpn-changes" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="What a VPN Changes">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>A VPN moves trust, it does not remove it.</strong> This single sentence resolves most confusion about the technology.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>A VPN Does</th> <th>A VPN Does Not</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td>Hide traffic from the local network operator</td> <td>Hide traffic from the sites you visit</td> </tr> <tr> <td>Change your apparent source address</td> <td>Make you anonymous to a logged-in service</td> </tr> <tr> <td>Protect traffic on untrusted WiFi</td> <td>Protect against malware on your device</td> </tr> <tr> <td>Shift DNS resolution to the provider</td> <td>Prevent fingerprinting by the destination site</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>A paid, reputable VPN provider is the recommendation for two scenarios:</strong> using untrusted WiFi, and preventing an internet provider from compiling a browsing record.</p> <p>Two configuration points matter:</p> <ul> <li><strong>Use WireGuard or OpenVPN.</strong> Avoid PPTP and SSTP, which are obsolete protocols with known weaknesses</li> <li><strong>Confirm DNS goes through the tunnel.</strong> A DNS leak sends your lookups in plaintext outside the tunnel, which defeats part of the purpose</li> </ul> <p><strong>The honest limit:</strong> a VPN provider sees everything your internet provider would have seen. You are choosing who holds the record, not eliminating it.</p> <p><em>If your requirement is anonymity rather than confidentiality, Tor is the appropriate tool and a VPN is not. Tor routes through multiple relays so no single party sees both who you are and what you requested.</em></p> <h2 id="dns-two-separate-problems"> <a href="#dns-two-separate-problems" title="DNS: Two Separate Problems">DNS: Two Separate Problems</a> <a href="#dns-two-separate-problems" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="DNS: Two Separate Problems">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>People treat “secure DNS” as one thing. It is two, and they are solved differently.</strong></p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Problem</th> <th>What Is At Risk</th> <th>Solution</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Privacy</strong></td> <td>Your provider observes every domain you resolve</td> <td>DNS over HTTPS or DNS over TLS</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Integrity</strong></td> <td>An attacker in the path returns a forged answer</td> <td>DNSSEC validation, plus encryption</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>DNS-over-HTTPS addresses privacy. DNSSEC addresses integrity.</strong> Encrypting your DNS does not validate the answers, and validating them does not hide the questions.</p> <p>Two honest caveats about encrypted DNS:</p> <ul> <li><strong>It moves trust rather than eliminating it.</strong> Your resolver sees your queries instead of your internet provider, so the resolver’s policy is the thing to evaluate</li> <li><strong>It bypasses network-level filtering</strong>, including parental controls and corporate policy, which is not always what you want</li> </ul> <p><em>One genuine security benefit beyond privacy: encrypted DNS removes DNS spoofing as a practical attack path on hostile networks, which matters on public WiFi.</em></p> <p>Inspect the addressing of a network with local tools: the <strong> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="CIDR Subnet Calculator"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/cidr-calculator/"> <a href="/cidr-calculator/" rel="follow me" >CIDR Subnet Calculator</a> </span> </strong> for IPv4 ranges, and the <strong> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="IPv6 Address Expander"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/ipv6-expander/"> <a href="/ipv6-expander/" rel="follow me" >IPv6 Address Expander</a> </span> </strong> for the addresses most home networks now also carry.</p> <h2 id="wifi-exposure-beyond-your-network"> <a href="#wifi-exposure-beyond-your-network" title="WiFi Exposure Beyond Your Network">WiFi Exposure Beyond Your Network</a> <a href="#wifi-exposure-beyond-your-network" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="WiFi Exposure Beyond Your Network">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Your network name is public.</strong> Every device broadcasting an SSID is announcing it to anything in range, and crowdsourced wardriving projects have been cataloguing those observations for years.</p> <p>The practical implications:</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Practice</th> <th>Reason</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Do not put personal details in the SSID</strong></td> <td>Names, flat numbers, and device models identify both you and your hardware</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Know SSIDs and locations get published</strong></td> <td>Crowdsourced databases map networks to places, which correlates to a physical address</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Enable MAC randomization on devices</strong></td> <td>Reduces the ability to track one device across multiple networks</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Understand hiding the SSID is weak</strong></td> <td>It is trivially discoverable from client traffic, and it breaks some devices</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><em>This site maintains two mapping projects in this space, both useful for understanding what public WiFi observations reveal: <strong> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="OpenRoaming and Hotspot 2.0 Map"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/sibling-sites/"> <a href="/sibling-sites/" rel="follow me" >OpenRoaming and Hotspot 2.0 Map</a> </span> </strong> and <strong> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Flock Finder"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/sibling-sites/"> <a href="/sibling-sites/" rel="follow me" >Flock Finder</a> </span> </strong>. They are demonstrations of how much is inferable from passive scanning rather than tools for your own network.</em></p> <p><strong>Assess your own exposure</strong> by checking what your neighbourhood already reveals, then decide whether your SSID adds anything an observer did not already have.</p> <script type="application/ld+json"> { "@context": "https://schema.org/", "@type": "ImageObject", "contentUrl": "https:\/\/simeononsecurity.com\/network-router-hardening-and-dns-paths.webp", "caption": "Diagram showing a home router with hardened settings, separate device segments, and two DNS paths illustrating plaintext lookups compared with encrypted lookups through a tunnel", "license": "https://simeononsecurity.com/termsandconditions/", "acquireLicensePage": href="#the-network-record" title="The Network Record">The Network Record</a> <a href="#the-network-record" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="The Network Record">#</a> </h2> <div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" style="color:#f8f8f2;background-color:#272822;-moz-tab-size:4;-o-tab-size:4;tab-size:4;-webkit-text-size-adjust:none;"><code class="language-text" data-lang="text"><span style="display:flex;"><span>NETWORK RECORD </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Router model: ______________________ </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Firmware version: ______________________ auto-update: on / off </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Admin password changed: yes / no </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>WiFi security: WPA3 / WPA2 / other </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>WiFi passphrase: in vault? yes / no </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Disabled: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> WPS: yes / no </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> UPnP: yes / no </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> Remote administration: yes / no </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> Cloud management: yes / no </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>DNS: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> Resolver: ______________________ </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> Encryption: DoH / DoT / none </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> DNSSEC validation: on / off / unknown </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> Leak test passed: yes / no </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Segments: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> Guest network: enabled / disabled </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> IoT network: enabled / disabled / unsupported </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> Devices on guest: ______________________ </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Forwarded ports (should be empty or intentional): </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> - ______________________ purpose: __________ </span></span></code></pre></div><h2 id="next-steps"> <a href="#next-steps" title="Next Steps">Next Steps</a> <a href="#next-steps" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Next Steps">#</a> </h2> <ol> <li><strong>Continue to Module 7</strong> and reduce what your phone reports: <strong> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Mobile Device Security"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/personal-security-course/mobile-devices/"> <a href="/personal-security-course/mobile-devices/" rel="follow me" >Mobile Device Security</a> </span> </strong></li> <li><strong>Change the router admin password and disable WPS and UPnP</strong> now, which takes about five minutes</li> <li><strong>Review the port forwarding list</strong> and remove anything you do not recognize</li> <li><strong>Check for DNS leaks</strong> if you use a VPN, then confirm validation separately</li> <li><strong>Explore addressing</strong> with the <strong> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="CIDR Calculator"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/cidr-calculator/"> <a href="/cidr-calculator/" rel="follow me" >CIDR Calculator</a> </span> </strong> and <strong> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="IPv6 Expander"> <meta item.title: Module 7: Mobile Device Security
item.description: A phone is a sensor platform which travels with you. This module covers carrier-level protections including SIM swap defense, permission and app inventory, stalkerware detection, and why the keyboard matters.
item.content:encoded: <h4 id="-return-to-the-personal-security-course"> <a href="#-return-to-the-personal-security-course" title=" ← Return to the Personal Security Course "> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="← Return to the Personal Security Course"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/personal-security-course-start/"> <a href="/personal-security-course-start/" rel="follow me" >← Return to the Personal Security Course</a> </span> </a> <a href="#-return-to-the-personal-security-course" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title=" ← Return to the Personal Security Course ">#</a> </h4> <p><strong>A phone is a sensor platform which travels with you.</strong> It knows your location continuously, holds a camera and two microphones, carries your authenticated sessions, and receives your second-factor codes. Losing control of it compromises almost everything in Module 1.</p> <p>This module covers the carrier layer, which most guides skip, then permissions, app inventory, stalkerware, and the input methods people never think about.</p> <p><em>Budget about 30 minutes. The SIM PIN and the permission audit are the two highest-yield actions.</em></p> <h2 id="what-you-will-learn"> <a href="#what-you-will-learn" title="What You Will Learn">What You Will Learn</a> <a href="#what-you-will-learn" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="What You Will Learn">#</a> </h2> <ul> <li><strong>Explain</strong> why the phone number is a security asset rather than a mere identifier</li> <li><strong>Configure</strong> carrier-level protections against SIM swap</li> <li><strong>Audit</strong> app permissions and background activity</li> <li><strong>Recognize</strong> the indicators of stalkerware and the correct response</li> <li><strong>Evaluate</strong> third-party keyboards, launchers, and input methods</li> <li><strong>Produce</strong> a mobile record listing encryption status, carrier PIN, and audited permissions</li> </ul> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Term</th> <th>Meaning</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>SIM swap</strong></td> <td>Moving your number to another SIM, which redirects calls and messages</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Carrier PIN</strong></td> <td>A passcode required before a provider changes your SIM or plan</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Juice jacking</strong></td> <td>Data theft through a charging cable which also carries data</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Stalkerware</strong></td> <td>Monitoring software installed by someone with physical device access</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Sandboxing</strong></td> <td>Isolating an app so it cannot read other apps’ data</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <h2 id="why-the-phone-deserves-its-own-module"> <a href="#why-the-phone-deserves-its-own-module" title="Why the Phone Deserves Its Own Module">Why the Phone Deserves Its Own Module</a> <a href="#why-the-phone-deserves-its-own-module" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Why the Phone Deserves Its Own Module">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Three properties make a phone a different risk category from a laptop.</strong></p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Property</th> <th>Consequence</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Continuous location</strong></td> <td>Movement patterns are recorded, and location is inferable without GPS</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Always-present sensors</strong></td> <td>Camera, microphone, accelerometer, and Bluetooth radios</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>It receives your second factors</strong></td> <td>SMS and push codes arrive here, so compromise escalates to every account</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>The third property is the one to internalize.</strong> A phone is not only a device holding your data. It is the delivery mechanism for the factor protecting your other accounts, which is why the carrier layer matters so much.</p> <p><em>This is also why Module 1 recommends passkeys and hardware keys over SMS. Moving the factor off the phone removes an entire attack path.</em></p> <h2 id="the-carrier-layer"> <a href="#the-carrier-layer" title="The Carrier Layer">The Carrier Layer</a> <a href="#the-carrier-layer" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="The Carrier Layer">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Your phone number is an asset which many services trust as proof of identity.</strong> The trust is the vulnerability.</p> <h3 id="set-a-carrier-pin"> <a href="#set-a-carrier-pin" title="Set a Carrier PIN">Set a Carrier PIN</a> <a href="#set-a-carrier-pin" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Set a Carrier PIN">#</a> </h3> <p><strong>This is the single most valuable phone action and it takes about ten minutes.</strong></p> <p>A carrier PIN is a passcode your provider requires before changing your SIM, porting your number, or altering your plan. Without it, an attacker who knows your personal details convinces a support agent to move your number to their device. With it, the conversation fails.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Attack</th> <th>Effect Without a PIN</th> <th>Effect With a PIN</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>SIM swap</strong></td> <td>Attacker receives your calls and SMS</td> <td>Blocked at the provider</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Number porting</strong></td> <td>Your number moves to another carrier</td> <td>Requires the passcode</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Account recovery</strong></td> <td>SMS-based recovery routes to the attacker</td> <td>Recovery codes stay with you</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>Two supporting steps:</p> <ul> <li><strong>Port-freeze your number</strong> where the provider offers it, which blocks unauthorized transfers</li> <li><strong>Reduce your number’s exposure</strong>, since it is both a tracking identifier and a link between datasets</li> </ul> <p><strong>A secondary number or virtual number for account recovery is worth considering</strong> if you register with many services. Keeping the recovery number separate from the number you publish limits what a single compromise reaches.</p> <p><em>This connects directly to Module 1. SMS as a second factor is only as strong as the carrier protections behind it.</em></p> <h2 id="permissions-and-app-inventory"> <a href="#permissions-and-app-inventory" title="Permissions and App Inventory">Permissions and App Inventory</a> <a href="#permissions-and-app-inventory" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Permissions and App Inventory">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Every installed app is code with a set of granted permissions</strong>, and most people have never reviewed the list.</p> <h3 id="start-with-the-inventory"> <a href="#start-with-the-inventory" title="Start With the Inventory">Start With the Inventory</a> <a href="#start-with-the-inventory" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Start With the Inventory">#</a> </h3> <ul> <li><strong>Uninstall what you do not use.</strong> An unused app still holds its permissions and still runs in the background</li> <li><strong>Prefer official app stores</strong>, where applications are reviewed and cryptographically signed, though review is not a guarantee</li> <li><strong>Prefer the browser over a dedicated app</strong> for services you use occasionally, since a website receives no standing permissions</li> </ul> <h3 id="then-audit-permissions"> <a href="#then-audit-permissions" title="Then Audit Permissions">Then Audit Permissions</a> <a href="#then-audit-permissions" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Then Audit Permissions">#</a> </h3> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Permission</th> <th>Grant Only When</th> <th>Warning Sign</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Location</strong></td> <td>Navigation or a genuine local need</td> <td>A shopping or social app requesting precise location at all times</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Microphone</strong></td> <td>Voice features you use</td> <td>Any app without a voice function</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Camera</strong></td> <td>Photography or scanning</td> <td>An app requesting camera without a stated use</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Contacts</strong></td> <td>Messaging or calling apps</td> <td>A game or utility reading your address book</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Files and photos</strong></td> <td>Editing apps</td> <td>An app requesting your entire library for one image</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>Set location to approximate rather than precise</strong> where the platform offers the choice. A weather app does not need your street address.</p> <p>Two further steps reduce background collection:</p> <ul> <li><strong>Restrict background activity</strong> per app, which limits both battery drain and data collection</li> <li><strong>Disable connectivity you are not using.</strong> Bluetooth, WiFi, and NFC left enabled are all continuously broadcast</li> </ul> <p><em>Restarting the device weekly clears in-memory state and is a low-cost habit worth keeping.</em></p> <h2 id="stalkerware"> <a href="#stalkerware" title="Stalkerware">Stalkerware</a> <a href="#stalkerware" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Stalkerware">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Stalkerware is monitoring software installed by someone with access to your device</strong>, frequently a partner or former partner. It differs from other malware because the attacker is known to you.</p> <p>Indicators worth noticing:</p> <ul> <li><strong>Battery draining faster than usual</strong> or the device running warm while idle</li> <li><strong>Unfamiliar apps</strong>, especially ones with generic or system-sounding names</li> <li><strong>Settings you did not change</strong>, particularly accessibility services and device administrators</li> <li><strong>Someone showing knowledge of your activity</strong> which they should not have</li> </ul> <p><strong>Check accessibility services and device administrators directly.</strong> Stalkerware frequently uses accessibility permissions, which are broad and easy to overlook.</p> <blockquote> <p><strong>Warning: do not remove stalkerware on a device you believe is monitored without a safety plan. Removal is often detectable, and the person who installed it often escalates. Consider using a different device to seek advice before acting.</strong></p> </blockquote> <p><em>The correct response to suspected stalkerware on a device you control is often a factory reset rather than an uninstall, since a reset is more thorough. Follow it with a new passcode the other person has never seen.</em></p> <h2 id="input-methods-and-physical-ports"> <a href="#input-methods-and-physical-ports" title="Input Methods and Physical Ports">Input Methods and Physical Ports</a> <a href="#input-methods-and-physical-ports" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Input Methods and Physical Ports">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>The keyboard sees everything you type</strong>, including passwords before they reach the vault.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Input Method</th> <th>Consideration</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Stock keyboard</strong></td> <td>Maintained by the platform vendor and covered by system updates</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Third-party keyboard</strong></td> <td>Receives every keystroke, including passwords. Some also serve ads</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Cloud-based prediction</strong></td> <td>Sends context to a server to improve suggestions</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>Use the stock keyboard, or a third-party keyboard with a genuine reputation and cloud features disabled.</strong> The convenience gain rarely justifies the exposure.</p> <p>Two physical considerations:</p> <ul> <li><strong>Avoid public charging ports where possible.</strong> A USB port carries data as well as power, so prefer your own adapter or a power-only cable</li> <li><strong>Enable erase-after-failed-attempts</strong> if the platform supports it, which limits the value of a stolen locked device</li> </ul> <p><em>Combined with Module 1’s guidance on avoiding four-digit PINs, these two settings make a stolen phone substantially less useful to whoever holds it.</em></p> <script type="application/ld+json"> { "@context": "https://schema.org/", "@type": "ImageObject", "contentUrl": "https:\/\/simeononsecurity.com\/mobile-device-carrier-permission-risk-layers.webp", "caption": "Diagram showing mobile security layers from the carrier SIM protections at the bottom through operating system encryption, app permissions, and input methods such as keyboards", "license": "https://simeononsecurity.com/termsandconditions/", "acquireLicensePage": "https://simeononsecurity.com/contactus/", "creditText": "SimeonOnSecurity", "creator": { "@type": "Person", "name": "SimeonOnSecurity" }, "copyrightNotice": "SimeonOnSecurity", "associatedArticle": { "@type": "NewsArticle", "headline": "simeononsecurity", "url": "https:\/\/simeononsecurity.com\/", "datePublished": "2026-10-02 21:20:37.608716371 \u002b0000 UTC m=\u002b337.333442136", "author": { "@type": "Person", "name": "SimeonOnSecurity", "url": "https:\/\/simeononsecurity.com\/authors\/simeononsecurity" } } } </script> <center> <figure align="center" style="text-align: center; margin: 0 auto;" itemscope itemtype="http://schema.org/ImageObject"> <meta property="article:published_time" content="2026-10-02 21:20:37.608716371 +0000 UTC m=+337.333442136"> <meta property="article:author" content="SimeonOnSecurity"> <meta property="article:author:url" content="https://simeononsecurity.com/authors/simeononsecurity"> <meta property="og:license" content="https://simeononsecurity.com/termsandconditions/"> <meta property="og:see_also" content="https://simeononsecurity.com/contactus/"> <meta property="og:copyright" content="SimeonOnSecurity"> <img align="center" style="text-align: center; margin: 0 auto; max-width: 80%; max-height: 600px; min-width: 100px; min-height: 100px; height: auto; width: auto;" src="https://simeononsecurity.com/mobile-device-carrier-permission-risk-layers.webp" alt="Diagram showing mobile security layers from the carrier SIM protections at the bottom through operating system encryption, app permissions, and input methods such as keyboards"loading="lazy" fetchpriority="low" itemprop="contentUrl" /> </figure> </center> <h2 id="the-mobile-record"> <a href="#the-mobile-record" title="The Mobile Record">The Mobile Record</a> <a href="#the-mobile-record" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="The Mobile Record">#</a> </h2> <div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" style="color:#f8f8f2;background-color:#272822;-moz-tab-size:4;-o-tab-size:4;tab-size:4;-webkit-text-size-adjust:none;"><code class="language-text" data-lang="text"><span style="display:flex;"><span>MOBILE RECORD </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Device: ______________________ </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>OS version: ______________________ auto-update: on / off </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Device encryption: on / off / unknown </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Lock method: PIN (length: __) / passphrase / biometric </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Erase after N attempts: enabled / disabled </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Carrier: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> Provider: ______________________ </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> Carrier PIN set: yes / no </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> Port freeze: yes / no / unavailable </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> Recovery number: separate / same as primary </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Permissions audited: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> Location set to approximate: yes / no </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> Apps with microphone: ______ revoked: ______ </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> Apps with camera: ______ revoked: ______ </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> Apps with contacts: ______ revoked: ______ </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Uninstalled this session: ______________________ </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Accessibility services reviewed: yes / no </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Keyboard: stock / third-party: __________ </span></span></code></pre></div><h2 id="next-steps"> <a href="#next-steps" title="Next Steps">Next Steps</a> <a href="#next-steps" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Next Steps">#</a> </h2> <ol> <li><strong>Continue to Module 8</strong> and secure the machine your accounts and files live on: <strong> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Personal Computer Security"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/personal-security-course/personal-computers/"> <a href="/personal-security-course/personal-computers/" rel="follow me" >Personal Computer Security</a> </span> </strong></li> <li><strong>Set a carrier PIN and port freeze today.</strong> This is the highest-value ten minutes in the module</li> <li><strong>Audit accessibility services and device administrators</strong> for anything you did not enable</li> <li><strong>Switch location permissions to approximate</strong> for apps which do not need precision</li> <li><strong>Review your keyboard</strong> and disable cloud prediction if you keep a third-party one</li> <li><strong>Read the organizational counterpart</strong>: <strong> <span
