href="/checklists/mobile-device-security-checklist/" rel="follow me" >Mobile Device Security Checklist</a> </span> </strong></li> </ol> Read More at https://simeononsecurity.com/

item.title: Module 8: Personal Computer Security
item.description: Updates, encryption, and backups matter more than anything else on a desktop. This module covers those three, then least privilege, endpoint integrity, attack surface reduction, and isolation techniques.
item.content:encoded: <h4 id="-return-to-the-personal-security-course"> <a href="#-return-to-the-personal-security-course" title=" ← Return to the Personal Security Course "> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="← Return to the Personal Security Course"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/personal-security-course-start/"> <a href="/personal-security-course-start/" rel="follow me" >← Return to the Personal Security Course</a> </span> </a> <a href="#-return-to-the-personal-security-course" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title=" ← Return to the Personal Security Course ">#</a> </h4> <p><strong>On a desktop, three controls carry more weight than everything else combined:</strong> updates, disk encryption, and backups. The remaining controls reduce the consequences when one of those three fails.</p> <p>This module covers those three first, then least privilege, endpoint integrity, attack surface reduction, and the isolation techniques which matter for readers who run untrusted software.</p> <p><em>Budget about 45 minutes. Encryption and the backup check are the two items to finish today.</em></p> <h2 id="what-you-will-learn"> <a href="#what-you-will-learn" title="What You Will Learn">What You Will Learn</a> <a href="#what-you-will-learn" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="What You Will Learn">#</a> </h2> <ul> <li><strong>Sequence</strong> desktop controls by consequence rather than by popularity</li> <li><strong>Enable</strong> full disk encryption on Windows, macOS, or Linux</li> <li><strong>Apply</strong> least privilege to daily work rather than only to servers</li> <li><strong>Reduce</strong> the listening attack surface by closing services and ports</li> <li><strong>Isolate</strong> risky activity with virtual machines and separate accounts</li> <li><strong>Produce</strong> a computer record listing encryption, backup, and privilege configuration</li> </ul> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Term</th> <th>Meaning</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Full disk encryption</strong></td> <td>Encrypting the entire volume so a stolen device yields no readable data</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Least privilege</strong></td> <td>Operating with the minimum rights needed for the task at hand</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Attack surface</strong></td> <td>The set of services, ports, and interfaces reachable by an attacker</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Keystroke injection</strong></td> <td>A device which presents itself as a keyboard and types commands</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Mandatory access control</strong></td> <td>A policy layer which restricts programs beyond file permissions</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Canary token</strong></td> <td>A decoy file or credential which alerts you when it is touched</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <h2 id="the-three-controls-which-matter-most"> <a href="#the-three-controls-which-matter-most" title="The Three Controls Which Matter Most">The Three Controls Which Matter Most</a> <a href="#the-three-controls-which-matter-most" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="The Three Controls Which Matter Most">#</a> </h2> <h3 id="1-automatic-updates"> <a href="#1-automatic-updates" title="1. Automatic Updates">1. Automatic Updates</a> <a href="#1-automatic-updates" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="1. Automatic Updates">#</a> </h3> <p><strong>Most successful compromises exploit a vulnerability with an available patch.</strong> Update lag is the exploitable window.</p> <ul> <li><strong>Enable automatic updates</strong> for the operating system and restart when prompted</li> <li><strong>Update applications separately.</strong> Browsers, document readers, and media players are common targets</li> <li><strong>Include firmware and drivers</strong> where the vendor supports automatic delivery</li> </ul> <p><em>A pending restart means a pending vulnerability. Treat the notification as unfinished work rather than an interruption.</em></p> <h3 id="2-full-disk-encryption"> <a href="#2-full-disk-encryption" title="2. Full Disk Encryption">2. Full Disk Encryption</a> <a href="#2-full-disk-encryption" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="2. Full Disk Encryption">#</a> </h3> <p><strong>Encryption converts a stolen device from a data breach into a hardware loss.</strong> Without it, anyone holding the machine reads your vault, your sessions, and your files.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Platform</th> <th>Feature</th> <th>Where to Check</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Windows</strong></td> <td>BitLocker or Device Encryption</td> <td>Settings, Privacy and Security, Device encryption</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>macOS</strong></td> <td>FileVault</td> <td>System Settings, Privacy and Security, FileVault</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Linux</strong></td> <td>LUKS</td> <td>Confirm root and home volumes at install time</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>Verify your recovery key is stored somewhere other than the encrypted disk.</strong> A recovery key only on the encrypted volume is not a recovery key.</p> <p><em>Turning the device fully off rather than leaving it in standby matters once encryption is enabled. A suspended machine often holds keys in memory.</em></p> <h3 id="3-backups"> <a href="#3-backups" title="3. Backups">3. Backups</a> <a href="#3-backups" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="3. Backups">#</a> </h3> <p><strong>A tested backup is the only control which survives ransomware, theft, and hardware failure alike.</strong></p> <ul> <li><strong>Keep one local copy</strong> for fast restores</li> <li><strong>Keep one encrypted offsite copy</strong> for fire and theft</li> <li><strong>Keep one offline or write-only copy</strong> for ransomware which reaches your synced storage</li> </ul> <p><strong>Test a restore.</strong> A backup never restored is an assumption.</p> <h2 id="least-privilege-on-a-desktop"> <a href="#least-privilege-on-a-desktop" title="Least Privilege on a Desktop">Least Privilege on a Desktop</a> <a href="#least-privilege-on-a-desktop" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Least Privilege on a Desktop">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Most people work as an administrator all day</strong>, which means every process they launch inherits those rights. Least privilege is not a server-only concept.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Practice</th> <th>Why It Matters</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Use a standard account for daily work</strong></td> <td>Malware inherits the account’s rights, not the machine’s</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Elevate only for administrative tasks</strong></td> <td>Limits what runs with full rights</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Do not link the machine to a cloud account</strong></td> <td>A local account avoids syncing settings and browsing data to a vendor</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Review installed applications</strong></td> <td>Fewer applications means fewer update obligations and fewer targets</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Lock the screen on idle</strong></td> <td>An unlocked machine is a complete compromise</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>Separate accounts are the simplest compartmentalization available.</strong> One account for daily use, one for administrative work, and one for anything untrusted. On Linux and macOS the separation is native. On Windows it requires creating additional local accounts rather than using the built-in administrator.</p> <p><em>The measurement for this module is not how many controls you enabled. It is how much an attacker gains from compromising one account.</em></p> <h2 id="endpoint-integrity"> <a href="#endpoint-integrity" title="Endpoint Integrity">Endpoint Integrity</a> <a href="#endpoint-integrity" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Endpoint Integrity">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>These controls answer a different question: is the machine currently trustworthy?</strong></p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Control</th> <th>What It Addresses</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Built-in platform protections</strong></td> <td>Defender, Gatekeeper, or the Linux equivalents, which are adequate for most users</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Avoid commercial free antivirus</strong></td> <td>Many monetize telemetry, and some add attack surface rather than reducing it</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Periodic rootkit checks</strong></td> <td>Tools such as <code>chkrootkit</code> or <code>rkhunter</code> on Linux, and vendor tooling elsewhere</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Watch for hardware keyloggers</strong></td> <td>Inspect the connection between keyboard and machine after the device has been unattended</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Guard against keystroke injection</strong></td> <td>A device presenting as a keyboard types commands instantly. USB filtering tools address it</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Block camera and microphone physically</strong></td> <td>A physical cover defeats software which has already compromised the device</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" style="color:#f8f8f2;background-color:#272822;-moz-tab-size:4;-o-tab-size:4;tab-size:4;-webkit-text-size-adjust:none;"><code class="language-bash" data-lang="bash"><span style="display:flex;"><span><span style="color:#75715e"># Linux: check what is listening on external interfaces</span> </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>ss -tulpn </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span><span style="color:#75715e"># Confirm a hardware keystroke filter is active before trusting the machine</span> </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>lsusb | head </span></span></code></pre></div><p><strong>Physical access defeats most software controls.</strong> A BIOS or UEFI password raises the effort for casual access, and it does not stop someone with the disk removed. Treat it as friction rather than protection.</p> <p><em>Canary tokens are worth knowing about. A decoy file or credential which alerts you when opened gives early warning something has access it should not. Self-hosted canary services and file-integrity monitoring both implement the idea.</em></p> <h2 id="attack-surface-reduction"> <a href="#attack-surface-reduction" title="Attack Surface Reduction">Attack Surface Reduction</a> <a href="#attack-surface-reduction" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Attack Surface Reduction">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Every listening service is a path in.</strong> The goal is a smaller list, not a longer one.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Target</th> <th>Action</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Listening ports</strong></td> <td>Identify what listens, then disable what you do not use</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>SSH</strong></td> <td>Disable password authentication in favor of keys, change the default port, and restrict source addresses</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>File and print sharing</strong></td> <td>Disable protocols you do not use, especially legacy SMB versions</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Remote access features</strong></td> <td>Disable remote desktop and remote assistance unless actively used</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Voice assistants</strong></td> <td>Disable or limit always-listening features</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Vendor telemetry</strong></td> <td>Reduce usage data and diagnostic reporting to the minimum offered</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Secure Boot</strong></td> <td>Keep it enabled, which complicates bootloader tampering</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" style="color:#f8f8f2;background-color:#272822;-moz-tab-size:4;-o-tab-size:4;tab-size:4;-webkit-text-size-adjust:none;"><code class="language-bash" data-lang="bash"><span style="display:flex;"><span><span style="color:#75715e"># Linux: verify SSH will not accept passwords</span> </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>grep -E <span style="color:#e6db74">'^PasswordAuthentication|^PermitRootLogin'</span> /etc/ssh/sshd_config </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span><span style="color:#75715e"># List enabled services to decide what deserves to stay</span> </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>systemctl list-unit-files --state<span style="color:#f92672">=</span>enabled </span></span></code></pre></div><p><strong>On Windows, the equivalent exercise is reviewing startup items and optional features.</strong> Disabling unused services reduces both collection and attack surface, at the cost of some convenience.</p> <p><em>Our organizational counterpart covers the server-side version of this exercise: <strong> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Patch Management Checklist"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/checklists/patch-management-checklist/"> <a href="/checklists/patch-management-checklist/" rel="follow me" >Patch Management Checklist</a> </span> </strong>.</em></p> <h2 id="isolation-for-risky-activity"> <a href="#isolation-for-risky-activity" title="Isolation for Risky Activity">Isolation for Risky Activity</a> <a href="#isolation-for-risky-activity" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Isolation for Risky Activity">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>When you must run something untrusted, isolation limits what a compromise reaches.</strong> These techniques cost convenience, so reserve them for the cases which justify it.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Technique</th> <th>Isolation Level</th> <th>Best For</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Separate user account</strong></td> <td>Low, shares the kernel</td> <td>Keeping work and personal data apart</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Container</strong></td> <td>Moderate, shares the kernel</td> <td>Running a service in a defined environment</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Virtual machine</strong></td> <td>High, separate kernel</td> <td>Testing unknown software and browsing risky sites</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Dedicated hardware</strong></td> <td>Highest</td> <td>Any activity you never want correlated with your identity</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Mandatory access control</strong></td> <td>Orthogonal, restricts programs</td> <td>Confining applications even after compromise</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>A virtual machine is the practical option for most readers</strong> who want to inspect suspicious files or software. Remember containers share the host kernel, so a kernel vulnerability crosses the boundary. Our analysis of <strong> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="why containers are no longer a security boundary"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/articles/containers-no-longer-security-boundary-2026/"> <a href="/articles/containers-no-longer-security-boundary-2026/" rel="follow me" >why containers are no longer a security boundary</a> </span> </strong> covers exactly this failure mode for the 2026 vulnerability families.</p> <p><strong>Mandatory access control</strong> is worth knowing on Linux, where AppArmor or SELinux confines what an application does regardless of its user’s rights. Enabling it adds a layer which survives a compromised process.</p> <p><em>Compartmentalization is the underlying principle for all five rows. Ask what a compromise of this account or this virtual machine would reach, then reduce it until the answer is acceptable.</em></p> <script type="application/ld+json"> { "@context": "https://schema.org/", "@type": "ImageObject", "contentUrl": "https:\/\/simeononsecurity.com\/personal-computer-controls-by-consequence.webp", "caption": "Diagram ranking desktop security controls by consequence, with updates, disk encryption, and tested backups at the top and isolation techniques such as virtual machines and compartmentalization at the bottom", "license": "https://simeononsecurity.com/termsandconditions/", "acquireLicensePage": "https://simeononsecurity.com/contactus/", "creditText": "SimeonOnSecurity", "creator": { "@type": "Person", "name": "SimeonOnSecurity" }, "copyrightNotice": "SimeonOnSecurity", "associatedArticle": { "@type": "NewsArticle", "headline": "simeononsecurity", "url": "https:\/\/simeononsecurity.com\/", "datePublished": itemprop="contentUrl" /> </figure> </center> <h2 id="the-computer-record"> <a href="#the-computer-record" title="The Computer Record">The Computer Record</a> <a href="#the-computer-record" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="The Computer Record">#</a> </h2> <div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" style="color:#f8f8f2;background-color:#272822;-moz-tab-size:4;-o-tab-size:4;tab-size:4;-webkit-text-size-adjust:none;"><code class="language-text" data-lang="text"><span style="display:flex;"><span>COMPUTER RECORD </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Device: ______________________ </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>OS and version: ______________________ auto-update: on / off </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>The three controls: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> Disk encryption: enabled / disabled recovery key stored at: __________ </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> Backup local: ______________________ last restore test: __________ </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> Backup offsite: ______________________ encrypted: yes / no </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> Backup offline: ______________________ </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Privilege: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> Daily account type: standard / administrator </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> Separate admin account: yes / no </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> Cloud account linked: yes / no </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Attack surface: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> Listening ports reviewed: yes / no </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> SSH password auth: disabled / not applicable / not reviewed </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> Sharing services off: file / print / both / none </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> Remote desktop: disabled / enabled </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> Secure Boot: enabled / disabled / unavailable </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Integrity: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> Platform protections: enabled / disabled </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> Rootkit check run: yes / never </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> Camera cover: yes / no </span></span></code></pre></div><h2 9</strong> and decide what earns a place on your network: <strong> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Smart Home and IoT"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/personal-security-course/smart-home/"> <a href="/personal-security-course/smart-home/" rel="follow me" >Smart Home and IoT</a> </span> </strong></li> <li><strong>Confirm disk encryption is on</strong> and the recovery key is stored off the device</li> <li><strong>Restore one file from your backup</strong> to prove the backup works</li> <li><strong>Review what listens on external interfaces</strong> and disable anything you do not recognize</li> <li><strong>Read the container boundary analysis</strong> before treating a container as isolation: <strong> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Containers Are No Longer a Security Boundary"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/articles/containers-no-longer-security-boundary-2026/"> <a href="/articles/containers-no-longer-security-boundary-2026/" rel="follow me" >Containers Are No Longer a Security Boundary</a> </span> </strong></li> <li><strong>Read the organizational counterpart</strong>: <strong> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Patch Management </strong></li> </ol> Read More at https://simeononsecurity.com/

item.title: Module 9: Smart Home and IoT
item.description: Smart devices trade data for convenience, and the trade is rarely disclosed clearly. This module covers the purchase decision, network segmentation for IoT, voice assistant specifics, and wearables.
item.content:encoded: <h4 id="-return-to-the-personal-security-course"> <a href="#-return-to-the-personal-security-course" title=" ← Return to the Personal Security Course "> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="← Return to the Personal Security Course"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/personal-security-course-start/"> <a href="/personal-security-course-start/" rel="follow me" >← Return to the Personal Security Course</a> </span> </a> <a href="#-return-to-the-personal-security-course" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title=" ← Return to the Personal Security Course ">#</a> </h4> <p><strong>A smart device is a sensor with a network connection attached.</strong> A speaker holds a microphone, a camera holds a lens and often a microphone, a thermostat learns occupancy, and a lock reports who comes and goes. Each one is a small computer with its own update history and its own data practices.</p> <p>This module covers the purchase decision, network segmentation for devices you did not build, voice assistant specifics, and wearables.</p> <p><em>Budget about 30 minutes. The segmentation decision has more effect than any individual device setting.</em></p> <h2 id="what-you-will-learn"> <a href="#what-you-will-learn" title="What You Will Learn">What You Will Learn</a> <a href="#what-you-will-learn" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="What You Will Learn">#</a> </h2> <ul> <li><strong>Evaluate</strong> a smart device against its data practices rather than its feature list</li> <li><strong>Segment</strong> IoT devices onto a separate network from your computers</li> <li><strong>Explain</strong> what voice assistants retain and what changes when you disable recording</li> <li><strong>Assess</strong> wearables as a continuous biometric collection platform</li> <li><strong>Decide</strong> which home functions should never connect to the internet</li> <li><strong>Produce</strong> a smart home record listing devices, network segment, and firmware status</li> </ul> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Term</th> <th>Meaning</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>IoT</strong></td> <td>Internet of Things, meaning network-connected devices beyond computers and phones</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Segmentation</strong></td> <td>Placing devices on separate network segments so they cannot reach each other</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Default credential</strong></td> <td>The factory username and password, which is published for most devices</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Voice assistant</strong></td> <td>A device or service which listens for a wake phrase and processes audio remotely</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Telemetry</strong></td> <td>Usage data a device reports back to its vendor</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <h2 id="the-trade-stated-plainly"> <a href="#the-trade-stated-plainly" title="The Trade, Stated Plainly">The Trade, Stated Plainly</a> <a href="#the-trade-stated-plainly" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="The Trade, Stated Plainly">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Smart home devices are convenient, and the price is data.</strong> The question is not whether a device collects, it is whether the collection is worth what the device does for you.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Category</th> <th>Typical Collection</th> <th>Honest Assessment</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Smart speaker</strong></td> <td>Audio snippets, wake events, queries, and household presence patterns</td> <td>High collection, moderate convenience</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Indoor camera</strong></td> <td>Continuous video, motion events, and audio</td> <td>High collection, and high breach impact</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Smart lock</strong></td> <td>Entry and exit events, user identity per event</td> <td>High sensitivity if the vendor account is compromised</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Thermostat</strong></td> <td>Occupancy inference and schedule</td> <td>Reveals when the property is empty</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Smart lighting</strong></td> <td>Usage schedules, and sometimes presence inference</td> <td>Lower sensitivity, and often the best value</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Fitness wearable</strong></td> <td>Continuous heart rate, sleep, location, and movement</td> <td>Extensive biometric data with weak resale controls</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>Two device types deserve the strongest scrutiny: cameras and microphones.</strong> A camera breach is a direct view into your home, and the historical record of smart camera incidents is long.</p> <p><em>Ask the inverse question when considering a purchase: what is the worst outcome if this vendor is breached, and would I accept the outcome for what the device does?</em></p> <h2 id="what-earns-a-place-on-your-network"> <a href="#what-earns-a-place-on-your-network" title="What Earns a Place on Your Network">What Earns a Place on Your Network</a> <a href="#what-earns-a-place-on-your-network" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="What Earns a Place on Your Network">#</a> </h2> <p>Run this before buying, not after.</p> <ol> <li><strong>Does it require an internet connection to function?</strong> Some devices work entirely locally, which removes the vendor from your threat model</li> <li><strong>Does the vendor publish a privacy policy with specifics</strong>, or only generalities</li> <li><strong>Does it support local control</strong> through a standard protocol rather than a vendor cloud</li> <li><strong>Is there a firmware update history</strong>, and how recent is the last one</li> <li><strong>Does it require a cloud account</strong>, and does your identity need to be real</li> </ol> <p><strong>Prefer devices with a local control path.</strong> A camera or bulb which works over your own network without a vendor cloud removes an entire category of risk, including the vendor’s breach becoming your breach.</p> <h2 id="segmentation-the-highest-value-step"> <a href="#segmentation-the-highest-value-step" title="Segmentation: The Highest-Value Step">Segmentation: The Highest-Value Step</a> <a href="#segmentation-the-highest-value-step" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Segmentation: The Highest-Value Step">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Put IoT devices on their own network segment.</strong> This is the single change which limits what a compromised device reaches.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Setup</th> <th>Effect</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Guest network for IoT</strong></td> <td>Available on most routers, and separates devices from your computers</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Dedicated VLAN</strong></td> <td>Stronger isolation where the router supports it</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Per-device blocking</strong></td> <td>Firewall rules denying outbound access for devices which do not need it</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>Three rules for the IoT segment:</p> <ul> <li><strong>No IoT device reaches your computers or network storage.</strong> Guest isolation usually handles this</li> <li><strong>Deny internet access where the device does not need it</strong>, which applies to many bulbs and sensors</li> <li><strong>Rename every device</strong> to something generic, so a device list does not describe your hardware to anyone who sees it</li> </ul> <p><em>Our <strong> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Network Security Checklist"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/checklists/network-security-checklist/"> <a href="/checklists/network-security-checklist/" rel="follow me" >Network Security Checklist</a> </span> </strong> covers the segment design in more depth, and Module 6 covers the router configuration.</em></p> <h2 id="voice-assistants"> <a href="#voice-assistants" title="Voice Assistants">Voice Assistants</a> <a href="#voice-assistants" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Voice Assistants">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>A voice assistant is a microphone with a network connection and a retention policy.</strong></p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Setting</th> <th>What It Changes</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Delete voice recordings</strong></td> <td>Removes stored audio, and review whether it also removes transcripts</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Disable voice purchases</strong></td> <td>Prevents spoken authorization of transactions</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Turn off personalization</strong></td> <td>Reduces profile building from your queries</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Mute the microphone physically</strong></td> <td>The only reliable guarantee nothing is captured</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Review linked accounts and skills</strong></td> <td>Third-party skills inherit access you granted once</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>The physical mute matters most.</strong> Software mute depends on the implementation being correct, and physical mute removes the microphone from the circuit.</p> <p><em>Consider whether the assistant needs to exist in bedrooms or rooms where you discuss sensitive matters. A microphone in a bedroom is a different risk from one in a kitchen.</em></p> <h2 id="wearables"> <a href="#wearables" title="Wearables">Wearables</a> <a href="#wearables" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Wearables">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>A wearable collects continuously</strong>, which distinguishes it from a phone in a pocket.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Data</th> <th>What It Reveals</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Heart rate</strong></td> <td>Sleep quality, stress response, and arousal</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Movement and steps</strong></td> <td>Routine, activity level, and often when you are home</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Sleep patterns</strong></td> <td>Bedtime and wake times, and disturbances</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Location</strong></td> <td>Journeys and stops, frequently at fine granularity</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Audio</strong></td> <td>Some devices record continuously for later processing</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>The privacy problem is not only the vendor. <strong>Health and lifestyle data is attractive to insurers, employers, and data brokers</strong>, and resale restrictions vary by jurisdiction.</p> <p><em>Our dedicated analysis of the trade-offs: <strong> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Privacy-First Smartwatch Options for Data-Savvy Users"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/articles/smartwatches-for-privacy-and-security-enthusiasts/"> <a href="/articles/smartwatches-for-privacy-and-security-enthusiasts/" rel="follow me" >Privacy-First Smartwatch Options for Data-Savvy Users</a> </span> </strong>.</em></p> <h2 id="what-should-never-connect"> <a href="#what-should-never-connect" title="What Should Never Connect">What Should Never Connect</a> <a href="#what-should-never-connect" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="What Should Never Connect">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Some functions do not belong on the internet at all.</strong></p> <ul> <li><strong>Life-safety systems.</strong> Smoke detectors, carbon monoxide alarms, and medical devices should not depend on a cloud service or a network connection</li> <li><strong>Access control for anything critical.</strong> A lock which fails open or fails unusable during an outage is worse than a mechanical alternative</li> <li><strong>Water and heating controls</strong> in a property you do not visit often, where a failure is expensive and remote</li> <li><strong>Anything in an outbuilding</strong> with unreliable connectivity, where offline behaviour matters</li> </ul> <p><strong>The test is the failure mode.</strong> Ask what happens when the internet is down, when the vendor shuts down, or when the account is locked. If the answer is unacceptable, the device belongs on a local-only path or nowhere.</p> <p><em>Many vendors have discontinued cloud services for products still in use. A device which depends entirely on the service becomes a paperweight, or worse, a lock you cannot open.</em></p> <script type="application/ld+json"> { "@context": "https://schema.org/", "@type": "ImageObject", "contentUrl": "https:\/\/simeononsecurity.com\/smart-home-iot-segmentation-and-data-flow.webp", "caption": "Diagram showing a home network with IoT devices isolated on a separate item.title: Personal Security Checklist 2026: Where to Start and What to Skip
item.category: "Personal Security" , "Privacy" , "Digital Hygiene" , "Account Security" , "Threat Modeling" , "Consumer Security" , "Password Management" , "Data Protection"
item.description: Most personal security advice is a flat list of 300 tips with no order. Here is the same advice ranked by real impact, with the five steps which stop most attacks and the common habits worth abandoning.
item.content:encoded: <p><strong>Every personal security guide hands you the same thing: a long flat list of hundreds of tips with no ranking.</strong> You are told to disable WebRTC, spoof your canvas fingerprint, and rotate your user agent, in the same breath as setting up a password manager and turning on auto-updates.</p> <p><em>Those items are not equally valuable, and treating them as equal is why so many people do the easy ones, skip the important ones, and remain exactly as exposed.</em></p> <p>This article keeps the topic and drops the false equivalence. The same advice, ordered by what removes the most risk for the least effort, plus an honest look at the habits worth abandoning.</p> <h2 id="the-short-answer"> <a href="#the-short-answer" title="The Short Answer">The Short Answer</a> <a href="#the-short-answer" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="The Short Answer">#</a> </h2> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Question</th> <th>Short Answer</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>What stops the most attacks?</strong></td> <td>A password manager, phishing-resistant second factors, and prompt updates. Three habits cover the majority of real-world account compromise</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>What is the single biggest upgrade available today?</strong></td> <td><strong>Passkeys or a hardware security key.</strong> Both defeat phishing entirely, because the credential never leaves your device</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>What is overrated?</strong></td> <td>Complex passwords you memorize, password rotation schedules, and most browser fingerprint tweaks</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>What is underrated?</strong></td> <td>Backups, account recovery setup, and physical security of your devices</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Does order matter?</strong></td> <td>Yes, and more than completeness. <strong>Tier 1 done today beats all 300 items done eventually</strong></td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>How long does Tier 1 take?</strong></td> <td>About two hours, once</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <h2 id="why-order-beats-completeness"> <a href="#why-order-beats-completeness" title="Why Order Beats Completeness">Why Order Beats Completeness</a> <a href="#why-order-beats-completeness" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Why Order Beats Completeness">#</a> </h2> <p>A comprehensive checklist typically catalogs several hundred entries and tags each one <strong>Essential</strong>, <strong>Optional</strong>, or <strong>Advanced</strong>. The tag is useful as a filter, and it is a poor substitute for a ranking, because every item carries the same label regardless of how much risk it removes.</p> <p><strong>My argument: even three tiers is not enough resolution</strong>, because “Essential” lumps together items with wildly different risk reduction. Compare two entries both marked Essential:</p> <ul> <li><strong>Enable 2FA</strong> removes an entire class of account takeover.</li> <li><strong>Disable WebRTC</strong> closes a local IP disclosure which matters to a small subset of users.</li> </ul> <p>Both belong on a complete list. Only one belongs in your first hour.</p> <p><strong>The correct ordering principle is a ratio.</strong> Rank every action by risk removed divided by effort required, then work top down. The ordering looks like this:</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Tier</th> <th>Purpose</th> <th>Effort</th> <th>Blocks</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>1. Stop the attack</strong></td> <td>Close the paths attackers use today</td> <td>~2 hours</td> <td>Credential theft, phishing, malware, device theft</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>2. Contain the damage</strong></td> <td>Limit blast radius when something fails</td> <td>~1 hour</td> <td>Single point of failure, account lockout, identity fraud</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>3. Reduce exposure</strong></td> <td>Shrink your data footprint</td> <td>Ongoing</td> <td>Profiling, tracking, targeted social engineering</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>4. Physical and human</strong></td> <td>Cover the layer software misses</td> <td>~30 minutes</td> <td>Device seizure, shoulder surfing, voice phishing</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><em>Work downward. Do not skip to Tier 3 because it is more interesting.</em> <script type="application/ld+json"> { "@context": "https://schema.org/", "@type": "ImageObject", "contentUrl": "https:\/\/simeononsecurity.com\/personal-security-tiers-ranked-by-impact.webp", "caption": "Diagram showing four tiers of personal security actions ranked by risk removed against effort required, from stopping attacks down to physical and human controls", "license": "https://simeononsecurity.com/termsandconditions/", "acquireLicensePage": "https://simeononsecurity.com/contactus/", "creditText": "SimeonOnSecurity", "creator": { "@type": "Person", "name": "SimeonOnSecurity" }, "copyrightNotice": "SimeonOnSecurity", "associatedArticle": { "@type": "NewsArticle", "headline": "simeononsecurity", "url": "https:\/\/simeononsecurity.com\/", "datePublished": "2026-10-02 21:20:37.633694495 \u002b0000 UTC m=\u002b337.358420257", "author": { "@type": "Person", "name": "SimeonOnSecurity", "url": "https:\/\/simeononsecurity.com\/authors\/simeononsecurity" } } } </script> <center> <figure align="center" style="text-align: center; margin: 0 auto;" itemscope itemtype="http://schema.org/ImageObject"> <meta property="article:published_time" content="2026-10-02 21:20:37.633694495 +0000 UTC m=+337.358420257"> <meta property="article:author" content="SimeonOnSecurity"> <meta property="article:author:url" content="https://simeononsecurity.com/authors/simeononsecurity"> <meta property="og:license" content="https://simeononsecurity.com/termsandconditions/"> <meta property="og:see_also" content="https://simeononsecurity.com/contactus/"> <meta property="og:copyright" content="SimeonOnSecurity"> <img align="center" style="text-align: center; margin: 0 auto; max-width: 80%; max-height: 600px; min-width: 100px; min-height: 100px; height: auto; width: auto;" src="https://simeononsecurity.com/personal-security-tiers-ranked-by-impact.webp" alt="Diagram showing four tiers of personal security actions ranked by risk removed against effort required, from stopping attacks down to physical and human controls"loading="lazy" fetchpriority="low" itemprop="contentUrl" /> </figure> </center> </p> <h2 id="tier-1-stop-the-attack"> <a href="#tier-1-stop-the-attack" title="Tier 1: Stop the Attack">Tier 1: Stop the Attack</a> <a href="#tier-1-stop-the-attack" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Tier 1: Stop the Attack">#</a> </h2> <p>Five items, roughly two hours total, and they address the paths attackers use.</p> <h3 id="1-a-password-manager-with-unique-passwords-everywhere"> <a href="#1-a-password-manager-with-unique-passwords-everywhere" title="1. A Password Manager, With Unique Passwords Everywhere">1. A Password Manager, With Unique Passwords Everywhere</a> <a href="#1-a-password-manager-with-unique-passwords-everywhere" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="1. A Password Manager, With Unique Passwords Everywhere">#</a> </h3> <p><strong>Credential stuffing is the dominant account takeover method</strong>, and it works because people reuse passwords. When one site leaks, attackers replay those credentials across every other site, automatically and at scale.</p> <p>A password manager fixes the root cause by making reuse impossible to do by accident. It generates a distinct high-entropy password per account and fills it for you.</p> <p>The important detail most advice omits: <strong>your manager password is now the single point of failure</strong>, so it needs to be long and memorized, and it is the one password you never store anywhere else. A multi-word passphrase of five or six random words is stronger than a short complex string and far easier to recall.</p> <p>Two legitimate architectures exist:</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Approach</th> <th>Strength</th> <th>Trade-off</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Cloud-synced</strong> (Bitwarden and similar)</td> <td>Convenient, syncs across devices, easy recovery</td> <td>You trust the vendor’s encryption and availability</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Offline file-based</strong> (KeePassXC and similar)</td> <td>Full control, no vendor dependency</td> <td>You own backup and synchronization</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><em>Pick either. The gap between them is far smaller than the gap between using a manager and not using one.</em></p> <p>See our full comparison in <strong> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Best Password Managers 2026: Bitwarden vs KeePassXC"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/articles/bitwarden-and-keepassxc-vs-the-rest/"> <a href="/articles/bitwarden-and-keepassxc-vs-the-rest/" rel="follow me" >Best Password Managers 2026: Bitwarden vs KeePassXC</a> </span> </strong> and the guide to <strong> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Creating Strong Passwords in 2026"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/articles/how-to-create-strong-passwords/"> <a href="/articles/how-to-create-strong-passwords/" rel="follow me" >Creating Strong Passwords in 2026</a> </span> </strong>.</p> <h3 id="2-phishing-resistant-second-factors"> <a href="#2-phishing-resistant-second-factors" title="2. Phishing-Resistant Second Factors">2. Phishing-Resistant Second Factors</a> <a href="#2-phishing-resistant-second-factors" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="2. Phishing-Resistant Second Factors">#</a> </h3> <p>Second factors are not interchangeable. They differ enormously in what they resist.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Method</th> <th>Stops Credential Stuffing</th> <th>Stops Phishing</th> <th>Stops Session Token Theft</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>SMS codes</strong></td> <td>Yes</td> <td>Partially, via SIM swap</td> <td>No</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Authenticator app codes</strong></td> <td>Yes</td> <td>Partially, via real-time relay</td> <td>No</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Push approval</strong></td> <td>Yes</td> <td>Weakly, via prompt bombing</td> <td>No</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Passkeys or hardware key</strong></td> <td>Yes</td> <td><strong>Yes</strong></td> <td>Yes</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>Passkeys and FIDO2 hardware keys are the only options on the list which defeat phishing.</strong> The reason is structural rather than incremental: the credential is bound to the origin, so a lookalike domain receives nothing usable. There is no code for a victim to read aloud to an attacker.</p> <p>A related threat deserves naming, because it defeats methods people assume are safe. <strong>Infostealer malware now harvests browser cookies directly</strong>, which lets an attacker reuse an authenticated session without ever needing your password or your second factor. This is why the final column matters, and it is also why <strong>Tier 1 item 3 is not optional</strong>.</p> <p><em>Priority order inside this item: passkeys where offered, hardware key for email and finance, authenticator app for everything else, SMS only where nothing better exists.</em></p> <script type="application/ld+json"> { "@context": "https://schema.org/", "@type": "ImageObject", "contentUrl": "https:\/\/simeononsecurity.com\/phishing-resistant-second-factor-comparison.webp", "caption": "Diagram comparing SMS codes, authenticator apps, push approval, and passkeys against credential stuffing, phishing, and session token theft, with passkeys defeating all three", "license": "https://simeononsecurity.com/termsandconditions/", "acquireLicensePage": "https://simeononsecurity.com/contactus/", "creditText": "SimeonOnSecurity", "creator": { "@type": "Person", "name": "SimeonOnSecurity" }, "copyrightNotice": "SimeonOnSecurity", "associatedArticle": { "@type": "NewsArticle", "headline": "simeononsecurity", "url": "https:\/\/simeononsecurity.com\/", "datePublished": "2026-10-02 21:20:37.634129385 \u002b0000 UTC m=\u002b337.358855130", "author": { "@type": "Person", "name": "SimeonOnSecurity", "url": "https:\/\/simeononsecurity.com\/authors\/simeononsecurity" } } } </script> <center> <figure align="center" style="text-align: center; margin: 0 auto;" itemscope itemtype="http://schema.org/ImageObject"> <meta property="article:published_time" content="2026-10-02 21:20:37.634129385 +0000 UTC m=+337.358855130"> <meta property="article:author" content="SimeonOnSecurity"> <meta property="article:author:url" content="https://simeononsecurity.com/authors/simeononsecurity"> <meta property="og:license" content="https://simeononsecurity.com/termsandconditions/"> <meta property="og:see_also" content="https://simeononsecurity.com/contactus/"> <meta property="og:copyright" content="SimeonOnSecurity"> <img align="center" style="text-align: center; margin: 0 auto; max-width: 80%; max-height: 600px; min-width: 100px; min-height: 100px; height: auto; width: auto;" src="https://simeononsecurity.com/phishing-resistant-second-factor-comparison.webp" alt="Diagram comparing SMS codes, authenticator apps, push approval, and passkeys against credential stuffing, phishing, and session token theft, with passkeys defeating all three"loading="lazy" fetchpriority="low" itemprop="contentUrl" /> </figure> </center> <p>Generate and verify time-based codes locally with our <strong> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="TOTP and HOTP Generator"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/totp-generator/"> <a href="/totp-generator/" rel="follow me" >TOTP and HOTP Generator</a> </span> </strong>, which reads a Base32 secret or an <code>otpauth://</code> URI and runs entirely in your browser.</p> <h3 id="3-automatic-updates-everywhere"> <a href="#3-automatic-updates-everywhere" title="3. Automatic Updates, Everywhere">3. Automatic Updates, Everywhere</a> <a href="#3-automatic-updates-everywhere" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="3. Automatic Updates, Everywhere">#</a> </h3> <p><strong>Most successful intrusions exploit a vulnerability for which a patch already exists.</strong> Update lag is the gap attackers live in.</p> <p>The practical move is not to become diligent about updating. It is to remove the decision entirely by enabling automatic updates on every layer:</p> <ul> <li><strong>Operating system</strong>: Windows Update, macOS Software Update, or unattended-upgrades on Linux</li> <li><strong>Browsers</strong>: leave auto-update enabled and restart when prompted, since a pending restart means a pending unpatched browser</li> <li><strong>Phone</strong>: enable automatic app updates, not only OS updates</li> <li><strong>Router</strong>: this is the layer people forget, and it is externally reachable</li> </ul> <p><strong>A browser sitting on a restart prompt is running vulnerable code.</strong> This single habit closes more exposure than most Tier 3 items combined.</p> <p><em>Our kernel-escape analysis in <strong> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Containers Are No Longer a Security Boundary"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/articles/containers-no-longer-security-boundary-2026/"> <a href="/articles/containers-no-longer-security-boundary-2026/" rel="follow me" >Containers Are No Longer a Security Boundary</a> </span> </strong> shows how quickly the patch window matters when a privilege escalation is involved.</em></p> <h3 id="4-device-encryption-and-a-real-lock-screen"> <a href="#4-device-encryption-and-a-real-lock-screen" title="4. Device Encryption and a Real Lock Screen">4. Device Encryption and a Real Lock Screen</a> <a href="#4-device-encryption-and-a-real-lock-screen" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="4. Device Encryption and a Real Lock Screen">#</a> </h3> <p><strong>Full-disk encryption converts a stolen device from a data breach into a hardware loss.</strong> Without it, anyone holding your laptop or phone reads everything on it, including your password manager vault and your active session tokens.</p> <p>Every mainstream platform offers it, and on some it is not enabled by default:</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Platform</th> <th>Feature</th> <th>Check</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Windows</strong></td> <td>BitLocker or Device Encryption</td> <td>Settings, then Privacy and Security, then Device encryption</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>macOS</strong></td> <td>FileVault</td> <td>System Settings, then Privacy and Security, then FileVault</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Linux</strong></td> <td>LUKS</td> <td>Confirm the root and home volumes are encrypted at install</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>iOS and Android</strong></td> <td>On by default once a passcode is set</td> <td>Set a passcode, then confirm encryption is active</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>Two rules matter alongside encryption:</p> <ul> <li><strong>Use a passphrase or long PIN, not a four-digit code.</strong> Email and finance accounts deserve your strongest phone lock, because the passcode gates everything else on the device.</li> <li><strong>Prefer a PIN to biometrics if you face legal or coercion risk.</strong> Biometrics are convenient and hard to forget, and in some jurisdictions compelled fingerprints or faces carry different protections than compelled knowledge.</li> </ul> <h3 id="5-backups-tested-once"> <a href="#5-backups-tested-once" title="5. Backups, Tested Once">5. Backups, Tested Once</a> <a href="#5-backups-tested-once" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="5. Backups, Tested Once">#</a> </h3> <p><strong>Ransomware and hardware failure both end with the same outcome, and a backup is the only control which survives either.</strong> This is the item people most often skip, and the one they most regret skipping.</p> <p>The standard shape is <strong>3-2-1</strong>: three copies, on two media types, with one offsite. For an individual, the shape becomes:</p> <ul> <li><strong>One local copy</strong> for fast recovery</li> <li><strong>One encrypted offsite copy</strong> for ransomware and fire</li> <li><strong>One offline or write-only copy</strong> for the case where ransomware reaches your synced storage</li> </ul> <p><em>The last point matters most and gets implemented least. Synchronized storage is not a backup. Ransomware and accidental deletion replicate.</em></p> <p><strong>Test a restore at least once.</strong> A backup never restored is a hypothesis.</p> <h2 id="tier-2-contain-the-damage"> <a href="#tier-2-contain-the-damage" title="Tier 2: Contain the Damage">Tier 2: Contain the Damage</a> <a href="#tier-2-contain-the-damage" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Tier 2: Contain the Damage">#</a> </h2> <p>Tier 1 assumes nothing fails. Tier 2 assumes something will, and limits the consequences.</p> <h3 id="6-stop-reusing-your-email-address"> <a href="#6-stop-reusing-your-email-address" title="6. Stop Reusing Your Email Address">6. Stop Reusing Your Email Address</a> <a href="#6-stop-reusing-your-email-address" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="6. Stop Reusing Your Email Address">#</a> </h3> <p><strong>Your email address is the join key between every database which has ever leaked.</strong> Using one address everywhere means one breach correlates with all your others, and it hands social engineers a verified starting point.</p> <p><strong>Aliasing solves both problems.</strong> Generate a unique address per service, and the address itself becomes a label:</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Benefit</th> <th>Why It Matters</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Breach attribution</strong></td> <td>When spam arrives at one alias, you learn which service leaked or sold your address</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Instant blocking</strong></td> <td>Disable a single alias without touching your real inbox</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Correlation resistance</strong></td> <td>Different addresses prevent linking your accounts into one profile</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Phishing detection</strong></td> <td>Mail to an alias no longer in use is obviously fraudulent</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>Subaddressing</strong> (<code>you+service@example.com</code>) is a weaker version. It tracks who leaked your address, and it exposes your real address in the process, so it offers no correlation resistance.</p> <p><em>If you own a domain, catch-all aliasing gives you this for free. Otherwise, dedicated alias providers do the same job.</em></p> <h3 id="7-account-recovery-is-the-real-attack-surface"> <a href="#7-account-recovery-is-the-real-attack-surface" title="7. Account Recovery Is the Real Attack Surface">7. Account Recovery Is the Real Attack Surface</a> <a href="#7-account-recovery-is-the-real-attack-surface" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="7. Account Recovery Is the Real Attack Surface">#</a> </h3> <p><strong>Attackers increasingly skip the front door and target recovery instead.</strong> Recovery must be able to survive a lost device, and it must not become the weakest link.</p> <p>Configure these, in order:</p> <ul> <li><strong>Save backup codes offline.</strong> Print them or store them on encrypted media, and keep them <strong>separate from your password manager</strong>, since a compromise of one should not hand over the other.</li> <li><strong>Prefer recovery keys to security questions.</strong> Answers to questions about your mother’s maiden name or first car are frequently public record.</li> <li><strong>Use false answers if a site forces questions.</strong> Store them in your manager alongside the account.</li> <li><strong>Register a second device or key</strong> where the service allows it, so one failure is not a lockout.</li> <li><strong>Remove stale recovery contacts and phone numbers</strong>, because an old number is now someone else’s.</li> </ul> <blockquote> <p><strong>Warning: losing your second factor without recovery codes frequently means permanent account loss, and support teams will not restore access to a properly secured account.</strong> Set recovery up at the same time you enable the second factor.</p> </blockquote> <script type="application/ld+json"> { from ransomware and accidental deletion"loading="lazy" fetchpriority="low" itemprop="contentUrl" /> </figure> </center> <h3 id="8-breach-monitoring-which-tells-you-early"> <a href="#8-breach-monitoring-which-tells-you-early" title="8. Breach Monitoring Which Tells You Early">8. Breach Monitoring Which Tells You Early</a> <a href="#8-breach-monitoring-which-tells-you-early" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="8. Breach Monitoring Which Tells You Early">#</a> </h3> <p><strong>The value of a breach notification is entirely about timing.</strong> You want to learn about a leak while the password is still valid somewhere.</p> <ul> <li><strong>Have I Been Pwned</strong> sends alerts when your address appears in a new dataset, and offers domain-wide notification if you own a domain and use aliases.</li> <li><strong>Your password manager is the better signal</strong>, because it knows which vault entries correspond to a notified service and flags them directly.</li> </ul> <p><em>The useful workflow is short: alert arrives, change the password for the affected account, and change it anywhere the old one was reused. This is the payoff for Tier 1 item 1, since unique passwords reduce the second step to nothing.</em></p> <h3 id="9-credit-freeze-before-you-need-it"> <a href="#9-credit-freeze-before-you-need-it" title="9. Credit Freeze Before You Need It">9. Credit Freeze Before You Need It</a> <a href="#9-credit-freeze-before-you-need-it" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="9. Credit Freeze Before You Need It">#</a> </h3> <p><strong>A credit freeze is the strongest available defense against new-account identity fraud</strong>, and it costs nothing. It blocks lenders from pulling your file to open accounts in your name.</p> <p>In the United States, freezing is available at each of the three major bureaus, and unfreezing for a legitimate application is temporary and reversible. The sequence is:</p> <ol> <li><strong>Freeze at all three bureaus</strong>, not one. Each holds a separate file.</li> <li><strong>Store the unfreeze PINs</strong> in your password manager.</li> <li><strong>Unfreeze temporarily</strong> when applying for credit, then re-freeze.</li> </ol> <p><em>Do this before you need it. Discovering the process mid-fraud, while also disputing accounts, is the worst possible time to learn it.</em></p> <h2 id="tier-3-reduce-exposure"> <a href="#tier-3-reduce-exposure" title="Tier 3: Reduce Exposure">Tier 3: Reduce Exposure</a> <a href="#tier-3-reduce-exposure" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Tier 3: Reduce Exposure">#</a> </h2> <p>Tier 3 is about shrinking your data footprint. It matters, and it sits below the items above because it does not block account takeover.</p> <h3 id="10-harden-the-browser-you-use"> <a href="#10-harden-the-browser-you-use" title="10. Harden the Browser You Use">10. Harden the Browser You Use</a> <a href="#10-harden-the-browser-you-use" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="10. Harden the Browser You Use">#</a> </h3> <p><strong>The browser is where most personal data exposure happens</strong>, and two changes cover most of it:</p> <ul> <li><strong>Install a content blocker.</strong> Ads and trackers are the primary collection mechanism on the web, and blocking them removes both the tracking and a substantial attack surface. Choose one reputable blocker rather than several.</li> <li><strong>Cut extensions to what you use.</strong> <strong>Extensions read and modify page content</strong>, which makes an abandoned or malicious extension a direct path to your sessions. Review the list quarterly.</li> </ul> <p><em>Browser fingerprint randomization is worth understanding and is rarely worth prioritizing. It is not zero value. It is simply low yield compared to items 1 through 5, and it breaks sites.</em></p> <p>See the full breakdown in <strong> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Best Privacy Browsers 2026: LibreWolf vs Brave vs Tor"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/articles/best-privacy-browsers-librewolf-brave-firefox-tor/"> <a href="/articles/best-privacy-browsers-librewolf-brave-firefox-tor/" rel="follow me" >Best Privacy Browsers 2026: LibreWolf vs Brave vs Tor</a> </span> </strong>.</p> <h3 id="11-encrypt-your-dns"> <a href="#11-encrypt-your-dns" title="11. Encrypt Your DNS">11. Encrypt Your DNS</a> <a href="#11-encrypt-your-dns" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="11. Encrypt Your DNS">#</a> </h3> <p><strong>Plain DNS is unencrypted and observable, which lets your network operator and anyone in the path see every domain you resolve.</strong> DNS-over-HTTPS or DNS-over-TLS encrypts the lookup.</p> <p>Two honest caveats:</p> <ul> <li><strong>DoH moves trust rather than removing it.</strong> Your resolver now sees your queries instead of your ISP. Choosing a resolver with a published privacy policy is the point, not the protocol alone.</li> <li><strong>DoH bypasses network-level filtering</strong>, including the parental and corporate controls many people rely on.</li> </ul> <p><em>One genuine security benefit beyond privacy: encrypted DNS removes DNS spoofing as a practical attack path on hostile networks.</em></p> <h3 id="12-strip-metadata-before-you-share"> <a href="#12-strip-metadata-before-you-share" title="12. Strip Metadata Before You Share">12. Strip Metadata Before You Share</a> <a href="#12-strip-metadata-before-you-share" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="12. Strip Metadata Before You Share">#</a> </h3> <p><strong>Photos carry more than pixels.</strong> Most phone cameras embed EXIF data including GPS coordinates, timestamps, and device identifiers.</p> <p><strong>This matters more for documents than for photos.</strong> A shared PDF or office file often retains author names, edit history, and internal file paths, which is how internal documents leak organizational detail.</p> <p>Our <strong> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="EXIF Viewer"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/exif-viewer/"> <a href="/exif-viewer/" rel="follow me" >EXIF Viewer</a> </span> </strong> reads metadata from an image locally, so you see what a photo exposes without uploading it. <strong> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="URL Parser"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/url-parser/"> <a href="/url-parser/" rel="follow me" >URL Parser</a> </span> </strong> does the equivalent for links, surfacing tracking parameters and credentials embedded in the authority before you paste a URL into a chat.</p> <h2 id="tier-4-physical-and-human"> <a href="#tier-4-physical-and-human" title="Tier 4: Physical and Human">Tier 4: Physical and Human</a> <a href="#tier-4-physical-and-human" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Tier 4: Physical and Human">#</a> </h2> <p>This tier takes about thirty minutes and covers what no software control reaches.</p> <h3 id="13-physical-control-of-your-devices"> <a href="#13-physical-control-of-your-devices" title="13. Physical Control of Your Devices">13. Physical Control of Your Devices</a> <a href="#13-physical-control-of-your-devices" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="13. Physical Control of Your Devices">#</a> </h3> <ul> <li><strong>Lock screens everywhere</strong>, with a short timeout. An unlocked laptop is a full account compromise.</li> <li><strong>Never leave devices visible in a vehicle.</strong> This is a theft prevention item, and theft is a data loss item.</li> <li><strong>Carry a privacy screen</strong> in public spaces, which defeats most shoulder surfing.</li> <li><strong>Inspect public charging</strong> before plugging in. Prefer a power-only cable or your own wall adapter over an unknown USB port.</li> </ul> <h3 id="14-verify-people-not-messages"> <a href="#14-verify-people-not-messages" title="14. Verify People, Not Messages">14. Verify People, Not Messages</a> <a href="#14-verify-people-not-messages" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="14. Verify People, Not Messages">#</a> </h3> <p><strong>Voice and video phishing now defeats the assumption a familiar voice proves identity.</strong> Cloned voices from a few seconds of public audio are routine, and the request usually carries urgency and a payment or credential ask.</p> <p>The countermeasure is out of band:</p> <ol> <li><strong>Hang up and call back</strong> on a number you already had, not one supplied by the caller.</li> <li><strong>Treat urgency as a signal, not a reason.</strong> Pressure to act immediately is the mechanism, not a side detail.</li> <li><strong>Agree a verification phrase</strong> with family members who might be impersonated.</li> <li><strong>Never move money on the strength of a voice call or message alone.</strong></li> </ol> <p><em>This is the highest-yield item in Tier 4 and it costs nothing.</em></p> <h3 id="15-documents-and-disposal"> <a href="#15-documents-and-disposal" title="15. Documents and Disposal">15. Documents and Disposal</a> <a href="#15-documents-and-disposal" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="15. Documents and Disposal">#</a> </h3> <ul> <li><strong>Shred or redact</strong> documents carrying account numbers, identity numbers, or medical detail.</li> <li><strong>Watermark documents</strong> shared for a specific purpose, with the recipient and date. It costs nothing and traces a leak.</li> <li><strong>Opt out of people-search sites</strong>, and expect to repeat the process, because listings reappear.</li> <li><strong>Review public records</strong> and request removal where possible.</li> </ul> <p><em>Our <strong> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Physical Security Checklist"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/checklists/physical-security-checklist/"> <a href="/checklists/physical-security-checklist/" rel="follow me" >Physical Security Checklist</a> </span> </strong> covers this layer in more depth.</em></p> <h2 id="what-most-people-get-backwards"> <a href="#what-most-people-get-backwards" title="What Most People Get Backwards">What Most People Get Backwards</a> <a href="#what-most-people-get-backwards" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="What Most People Get Backwards">#</a> </h2> <p>Eight habits worth abandoning, each with the reason it persists and what to do instead.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Habit</th> <th>Why It Persists</th> <th>Do This Instead</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Memorizing short complex passwords</strong></td> <td>Complexity rules were the guidance for years</td> <td>Use a manager and a long passphrase for the vault</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Rotating passwords on a schedule</strong></td> <td>Legacy compliance policy</td> <td>Change on breach notification or suspected compromise, not on a calendar</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Relying on SMS for critical accounts</strong></td> <td>It is the default offered</td> <td>Move email, finance, and identity accounts to passkeys or a hardware key</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Storing 2FA codes in the same manager as passwords</strong></td> <td>Convenience</td> <td>Separate the two, so one compromise does not yield both factors</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Treating synced cloud storage as a backup</strong></td> <td>It looks like one</td> <td>Add an offline or write-only copy</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Chasing browser fingerprint perfection</strong></td> <td>It is measurable, so it feels actionable</td> <td>Do items 1 through 5 first</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Answering security questions honestly</strong></td> <td>It feels required</td> <td>Use false answers stored in your manager</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Assuming HTTPS means safe</strong></td> <td>The padlock is reassuring</td> <td>Verify the domain, since most phishing sites hold valid certificates</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>The pattern across all eight: <strong>each one is visible and measurable, which is why it attracts attention, and each one sits below a higher-yield item.</strong> Anyone optimizing fingerprint entropy before setting up a password manager has the ordering inverted.</p> <blockquote> <p><strong>Common Mistake: treating password managers as a risk because they concentrate secrets.</strong> They do concentrate risk, and the alternative is password reuse across dozens of sites. Concentration you control beats dispersion you do not.</p> </blockquote> <h2 id="do-it-without-handing-over-your-data"> <a href="#do-it-without-handing-over-your-data" title="Do It Without Handing Over Your Data">Do It Without Handing Over Your Data</a> <a href="#do-it-without-handing-over-your-data" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Do It Without Handing Over Your Data">#</a> </h2> <p>A practical problem runs through this whole topic. <strong>The tools which help you secure your accounts often ask for the same secrets you are trying to protect.</strong></p> <p>A password strength checker which posts your password to a server is a liability. A hash calculator which uploads the file defeats the purpose. A certificate tool which fetches your hostname tells a third party which sites you operate.</p> <p><strong>Every tool below runs entirely in your browser</strong>, with no upload and no account. This is a stated policy on this site, and the exceptions are named openly rather than buried.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Task</th> <th>Tool</th> <th>What It Handles</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Create a strong password</strong></td> <td><strong> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Password Generator"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/password-generator/"> <a href="/password-generator/" rel="follow me" >Password Generator</a> </span> </strong></td> <td><code>crypto.getRandomValues</code> with rejection sampling to avoid modulo bias, plus the entropy of your chosen settings</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Check a password’s strength</strong></td> <td><strong> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Password Strength Checker"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/password-checker/"> <a href="/password-checker/" rel="follow me" >Password Strength Checker</a> </span> </strong></td> <td>Scores a candidate locally, including pattern and reuse detection</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Set up a second factor</strong></td> <td><strong> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="TOTP and HOTP Generator"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/totp-generator/"> <a href="/totp-generator/" rel="follow me" >TOTP and HOTP Generator</a> </span> </strong></td> <td>Reads a Base32 secret or <code>otpauth://</code> URI, verifies codes across time windows</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Inspect a site’s certificate</strong></td> <td><strong> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="SSL Certificate Information"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/ssl-certificate-info/"> <a href="/ssl-certificate-info/" rel="follow me" >SSL Certificate Information</a> </span> </strong></td> <td>Subject, validity, key strength, SANs, and weak-algorithm flags</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Check a certificate chain</strong></td> <td><strong> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="SSL Chain Tester"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/ssl-chain-tester/"> <a href="/ssl-chain-tester/" rel="follow me" >SSL Chain Tester</a> </span> </strong></td> <td>Orders the chain and verifies every signature, catching missing intermediates</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Verify a download or file</strong></td> <td><strong> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Hash Calculator"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/hash-calculator/"> <a href="/hash-calculator/" rel="follow me" >Hash Calculator</a> </span> </strong></td> <td>MD5 through SHA-512 to confirm integrity against a published digest</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Generate unique identifiers</strong></td> <td><strong> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="UUID Generator"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/uuid-generator/"> <a href="/uuid-generator/" rel="follow me" >UUID Generator</a> </span> </strong></td> <td>Version 4 identifiers with correct version and variant bits</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Inspect a suspicious link</strong></td> <td><strong> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="URL Parser"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/url-parser/"> <a href="/url-parser/" rel="follow me" >URL Parser</a> </span> </strong></td> <td>Decodes the path, lists parameters, and flags credentials in the authority</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Check photo metadata</strong></td> <td><strong> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="EXIF Viewer"> <meta itemprop="url" <td><strong>Measure encoding or encryption</strong></td> <td><strong> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Entropy Analyzer"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/entropy-analyzer/"> <a href="/entropy-analyzer/" rel="follow me" >Entropy Analyzer</a> </span> </strong></td> <td>Shannon entropy to distinguish repetitive data from encoded or encrypted content</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Neutralize an indicator safely</strong></td> <td><strong> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="IOC Defang and Refang"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/ioc-defang-refang/"> <a href="/ioc-defang-refang/" rel="follow me" >IOC Defang and Refang</a> </span> </strong></td> <td>Defangs URLs and addresses so they are inert when shared</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><em>The principle behind the table: if a tool needs the secret, the tool should run where the secret lives. See <strong> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="All Tools"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/tools/"> <a href="/tools/" rel="follow me" >All Tools</a> </span> </strong> for the complete set, including which few make network requests and why.</em></p> <h2 id="the-threat-model-question"> <a href="#the-threat-model-question" title="The Threat Model Question">The Threat Model Question</a> <a href="#the-threat-model-question" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="The Threat Model Question">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>The correct checklist depends on who you are defending against</strong>, and skipping this question produces effort in the wrong places.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Your Situation</th> <th>Realistic Adversary</th> <th>Where to Focus</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Most individuals</strong></td> <td>Opportunistic criminals, automated credential stuffing, indiscriminate phishing</td> <td>Tiers 1 and 2, plus devices you carry</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>High-profile or public role</strong></td> <td>Targeted phishing, doxxing, account takeover attempts</td> <td>Add compartmentalization, aliasing, and consider a monitored social footprint</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Journalist, activist, or legal risk</strong></td> <td>State or well-resourced adversaries, device seizure</td> <td>Add Tor, dedicated devices, and operational discipline around identity separation</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Small business owner</strong></td> <td>Business email compromise, invoice fraud, payment redirection</td> <td>Add out-of-band payment verification for every transfer</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Technical professional</strong></td> <td>Supply chain, credential theft, targeting through dependencies</td> <td>Add hardware keys, code-signing practices, and separation of work and personal identity</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>The honest reading of the table.</strong> For most people, the majority of realistic risk sits in Tiers 1 and 2. The advanced items matter enormously for the people who need them, and they are frequently adopted by people who do not.</p> <p><em>Our <strong> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="How to Form Your Own Personal Threat Model"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/articles/how-to-form-your-own-personal-threat-model-safeguard-online-security/"> <a href="/articles/how-to-form-your-own-personal-threat-model-safeguard-online-security/" rel="follow me" >How to Form Your Own Personal Threat Model</a> </span> </strong> walks through building this assessment for yourself.</em></p> <h2 id="key-takeaways"> <a href="#key-takeaways" title="Key Takeaways">Key Takeaways</a> <a href="#key-takeaways" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Key Takeaways">#</a> </h2> <ul> <li><strong>Order beats completeness.</strong> Five items in Tier 1 remove more realistic risk than all 300 items on a comprehensive list performed randomly.</li> <li><strong>Passkeys and hardware keys are the only second factors which defeat phishing</strong>, because the credential is bound to the origin and never leaves your device.</li> <li><strong>Infostealer malware harvests session cookies directly</strong>, so session token theft is why the weakest second factor is not enough on its own.</li> <li><strong>Encryption turns a stolen device into a hardware loss</strong> instead of a data breach. Confirm it is enabled, because it is not universal by default.</li> <li><strong>Synchronized storage is not a backup.</strong> Add an offline or write-only copy, and test a restore once.</li> <li><strong>Account recovery is the new attack surface.</strong> Save backup codes offline and separate from your password manager.</li> <li><strong>Aliasing breaks the correlation</strong> between every leaked database which holds your address.</li> <li><strong>Most advice you see optimized is low yield.</strong> Fingerprint tweaks and user-agent spoofing sit far below a password manager and automatic updates.</li> <li><strong>The right checklist depends on your adversary.</strong> Advanced items matter enormously for the people who need them, and they are often adopted by people who do not.</li> </ul> <h2 id="next-steps"> <a href="#next-steps" title="Next Steps">Next Steps</a> <a href="#next-steps" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Next Steps">#</a> </h2> <ol> <li><strong>Do Tier 1 today</strong>, which takes about two hours: a password manager, a phishing-resistant second factor, automatic updates, device encryption, and one tested backup.</li>
