item.title: Personal Security Course
item.category: "Personal Security" , "Privacy" , "Digital Hygiene" , "Account Security" , "Consumer Security" , "Threat Modeling" , "Data Protection"
item.description: A twelve module course covering the security and privacy of one person rather than one organization. Each module moves from definitions to comparisons, decisions, and a record you create for yourself.
item.content:encoded: <p><strong>This course treats the individual as the asset.</strong> This is the opposite of most security training, which teaches you to defend an organization and then assumes your personal life works the same way.</p> <p>The difference matters. You do not have a security team, a managed detection service, or a compliance officer. You have a limited amount of time and a threat model shaped by who you are. <strong>The course is built around the constraint.</strong></p> <p><em>Every module ends with something you produce: a decision, a configuration, or a record. Reading without acting teaches nothing.</em></p> <h2 id="what-you-will-learn"> <a href="#what-you-will-learn" title="What You Will Learn">What You Will Learn</a> <a href="#what-you-will-learn" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="What You Will Learn">#</a> </h2> <p>The course runs in a fixed order, from account credentials up to the physical layer. Each module builds on the previous one, and the ordering is deliberate rather than alphabetical.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Module</th> <th>Focus</th> <th>Reader outcome</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>1. Authentication</strong></td> <td>Credentials and second factors</td> <td>Choose a vault architecture and a phishing-resistant factor</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>2. Web Browsing</strong></td> <td>Tracking and browser exposure</td> <td>Harden one browser and understand what remains</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>3. Email</strong></td> <td>The recovery gateway</td> <td>Separate addresses and control remote content</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>4. Messaging</strong></td> <td>Conversation privacy</td> <td>Evaluate a messenger against real criteria</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>5. Social Media</strong></td> <td>Public exposure</td> <td>Reduce what your profile reveals</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>6. Networks</strong></td> <td>Traffic and routing</td> <td>Configure a router and judge a VPN claim</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>7. Mobile Devices</strong></td> <td>Sensors and tracking</td> <td>Cut permissions and background collection</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>8. Personal Computers</strong></td> <td>The operating system</td> <td>Enable encryption, updates, and least privilege</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>9. Smart Home</strong></td> <td>Microphones and cameras</td> <td>Decide what earns a place on your network</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>10. Personal Finance</strong></td> <td>Money and identity</td> <td>Freeze credit and limit card exposure</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>11. Human Aspect</strong></td> <td>Social engineering</td> <td>Build verification habits which survive pressure</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>12. Physical Security</strong></td> <td>The world outside the screen</td> <td>Reduce public exposure and device seizure risk</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <h2 id="how-this-course-differs-from-a-compliance-checklist"> <a href="#how-this-course-differs-from-a-compliance-checklist" title="How This Course Differs From a Compliance Checklist">How This Course Differs From a Compliance Checklist</a> <a href="#how-this-course-differs-from-a-compliance-checklist" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="How This Course Differs From a Compliance Checklist">#</a> </h2> <p>A compliance checklist asks whether a control exists. <strong>This course asks whether a control changes your outcome</strong>, which is a different question with a different answer.</p> <p>Three commitments shape every module:</p> <ul> <li><strong>Priority is explicit.</strong> Items carry an impact ranking, so you know what to do first when time is short.</li> <li><strong>Trade-offs are named.</strong> Every recommendation carries its cost, because advice without cost is marketing.</li> <li><strong>Tools are optional.</strong> Where a client-side tool helps, the module links one. None require an account or an upload.</li> </ul> <p><em>The most commonly skipped item across all twelve modules is the backup. The most commonly over-prioritized is browser fingerprint randomization. Both are corrected in the modules where they appear.</em></p> <h2 id="the-modules"> <a href="#the-modules" title="The Modules">The Modules</a> <a href="#the-modules" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="The Modules">#</a> </h2> <h3 id="part-one-accounts-and-identity"> <a href="#part-one-accounts-and-identity" title="Part One: Accounts and Identity">Part One: Accounts and Identity</a> <a href="#part-one-accounts-and-identity" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Part One: Accounts and Identity">#</a> </h3> <ul> <li> <h4 id="module-1-authentication-and-credentials"> <a href="#module-1-authentication-and-credentials" title=" Module 1: Authentication and Credentials "> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Module 1: Authentication and Credentials"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/personal-security-course/authentication/"> <a href="/personal-security-course/authentication/" rel="follow me" >Module 1: Authentication and Credentials</a> </span> </a> <a href="#module-1-authentication-and-credentials" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title=" Module 1: Authentication and Credentials ">#</a> </h4> </li> <li> <h4 id="module-2-web-browsing-and-tracking"> <a href="#module-2-web-browsing-and-tracking" title=" Module item.title: Containers Are No Longer a Security Boundary: Kernel Escapes in 2026
item.description: AI-driven kernel bug hunting produced four new local privilege escalation families in 2026, all of which escape containers. Here is how they work, why patching is losing ground, and where microVMs fit.
item.content:encoded: <p><strong>Containers share one kernel, and in 2026 four separate vulnerability families proved a single kernel bug is enough to walk out of a container and onto the host.</strong> Copy Fail, Dirty Frag, Fragnesia, and CVE-2026-80521 each grant root to an unprivileged local user, and every one of them crosses the container boundary.</p> <p><em>The uncomfortable part is not the bugs themselves. It is how cheaply AI now finds them, and how one patch created another.</em></p> <p>This article explains how containers isolate workloads, why the isolation now rests on a shrinking foundation, what each 2026 vulnerability does, and which isolation technology is worth trusting instead.</p> <h2 id="the-short-answer"> <a href="#the-short-answer" title="The Short Answer">The Short Answer</a> <a href="#the-short-answer" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="The Short Answer">#</a> </h2> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Question</th> <th>Short Answer</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Do containers isolate?</strong></td> <td>Yes, for process and filesystem separation. All containers share one kernel, so kernel bugs are a shared risk</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Why now?</strong></td> <td>AI-assisted bug hunting collapsed the cost of finding kernel flaws. Nearly <strong>6,000 kernel CVEs</strong> are published as of September 2026</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>What breaks the boundary?</strong></td> <td>Any local privilege escalation in the kernel. Escaping needs no container misconfiguration</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Is patching enough?</strong></td> <td>It is necessary and it is losing the race. One 2026 patch <strong>introduced a new exploitable bug</strong></td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>What works better?</strong></td> <td>MicroVMs such as Firecracker or Kata Containers, which give each workload its own kernel</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Is the alternative perfect?</strong></td> <td>No. The hypervisor is code too. The attack surface is orders of magnitude smaller, and the difference is the point</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <h2 id="how-containers-isolate"> <a href="#how-containers-isolate" title="How Containers Isolate">How Containers Isolate</a> <a href="#how-containers-isolate" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="How Containers Isolate">#</a> </h2> <p>Understanding the boundary starts with understanding what a container is not.</p> <p><strong>A container is not a virtual machine.</strong> There is no second kernel, no emulated hardware, and no hypervisor between your process and the metal. When you run a container image, you are running a process on your existing kernel with a modified view of the system.</p> <p>The mechanism is the <strong><code>clone</code> syscall</strong>. Where <code>fork</code> copies a process address space, <code>clone</code> creates a child process while giving the caller precise control over which pieces of execution context get shared and which get replaced. Docker passes <code>clone</code> a set of <strong>namespaces</strong>:</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Namespace</th> <th>What It Fakes</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Mount</strong></td> <td>A private filesystem root, so the container sees its own tree instead of yours</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>PID</strong></td> <td>Its own process numbering, so <code>PID 1</code> is the container’s first process, not <code>systemd</code></td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>User</strong></td> <td>An identity mapping where container “root” maps to an unprivileged host user</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Network</strong></td> <td>Private interfaces, routing tables, and ports</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>IPC</strong></td> <td>Isolated shared memory and message queues</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>UTS</strong></td> <td>Its own hostname and domain name</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Cgroup</strong></td> <td>A private view of resource limits</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>Add a <strong>union filesystem</strong> layered over an image, and the result <em>feels</em> like a separate computer. <code>id</code> inside the container reports <code>uid=0(root)</code>. The filesystem looks like a minimal Ubuntu. A process listing shows only its own processes.</p> <p><strong>None of this is a security boundary at the syscall level.</strong> When a process inside the container opens a file, allocates memory, or touches a network socket, the same kernel handles the request for every other container on the host. Namespaces change <em>what the process sees</em>, not <em>what the kernel will do for it</em>.</p> <p><em>The kernel is the real boundary between container and host. Everything else is presentation.</em></p> <script type="application/ld+json"> { "@context": "https://schema.org/", "@type": "ImageObject", "contentUrl": "https:\/\/simeononsecurity.com\/container-namespace-isolation-shared-kernel.webp", "caption": "Diagram showing three containers built from the same kernel, with mount, PID, user, and network namespaces separating their views while all syscalls still route to one shared kernel underneath", "license": "https://simeononsecurity.com/termsandconditions/", "acquireLicensePage": "https://simeononsecurity.com/contactus/", "creditText": "SimeonOnSecurity", "creator": { "@type": "Person", "name": "SimeonOnSecurity" }, "copyrightNotice": "SimeonOnSecurity", "associatedArticle": { "@type": "NewsArticle", "headline": "simeononsecurity", "url": "https:\/\/simeononsecurity.com\/", "datePublished": "2026-10-02 21:20:37.650637429 \u002b0000 UTC m=\u002b337.375363174", "author": { "@type": "Person", "name": "SimeonOnSecurity", "url": "https:\/\/simeononsecurity.com\/authors\/simeononsecurity" } } } </script> <center> <figure align="center" style="text-align: center; margin: 0 auto;" itemscope itemtype="http://schema.org/ImageObject"> <meta property="article:published_time" content="2026-10-02 21:20:37.650637429 +0000 UTC m=+337.375363174"> <meta property="article:author" content="SimeonOnSecurity"> <meta property="article:author:url" content="https://simeononsecurity.com/authors/simeononsecurity"> <meta property="og:license" content="https://simeononsecurity.com/termsandconditions/"> <meta property="og:see_also" content="https://simeononsecurity.com/contactus/"> <meta property="og:copyright" content="SimeonOnSecurity"> <img align="center" style="text-align: center; margin: 0 auto; max-width: 80%; max-height: 600px; min-width: 100px; min-height: 100px; height: auto; width: auto;" src="https://simeononsecurity.com/container-namespace-isolation-shared-kernel.webp" alt="Diagram showing three containers built from the same kernel, with mount, PID, user, and network namespaces separating their views while all syscalls still route to one shared kernel underneath"loading="lazy" fetchpriority="low" itemprop="contentUrl" /> </figure> </center> <script> function loadLiteYouTubeScript() { if (document.querySelector('script[src^="/p/jsdelivr/npm/@justinribeiro/lite-youtube@1.5.0/lite-youtube.js"]')) { console.log('Lite YouTube script is already loaded.'); return; } var scriptTag = document.createElement('script'); scriptTag.src = '/p/jsdelivr/npm/@justinribeiro/lite-youtube@1.5.0/lite-youtube.js'; scriptTag.setAttribute('defer', ''); scriptTag.setAttribute('type', 'module'); scriptTag.setAttribute('fetchpriority', 'low'); document.body.appendChild(scriptTag); } document.addEventListener('DOMContentLoaded', function () { if (typeof yieldToMain === 'function') { yieldToMain(loadLiteYouTubeScript, "user-visible"); } else { loadLiteYouTubeScript(); } }); </script> <style scoped> .lite-youtube-fallback { aspect-ratio: 16 / 9; display: flex; justify-content: center; align-items: center; flex-direction: column; gap: 1em; padding: 1em; background-color: #000; color: #fff; text-decoration: none; } .lite-youtube-fallback::before { display: block; content: ''; border: solid transparent; border-width: 2em 0 2em 3em; border-left-color: red; } .lite-youtube-fallback:hover::before { border-left-color: #fff; } .lite-youtube-fallback:focus { outline: 2px solid red; } </style><div itemscope itemtype="http://schema.org/VideoObject http://schema.org/LearningResource" style="position: relative; padding-bottom: 56.25%; height: 0; overflow: hidden;"> <meta itemprop="name" content="the change is finally coming"> <meta itemprop="description" content="YouTube Video"> <meta itemprop="thumbnailUrl" content="https://img.youtube.com/vi/9-2CSJC114k/maxresdefault.jpg"> <meta itemprop="contentUrl" content="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9-2CSJC114k"> <meta itemprop="learningResourceType" content="Concept Overview"> <meta itemprop="educationalLevel" content="High school (US)"> <lite-youtube videoid="9-2CSJC114k" videotitle="the change is finally coming" videoplay="" nocookie posterloading="lazy" loading="lazy" params=""> <noscript> <a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9-2CSJC114k" class="lite-youtube-fallback" style="position: absolute; top: 0; left: 0; width: 100%; height: 100%; border:0;" title="the change is finally coming"> <span class="lyt-visually-hidden"></span> </a> </noscript> </lite-youtube> </div> <script type="application/ld+json"> { "@context": "https://schema.org", "@type": ["VideoObject", "LearningResource"], "name": "the change is finally coming", "description": "YouTube Video", "thumbnailUrl": ["https:\/\/img.youtube.com\/vi\/9-2CSJC114k\/maxresdefault.jpg"], "contentUrl": "https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9-2CSJC114k", "learningResourceType": "Concept Overview", "educationalLevel": "High school (US)" } </script> <h2 id="the-boundary-is-code-and-code-has-bugs"> <a href="#the-boundary-is-code-and-code-has-bugs" title="The Boundary Is Code, and Code Has Bugs">The Boundary Is Code, and Code Has Bugs</a> <a href="#the-boundary-is-code-and-code-has-bugs" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="The Boundary Is Code, and Code Has Bugs">#</a> </h2> <p>Every action a container performs goes through the <strong>syscall interface</strong>. Opening a file, reading memory, writing to a socket, changing a UID: the kernel mediates all of it, because the kernel does not want processes touching the CPU, the filesystem, or the network directly.</p> <p>The mediation is the security model, and mediation is implemented as code. Specifically, it is roughly <strong>30 million lines</strong> of it.</p> <p>A local privilege escalation (LPE) is what happens when a process exploits a flaw in the mediating code to gain privileges it was never granted. <strong>LPEs are not new.</strong> They have existed since the earliest kernel mediation, and the industry lived with a steady trickle of them for decades.</p> <p><strong>Dirty Pipe in 2022</strong> is the reference point most people know. It abused a flaw in pipe buffer handling to overwrite read-only files, and it was treated as breaking news because bugs of such severity arrived <strong>roughly once a year or two</strong>. You patched, you moved on, and the assumption held: no large defect sat undiscovered in code a million people read.</p> <p><em>The assumption no longer holds.</em></p> <h2 id="what-changed-in-2026"> <a href="#what-changed-in-2026" title="What Changed in 2026">What Changed in 2026</a> <a href="#what-changed-in-2026" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="What Changed in 2026">#</a> </h2> <p>The change is not attacker skill. It is how <strong>finding kernel memory-corruption bugs became an engineering task instead of a research career</strong>.</p> <p>Three data points from this year make the shift concrete:</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Finding</th> <th>Who Found It</th> <th>How</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Copy Fail</strong> (CVE-2026-31431)</td> <td>Taeyang Lee, Theori</td> <td>Assisted by <strong>Xint Code</strong>, an AI static analysis tool. Roughly <strong>one hour of scan time</strong> against the Linux crypto subsystem</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>CVE-2026-80521</strong></td> <td>Zhenpeng (Leo) Lin, DepthFirst</td> <td>Found with <strong>dfs-large1</strong>, an in-house AI model trained for vulnerability detection</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>CVE-2026-80521</strong>, independently</td> <td>Kyle, <strong>OpenAI</strong></td> <td>The same bug, found separately, reported the same day</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>Read the third row again. Two organizations using different AI tooling arrived at <strong>the same AF_UNIX use-after-free</strong> and reported it to <code>security@kernel.org</code> on the <strong>same day</strong>. This is not a coincidence of talent. It is a repeatable process producing the same answer twice.</p> <p>DepthFirst states the scale directly: <strong>nearly 6,000 kernel CVEs published as of September 2026</strong>. The count climbs on a curve tracking the availability of AI assistance, not the number of kernel developers.</p> <p><em>When one hour of AI scan time finds a decade-old bug in the crypto subsystem, the economics of kernel exploitation have inverted.</em></p> <h2 id="four-escapes-one-year"> <a href="#four-escapes-one-year" title="Four Escapes, One Year">Four Escapes, One Year</a> <a href="#four-escapes-one-year" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Four Escapes, One Year">#</a> </h2> <p>Each of these grants root from an unprivileged local account. None requires a container misconfiguration, a privileged flag, or a network foothold.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Vulnerability</th> <th>CVE</th> <th>Subsystem</th> <th>Primitive</th> <th>Found By</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Copy Fail</strong></td> <td>CVE-2026-31431</td> <td><code>algif_aead</code> / AF_ALG</td> <td>4-byte write into any readable file’s page cache</td> <td>Theori, AI-assisted</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Dirty Frag</strong></td> <td>CVE-2026-43284 + CVE-2026-43500</td> <td>XFRM ESP, RxRPC</td> <td>4-byte page-cache write via two chained variants</td> <td>Hyunwoo Kim</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Fragnesia</strong></td> <td>CVE-2026-46300</td> <td>XFRM ESP-in-TCP</td> <td>Single-byte page-cache writes</td> <td>Hyunwoo Kim</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>AF_UNIX UAF</strong></td> <td>CVE-2026-80521</td> <td>AF_UNIX sockets</td> <td>Use-after-free in <code>unix_vertex</code> garbage collection</td> <td>DepthFirst, AI-assisted</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>All four share a design pattern worth noticing. <strong>They attack the page cache rather than the disk.</strong></p> <h3 id="copy-fail-a-logic-flaw-with-no-race"> <a href="#copy-fail-a-logic-flaw-with-no-race" title="Copy Fail: A Logic Flaw With No Race">Copy Fail: A Logic Flaw With No Race</a> <a href="#copy-fail-a-logic-flaw-with-no-race" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Copy Fail: A Logic Flaw With No Race">#</a> </h3> <p>Copy Fail is the cleanest of the four, and the most alarming.</p> <p>Almost every Linux LPE needs a timing window or a kernel-specific memory offset. <strong>Copy Fail needs neither.</strong> It is a straight-line logic flaw in <code>algif_aead</code>, the module providing userspace access to authenticated encryption through AF_ALG.</p> <p>The chain runs <code>splice()</code> to place a page-cache page into the operation, then abuses the in-place AEAD path to write <strong>four controlled bytes</strong> into that page. The corrupted page is <strong>never marked dirty</strong>, so it is never written back to disk. The file on disk stays pristine, which means checksum and integrity verification pass while the in-memory copy carries your modification.</p> <p>One <strong>732-byte Python script</strong> roots every Linux distribution released since 2017. The bug was introduced by a <strong>2017 optimization</strong> to <code>algif_aead</code>, and the 2026 patch simply reverts the optimization. Mainline commit <code>a664bf3d603d</code>.</p> <p><em>The bug sat in every mainstream distribution for nearly a decade, and an AI tool found it in about an hour.</em></p> <h3 id="dirty-frag-two-variants-which-cover-each-other"> <a href="#dirty-frag-two-variants-which-cover-each-other" title="Dirty Frag: Two Variants Which Cover Each Other">Dirty Frag: Two Variants Which Cover Each Other</a> <a href="#dirty-frag-two-variants-which-cover-each-other" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Dirty Frag: Two Variants Which Cover Each Other">#</a> </h3> <p>Dirty Frag describes its own lineage precisely. <strong>Dirty Pipe overwrites <code>struct pipe_buffer</code>. Dirty Frag overwrites the <code>frag</code> of <code>struct sk_buff</code>.</strong></p> <p>It is <strong>two vulnerabilities chained</strong>, and the chaining is the clever part:</p> <ul> <li><strong>CVE-2026-43284</strong> abuses <code>esp_input()</code> skipping the copy-on-write path before running in-place decryption on a spliced fragment. It requires the privilege to create a <strong>user namespace</strong>, which some distributions restrict.</li> <li><strong>CVE-2026-43500</strong> abuses <code>rxkad_verify_packet_1()</code> performing an in-place decrypt on the fragment. It needs no namespace privilege, but the <code>rxrpc</code> module is missing from most distributions. Ubuntu loads it by default.</li> </ul> <p><strong>Either variant alone has a blind spot. Together they cover each other.</strong> Where user namespaces are allowed, the ESP path runs first. Where it is blocked but <code>rxrpc</code> is present, the RxRPC path runs instead. One exploit binary then works across distributions, and the RxRPC variant reaches root by blanking a field in <code>/etc/passwd</code> and letting PAM’s <code>nullok</code> accept an empty password.</p> <p><strong>The finding which matters most for defenders:</strong> Dirty Frag triggers <strong>regardless of <code>algif_aead</code> availability</strong>. The widely circulated Copy Fail mitigation, which blacklists the module, <strong>does not protect against Dirty Frag at all.</strong></p> <h3 id="fragnesia-the-patch-which-created-a-bug"> <a href="#fragnesia-the-patch-which-created-a-bug" title="Fragnesia: The Patch Which Created a Bug">Fragnesia: The Patch Which Created a Bug</a> <a href="#fragnesia-the-patch-which-created-a-bug" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Fragnesia: The Patch Which Created a Bug">#</a> </h3> <p>Fragnesia is the same class as Dirty Frag, aimed at the XFRM <strong>ESP-in-TCP</strong> path, and it is the most instructive entry in the set.</p> <p>The vulnerability exploits improper handling of shared page fragments during <code>skb</code> coalescing. An attacker splices file-backed pages into a TCP receive queue before the socket switches into <code>espintcp</code> upper-layer-protocol mode. Once ESP processing activates, the kernel decrypts the queued data <strong>in place</strong>, and AES-GCM keystream manipulation corrupts the underlying page cache. The attacker gains repeated <strong>single-byte writes</strong> into cached file pages.</p> <p>The exploit reaches root by overwriting the first bytes of <code>/usr/bin/su</code> with a small ELF payload. <strong>The change exists only in memory and never touches the on-disk binary.</strong></p> <p>Unprivileged <strong>user and network namespaces</strong> provide <code>CAP_NET_ADMIN</code> inside an isolated namespace, then NETLINK_XFRM installs a crafted security association.</p> <p><em>Here is the sentence to sit with:</em> Fragnesia emerged as <strong>an unintended side effect of one of the patches for the original Dirty Frag vulnerabilities</strong>. Patching Dirty Frag produced a new, independently exploitable root bug.</p> <h3 id="cve-2026-80521-the-container-escape-which-won-kernelctf"> <a href="#cve-2026-80521-the-container-escape-which-won-kernelctf" title="CVE-2026-80521: The Container Escape Which Won kernelCTF">CVE-2026-80521: The Container Escape Which Won kernelCTF</a> <a href="#cve-2026-80521-the-container-escape-which-won-kernelctf" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="CVE-2026-80521: The Container Escape Which Won kernelCTF">#</a> </h3> <p>The AF_UNIX race is the one which removes any argument this is theoretical.</p> <p>The vulnerability is a <strong>heap use-after-free</strong> in the garbage collection mechanism for <code>SCM_RIGHTS</code> messages, which is how processes pass file descriptors to each other. A race during collection of a circular socket reference frees a <code>struct unix_vertex</code> while a surviving socket’s SCC ring still holds a pointer to it. The next collection pass walks the stale ring and dereferences freed memory.</p> <p>The reason it matters beyond Linux generally: <strong>AF_UNIX underpins local IPC.</strong> Local databases, <code>systemd</code>, and Docker itself all depend on it. DepthFirst notes the vulnerability impacts most OS-level sandboxes built on the kernel, <strong>including <code>nsjail</code>, <code>Firejail</code>, and <code>Bubblewrap</code></strong>, plus modern container runtimes.</p> <p>DepthFirst won a <strong>Google kernelCTF slot</strong> with it on <strong>July 24, 2026</strong>, received confirmation in the <code>lts-6.12.95</code> slot on <strong>August 5</strong>, reported it to <code>security@kernel.org</code> the same day, and learned <strong>Kyle from OpenAI had reported the same bug.</strong> The upstream patch landed <strong>August 6</strong>. Research published <strong>September 22</strong>.</p> <p>They released a working exploit targeting <strong>Ubuntu 26.04</strong>, plus a second exploit for CVE-2026-52910 escaping <strong>Ubuntu 24.04</strong>.</p> <script type="application/ld+json"> { "@context": "https://schema.org/", "@type": "ImageObject", "contentUrl": "https:\/\/simeononsecurity.com\/kernel-page-cache-overwrite-container-escape.webp", "caption": "Diagram showing an unprivileged process inside a container corrupting a page-cache page to modify a setuid binary in memory, escalating to root and stepping outside the container boundary onto the host kernel", "license": "https://simeononsecurity.com/termsandconditions/", "acquireLicensePage": "https://simeononsecurity.com/contactus/", "creditText": "SimeonOnSecurity", "creator": { "@type": "Person", "name": "SimeonOnSecurity" }, "copyrightNotice": "SimeonOnSecurity", "associatedArticle": { "@type": "NewsArticle", "headline": "simeononsecurity", "url": "https:\/\/simeononsecurity.com\/", "datePublished": "2026-10-02 21:20:37.651173211 \u002b0000 UTC m=\u002b337.375898957", "author": { "@type": "Person", "name": "SimeonOnSecurity", "url": "https:\/\/simeononsecurity.com\/authors\/simeononsecurity" } } } </script> <center> <figure align="center" style="text-align: center; margin: 0 auto;" itemscope itemtype="http://schema.org/ImageObject"> <meta property="article:published_time" content="2026-10-02 21:20:37.651173211 +0000 UTC m=+337.375898957"> <meta property="article:author" content="SimeonOnSecurity"> <meta property="article:author:url" content="https://simeononsecurity.com/authors/simeononsecurity"> <meta property="og:license" content="https://simeononsecurity.com/termsandconditions/"> <meta property="og:see_also" content="https://simeononsecurity.com/contactus/"> <meta property="og:copyright" content="SimeonOnSecurity"> <img align="center" style="text-align: center; margin: 0 auto; max-width: 80%; max-height: 600px; min-width: 100px; min-height: 100px; height: auto; width: auto;" src="https://simeononsecurity.com/kernel-page-cache-overwrite-container-escape.webp" alt="Diagram showing an unprivileged process inside a container corrupting a page-cache page to modify a setuid binary in memory, escalating to root and stepping outside the container boundary onto the host kernel"loading="lazy" fetchpriority="low" itemprop="contentUrl" /> </figure> </center> <h2 id="why-the-mitigation-advice-keeps-failing"> <a href="#why-the-mitigation-advice-keeps-failing" title="Why the Mitigation Advice Keeps Failing">Why the Mitigation Advice Keeps Failing</a> <a href="#why-the-mitigation-advice-keeps-failing" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Why the Mitigation Advice Keeps Failing">#</a> </h2> <p>Defenders have been handed three rounds of workarounds this year, and each one has been partially wrong.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Mitigation</th> <th>What It Stops</th> <th>What It Misses</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td>Blacklist <strong><code>algif_aead</code></strong></td> <td>Copy Fail</td> <td><strong>Nothing in Dirty Frag</strong>, which ignores the module entirely</td> </tr> <tr> <td>Blacklist <strong><code>esp4</code>, <code>esp6</code>, <code>rxrpc</code></strong></td> <td>Dirty Frag, Fragnesia</td> <td>Teams needing IPsec. Also misses entirely new subsystems</td> </tr> <tr> <td>Restrict <strong>unprivileged user namespaces</strong></td> <td>The ESP variants</td> <td>The RxRPC variant needs no namespace. AppArmor policy is a <strong>partial</strong> mitigation only</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Patch the kernel</strong></td> <td>The patched bug</td> <td>The next bug, and any bug a patch introduces</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>Two patterns stand out.</p> <p><strong>First, the workarounds conflict with each other.</strong> Copy Fail is mitigated by disabling <code>algif_aead</code>. Dirty Frag explicitly triggers <strong>whether or not</strong> the module exists. Fragnesia needs <code>esp4</code> and <code>esp6</code> disabled, which is a problem for anyone running IPsec. There is no single module blacklist covering the family.</p> <p><strong>Second, and worse, patching is not a clean win.</strong> Fragnesia was introduced <strong>by the patch for Dirty Frag</strong>. Every patch carries risk of new logic errors, and in this subsystem a logic error becomes a root exploit.</p> <p><em>The uncomfortable conclusion: these vulnerabilities are all in the page cache, all reachable from unprivileged code, and all found by tooling which improves every quarter. No blocklist stays complete.</em></p> <h2 id="the-counter-argument-answered-honestly"> <a href="#the-counter-argument-answered-honestly" title="The Counter-Argument, Answered Honestly">The Counter-Argument, Answered Honestly</a> <a href="#the-counter-argument-answered-honestly" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="The Counter-Argument, Answered Honestly">#</a> </h2> <p>There is a fair objection, and it deserves a straight answer: <strong>hypervisors have bugs too.</strong></p> <p>The KVM attack surface is real. Google runs <strong>kvmCTF</strong> specifically because it wants those bugs found, and the program pays generously for them:</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Tier</th> <th>Reward</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Full VM escape</strong></td> <td><strong>$250,000</strong></td> </tr> <tr> <td>Arbitrary memory write</td> <td>$100,000</td> </tr> <tr> <td>Arbitrary memory read</td> <td>$50,000</td> </tr> <tr> <td>Relative memory write</td> <td>$50,000</td> </tr> <tr> <td>Denial of Service</td> <td>$20,000</td> </tr> <tr> <td>Relative memory read</td> <td>$10,000</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>Awards do not stack, the target is a Linux LTS kernel with KVM, and the guest is Debian 12.5. The goal is a <strong>guest-to-host attack</strong>.</p> <p><strong>Hyunwoo Kim, the same researcher who found Dirty Frag, also collects KVM bounties</strong> and has won the full $250,000 for a VM escape. So the honest summary: both layers have flaws, and the person finding them is sometimes the same person.</p> <p><strong>But compare the scales:</strong></p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th></th> <th>Linux Kernel</th> <th>KVM Hypervisor</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>CVEs in 2026</strong></td> <td>Nearly <strong>6,000</strong></td> <td>A handful, with individual researchers finding a few per year</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Reachable from</strong></td> <td>Any unprivileged process, through the syscall interface</td> <td>Only by code already running inside a guest</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Attack surface</strong></td> <td>Everything: networking, filesystems, crypto, IPC, drivers</td> <td>The virtual device and hypercall interface</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Bug class</strong></td> <td>Any memory-safety or logic flaw in 30M lines</td> <td>Confined to the virtualization boundary</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><em>The difference is orders of magnitude, not a factor of two. The gap is why microVMs change the risk calculus.</em></p> <h2 id="what-provides-a-real-boundary"> <a href="#what-provides-a-real-boundary" title="What Provides a Real Boundary">What Provides a Real Boundary</a> <a href="#what-provides-a-real-boundary" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="What Provides a Real Boundary">#</a> </h2> <p>A <strong>microVM</strong> gives each workload its own <strong>kernel instance</strong> running on hardware-enforced virtualization, rather than sharing the host kernel through namespaces.</p> <p>The stack has three layers worth naming:</p> <ul> <li><strong>The CPU</strong> provides hardware mechanisms to isolate one memory region from another.</li> <li><strong>KVM</strong> exposes those mechanisms to the Linux kernel, so the kernel acts as a hypervisor.</li> <li><strong>A VMM (virtual machine monitor)</strong>, such as Firecracker or QEMU, drives KVM to create and run the guest.</li> </ul> <p>Because the guest runs its own kernel, a kernel exploit <strong>inside the guest</strong> compromises only the guest. There is no shared kernel to attack. An attacker must then escape the hypervisor itself, which is the smaller surface KVM bugs occupy.</p> <p>Two implementations matter in practice, and both are named in DepthFirst’s recommendation:</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Technology</th> <th>Approach</th> <th>Notes</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Firecracker</strong></td> <td>Purpose-built VMM, minimal device model</td> <td>AWS-built, designed specifically for multi-tenant isolation at scale</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Kata Containers</strong></td> <td>OCI-compatible runtime wrapping a microVM</td> <td>Runs standard container images with a VM boundary underneath</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>Kata is the easier migration for most teams, because it accepts the container images and tooling already in use. <strong>Firecracker is the smaller attack surface</strong>, because it implements far less device emulation than a general-purpose VMM.</p> <script type="application/ld+json"> { "@context": "https://schema.org/", "@type": "ImageObject", "contentUrl": "https:\/\/simeononsecurity.com\/microvm-vs-container-isolation-boundary.webp", "caption": "Diagram comparing container isolation through shared kernel namespaces against microVM isolation where each workload runs its own kernel on top of KVM and a virtual machine monitor", "license": "https://simeononsecurity.com/termsandconditions/", "acquireLicensePage": "https://simeononsecurity.com/contactus/", "creditText": "SimeonOnSecurity", "creator": { "@type": "Person", "name": "SimeonOnSecurity" }, "copyrightNotice": "SimeonOnSecurity", "associatedArticle": { "@type": "NewsArticle", "headline": "simeononsecurity", "url": "https:\/\/simeononsecurity.com\/", "datePublished": "2026-10-02 21:20:37.651498583 \u002b0000 UTC m=\u002b337.376224329", "author": { "@type": "Person", "name": "SimeonOnSecurity", "url": "https:\/\/simeononsecurity.com\/authors\/simeononsecurity" } } } </script> <center> <figure align="center" style="text-align: center; margin: 0 auto;" itemscope itemtype="http://schema.org/ImageObject"> <meta property="article:published_time" content="2026-10-02 21:20:37.651498583 +0000 UTC m=+337.376224329"> <meta property="article:author" content="SimeonOnSecurity"> <meta property="article:author:url" content="https://simeononsecurity.com/authors/simeononsecurity"> <meta property="og:license" content="https://simeononsecurity.com/termsandconditions/"> <meta property="og:see_also" content="https://simeononsecurity.com/contactus/"> <meta property="og:copyright" content="SimeonOnSecurity"> <img align="center" style="text-align: center; margin: 0 auto; max-width: 80%; max-height: 600px; min-width: 100px; min-height: 100px; height: auto; width: auto;" src="https://simeononsecurity.com/microvm-vs-container-isolation-boundary.webp" alt="Diagram comparing container isolation through shared kernel namespaces against microVM isolation where each workload runs its own kernel on top of KVM and a virtual machine monitor"loading="lazy" fetchpriority="low" itemprop="contentUrl" /> </figure> </center> <h2 id="what-to-do-now"> <a href="#what-to-do-now" title="What To Do Now">What To Do Now</a> <a href="#what-to-do-now" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="What To Do Now">#</a> </h2> <p>Not every container needs a microVM. The decision hinges on <strong>whose code runs inside it</strong>.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Your Situation</th> <th>Risk</th> <th>What To Do</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>You run your own code</strong>, single tenant</td> <td>Low</td> <td>Keep containers. Patch promptly, drop capabilities, keep a read-only root filesystem</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Multi-tenant hosts</strong>, shell access for users</td> <td><strong>High</strong></td> <td>Move untrusted workloads to microVMs. This is the case DepthFirst calls out first</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>CI runners executing untrusted PRs</strong></td> <td><strong>High</strong></td> <td>A pull request becomes root on the runner. Isolate each job in its own VM</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Notebooks, agent sandboxes, serverless</strong></td> <td><strong>High</strong></td> <td>Tenant code becomes host root. MicroVM per tenant</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Kubernetes clusters</strong></td> <td><strong>Elevated</strong></td> <td>The page cache is shared across the host. A pod with the right primitives compromises the node and crosses tenant boundaries</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>The unifying principle is simple. <strong>Containers are an excellent packaging and process-isolation tool.</strong> They were never designed to contain hostile code, and the industry quietly borrowed them for the job because they were convenient and cheap.</p> <h3 id="hardening-which-helps-regardless"> <a href="#hardening-which-helps-regardless" title="Hardening Which Helps Regardless">Hardening Which Helps Regardless</a> <a href="#hardening-which-helps-regardless" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Hardening Which Helps Regardless">#</a> </h3> <p>None of this substitutes for a VM boundary, and all of it removes easy paths:</p> <div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" style="color:#f8f8f2;background-color:#272822;-moz-tab-size:4;-o-tab-size:4;tab-size:4;-webkit-text-size-adjust:none;"><code class="language-bash" data-lang="bash"><span style="display:flex;"><span><span style="color:#75715e"># Disable the modules the page-cache family abuses, where they are not needed</span> </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>printf <span style="color:#e6db74">'install algif_aead /bin/false\ninstall esp4 /bin/false\ninstall esp6 /bin/false\ninstall rxrpc /bin/false\n'</span> <span style="color:#ae81ff">\ </span></span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> > /etc/modprobe.d/harden-pagecache-family.conf </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>rmmod algif_aead esp4 esp6 rxrpc 2>/dev/null <span style="color:#f92672">||</span> true </span></span></code></pre></div><div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" style="color:#f8f8f2;background-color:#272822;-moz-tab-size:4;-o-tab-size:4;tab-size:4;-webkit-text-size-adjust:none;"><code class="language-bash" data-lang="bash"><span style="display:flex;"><span><span style="color:#75715e"># Restrict unprivileged user namespaces, which gates the ESP variants</span> </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span><span style="color:#75715e"># Debian and Ubuntu: this is a partial mitigation, not a complete one</span> </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>sysctl -w kernel.unprivileged_userns_clone<span style="color:#f92672">=</span><span style="color:#ae81ff">0</span> </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span><span style="color:#75715e"># If exploitation is suspected, drop the page cache to discard modified in-memory binaries</span> </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>echo <span style="color:#ae81ff">1</span> | tee /proc/sys/vm/drop_caches </span></span></code></pre></div><div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" style="color:#f8f8f2;background-color:#272822;-moz-tab-size:4;-o-tab-size:4;tab-size:4;-webkit-text-size-adjust:none;"><code class="language-text" data-lang="text"><span style="display:flex;"><span># Detection starting points </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>- Unexpected unshare(CLONE_NEWUSER) from a workload with no legitimate reason </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>- NETLINK_XFRM activity, or XFRM security associations appearing outside IPsec hosts </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>- Requests to bind AF_ALG sockets </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>- Loads of esp4, esp6, or rxrpc on hosts running neither IPsec nor AFS </span></span></code></pre></div><blockquote> <p><strong>Warning: <code>drop_caches</code> discards the modified in-memory copy, which clears the corruption, but it does not remove an attacker who already reached root. Treat it as incident response, not remediation.</strong></p> </blockquote> <h3 id="the-patching-cadence-problem"> <a href="#the-patching-cadence-problem" title="The Patching Cadence Problem">The Patching Cadence Problem</a> <a href="#the-patching-cadence-problem" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="The Patching Cadence Problem">#</a> </h3> <p>Even with the best intentions, kernel patching has become a race:</p> <ul> <li>Nearly <strong>6,000 CVEs</strong> published this year means the volume alone outpaces most maintenance windows.</li> <li><strong>A patch introduces a bug.</strong> Fragnesia proved it, in this exact subsystem.</li> <li><strong>The mitigation list expires.</strong> <code>algif_aead</code> was the answer in April. By May it covered nothing in Dirty Frag.</li> </ul> <p><em>Speed of patching is necessary and insufficient. The architecture decides whether a missed patch is a contained incident or a host compromise.</em></p> <h2 id="the-harder-question-who-is-the-adversary"> <a href="#the-harder-question-who-is-the-adversary" title="The Harder Question: Who Is the Adversary?">The Harder Question: Who Is the Adversary?</a> <a href="#the-harder-question-who-is-the-adversary" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="The Harder Question: Who Is the Adversary?">#</a> </h2> <p>The technical answer is clear. The strategic answer depends on a question most teams skip.</p> <p><strong>If your threat model is a curious user or a careless developer, containers remain adequate.</strong> A container escape requires local code execution plus a kernel exploit. Neither is casual, and the operational cost of moving everything to microVMs is real.</p> <p><strong>If your threat model includes an adversary who runs code on your infrastructure, containers are now a speed bump.</strong> DepthFirst’s conclusion is worth quoting rather than paraphrasing:</p> <blockquote> <p>“The barrier to entry for weaponizing these vulnerabilities has dropped so significantly that we must assume attackers already have the capability to escape standard containers at will.”</p> </blockquote> <p>This is a security vendor with a product to sell arguing for a specific architecture, and the skepticism it deserves is fair. <strong>The argument does not depend on the vendor, though.</strong> The 6,000 CVE count is public, the exploits are published, and the kernel is shared by design.</p> <p><em>The honest framing: containers are a boundary of decreasing value against an attacker with a foothold, and a boundary of undiminished value against everything else.</em></p> <h2 id="the-verdict"> <a href="#the-verdict" title="The Verdict">The Verdict</a> <a href="#the-verdict" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="The Verdict">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Containers remain the right tool for packaging, deployment, and process separation. They are no longer a reliable security boundary against hostile code.</strong></p> <p>Three claims, ordered by confidence:</p> <ol> <li> <p><strong>The technical premise is settled.</strong> Containers share the host kernel. Every one of the four vulnerabilities in this article escaped the boundary from an unprivileged account, and the exploits are public.</p> </li> <li> <p><strong>AI changed the pace, not the principle.</strong> Kernel LPEs have always existed. Finding one now costs roughly <strong>an hour of AI scan time</strong> instead of months of expert effort, and two organizations independently found the same zero-day on the same day.</p> </li> <li> <p><strong>The migration is a real cost, and so is not migrating.</strong> Firecracker and Kata both add overhead, operational complexity, and a new set of skills. The trade is straightforward: accept the overhead, or accept that a kernel bug is a host compromise.</p> </li> </ol> <p><strong>If you run multi-tenant infrastructure or execute untrusted code, start planning the microVM migration now.</strong> Not because the sky is falling, but because the trajectory is unambiguous and the migration takes quarters rather than weeks.</p> <p><strong>If you run single-tenant containers of your own code, keep them.</strong> Patch the kernel faster than you are used to, disable the modules you do not need, and revisit the decision when untrusted code enters the picture.</p> <p><em>The era of treating the kernel as an unconditionally trusted boundary is ending. Infrastructure which assumes the kernel will be breached is infrastructure which survives the breach.</em></p> <h2 id="key-takeaways"> <a href="#key-takeaways" title="Key Takeaways">Key Takeaways</a> <a href="#key-takeaways" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Key Takeaways">#</a> </h2> <ul> <li><strong>Containers share the host kernel.</strong> Isolation comes from <code>clone</code> syscall namespaces, not hardware virtualization, so a kernel bug is a container bug.</li> <li><strong>Four 2026 vulnerabilities escaped the boundary</strong> from unprivileged local accounts: Copy Fail, Dirty Frag, Fragnesia, and CVE-2026-80521. All four target the page cache.</li> <li><strong>Nearly 6,000 kernel CVEs</strong> were published as of September 2026, and AI tooling is the accelerant. <strong>Copy Fail was found in about an hour</strong> of AI scan time.</li> <li><strong>Fragnesia was introduced by the patch for Dirty Frag.</strong> Patching produced a new root bug in the same subsystem.</li> <li><strong>The Copy Fail workaround does not stop Dirty Frag.</strong> Blacklisting <code>algif_aead</code> covers one vulnerability and nothing else in the family.</li> <li><strong>CVE-2026-80521 also broke <code>nsjail</code>, <code>Firejail</code>, and <code>Bubblewrap</code></strong>, not only container runtimes.</li> <li><strong>MicroVMs change the risk calculus</strong> by giving each workload its own kernel. KVM has bugs, but the surface is orders of magnitude smaller.</li> <li><strong>Choose based on who runs the code.</strong> Your own code in a single-tenant container is a low risk. Untrusted code on a shared host is a host-compromise risk.</li> </ul> <h2 id="next-steps"> <a href="#next-steps" title="Next Steps">Next Steps</a> <a href="#next-steps" class="h-anchor" item.title: Claude Cowork and Claude Code With Local Models: 2026 Setup Guide
item.category: "Local AI" , "AI Coding Tools" , "Self-Hosted AI" , "Developer Tools" , "Privacy" , "Open Source Models" , "Automation" , "AI Hardware"
item.description: Ollama connects Claude Desktop and Claude Code to local models through an Anthropic-compatible API. Here is the correct setup for each, the environment variable most guides omit, which models to use in September 2026, and which features stay cloud-only.
item.content:encoded: <p><strong>Claude’s agentic tools now run against models on your own hardware, with no API key, no subscription, and no data leaving the machine.</strong> Ollama exposes an Anthropic-compatible API, and both Claude Code and Claude Desktop connect to it in a few commands.</p> <p><em>Most guides get one important detail wrong. They describe Claude Cowork, then hand you setup steps which configure the command-line tool instead. Those are two different integrations, and only one of them gives you Cowork.</em></p> <p>This guide covers both paths separately, the environment variable the popular tutorials skip, which models to pair with each in September 2026, and the features which stay cloud-only no matter what you configure.</p> <h2 id="the-short-answer"> <a href="#the-short-answer" title="The Short Answer">The Short Answer</a> <a href="#the-short-answer" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="The Short Answer">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Ollama connects to Claude in two distinct ways, and picking the wrong one is the most common reason people finish a setup guide with a working terminal and no Cowork.</strong></p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Integration</th> <th>What You Get</th> <th>Setup Path</th> <th>Platform</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Claude Desktop</strong></td> <td>Cowork, subagents, web search, auto mode</td> <td>Ollama app, then <strong>Apps</strong> and <strong>Connect Claude</strong></td> <td><strong>macOS only</strong></td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Claude Code</strong></td> <td>The CLI coding agent with tool calling and file edits</td> <td><code>ollama launch claude</code>, or environment variables</td> <td>macOS, Linux, Windows</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>If you want Cowork, use the Claude Desktop integration.</strong> It is a graphical flow in the Ollama app, and it is macOS-only while Windows support is still listed as coming soon.</p> <p><strong>If you want an agent in your terminal, use Claude Code.</strong> One command does it.</p> <p><em>Both are free. The only cost is the hardware and the electricity.</em></p> <h2 id="two-integrations-not-one"> <a href="#two-integrations-not-one" title="Two Integrations, Not One">Two Integrations, Not One</a> <a href="#two-integrations-not-one" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Two Integrations, Not One">#</a> </h2> <p>The confusion starts with the naming. <strong>Claude Cowork is a feature inside Claude Desktop</strong>, not a separate application, and not a synonym for Claude Code.</p> <p>Ollama’s documentation lists them on separate pages under separate headings. Claude Desktop sits under <strong>Assistants</strong>, alongside OpenClaw and Hermes. Claude Code sits under <strong>Coding</strong>, alongside OpenCode, Cline, and Codex CLI.</p> <p>The distinction matters because the setup differs completely:</p> <ul> <li><strong>Claude Desktop</strong> is configured through the Ollama application interface. You do not touch a shell profile.</li> <li><strong>Claude Code</strong> is configured through environment variables or a single launch command.</li> </ul> <p>A guide which tells you to export <code>ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL</code> and run <code>claude</code> has configured the command-line tool. If you followed those steps expecting the Cowork desktop experience, <strong>nothing in your setup is broken. You configured a different product.</strong></p> <h2 id="setup-claude-desktop-and-cowork"> <a href="#setup-claude-desktop-and-cowork" title="Setup: Claude Desktop and Cowork">Setup: Claude Desktop and Cowork</a> <a href="#setup-claude-desktop-and-cowork" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Setup: Claude Desktop and Cowork">#</a> </h2> <p>This path runs through the Ollama application rather than the terminal.</p> <h3 id="prerequisites"> <a href="#prerequisites" title="Prerequisites">Prerequisites</a> <a href="#prerequisites" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Prerequisites">#</a> </h3> <ul> <li><strong>Ollama installed</strong>, on macOS. Windows support is documented as coming soon.</li> <li><strong>A model downloaded first</strong> if you plan to run locally. For a cloud model, sign in to Ollama and enable cloud models. Some cloud models require a paid plan.</li> <li><strong>Claude installed.</strong> If it is missing, Ollama offers to download it during setup.</li> </ul> <h3 id="the-steps"> <a href="#the-steps" title="The Steps">The Steps</a> <a href="#the-steps" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="The Steps">#</a> </h3> <ol> <li>Open Ollama and select <strong>Apps</strong>.</li> <li>Select <strong>Connect Claude</strong>.</li> <li>Follow the setup prompts. Install Claude if prompted, and restart it when asked.</li> </ol> <p>This is the whole flow. To change models afterward, open <strong>Ollama Settings</strong>, go to <strong>Apps</strong>, choose your models, and select <strong>Restart Claude</strong>.</p> <h3 id="what-carries-over"> <a href="#what-carries-over" title="What Carries Over">What Carries Over</a> <a href="#what-carries-over" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="What Carries Over">#</a> </h3> <p>Ollama’s documentation lists four features as supported through this integration:</p> <ul> <li><strong>Cowork</strong>, for completing difficult tasks</li> <li><strong>Subagents</strong>, for splitting larger tasks across agents</li> <li><strong>Web search</strong>, provided by default through Ollama’s search</li> <li><strong>Auto mode</strong>, which lets the agent decide when to ask before making changes</li> </ul> <p><em>Cowork appears in this list, which is the part worth noting. It is available through this integration and not through the command-line one.</em></p> <h3 id="disconnecting"> <a href="#disconnecting" title="Disconnecting">Disconnecting</a> <a href="#disconnecting" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Disconnecting">#</a> </h3> <p>Disconnecting restores Claude’s previous configuration, so the change is not destructive.</p> <ul> <li>Through the interface, open <strong>Apps</strong> and disconnect Claude, then restart Claude when prompted.</li> <li>From a terminal, run <code>ollama launch claude-desktop --restore</code>.</li> <li><strong>Quitting Ollama while Claude is connected also restores Claude’s usual configuration.</strong> If you want the local setup to persist, leave Ollama running.</li> </ul> <script type="application/ld+json"> { "@context": "https://schema.org/", "@type": "ImageObject", "contentUrl": "https:\/\/simeononsecurity.com\/claude-desktop-ollama-integration-flow.webp", "caption": "Diagram showing the Ollama application Apps panel connecting to Claude Desktop, with model selection routed through Ollama settings and a restore path back to the original configuration", "license": "https://simeononsecurity.com/termsandconditions/", "acquireLicensePage": "https://simeononsecurity.com/contactus/", "creditText": "SimeonOnSecurity", "creator": { "@type": "Person", "name": "SimeonOnSecurity" }, "copyrightNotice": "SimeonOnSecurity", "associatedArticle": { "@type": "NewsArticle", "headline": "simeononsecurity", "url": "https:\/\/simeononsecurity.com\/", "datePublished": "2026-10-02 21:20:37.660402496 \u002b0000 UTC m=\u002b337.385128241", "author": { "@type": "Person", "name": "SimeonOnSecurity", "url": "https:\/\/simeononsecurity.com\/authors\/simeononsecurity" } } } </script> <center> <figure align="center" style="text-align: center; margin: 0 auto;" itemscope itemtype="http://schema.org/ImageObject"> <meta property="article:published_time" content="2026-10-02 21:20:37.660402496 +0000 UTC m=+337.385128241"> <meta property="article:author" content="SimeonOnSecurity"> <meta property="article:author:url" content="https://simeononsecurity.com/authors/simeononsecurity"> <meta property="og:license" content="https://simeononsecurity.com/termsandconditions/"> <meta property="og:see_also" content="https://simeononsecurity.com/contactus/"> <meta property="og:copyright" content="SimeonOnSecurity"> <img align="center" style="text-align: center; margin: 0 auto; max-width: 80%; max-height: 600px; min-width: 100px; min-height: 100px; height: auto; width: auto;" src="https://simeononsecurity.com/claude-desktop-ollama-integration-flow.webp" alt="Diagram showing the Ollama application Apps panel connecting to Claude Desktop, with model selection routed through Ollama settings and a restore path back to the original configuration"loading="lazy" fetchpriority="low" itemprop="contentUrl" /> </figure> </center> <h2 id="setup-claude-code-from-the-cli"> <a href="#setup-claude-code-from-the-cli" title="Setup: Claude Code From the CLI">Setup: Claude Code From the CLI</a> <a href="#setup-claude-code-from-the-cli" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Setup: Claude Code From the CLI">#</a> </h2> <p>This is the path covered by almost every guide, and for terminal work it is the right one.</p> <h3 id="the-one-command-method"> <a href="#the-one-command-method" title="The One-Command Method">The One-Command Method</a> <a href="#the-one-command-method" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="The One-Command Method">#</a> </h3> <div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" style="color:#f8f8f2;background-color:#272822;-moz-tab-size:4;-o-tab-size:4;tab-size:4;-webkit-text-size-adjust:none;"><code class="language-bash" data-lang="bash"><span style="display:flex;"><span>ollama launch claude </span></span></code></pre></div><p>The command sets the required environment variables, points Claude Code at your local Ollama instance, and starts it. Choose a model from the list and press Enter. To name the model up front, add the flag:</p> <div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" style="color:#f8f8f2;background-color:#272822;-moz-tab-size:4;-o-tab-size:4;tab-size:4;-webkit-text-size-adjust:none;"><code class="language-bash" data-lang="bash"><span style="display:flex;"><span>ollama launch claude --model qwen3.5 </span></span></code></pre></div><p><em>The wrapper handles the environment for you. Read the next section anyway, because knowing what it sets is how you debug it later.</em></p> <h3 id="the-manual-environment-variables"> <a href="#the-manual-environment-variables" title="The Manual Environment Variables">The Manual Environment Variables</a> <a href="#the-manual-environment-variables" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="The Manual Environment Variables">#</a> </h3> <div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" style="color:#f8f8f2;background-color:#272822;-moz-tab-size:4;-o-tab-size:4;tab-size:4;-webkit-text-size-adjust:none;"><code class="language-bash" data-lang="bash"><span style="display:flex;"><span>export ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN<span style="color:#f92672">=</span>ollama </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY<span style="color:#f92672">=</span><span style="color:#e6db74">""</span> </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>export ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL<span style="color:#f92672">=</span>http://localhost:11434 </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>claude --model qwen3.5 </span></span></code></pre></div><p><strong>The second line is the one popular guides omit.</strong> Setting <code>ANTHROPIC_API_KEY</code> to an empty string prevents an existing real key in your environment from interfering with the local connection. If you publish a guide with the variables printed on a page and leave the line out, readers with a key already exported get a confusing failure.</p> <p>To avoid modifying your shell profile, pass everything inline:</p> <div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" style="color:#f8f8f2;background-color:#272822;-moz-tab-size:4;-o-tab-size:4;tab-size:4;-webkit-text-size-adjust:none;"><code class="language-bash" data-lang="bash"><span style="display:flex;"><span>ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN<span style="color:#f92672">=</span>ollama ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL<span style="color:#f92672">=</span>http://localhost:11434 ANTHROPIC_API_KEY<span style="color:#f92672">=</span><span style="color:#e6db74">""</span> claude --model kimi-k2.7-code:cloud </span></span></code></pre></div><p>Two details worth knowing from the official documentation:</p> <ul> <li><strong><code>ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN</code> carries the bearer authentication</strong>, which is why it holds the literal string <code>ollama</code> in local mode.</li> <li><strong>Claude’s own settings files override shell variables.</strong> If a connection behaves oddly after you export new values, check those settings and then run <code>/status</code> inside Claude Code to see which endpoint is in use.</li> </ul> <h3 id="connecting-straight-to-ollama-cloud"> <a href="#connecting-straight-to-ollama-cloud" title="Connecting Straight to Ollama Cloud">Connecting Straight to Ollama Cloud</a> <a href="#connecting-straight-to-ollama-cloud" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Connecting Straight to Ollama Cloud">#</a> </h3> <p>You do not need Ollama installed at all for this route. Set an API key and point Claude Code at Ollama’s hosted endpoint:</p> <div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" style="color:#f8f8f2;background-color:#272822;-moz-tab-size:4;-o-tab-size:4;tab-size:4;-webkit-text-size-adjust:none;"><code class="language-bash" data-lang="bash"><span style="display:flex;"><span>ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL<span style="color:#f92672">=</span>https://ollama.com <span style="color:#ae81ff">\ </span></span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN<span style="color:#f92672">=</span><span style="color:#e6db74">"</span>$OLLAMA_API_KEY<span style="color:#e6db74">"</span> <span style="color:#ae81ff">\ </span></span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>ANTHROPIC_API_KEY<span style="color:#f92672">=</span><span style="color:#e6db74">""</span> <span style="color:#ae81ff">\ </span></span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>claude --model glm-5.3-flash </span></span></code></pre></div><p><strong>One caveat applies here.</strong> Ollama’s documentation notes hosted web search and advanced tool controls are not fully supported on this route. Basic chat, file edits, and tool calling work with compatible models.</p> <h2 id="model-choices-for-september-2026"> <a href="#model-choices-for-september-2026" title="Model Choices for September 2026">Model Choices for September 2026</a> <a href="#model-choices-for-september-2026" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Model Choices for September 2026">#</a> </h2> <p>The model lineup moved a long way during 2026, so advice written in the spring is worth rechecking. Here is where things stand now.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Model</th> <th>Type</th> <th>Context</th> <th>Why Pick It</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Qwen3.8 27B</strong></td> <td>Local, 18 GB</td> <td>256K</td> <td>Current best local all-rounder with vision, tool calling, and thinking control</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Qwen3 Coder Next</strong></td> <td>Local, MoE 80B total / 3B active</td> <td>256K</td> <td>Built for always-on coding agents, non-thinking mode for speed</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Qwen3.6 35B A3B</strong></td> <td>Local, MoE 35B / 3B active</td> <td>262K</td> <td>Apache 2.0 and efficient on modest memory</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>kimi-k2.7-code:cloud</strong></td> <td>Cloud</td> <td>Large</td> <td>Coding-focused cloud model with no local hardware requirement</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>glm-5.3-flash</strong></td> <td>Cloud</td> <td>Large</td> <td>The model Ollama’s own documentation reaches for first</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>Start with Qwen3.8 27B if you have the memory.</strong> It runs locally with a 256K context window, native vision, tool calling, and thinking you toggle per request. On a card with 24 GB or more it is a comfortable daily driver.</p> <p><strong>Start with a cloud model if you do not.</strong> Pointing Claude Code at a hosted model costs nothing to try and removes the hardware question entirely, at the price of your code leaving the machine.</p> <h3 id="a-warning-about-ternary-models"> <a href="#a-warning-about-ternary-models" title="A Warning About Ternary Models">A Warning About Ternary Models</a> <a href="#a-warning-about-ternary-models" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="A Warning About Ternary Models">#</a> </h3> <p>If you read our <strong> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="local AI 2026 guide"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/articles/local-ai-2026-build-your-rig-now/"> <a href="/articles/local-ai-2026-build-your-rig-now/" rel="follow me" >local AI 2026 guide</a> </span> </strong>, you know ternary Bonsai 2 27B runs a full 27B model in <strong>5.53 GiB</strong>. It is tempting to reach for it here.</p> <p><strong>It will not work with this workflow.</strong> The ternary kernels live in Prism ML’s llama.cpp fork, and stock Ollama cannot load those files. A command like <code>ollama launch claude --model Ternary-Bonsai-2-27B</code> fails before inference starts. Use the standard Qwen3.8 27B pack for Claude Code, and reserve the ternary packs for a runtime built to handle them.</p> <p><em>Convenience and maximum efficiency pull in different directions here. The integrated tooling wants a standard GGUF.</em></p> <h2 id="set-a-64k-context-before-blaming-the-model"> <a href="#set-a-64k-context-before-blaming-the-model" title="Set a 64K Context Before Blaming the Model">Set a 64K Context Before Blaming the Model</a> <a href="#set-a-64k-context-before-blaming-the-model" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Set a 64K Context Before Blaming the Model">#</a> </h2> <p>Ollama’s documentation gives one direct instruction for repository work: choose a model and <strong>set a 64k or larger context window</strong>, raising it further for larger repositories.</p> <p>The reason is mechanical. Claude Code pulls file contents, diffs, and command output into the context window. A model left at a small default runs out of room partway through a task, and the failure looks like a reasoning problem rather than a settings problem.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Context</th> <th>What It Handles</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td>Under 32K</td> <td>Single-file edits and quick questions</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>64K</strong></td> <td>Multi-file work in a modest repository</td> </tr> <tr> <td>128K</td> <td>Larger repositories and long command output</td> </tr> <tr> <td>256K</td> <td>The full window on Qwen3.8 27B</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><em>If Claude Code loses the thread halfway through a task, check the context setting before you swap models.</em></p> <h2 id="verify-tool-calling-in-one-command"> <a href="#verify-tool-calling-in-one-command" title="Verify Tool Calling in One Command">Verify Tool Calling in One Command</a> <a href="#verify-tool-calling-in-one-command" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Verify Tool Calling in One Command">#</a> </h2> <p>Tool calling is the difference between an agent and a text generator, and it is worth confirming rather than assuming.</p> <p>Once Claude Code is running, ask it:</p> <div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" style="color:#f8f8f2;background-color:#272822;-moz-tab-size:4;-o-tab-size:4;tab-size:4;-webkit-text-size-adjust:none;"><code class="language-text" data-lang="text"><span style="display:flex;"><span>Read the current directory and list all files </span></span></code></pre></div><p><strong>If it lists real files, tool calling works.</strong> If it replies it would read the directory and describes what it expects to find, tool calling is not wired up. You are talking to a chat model with a coding prompt attached, and no amount of prompting fixes it.</p> <p>Work through the fixes in this order:</p> <ol> <li><strong>Switch to a model with confirmed tool support.</strong> Not every model implements it, and the difference is not visible from the parameter count.</li> <li><strong>Confirm the environment points at Ollama.</strong> Run <code>ollama --version</code> and check <code>ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL</code> is set to your local endpoint.</li> <li><strong>Run <code>/status</code> inside Claude Code.</strong> Any base URL or credential in Claude’s own settings overrides the shell variables you recently exported.</li> </ol> <h2 id="what-stays-cloud-only"> <a href="#what-stays-cloud-only" title="What Stays Cloud-Only">What Stays Cloud-Only</a> <a href="#what-stays-cloud-only" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="What Stays Cloud-Only">#</a> </h2> <p>Know the boundary before rebuilding a workflow around local inference.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Feature</th> <th>With Local Models</th> <th>Cloud</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td>Chat and file edits</td> <td>Yes</td> <td>Yes</td> </tr> <tr> <td>Tool calling</td> <td>Model-dependent</td> <td>Yes</td> </tr> <tr> <td>Subagents</td> <td>Yes</td> <td>Yes</td> </tr> <tr> <td>Web search</td> <td>Provided through Ollama</td> <td>Yes</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Cowork</strong></td> <td>Through the Claude Desktop integration</td> <td>Yes</td> </tr> <tr> <td>Auto mode</td> <td>Through the Claude Desktop integration</td> <td>Yes</td> </tr> <tr> <td>Scheduled prompts</td> <td>Through <code>/loop</code> in Claude Code</td> <td>Yes</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>Three caveats on the local side:</p> <ul> <li><strong>Multi-file reasoning degrades before speed does.</strong> A local model handles one file well, three files acceptably, and a whole repository poorly. Plan the task size around it.</li> <li><strong>Some cloud models require a paid Ollama plan</strong>, and cloud models need you signed in with them enabled.</li> <li><strong>The cloud-direct route has feature limits.</strong> Hosted web search and advanced tool controls are not fully supported when you skip the local installation.</li> </ul> <p><em>Local inference is excellent at bounded, verifiable work and worse at sprawling, ambiguous work. This is a useful line to organize around.</em></p> <h2 id="automate-it"> <a href="#automate-it" title="Automate It">Automate It</a> <a href="#automate-it" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Automate It">#</a> </h2> <p>Two features make this more than an interactive toy.</p> <h3 id="headless-runs-for-scripts-and-ci"> <a href="#headless-runs-for-scripts-and-ci" title="Headless Runs for Scripts and CI">Headless Runs for Scripts and CI</a> <a href="#headless-runs-for-scripts-and-ci" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Headless Runs for Scripts and CI">#</a> </h3> <p>The <code>--yes</code> flag skips the interactive selectors and pulls the model when needed. It requires <code>--model</code>, and anything after <code>--</code> goes straight to Claude Code:</p> <div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" style="color:#f8f8f2;background-color:#272822;-moz-tab-size:4;-o-tab-size:4;tab-size:4;-webkit-text-size-adjust:none;"><code class="language-bash" data-lang="bash"><span style="display:flex;"><span>ollama launch claude --model gemma4:cloud --yes -- -p <span style="color:#e6db74">"how does this repository work?"</span> </span></span></code></pre></div><p><strong>Watch the permission model here.</strong> Claude Code prompts before most actions, so a headless run either needs configured permission rules or an isolated environment. Do not point an unsupervised agent at a repository you care about.</p> <h3 id="scheduled-prompts-with-loop"> <a href="#scheduled-prompts-with-loop" title="Scheduled Prompts With /loop">Scheduled Prompts With <code>/loop</code></a> <a href="#scheduled-prompts-with-loop" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Scheduled Prompts With /loop">#</a> </h3> <p>Inside a Claude Code session, <code>/loop</code> runs a prompt or slash command on an interval:</p> <div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" style="color:#f8f8f2;background-color:#272822;-moz-tab-size:4;-o-tab-size:4;tab-size:4;-webkit-text-size-adjust:none;"><code class="language-text" data-lang="text"><span style="display:flex;"><span>/loop 30m Check my open PRs and summarize their status </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>/loop 1h Research the latest AI news and summarize key developments </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>/loop 15m Check for new GitHub issues and triage by priority </span></span></code></pre></div><p><em>This runs while the session is open. It is not a background daemon, so it ends when the session does.</em></p> <h2 id="troubleshooting"> <a href="#troubleshooting" title="Troubleshooting">Troubleshooting</a> <a href="#troubleshooting" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Troubleshooting">#</a> </h2> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Symptom</th> <th>Likely Cause</th> <th>Fix</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Connection refused</strong></td> <td>Ollama is not running</td> <td>Run <code>ollama serve</code>, and confirm with <code>curl http://localhost:11434/api/tags</code></td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Describes actions instead of performing them</strong></td> <td>The selected model lacks tool calling</td> <td>Switch to a model with confirmed tool support</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>A real API key gets used instead of the local endpoint</strong></td> <td><code>ANTHROPIC_API_KEY</code> is still exported</td> <td>Set it to an empty string, as shown above</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Cowork is missing after setup</strong></td> <td>The Claude Code CLI was configured instead of Claude Desktop</td> <td>Use the Ollama <strong>Apps</strong> flow for Cowork</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Generation is slow</strong></td> <td>Context set too high, or a dense model where a sparse one fits</td> <td>Lower the context, then try a mixture-of-experts model</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Exported variables have no effect</strong></td> <td>Claude’s settings files override shell variables</td> <td>Check the settings files, then run <code>/status</code></td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Background requests fail</strong></td> <td>Claude Code reaches for a small model for internal tasks</td> <td>Point the small-model override at the same local model</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><em>Two of these seven come down to the same thing. Most setup problems are a wrong endpoint or a model without tool calling.</em></p> <h2 id="key-takeaways"> <a href="#key-takeaways" title="Key Takeaways">Key Takeaways</a> <a href="#key-takeaways" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Key Takeaways">#</a> </h2> <ul> <li><strong>Claude Desktop and Claude Code are separate integrations.</strong> Cowork lives in Claude Desktop and is configured through the Ollama <strong>Apps</strong> panel on macOS. The CLI path does not give you Cowork.</li> <li><strong>One command starts the CLI route</strong>: <code>ollama launch claude</code>. The manual equivalent needs three variables, and <strong><code>ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=""</code> is the one most guides leave out</strong>.</li> <li><strong>You do not need a local install at all.</strong> Point Claude Code at <code>https://ollama.com</code> with an API key.</li> <li><strong>Set a 64K or larger context before judging a model.</strong> A small window mimics a reasoning failure.</li> <li><strong>Verify tool calling with one request.</strong> If the model describes what it would do, you have a text generator rather than an agent.</li> <li><strong>Ternary Bonsai packs do not work here.</strong> They need Prism ML’s llama.cpp fork, and stock Ollama cannot load them.</li> <li><strong>Disconnecting is safe.</strong> Quitting Ollama restores Claude’s previous configuration, and <code>ollama launch claude-desktop --restore</code> does it from the terminal.</li> </ul> <h2 id="next-steps"> <a href="#next-steps" title="Next Steps">Next Steps</a> <a href="#next-steps" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Next Steps">#</a> </h2> <ol> <li><strong>Install Ollama and pull a model</strong> with confirmed tool support before touching Claude: <strong> <span rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Ollama model library</a> </span> </strong></li> <li><strong>Read Ollama’s own Claude Code page</strong> for the current flags and model list: <strong> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Claude Code integration"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://docs.ollama.com/integrations/claude-code"> <a href="https://docs.ollama.com/integrations/claude-code" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Claude Code integration</a> </span> </strong></li> <li><strong>Use the Claude Desktop page</strong> if Cowork is what you want: <strong> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Claude Desktop integration"> <meta itemprop="url" if you want an always-on agent on a low-power box: <strong> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Which AI Models Can Run on a Raspberry Pi 4 or 5?">
