item.title: Local AI in 2026: A 27B Model Beats Sonnet 4.6, and the Hardware Window Is Closing
item.category: "Local AI" , "Self-Hosted AI" , "Open Source Models" , "AI Hardware" , "Machine Learning" , "Quantization" , "Homelab" , "Privacy" , "AI Economics" , "Consumer Hardware"
item.description: Qwen3.8 27B and its ternary repack Bonsai 2 27B now outscore Claude Sonnet 4.6 on the aggregate intelligence index while running on one consumer GPU. What changed, what the benchmarks show, and why memory pricing makes waiting the most expensive option.
item.content:encoded: <p><strong>A downloadable model which fits on a single consumer graphics card now outscores a frontier API model on the aggregate intelligence index.</strong> Qwen3.8 27B is an open-weight vision-language model released in August 2026. Its ternary repack, Bonsai 2 27B, squeezes the same weights into 5.53 GiB. Together they mark the moment local inference stopped being a hobbyist compromise and became a genuine substitute for a paid API.</p> <p><em>The hardware side of this story is closing fast. Memory prices are the worst they have been in two decades, and they are dragging graphics card prices up with them.</em></p> <p>This article covers what the benchmarks show, what the two models are under the hood, where the open model still loses, and why the next twelve months are the wrong time to wait.</p> <h2 id="the-short-answer"> <a href="#the-short-answer" title="The Short Answer">The Short Answer</a> <a href="#the-short-answer" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="The Short Answer">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>The intelligence gap between a local 27B model and a paid frontier-adjacent API model has closed, and the remaining advantages of the paid model are narrower than the price difference suggests.</strong></p> <p>Three things changed at once:</p> <ul> <li><strong>Open 27B models reached frontier-adjacent scores.</strong> Qwen3.8 27B posts a 33.7 Intelligence Index against Sonnet 4.6 at 30.1, on the same evaluation suite.</li> <li><strong>Ternary quantization cut the memory requirement by roughly two thirds.</strong> Bonsai 2 27B runs the full 27B model in <strong>5.53 GiB</strong>, which fits on cards costing a few hundred dollars.</li> <li><strong>Memory supply went in the wrong direction.</strong> Conventional DRAM contract prices rose <strong>90 to 95 percent</strong> quarter over quarter in early 2026, the steepest quarterly jump TrendForce has recorded, which pushed next-generation GPUs out to 2028.</li> </ul> <p><em>Buying or building now is the cheap option. This is not a sales pitch, it is what the supply data says.</em></p> <h2 id="watch-the-single-gpu-test"> <a href="#watch-the-single-gpu-test" title="Watch the Single-GPU Test">Watch the Single-GPU Test</a> <a href="#watch-the-single-gpu-test" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Watch the Single-GPU Test">#</a> </h2> <p>The claim above deserves a demonstration rather than a table. Bijan Bowen tested Bonsai 2 27B on a single-GPU machine and asked whether it is the best model available for a single card today.</p> <script> function loadLiteYouTubeScript() { if (document.querySelector('script[src^="/p/jsdelivr/npm/@justinribeiro/lite-youtube@1.5.0/lite-youtube.js"]')) { console.log('Lite YouTube script is already loaded.'); top: 0; left: 0; width: 100%; height: 100%; border:0;" title="Bonsai 2 27B First Test – Is THIS the BEST Single-GPU AI Model?"> <span class="lyt-visually-hidden"></span> </a> </noscript> </lite-youtube> </div> <script type="application/ld+json"> { "@context": "https://schema.org", "@type": ["VideoObject", "LearningResource"], "name": "Bonsai 2 27B First Test – Is THIS the BEST Single-GPU AI Model?", "description": "A first look at running the 27B Bonsai 2 ternary model on a single consumer GPU, covering speed, quality, and whether it beats the alternatives.", "thumbnailUrl": ["https:\/\/img.youtube.com\/vi\/OA5cICIzD-c\/maxresdefault.jpg"], "contentUrl": "https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OA5cICIzD-c", "learningResourceType": "Concept Overview", "educationalLevel": "High school (US)" } </script> <p><em>Watch for the output quality rather than the tokens-per-second figure. Speed is the easy part to fix.</em></p> <h2 id="two-names-one-model"> <a href="#two-names-one-model" title="Two Names, One Model">Two Names, One Model</a> <a href="#two-names-one-model" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Two Names, One Model">#</a> </h2> <p>The two models worth understanding here are not competitors. <strong>They are the same weights at two different precisions.</strong></p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th></th> <th>Qwen3.8 27B</th> <th>Ternary Bonsai 2 27B</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>What it is</strong></td> <td>The original open-weight model from Qwen</td> <td>A ternary repack of Qwen3.8-27B by Prism ML</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Weights on disk</strong></td> <td><strong>18 GB</strong></td> <td><strong>5.53 GiB</strong> (PTQ1_0) or <strong>6.70 GiB</strong> (PQ2_0)</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Parameters</strong></td> <td>27B dense</td> <td>26.90B, same architecture</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Context</strong></td> <td>256K</td> <td>262,144 tokens</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Vision</strong></td> <td>Yes, native</td> <td>Yes, separate CLIP projector pack</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Tool calling</strong></td> <td>Yes</td> <td>Yes</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>License</strong></td> <td>Apache 2.0</td> <td>Apache 2.0</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Runtime</strong></td> <td>Ollama, llama.cpp, MLX</td> <td><strong>Prism ML’s llama.cpp fork only</strong></td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>The Ollama library page for <code>qwen3.8</code> lists the 27B model at <strong>18 GB</strong> with a 256K context window, vision support, tool calling, and a separate MLX build for Apple Silicon. The ternary repack on Ollama is a mirror of Prism ML’s Apache-2.0 GGUF packs, republished with matching checksums.</p> <p><strong>So the practical question is not which model to choose.</strong> It is how much memory you are willing to spend for the same intelligence. The ternary version costs roughly a third of the memory and gives up little.</p> <script type="application/ld+json"> { "@context": "https://schema.org/", "@type": "ImageObject", "contentUrl": "https:\/\/simeononsecurity.com\/local-ai-architecture-comparison.webp", "caption": "Diagram comparing the memory footprint of the same 27B model at 18 GB standard precision against 5.53 GiB in ternary weights, showing both fitting into a single consumer GPU", "license": "https://simeononsecurity.com/termsandconditions/", "acquireLicensePage": "https://simeononsecurity.com/contactus/", "creditText": "SimeonOnSecurity", "creator": { "@type": "Person", "name": "SimeonOnSecurity" }, "copyrightNotice": "SimeonOnSecurity", "associatedArticle": { "@type": "NewsArticle", "headline": "simeononsecurity", "url": "https:\/\/simeononsecurity.com\/", "datePublished": "2026-10-02 21:20:37.669240184 \u002b0000 UTC m=\u002b337.393965945", "author": { "@type": "Person", "name": "SimeonOnSecurity", "url": "https:\/\/simeononsecurity.com\/authors\/simeononsecurity" } } } </script> <center> <figure align="center" style="text-align: center; margin: 0 auto;" itemscope itemtype="http://schema.org/ImageObject"> <meta property="article:published_time" content="2026-10-02 21:20:37.669240184 +0000 UTC m=+337.393965945"> <meta property="article:author" content="SimeonOnSecurity"> <meta property="article:author:url" content="https://simeononsecurity.com/authors/simeononsecurity"> <meta property="og:license" content="https://simeononsecurity.com/termsandconditions/"> <meta property="og:see_also" content="https://simeononsecurity.com/contactus/"> <meta property="og:copyright" content="SimeonOnSecurity"> <img align="center" style="text-align: center; margin: 0 auto; max-width: 80%; max-height: 600px; min-width: 100px; min-height: 100px; height: auto; width: auto;" src="https://simeononsecurity.com/local-ai-architecture-comparison.webp" alt="Diagram comparing the memory footprint of the same 27B model at 18 GB standard precision against 5.53 GiB in ternary weights, showing both fitting into a single consumer GPU"loading="lazy" fetchpriority="low" itemprop="contentUrl" /> </figure> </center> <h2 id="the-benchmark-comparison"> <a href="#the-benchmark-comparison" title="The Benchmark Comparison">The Benchmark Comparison</a> <a href="#the-benchmark-comparison" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="The Benchmark Comparison">#</a> </h2> <p>Artificial Analysis scores both models on the same suite. The results deserve to be read row by row rather than summarized, because the two models win in different places.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Benchmark</th> <th>Qwen3.8 27B</th> <th>Claude Sonnet 4.6</th> <th>Leader</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Intelligence Index</strong></td> <td><strong>33.7</strong></td> <td>30.1</td> <td>Open</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Coding Index</strong></td> <td><strong>68.1</strong></td> <td>63.0</td> <td>Open</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Agentic Index</strong></td> <td><strong>45.8</strong></td> <td>31.8</td> <td>Open</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>GPQA Diamond</strong></td> <td><strong>90.5%</strong></td> <td>87.5%</td> <td>Open</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Humanity’s Last Exam</strong></td> <td><strong>33.9%</strong></td> <td>33.6%</td> <td>Open</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>AA-LCR (long context)</strong></td> <td><strong>82.0%</strong></td> <td>80.0%</td> <td>Open</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>GDPval-AA</strong></td> <td><strong>45.4%</strong></td> <td>36.0%</td> <td>Open</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>CritPt (research physics)</strong></td> <td><strong>5.4%</strong></td> <td>3.1%</td> <td>Open</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Non-hallucination rate</strong></td> <td><strong>69.7%</strong></td> <td>51.6%</td> <td>Open</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>SciCode</strong></td> <td>46.6%</td> <td><strong>50.1%</strong></td> <td>Sonnet</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>AA-Omniscience accuracy</strong></td> <td>15.6%</td> <td><strong>40.9%</strong></td> <td>Sonnet</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><em>The open model leads nine of eleven comparable rows, including every aggregate index.</em></p> <h3 id="where-the-open-model-leads"> <a href="#where-the-open-model-leads" title="Where the Open Model Leads">Where the Open Model Leads</a> <a href="#where-the-open-model-leads" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Where the Open Model Leads">#</a> </h3> <p>The three aggregate indexes carry the headline. <strong>Intelligence 33.7 against 30.1, Coding 68.1 against 63.0, Agentic 45.8 against 31.8.</strong> The agentic gap is the widest of the three, and it matters most for anyone running automated multi-step workflows rather than single prompts.</p> <p>For percentile context, Artificial Analysis places Qwen3.8 27B <strong>better than 86 percent of models</strong> on the agentic index and 76 percent on coding. Sonnet 4.6 sits at 68 percent and 72 percent respectively. On graduate-level science reasoning the open model posts <strong>90.5 percent</strong> on GPQA Diamond.</p> <h3 id="where-sonnet-46-still-leads"> <a href="#where-sonnet-46-still-leads" title="Where Sonnet 4.6 Still Leads">Where Sonnet 4.6 Still Leads</a> <a href="#where-sonnet-46-still-leads" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Where Sonnet 4.6 Still Leads">#</a> </h3> <p>Two rows go the other way, and neither is minor.</p> <p><strong>AA-Omniscience measures whether a model answers knowledge questions correctly in the first place. Sonnet 4.6 scores 40.9 percent against 15.6 percent.</strong> This is a wide gap in factual reliability, and it is the strongest single argument for paying for a premium model.</p> <p>The non-hallucination row needs care. Qwen’s 69.7 percent against Sonnet’s 51.6 percent looks like a clean win, and in isolation it is. But the metric describes the share of <em>non-correct</em> answers which avoid fabrication. A model with lower accuracy produces more non-correct answers, so the two percentages describe different populations and are not directly comparable. <strong>Read the accuracy row first.</strong></p> <p>Sonnet also takes SciCode at 50.1 percent against 46.6 percent, and it reports figures on two evaluations the open model’s card does not list, IFBench and Terminal-Bench Hard. Those cannot be compared at all.</p> <h3 id="two-honest-caveats"> <a href="#two-honest-caveats" title="Two Honest Caveats">Two Honest Caveats</a> <a href="#two-honest-caveats" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Two Honest Caveats">#</a> </h3> <p><strong>The release dates are six months apart.</strong> Sonnet 4.6 shipped in February 2026. Qwen3.8 27B shipped in August 2026. A February frontier model against an August open model is not a like-for-like contest.</p> <p><strong>Sonnet 4.6 is no longer Anthropic’s frontier.</strong> Sonnet 5 and Opus 5 now sit above it in the lineup. The open 27B caught a mid-2026 flagship. It has not caught the current top of the stack, and anyone claiming otherwise is overreading the table.</p> <p><em>Benchmarks measure benchmark performance. The only score which matters is the one your own workload produces.</em></p> <h2 id="what-ternary-weights-change"> <a href="#what-ternary-weights-change" title="What Ternary Weights Change">What Ternary Weights Change</a> <a href="#what-ternary-weights-change" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="What Ternary Weights Change">#</a> </h2> <p>Bonsai 2 is not a smaller model. It is the same 26.90B model at a much lower numerical precision, and the published GGUF metadata makes the trade explicit.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Property</th> <th>Value</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Architecture</strong></td> <td><code>qwen35</code>, hybrid attention with full attention every fourth layer, plus state-space layers</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Parameters</strong></td> <td>26.90B</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Blocks</strong></td> <td>64</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Embedding width</strong></td> <td>5120</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Attention</strong></td> <td>24 query heads, 4 KV heads, key/value length 256</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Context</strong></td> <td>262,144 tokens, RoPE base 1e7</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Weight format</strong></td> <td>Ternary, group size 128. PQ2_0 at 2.13 bits per weight, PTQ1_0 at 1.75</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Vision tower</strong></td> <td>CLIP, 460.73M parameters, shipped as a separate projector pack</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>License</strong></td> <td>Apache 2.0</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>Ternary weights mean each parameter carries one of three values instead of sixteen.</strong> The compression is the entire point, and it is why a full 27B model fits in 5.53 GiB rather than 18 GB.</p> <h3 id="measured-throughput"> <a href="#measured-throughput" title="Measured Throughput">Measured Throughput</a> <a href="#measured-throughput" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Measured Throughput">#</a> </h3> <p>Benchmarked with <code>llama-bench</code> on an RTX 5090 32 GB, every layer offloaded, flash attention enabled, mean of three runs:</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Pack</th> <th>Weights</th> <th>Prefill (pp512)</th> <th>Decode (tg128)</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>PQ2_0</strong></td> <td>6.70 GiB</td> <td><strong>3802.74 tok/s</strong></td> <td><strong>135.41 tok/s</strong></td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>PTQ1_0</strong></td> <td>5.53 GiB</td> <td>1876.31 tok/s</td> <td>131.41 tok/s</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>PQ2_0 prefills <strong>2.03 times faster</strong> than PTQ1_0 while decode is a statistical tie, so PQ2_0 is the sensible default and PTQ1_0 is for when the last 1.2 GiB matters. Through <code>llama-server</code> with a 65K context, decode held at <strong>136.5 tok/s</strong> on a single streaming request.</p> <p><strong>Decode speed is the figure you feel in daily use.</strong> 135 tokens per second comfortably outruns reading speed. Latency is not the reason to run local inference, since a hosted API is fast enough. Cost, privacy, and control are.</p> <h3 id="the-catch-nobody-mentions"> <a href="#the-catch-nobody-mentions" title="The Catch Nobody Mentions">The Catch Nobody Mentions</a> <a href="#the-catch-nobody-mentions" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="The Catch Nobody Mentions">#</a> </h3> <p><strong>Stock Ollama cannot load these files.</strong> The ternary kernels live in Prism ML’s llama.cpp fork. Verified against Ollama 0.34.2, the load fails with <code>unsupported tensor "output.weight" size overflows</code>. The runtime recognizes the <code>qwen35</code> architecture but has no <code>pq2_0</code> or <code>ptq1_0</code> anywhere in its libraries, and no Hadamard activation runtime.</p> <p>There is a second trap worth knowing before you spend an evening on it. <strong>The F16 pack of this family looks like a safe fallback and is not.</strong> Its tensors are ordinary F16 and F32, so it parses and loads without complaint, then decodes incoherent text. The weights sit in a rotated basis declared in <code>prism.hadamard.*</code> metadata, and a runtime either applies the matching rotation or produces nonsense. At 50.1 GiB the F16 pack also will not fully offload to a 32 GB card.</p> <p><em>Read the model card before downloading. A community mirror is not a supported build, and this one says so plainly on the page.</em></p> <h2 id="the-moe-wave-behind-this"> <a href="#the-moe-wave-behind-this" title="The MoE Wave Behind This">The MoE Wave Behind This</a> <a href="#the-moe-wave-behind-this" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="The MoE Wave Behind This">#</a> </h2> <p>Dense 27B models are half the story. Mixture-of-experts models activate a small slice of their parameters per token, which changes the economics again.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Model</th> <th>Total / Active</th> <th>Context</th> <th>Note</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Qwen3.8 2.4T A95B</strong></td> <td>2.4T / 95B</td> <td>1.0M</td> <td>Open-weight sibling of Qwen3.8 Max</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Qwen3.6 35B A3B</strong></td> <td>35B / 3B</td> <td>262K</td> <td>Apache 2.0, hybrid sparse MoE</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Qwen3 Coder Next</strong></td> <td>80B / 3B</td> <td>256K</td> <td>Open weight, built for always-on coding agents</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>Qwen3 Coder Next is the one to watch for local work.</strong> 80B total parameters with only 3B active per token, positioned for always-on agent deployment inside CLI and IDE environments. A model activating 3B parameters generates at the speed of a 3B model while drawing on 80B of stored capability. The upstream notes describe performance comparable to models with 10 to 20 times the active compute.</p> <p><em>The dense 27B is the safe choice today. Sparse models are where the efficiency curve is still bending.</em></p> <script type="application/ld+json"> { "@context": "https://schema.org/", "@type": "ImageObject", "contentUrl": "https:\/\/simeononsecurity.com\/local-ai-moe-dense-tradeoff.webp", "caption": "Chart illustrating the difference between a dense 27B model activating all parameters per token and a sparse mixture-of-experts model activating only 3 billion of 80 billion parameters", "license": "https://simeononsecurity.com/termsandconditions/", "acquireLicensePage": "https://simeononsecurity.com/contactus/", "creditText": "SimeonOnSecurity", "creator": { "@type": "Person", "name": "SimeonOnSecurity" }, "copyrightNotice": "SimeonOnSecurity", "associatedArticle": { "@type": "NewsArticle", "headline": "simeononsecurity", "url": "https:\/\/simeononsecurity.com\/", "datePublished": "2026-10-02 21:20:37.669594147 \u002b0000 UTC m=\u002b337.394319894", "author": { "@type": "Person", "name": "SimeonOnSecurity", "url": "https:\/\/simeononsecurity.com\/authors\/simeononsecurity" } } } </script> <center> <figure align="center" style="text-align: center; margin: 0 auto;" itemscope itemtype="http://schema.org/ImageObject"> <meta property="article:published_time" content="2026-10-02 21:20:37.669594147 +0000 UTC m=+337.394319894"> <meta property="article:author" content="SimeonOnSecurity"> <meta property="article:author:url" content="https://simeononsecurity.com/authors/simeononsecurity"> <meta property="og:license" content="https://simeononsecurity.com/termsandconditions/"> <meta property="og:see_also" content="https://simeononsecurity.com/contactus/"> <meta property="og:copyright" content="SimeonOnSecurity"> <img align="center" style="text-align: center; margin: 0 auto; max-width: 80%; max-height: 600px; min-width: 100px; min-height: 100px; height: auto; width: auto;" src="https://simeononsecurity.com/local-ai-moe-dense-tradeoff.webp" alt="Chart illustrating the difference between a dense 27B model activating all parameters per token and a sparse mixture-of-experts model activating only 3 billion of 80 billion parameters"loading="lazy" fetchpriority="low" itemprop="contentUrl" /> </figure> </center> <h2 id="the-hardware-window-is-closing"> <a href="#the-hardware-window-is-closing" title="The Hardware Window Is Closing">The Hardware Window Is Closing</a> <a href="#the-hardware-window-is-closing" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="The Hardware Window Is Closing">#</a> </h2> <p>Here is the part of this story with a deadline attached.</p> <p>Local inference got cheap at the exact moment the memory it depends on started getting expensive. Those two trends are on a collision course, and the collision is already visible in retail pricing.</p> <h3 id="what-happened-to-memory-prices"> <a href="#what-happened-to-memory-prices" title="What Happened to Memory Prices">What Happened to Memory Prices</a> <a href="#what-happened-to-memory-prices" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="What Happened to Memory Prices">#</a> </h3> <p><strong>Conventional DRAM contract prices rose 90 to 95 percent quarter over quarter in the first quarter of 2026</strong>, the steepest quarterly increase TrendForce has on record. NAND flash climbed 55 to 60 percent in the same window.</p> <p>The pressure did not ease. TrendForce data puts second-quarter DRAM up another <strong>58 to 63 percent</strong> and NAND up 70 to 75 percent. Even the third-quarter moderation, DRAM up 13 to 18 percent and NAND up 10 to 15 percent, is inflation stacking on top of two record-setting quarters rather than relief.</p> <p>The cause is structural rather than cyclical. AI data center buildouts absorb memory capacity which used to serve phones, laptops, and game consoles, and memory makers allocate to the higher-margin orders first. Analysts tracking module supply project DRAM chip supply to module makers falling by more than 70 percent in 2027.</p> <p><strong>Intel’s chief executive put a number on it.</strong> Speaking at the AI Infrastructure Summit in Santa Clara on September 15, 2026, Lip-Bu Tan said memory prices had already risen “five, six, and seven times” over prior levels, and warned 70 to 80 percent of a low-cost laptop’s bill of materials now goes to memory alone. He has separately said there is no relief until 2028.</p> <p><em>Independent reporting on the per-area comparison between DRAM wafers and leading-edge logic wafers carries an important caveat. Spot prices are not contract prices, and DDR5 spot procurement is thin enough for the comparison to be suggestive rather than settled. The direction of travel is not in question.</em></p> <script type="application/ld+json"> { "@context": "https://schema.org/", "@type": "ImageObject", "contentUrl": "https:\/\/simeononsecurity.com\/local-ai-memory-price-trend-2026.webp", "caption": "Chart showing quarter over quarter DRAM contract price increases through 2026, beginning with a 90 to 95 percent jump in the first quarter and moderating to 13 to 18 percent by the third quarter", "license": "https://simeononsecurity.com/termsandconditions/", "acquireLicensePage": "https://simeononsecurity.com/contactus/", "creditText": "SimeonOnSecurity", "creator": { "@type": "Person", "name": "SimeonOnSecurity" }, "copyrightNotice": "SimeonOnSecurity", "associatedArticle": { "@type": "NewsArticle", "headline": "simeononsecurity", "url": "https:\/\/simeononsecurity.com\/", "datePublished": "2026-10-02 21:20:37.669962416 \u002b0000 UTC m=\u002b337.394688163", "author": { "@type": "Person", "name": "SimeonOnSecurity", "url": "https:\/\/simeononsecurity.com\/authors\/simeononsecurity" } } } </script> <center> <figure align="center" style="text-align: center; margin: 0 auto;" itemscope itemtype="http://schema.org/ImageObject"> <meta property="article:published_time" content="2026-10-02 21:20:37.669962416 +0000 UTC m=+337.394688163"> <meta property="article:author" content="SimeonOnSecurity"> <meta property="article:author:url" content="https://simeononsecurity.com/authors/simeononsecurity"> <meta property="og:license" content="https://simeononsecurity.com/termsandconditions/"> <meta property="og:see_also" content="https://simeononsecurity.com/contactus/"> <meta property="og:copyright" content="SimeonOnSecurity"> <img align="center" style="text-align: center; margin: 0 auto; max-width: 80%; max-height: 600px; min-width: 100px; min-height: 100px; height: auto; width: auto;" src="https://simeononsecurity.com/local-ai-memory-price-trend-2026.webp" alt="Chart showing quarter over quarter DRAM contract price increases through 2026, beginning with a 90 to 95 percent jump in the first quarter and moderating to 13 to 18 percent by the third quarter"loading="lazy" fetchpriority="low" itemprop="contentUrl" /> </figure> </center> <h3 id="what-it-did-to-graphics-cards"> <a href="#what-it-did-to-graphics-cards" title="What It Did to Graphics Cards">What It Did to Graphics Cards</a> <a href="#what-it-did-to-graphics-cards" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="What It Did to Graphics Cards">#</a> </h3> <p>Memory is a large share of a graphics card’s bill of materials, so DRAM pricing feeds straight into GPU pricing.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Card</th> <th>Early 2025</th> <th>September 2026</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Nvidia RTX 5090</strong></td> <td>$1,999</td> <td><strong>over $5,000</strong></td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Asus RTX 5080</strong></td> <td>$1,199</td> <td>$1,595</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>AMD RX 9070 XT</strong></td> <td>roughly $830</td> <td><strong>over $1,037</strong></td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>Those increases arrived in coordinated waves through 2026 rather than as isolated spikes. Nvidia raised prices in January, again in May on the RTX 5090 specifically, and again later in the year. AMD followed in August with an increase of at least 10 percent across select Radeon cards and GDDR6 memory kits, attributed directly to memory costs.</p> <p><strong>The next generation slipped instead of shipping.</strong> Nvidia’s RTX 60 series is now expected in 2028, skipping 2027 entirely, with memory availability cited as the cause.</p> <p><em>The card you buy today is not competing against a cheaper card next year. It is competing against a more expensive version of itself.</em></p> <h2 id="why-waiting-is-the-expensive-choice"> <a href="#why-waiting-is-the-expensive-choice" title="Why Waiting Is the Expensive Choice">Why Waiting Is the Expensive Choice</a> <a href="#why-waiting-is-the-expensive-choice" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Why Waiting Is the Expensive Choice">#</a> </h2> <p>The usual hardware advice is to wait for the next generation. In a supply-constrained memory market this advice works against you.</p> <p>Three points make the case.</p> <p><strong>Prices are already up and still climbing.</strong> A 90 to 95 percent quarterly jump in DRAM contract prices is not a blip which reverses on a quarterly cycle. TrendForce is forecasting further growth in the third quarter, not decline, and Intel’s chief executive has put relief at 2028.</p> <p><strong>There is no 2027 product to wait for.</strong> When next-generation consumer GPUs slip to 2028, the waiting strategy stretches to a two-year horizon. This is most of a hardware refresh cycle spent waiting for nothing.</p> <p><strong>The models are good enough already.</strong> This is the part which changed in 2026. Two years ago, local hardware bought a visibly compromised experience. Today the same money buys a 27B model at 135 tokens per second with a 262K context window, outscoring a premium API model on the aggregate intelligence index.</p> <p><em>If you were waiting for local models to get good, the wait is over. If you are waiting for hardware to get cheaper, the supply data says you are waiting until 2028.</em></p> <h2 id="what-to-build"> <a href="#what-to-build" title="What to Build">What to Build</a> <a href="#what-to-build" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="What to Build">#</a> </h2> <p>Matching hardware to the models above is straightforward, because ternary weights shrank the requirement.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Tier</th> <th>Memory</th> <th>What It Runs Comfortably</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Entry</strong></td> <td>8 to 12 GB VRAM</td> <td>Ternary 27B at 5.53 to 6.70 GiB, with headroom for context</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Practical</strong></td> <td>16 to 24 GB VRAM</td> <td>Full 18 GB Qwen3.8 27B, or the ternary pack at a long context</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Comfortable</strong></td> <td>32 GB VRAM</td> <td>Ternary 27B at the full 262K context, or an 80B MoE at 3B active</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Unified memory</strong></td> <td>64 to 128 GB</td> <td>Larger sparse MoE models on Apple Silicon or a unified-memory desktop</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>A few practical notes which matter more than the tier table:</p> <ul> <li><strong>Buy memory, not the flagship GPU.</strong> The 5.53 GiB ternary pack means the entry tier is genuinely usable. Spending the difference on system RAM and storage helps more than chasing a halo card at 2026 prices.</li> <li><strong>Unified-memory systems are the value play.</strong> A machine with 64 GB or more of shared memory runs larger sparse models at a fraction of the cost of a discrete card with the same capacity.</li> <li><strong>Power and cooling count.</strong> A rig running inference for hours behaves differently from one running benchmarks for minutes.</li> <li><strong>Run the ternary pack alongside a smaller model.</strong> A 3B model answers quick questions while the 27B handles the hard ones.</li> </ul> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <center> <meta itemprop="name" content="simeononsecurity"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://ollama.com/tobestyledintro/Ternary-Bonsai-2-27B"> <a href="https://ollama.com/tobestyledintro/Ternary-Bonsai-2-27B" title="simeononsecurity" target="_blank" class="markdown-btn" rel="noopener external" alt="simeononsecurity" target="_blank" > <button class="markdown-button"> Download Ternary Bonsai 2 27B </button> </a> <p></p> </center> </span> <h2 id="where-premium-models-still-earn-their-price"> <a href="#where-premium-models-still-earn-their-price" title="Where Premium Models Still Earn Their Price">Where Premium Models Still Earn Their Price</a> <a href="#where-premium-models-still-earn-their-price" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Where Premium Models Still Earn Their Price">#</a> </h2> <p>The case for the premium tier is real, and it is narrower than the marketing suggests.</p> <p><strong>Factual reliability is the honest answer.</strong> AA-Omniscience accuracy is 40.9 percent for Sonnet 4.6 against 15.6 percent for the open 27B. When a wrong answer costs a client, a diagnosis, or a legal position, a 25-point accuracy gap matters more than any aggregate index.</p> <p><strong>Long agentic chains are the second answer.</strong> Sonnet 4.6 reports 53.0 percent on Terminal-Bench Hard and 75.7 percent on τ²-Bench Telecom, which measure sustained tool use and multi-turn agent behavior. The open model’s card reports no comparable figures, and the absence is not encouraging.</p> <p><strong>The third answer is operational.</strong> A hosted API brings no driver updates, no quantization quirks, no fork of llama.cpp to track, and no rotated weight basis to get right. Someone else handles uptime and someone else gets paged at 3 AM.</p> <h3 id="the-question-worth-asking"> <a href="#the-question-worth-asking" title="The Question Worth Asking">The Question Worth Asking</a> <a href="#the-question-worth-asking" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="The Question Worth Asking">#</a> </h3> <p>So where does the premium tier stand outside the enterprise?</p> <p><strong>For knowledge-critical work, it still stands.</strong> Research, legal analysis, medical questions, financial modeling, and anything where a confident wrong answer is expensive. This is a genuine category, and the accuracy gap is a genuine reason to pay.</p> <p><strong>For generative work, the justification is thinning fast.</strong> Drafting, summarizing, refactoring code, reformatting data, classifying documents, and running automated pipelines are all tasks where output is verified before it is trusted. The accuracy gap costs little when a human or a test suite checks the result first. For those workloads, paying per token for a 30.1 index while a 33.7 index runs free on hardware you already own is a hard position to defend.</p> <p><strong>The decision has moved from capability to consequence.</strong> Two years ago the question was whether a local model was good enough to do the work at all. Today the question is what a mistake costs and how you would catch it.</p> <p><em>The enterprise premium buys reliability, compliance, and somebody else’s on-call rotation. Everyone else is paying for a difference which stops mattering the moment a test suite runs.</em></p> <h2 id="key-takeaways"> <a href="#key-takeaways" title="Key Takeaways">Key Takeaways</a> <a href="#key-takeaways" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Key Takeaways">#</a> </h2> <ul> <li><strong>A local 27B model now outscores Claude Sonnet 4.6 on the aggregate intelligence index</strong>, 33.7 against 30.1, and leads on coding, agentic tasks, long context, and graduate-level science reasoning.</li> <li><strong>Sonnet 4.6 still wins on factual accuracy</strong>, 40.9 percent against 15.6 percent on AA-Omniscience, which is the strongest remaining argument for the premium tier.</li> <li><strong>Ternary quantization is the change which makes this practical.</strong> Bonsai 2 27B runs the same 26.90B model in 5.53 GiB instead of 18 GB, and both are Apache 2.0.</li> <li><strong>Stock Ollama cannot run the ternary packs.</strong> They need Prism ML’s llama.cpp fork, and the F16 fallback silently produces incoherent output rather than failing.</li> <li><strong>Measured speed is 135 tokens per second decode</strong> on an RTX 5090, which outruns reading speed by a wide margin.</li> <li><strong>Memory prices are the reason to act now.</strong> DRAM contract prices rose 90 to 95 percent in a single quarter in 2026, and next-generation consumer GPUs slipped to 2028.</li> <li><strong>The RTX 5090 went from $1,999 to over $5,000</strong> in under two years, and every tier moved with it.</li> </ul> <h2 id="next-steps"> <a href="#next-steps" title="Next item.title: Mining Pearl (PRL) in 2026: Setup, Profitability, and Whether the Chain Is Useful
item.description: How to mine Pearl (PRL) with SRBMiner, what proof-of-useful-work computes, why margins compressed after launch, and an honest assessment of whether the chain produces anything anyone buys.
item.content:encoded: <p><strong>Pearl is the first proof-of-useful-work chain to reach real production scale, and the work it pays miners for is matrix multiplication rather than hashing.</strong> Mainnet launched on <strong>April 27, 2026</strong>, and within weeks it triggered a GPU mining rush built on a claim of securing a blockchain while producing AI compute in the same pass.</p> <p><em>The claim is technically real and economically unproven, and the gap between those two things is the whole story.</em></p> <p>This guide covers how to mine PRL, what the miner computes, why the margins compressed so quickly after launch, and a direct answer to whether the chain produces anything of value.</p> <h2 id="the-short-answer"> <a href="#the-short-answer" title="The Short Answer">The Short Answer</a> <a href="#the-short-answer" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="The Short Answer">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Pearl is a genuine technical achievement wrapped around a mining economics problem which every new coin faces.</strong></p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Question</th> <th>Short Answer</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>What is it?</strong></td> <td>A Bitcoin-derived L1 secured by proof-of-useful-work, where miners run noisy matrix multiplication instead of SHA-256</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>How do you mine it?</strong></td> <td>SRBMiner-MULTI with <code>--algorithm pearlhash</code> against a pool, or Pearl’s own vLLM miner against your own node</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Why was it profitable?</strong></td> <td>Launch-era emissions outpaced difficulty for a few weeks, then difficulty caught up</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Is it still profitable?</strong></td> <td>Hardware dependent, and the window is narrowing. See the margins section below</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Is the chain useful?</strong></td> <td><strong>The mechanism is, the marketplace is not yet.</strong> Details in the verdict section</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>The single most important thing to understand before you build a rig for this:</strong> the miner developer’s own release notes for version 3.6.8 state Pearl has an upgrade coming which will make consumer-grade GPUs “pretty much useless” for mining it. This is not an outside critic. This is the person writing the miner.</p> <h2 id="what-pearl-actually-is"> <a href="#what-pearl-actually-is" title="What Pearl Actually Is">What Pearl Actually Is</a> <a href="#what-pearl-actually-is" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="What Pearl Actually Is">#</a> </h2> <p>Pearl is an L1 blockchain built by <strong>Pearl Research Labs</strong> and described in its own repository as follows:</p> <blockquote> <p>“Pearl is an L1 blockchain based on the Proof-of-Useful-Work protocol, where mining is done as a by-product of arbitrary matrix multiplication.”</p> </blockquote> <p>The repository ships a full node, a wallet daemon, an SPV light client, a zero-knowledge proving system, and a GPU miner. It is licensed under the <strong>ISC License</strong>, a permissive copyfree license, and the chain infrastructure was forked from well-tested Bitcoin projects: <strong>btcd</strong> for the node, <strong>btcwallet</strong> for the wallet, and <strong>neutrino</strong> for the light client.</p> <p><strong>The design borrows deliberately from Bitcoin</strong>, down to a <strong>2.1 billion PRL maximum supply</strong>, exactly 100 times Bitcoin’s 21 million, with a declining block reward and roughly two-minute blocks.</p> <p><em>The plumbing is conservative on purpose. The novelty is entirely in the work function.</em></p> <h3 id="proof-of-useful-work-explained"> <a href="#proof-of-useful-work-explained" title="Proof-of-Useful-Work, Explained">Proof-of-Useful-Work, Explained</a> <a href="#proof-of-useful-work-explained" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Proof-of-Useful-Work, Explained">#</a> </h3> <p>Proof-of-useful-work is an old idea with a poor track record. The pitch has always been to replace Bitcoin’s deliberately wasteful hashing with computation producing something valuable on the side. Almost every previous attempt failed for the same reason: the “useful” work turned out to be either not useful, or not verifiable cheaply enough to secure a chain.</p> <p>Pearl implements it through a routine it calls <strong>NoisyGEMM</strong>. Mechanically, a miner runs noisy matrix multiplications on a GPU, hashes the result into a commitment, and wraps the work in a <strong>zero-knowledge proof</strong> so the chain verifies it cheaply.</p> <p>The scheme rests on a 2025 cryptography paper, <strong>“Proofs of Useful Work from Arbitrary Matrix Multiplication”</strong> by Komargodski, Schen, and Weinstein. The paper claims an overhead of roughly <strong>1 + o(1) against a naive matrix multiply</strong>, which is the load-bearing claim of the entire project. If securing the chain costs almost nothing on top of the underlying compute, then the compute is nearly free to produce.</p> <p><strong>The pitch is 2-for-1. One GPU pass, two outputs.</strong></p> <p>The claim is what separates Pearl from a decade of failed PoUW concepts. Most of them had no such bound.</p> <script type="application/ld+json"> { "@context": "https://schema.org/", "@type": "ImageObject", "contentUrl": "https:\/\/simeononsecurity.com\/pearl-noisygemm-proof-of-useful-work-flow.webp", "caption": "Diagram showing how Pearl proof-of-useful-work converts a GPU matrix multiplication into a hash commitment and a zero-knowledge proof which the chain verifies cheaply", "license": "https://simeononsecurity.com/termsandconditions/", "acquireLicensePage": "https://simeononsecurity.com/contactus/", "creditText": "SimeonOnSecurity", "creator": { "@type": "Person", "name": "SimeonOnSecurity" }, "copyrightNotice": "SimeonOnSecurity", "associatedArticle": { "@type": "NewsArticle", "headline": "simeononsecurity", "url": "https:\/\/simeononsecurity.com\/", "datePublished": "2026-10-02 21:20:37.684711197 \u002b0000 UTC m=\u002b337.409436943", "author": { "@type": "Person", "name": "SimeonOnSecurity", "url": "https:\/\/simeononsecurity.com\/authors\/simeononsecurity" } } } </script> <center> <figure align="center" style="text-align: center; margin: 0 auto;" itemscope itemtype="http://schema.org/ImageObject"> <meta property="article:published_time" content="2026-10-02 21:20:37.684711197 +0000 UTC m=+337.409436943"> <meta property="article:author" content="SimeonOnSecurity"> <meta property="article:author:url" content="https://simeononsecurity.com/authors/simeononsecurity"> <meta property="og:license" content="https://simeononsecurity.com/termsandconditions/"> <meta property="og:see_also" content="https://simeononsecurity.com/contactus/"> <meta property="og:copyright" content="SimeonOnSecurity"> <img align="center" style="text-align: center; margin: 0 auto; max-width: 80%; max-height: 600px; min-width: 100px; min-height: 100px; height: auto; width: auto;" src="https://simeononsecurity.com/pearl-noisygemm-proof-of-useful-work-flow.webp" alt="Diagram showing how Pearl proof-of-useful-work converts a GPU matrix multiplication into a hash commitment and a zero-knowledge proof which the chain verifies cheaply"loading="lazy" fetchpriority="low" itemprop="contentUrl" /> </figure> </center> <h3 id="what-the-miner-actually-computes"> <a href="#what-the-miner-actually-computes" title="What the Miner Actually Computes">What the Miner Actually Computes</a> <a href="#what-the-miner-actually-computes" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="What the Miner Actually Computes">#</a> </h3> <p>There are two paths, and they are not equivalent.</p> <p><strong>The official path</strong> ships in Pearl’s own repository. It has two components: <code>pearl-gateway</code>, which bridges to your node, and <code>vllm-miner</code>, which does the GPU work through vLLM. The gateway talks to a local <code>pearld</code> node over JSON-RPC and exposes a mining interface on a Unix socket or TCP port 8337.</p> <p><strong>The pool path</strong> is what most people run. SRBMiner-MULTI implements Pearl as the <code>pearlhash</code> algorithm, and you point it at a pool.</p> <p>The difference matters for the usefulness argument. <strong>The official miner loads a real language model.</strong> Pearl’s own documentation example runs <code>pearl-ai/Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct-pearl</code> inside Docker with GPU passthrough. This is a 70-billion-parameter model serving inference while the same pass secures the chain.</p> <p><em>Producing inference is genuine capability. Producing inference nobody buys is a cost centre with a blockchain attached. Keep those two ideas separate.</em></p> <h2 id="why-it-was-profitable-and-why-that-changed"> <a href="#why-it-was-profitable-and-why-that-changed" title="Why It Was Profitable, and Why That Changed">Why It Was Profitable, and Why That Changed</a> <a href="#why-it-was-profitable-and-why-that-changed" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Why It Was Profitable, and Why That Changed">#</a> </h2> <p>Pearl’s initial profitability was not a mystery, and it was not about AI. It was the standard new-coin emission curve.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>When</th> <th>What Happened</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>April 27, 2026</strong></td> <td>Mainnet launch</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Late May 2026</strong></td> <td>A GPU mining rush begins, five weeks into the chain’s life</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>June 2026</strong></td> <td>Estimated RTX 5090 daily revenue <strong>roughly halved</strong> as difficulty climbed</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Mid to late 2026</strong></td> <td>Miner software efficiency improves sharply, partly offsetting the decline</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>The compression mechanism is mechanical:</p> <ol> <li><strong>Launch emissions are large and difficulty is low.</strong> Early miners collect outsized rewards per unit of hashrate.</li> <li><strong>Those rewards attract hashrate.</strong> More GPUs point at the chain.</li> <li><strong>Difficulty rises to match.</strong> Reward per GPU falls.</li> </ol> <p>Pearl adds a second downward force, because its block reward declines by design. <strong>Revenue has two reasons to fall and difficulty has one reason to rise.</strong></p> <h3 id="the-countervailing-force-software-efficiency"> <a href="#the-countervailing-force-software-efficiency" title="The Countervailing Force: Software Efficiency">The Countervailing Force: Software Efficiency</a> <a href="#the-countervailing-force-software-efficiency" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="The Countervailing Force: Software Efficiency">#</a> </h3> <p>Margins did not collapse uniformly, because the miners kept getting faster. SRBMiner’s pearlhash changelog tracks the improvement:</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Version</th> <th>Pearlhash Change</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>3.6.1</strong></td> <td>Added B300 support. B300 SXM6 at <code>--gpu-cclock 1600</code> reported around <strong>706 TH/s at 920W</strong></td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>3.6.2</strong></td> <td>Improvements for H100, H200, and 4000 series</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>3.6.8</strong></td> <td>Hashrate improvement, mostly 3000 series</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>3.6.9</strong></td> <td><strong>Huge efficiency improvements.</strong> Same or better hashrate at much lower power across most architectures</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>For a home miner, electricity is the dominant operating cost.</strong> A release which holds hashrate while cutting power improves margin directly, with no change in token price or network difficulty. This is why a rig which looked marginal in June looks reasonable in September on identical hardware.</p> <p><em>Efficiency gains are a real tailwind and a temporary one, because the same improvements are available to everyone else pushing difficulty alongside you.</em></p> <h2 id="the-rank-penalty-softfork"> <a href="#the-rank-penalty-softfork" title="The Rank Penalty Softfork">The Rank Penalty Softfork</a> <a href="#the-rank-penalty-softfork" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="The Rank Penalty Softfork">#</a> </h2> <p>On the night of <strong>August 6, 2026</strong>, a softfork activated on Pearl at approximately <strong>02:00 UTC, block 96251</strong>. Many miners learned about it the next morning when their hashrate dropped.</p> <p>Pearl’s protocol has a <strong>noise rank</strong> parameter, and a higher rank made it easier to win a jackpot for the same amount of work. <strong>Some miners mined deliberately at high ranks and collected disproportionately large effective hashrate and rewards.</strong> The team investigated what it described as abnormal mining optimizations and responded with a penalty mechanism.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Rule Change</th> <th>Effect</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Minimum allowed rank</strong></td> <td>128</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Jackpot bound</strong></td> <td>Now scaled by the formula <code>128 / rank</code></td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Advantage of high ranks</strong></td> <td>Removed entirely</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>Impact on miners:</strong></p> <ul> <li>Mining above rank 128 cost those operators <strong>50% to 87.5% of effective hashrate</strong></li> <li>Mining at or below rank 128 cost almost nothing</li> </ul> <p>Two lessons apply to anyone starting now.</p> <p><strong>Your hashrate is a function of software and network rules, not only your GPU.</strong> A configuration that benchmarked well in July was not measuring what the operator assumed it was.</p> <p><strong>Update the miner when the network changes.</strong> Older versions either lose significant efficiency or stop working correctly under the new rules. Pool software was updated ahead of the fork, including PearlFortune v2.1.0 and Krig (Kryptex) v1.1.0, alongside miners such as Tw-pearl-miner v3.3.0 and Wildrig 0.49.8.</p> <p><em>A softfork which cuts a reward by up to 87.5% is the clearest possible argument for watching project announcements rather than only reading a payout dashboard.</em></p> <h2 id="the-two-ways-to-mine-pearl"> <a href="#the-two-ways-to-mine-pearl" title="The Two Ways to Mine Pearl">The Two Ways to Mine Pearl</a> <a href="#the-two-ways-to-mine-pearl" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="The Two Ways to Mine Pearl">#</a> </h2> <table> <thead> <tr> <th></th> <th>Pool Mining</th> <th>Official vLLM Miner</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Software</strong></td> <td>SRBMiner-MULTI</td> <td><code>pearl-gateway</code> plus <code>vllm-miner</code></td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Algorithm</strong></td> <td><code>pearlhash</code></td> <td>NoisyGEMM through vLLM</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Node required</strong></td> <td>No</td> <td><strong>Yes, a synced <code>pearld</code></strong></td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Payout</strong></td> <td>Pool, PPLNS or solo</td> <td>Direct to your mining address</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Runs a real model</strong></td> <td>No</td> <td><strong>Yes, for example Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct</strong></td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Setup effort</strong></td> <td>Low</td> <td>High, needs the CUDA toolkit and Python 3.12</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Best for</strong></td> <td>Getting hashrate on the network quickly</td> <td>Contributing compute to the network directly</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>Start with pool mining.</strong> It requires no node, no sync, and no model download, and it gets you hashrate and a payout address in minutes. Move to the official miner only if you specifically want to serve inference or run a node.</p> <script type="application/ld+json"> { "@context": "https://schema.org/", "@type": "ImageObject", "contentUrl": "https:\/\/simeononsecurity.com\/pearl-mining-pool-vs-vllm-miner-comparison.webp", "caption": "Diagram comparing Pearl pool mining with SRBMiner against the official vLLM miner, showing the node, gateway, and inference components required by each path", "license": "https://simeononsecurity.com/termsandconditions/", "acquireLicensePage": "https://simeononsecurity.com/contactus/", "creditText": "SimeonOnSecurity", "creator": { "@type": "Person", "name": "SimeonOnSecurity" }, "copyrightNotice": "SimeonOnSecurity", "associatedArticle": { "@type": "NewsArticle", "headline": "simeononsecurity", "url": "https:\/\/simeononsecurity.com\/", "datePublished": "2026-10-02 21:20:37.685093451 \u002b0000 UTC m=\u002b337.409819199", "author": { "@type": "Person", "name": "SimeonOnSecurity", "url": "https:\/\/simeononsecurity.com\/authors\/simeononsecurity" } } } </script> <center> <figure align="center" style="text-align: center; margin: 0 auto;" itemscope itemtype="http://schema.org/ImageObject"> <meta property="article:published_time" content="2026-10-02 21:20:37.685093451 +0000 UTC m=+337.409819199"> <meta property="article:author" content="SimeonOnSecurity"> <meta property="article:author:url" content="https://simeononsecurity.com/authors/simeononsecurity"> <meta property="og:license" content="https://simeononsecurity.com/termsandconditions/"> <meta property="og:see_also" content="https://simeononsecurity.com/contactus/"> <meta property="og:copyright" content="SimeonOnSecurity"> <img align="center" style="text-align: center; margin: 0 auto; max-width: 80%; max-height: 600px; min-width: 100px; min-height: 100px; height: auto; width: auto;" src="https://simeononsecurity.com/pearl-mining-pool-vs-vllm-miner-comparison.webp" alt="Diagram comparing Pearl pool mining with SRBMiner against the official vLLM miner, showing the node, gateway, and inference components required by each path"loading="lazy" fetchpriority="low" itemprop="contentUrl" /> </figure> </center> <h2 id="hardware-notes-for-consumer-gpus"> <a href="#hardware-notes-for-consumer-gpus" title="Hardware Notes for Consumer GPUs">Hardware Notes for Consumer GPUs</a> <a href="#hardware-notes-for-consumer-gpus" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Hardware Notes for Consumer GPUs">#</a> </h2> <p>Pearl is notable for what it does not demand. Hashrate Index noted the hardware profile is <strong>unusually light: low RAM, low storage, low CPU, and none of the expensive multi-fiber networking a real training cluster needs.</strong> One analyst described it as “a great way to use up equipment.”</p> <p>This is the honest appeal. <strong>Existing GPUs, including older ones, earn something.</strong></p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>GPU Class</th> <th>Observation</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>RTX 5090 and 4090</strong></td> <td>Highest revenue per card, and the segments where the early revenue halving was measured</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>RTX 3000 series</strong></td> <td>Specifically targeted by the 3.6.8 hashrate improvement. Still viable, efficiency matters more than raw speed</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Data center accelerators</strong></td> <td>H100, H200 and B300 were added and improved through 2026. This is where the hashrate race is heading</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Older or low-VRAM cards</strong></td> <td>Marginal. Check a live profitability calculator before building anything</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>The pattern across every release in 2026 is the same.</strong> Flagship accelerators were added first and improved most, because the hashrate is worth the most there. Consumer cards got attention when the 3000 series had headroom to recover.</p> <p><em>Efficiency tuning produces more revenue than chasing clock speed. This is the opposite of what most mining guides teach.</em></p> <h2 id="setting-it-up-on-linux"> <a href="#setting-it-up-on-linux" title="Setting It Up on Linux">Setting It Up on Linux</a> <a href="#setting-it-up-on-linux" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Setting It Up on Linux">#</a> </h2> <p>The pool route needs four things: the SRBMiner binary, a Pearl wallet address, a pool endpoint, and a service to keep it running.</p> <h3 id="get-a-wallet-address-first"> <a href="#get-a-wallet-address-first" title="Get a Wallet Address First">Get a Wallet Address First</a> <a href="#get-a-wallet-address-first" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Get a Wallet Address First">#</a> </h3> <p>Pearl mining addresses start with <strong><code>prl1</code></strong>. The official wallet is <strong>Oyster</strong>, the HD wallet daemon in Pearl’s repository, which exposes JSON-RPC and gRPC interfaces. Generate a <strong>Taproot</strong> mining address from it.</p> <p>Do not skip this step or reuse an address from another chain. <strong>Rewards sent to an address you do not control are gone.</strong></p> <h3 id="pool-ports-and-merge-mining"> <a href="#pool-ports-and-merge-mining" title="Pool, Ports, and Merge Mining">Pool, Ports, and Merge Mining</a> <a href="#pool-ports-and-merge-mining" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Pool, Ports, and Merge Mining">#</a> </h3> <p>The largest Pearl pool is LuckyPool, which offers ports tiered by expected hashrate:</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Port</th> <th>Starting Difficulty</th> <th>Recommended Hashrate</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>3360</strong></td> <td>2M</td> <td>Under 500 TH/s</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>3361</strong></td> <td>4M</td> <td>500 to 1000 TH/s</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>3362</strong></td> <td>8M</td> <td>Above 1000 TH/s</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>Choose the port matching your rig’s actual hashrate. <strong>A single consumer GPU belongs on 3360.</strong> Sending a small rig to a high-difficulty port means long gaps between shares and worse variance without any benefit.</p> <p>Two pool features are worth knowing about:</p> <ul> <li><strong>Solo mining</strong> works on any port by prefixing the wallet with <code>solo:</code>. You keep the whole block reward when you find one, and you earn nothing when you do not. With consumer hashrate, expect a long wait.</li> <li><strong>Nockchain merge mining</strong> earns NOCK alongside PRL for the same hashrate, by appending <code>+NOCK_ADDRESS</code> to your Pearl wallet. The pool pays NOCK on Nockchain itself, so a wrapped token address starting <code>0x</code> cannot receive it. <strong>Your miner must support merge mining, and a miner without it still mines Pearl normally.</strong></li> </ul> <p>The pool publishes both <code>luckypool.io</code> hosts and <code>lproute.com</code> route hosts. If your network blocks direct mining traffic, keep the port and swap the domain.</p> <h2 id="a-working-install-script"> <a href="#a-working-install-script" title="A Working Install Script">A Working Install Script</a> <a href="#a-working-install-script" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="A Working Install Script">#</a> </h2> <p>The script below provisions SRBMiner as a systemd service on a Debian or Ubuntu host. It detects every GPU, applies per-card overclock flags, verifies the download against the published MD5, writes the unit and a logrotate policy, and restarts the service.</p> <div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" style="color:#f8f8f2;background-color:#272822;-moz-tab-size:4;-o-tab-size:4;tab-size:4;-webkit-text-size-adjust:none;"><code class="language-bash" data-lang="bash"><span style="display:flex;"><span><span style="color:#75715e">#!/usr/bin/env bash </span></span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span><span style="color:#75715e"># install-pearl-miner.sh -- provision SRBMiner (Pearl / PRL) as a systemd service.</span> </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span><span style="color:#75715e"># Run: sudo bash install-pearl-miner.sh</span> </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>set -euo pipefail </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> </span></span><span prl1... add +NOCK_ADDRESS to merge mine</span> </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>WORKER<span style="color:#f92672">=</span><span style="color:#e6db74">"</span><span </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span><span style="color:#75715e"># RTX 3070-class tuning. MCORE is an absolute memory-clock lock, well below the</span> </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span><span style="color:#75715e"># card's stock 7001 MHz, so it is a deliberate efficiency underclock rather than</span> </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span><span style="color:#75715e"># a performance overclock. Set any value to "" to disable that flag.</span> </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>CCLOCK<span style="color:#f92672">=</span><span style="color:#e6db74">"</span><span style="color:#e6db74">${</span>CCLOCK<span style="color:#66d9ef">:-</span>1560<span style="color:#e6db74">}</span><span style="color:#e6db74">"</span> </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>MCLOCK<span style="color:#f92672">=</span><span style="color:#e6db74">"</span><span style="color:#e6db74">${</span>MCLOCK<span style="color:#66d9ef">:-</span>5001<span style="color:#e6db74">}</span><span style="color:#e6db74">"</span> </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>COFFSET<span style="color:#f92672">=</span><span style="color:#e6db74">"</span><span style="color:#e6db74">${</span>COFFSET<span style="color:#66d9ef">:-</span>150<span style="color:#e6db74">}</span><span style="color:#e6db74">"</span> </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>PLIMIT<span style="color:#f92672">=</span><span style="color:#e6db74">"</span><span style="color:#e6db74">${</span>PLIMIT<span style="color:#66d9ef">:-</span>180<span style="color:#e6db74">}</span><span style="color:#e6db74">"</span> </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>FAN<span style="color:#f92672">=</span><span style="color:#e6db74">"</span><span style="color:#e6db74">${</span>FAN<span style="color:#66d9ef">:-</span><span style="color:#e6db74">}</span><span style="color:#e6db74">"</span> </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>THERMAL<span style="color:#f92672">=</span><span style="color:#e6db74">"</span><span style="color:#e6db74">${</span>THERMAL<span style="color:#66d9ef">:-</span>88<span style="color:#e6db74">}</span><span style="color:#e6db74">"</span> </span></span></code></pre></div><p>The tuning block deserves a note, because it looks wrong at a glance. <strong><code>MCORE=5001</code> sits below the stock memory clock on a 3070.</strong> This is intentional. Pearl rewards memory efficiency, and locking memory lower cuts power draw more than it cuts hashrate. <strong>Do not copy overclock numbers from a hashrate database row without checking which GPU the row was benchmarked on.</strong> Benchmark rows are frequently captured on a different card than the one in your machine.</p> <div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0"
