running any mining binary.</strong> The releases publish per-file hashes, and a miner runs with root privileges reading your GPU. Skipping the check means trusting a download you never inspected.</p> <p>Two operational details in the service unit:</p> <div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" style="color:#f8f8f2;background-color:#272822;-moz-tab-size:4;-o-tab-size:4;tab-size:4;-webkit-text-size-adjust:none;"><code class="language-bash" data-lang="bash"><span style="display:flex;"><span>cat ><span style="color:#e6db74">"</span>$UNIT<span style="color:#e6db74">"</span> <span style="color:#e6db74"><<EOF </span></span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span><span style="color:#e6db74">[Unit] </span></span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span><span style="color:#e6db74">Description=Pearl (PRL) SRBMiner v$SRB_VERSION - $WORKER </span></span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span><span style="color:#e6db74">After=network.target </span></span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span><span style="color:#e6db74"> </span></span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span><span style="color:#e6db74">[Service] </span></span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span><span style="color:#e6db74">Type=simple </span></span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span><span style="color:#e6db74">User=root </span></span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span><span style="color:#e6db74">WorkingDirectory=$MINER_DIR </span></span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span><span style="color:#e6db74">ExecStart=$MINER_DIR/SRBMiner-MULTI --algorithm $ALGO --pool $POOL --wallet $WALLET --worker $WORKER --disable-cpu --gpu-reset-oc$OC$THERMAL_ARG --api-enable --api-port 21550 --api-rig-name $WORKER </span></span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span><span style="color:#e6db74">Restart=always </span></span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span><span style="color:#e6db74">RestartSec=10 </span></span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span><span style="color:#e6db74">StandardOutput=append:$LOG </span></span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span><span style="color:#e6db74">StandardError=append:$LOG </span></span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span><span style="color:#e6db74">LimitNOFILE=65536 </span></span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span><span style="color:#e6db74"> </span></span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span><span style="color:#e6db74">[Install] </span></span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span><span style="color:#e6db74">WantedBy=multi-user.target </span></span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span><span style="color:#e6db74">EOF</span> </span></span></code></pre></div><ul> <li><strong><code>--disable-cpu</code></strong> keeps the miner off the CPU, which matters on a machine doing anything else.</li> <li><strong><code>--shutdown-temperature 88</code></strong> stops the miner rather than cooking a card when a fan fails.</li> <li><strong><code>--gpu-reset-oc</code></strong> clears any previous clock settings before applying yours, which prevents stale settings from a prior run carrying over.</li> <li><strong><code>Restart=always</code> with <code>RestartSec=10</code></strong> survives driver hiccups, which are common on multi-GPU rigs.</li> <li><strong><code>--api-enable</code> opens a monitoring port.</strong> Confirm which interface port 21550 binds to and keep it off any untrusted network. A rig monitoring endpoint does not need to be reachable from outside the machine.</li> </ul> <p>Finally, log rotation, because mining logs grow without limit:</p> <div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" style="color:#f8f8f2;background-color:#272822;-moz-tab-size:4;-o-tab-size:4;tab-size:4;-webkit-text-size-adjust:none;"><code class="language-bash" data-lang="bash"><span style="display:flex;"><span>cat >/etc/logrotate.d/pearl-miner <span style="color:#e6db74"><<EOF </span></span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span><span style="color:#e6db74">$LOG { </span></span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span><span style="color:#e6db74"> weekly </span></span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span><span style="color:#e6db74"> rotate 4 </span></span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span><span style="color:#e6db74"> compress </span></span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span><span style="color:#e6db74"> delaycompress </span></span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span><span style="color:#e6db74"> missingok </span></span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span><span style="color:#e6db74"> notifempty </span></span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span><span style="color:#e6db74"> copytruncate </span></span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span><span style="color:#e6db74">} </span></span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span><span style="color:#e6db74">EOF</span> </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>systemctl daemon-reload </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>systemctl enable <span style="color:#e6db74">"</span>$SVC<span style="color:#e6db74">"</span> >/dev/null 2>&<span style="color:#ae81ff">1</span> <span style="color:#f92672">||</span> true </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>systemctl restart <span style="color:#e6db74">"</span>$SVC<span style="color:#e6db74">"</span> </span></span></code></pre></div><p><em><code>copytruncate</code> matters here. SRBMiner holds the log open, and a rotation which renames the file leaves the miner writing to a deleted inode, so the disk fills anyway.</em></p> <p>Monitor progress with a filtered tail rather than the raw log:</p> <div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" style="color:#f8f8f2;background-color:#272822;-moz-tab-size:4;-o-tab-size:4;tab-size:4;-webkit-text-size-adjust:none;"><code class="language-bash" data-lang="bash"><span style="display:flex;"><span>grep -aE <span style="color:#e6db74">'Hashrate|accepted|Pool:'</span> /var/log/pearl-miner.log | tail -20 </span></span></code></pre></div><h2 id="what-has-gone-wrong"> <a href="#what-has-gone-wrong" title="What Has Gone Wrong">What Has Gone Wrong</a> <a href="#what-has-gone-wrong" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="What Has Gone Wrong">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>A Pearl mining guide has to start with the problems, because all of them affect your payout.</strong> Four things went wrong between July and September 2026.</p> <h3 id="the-market-is-one-exchange-deep"> <a href="#the-market-is-one-exchange-deep" title="The Market Is One Exchange Deep">The Market Is One Exchange Deep</a> <a href="#the-market-is-one-exchange-deep" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="The Market Is One Exchange Deep">#</a> </h3> <p>On <strong>July 23, 2026</strong> PRL printed an all-time low of <strong>$0.1399</strong>, down from roughly <strong>87 cents</strong> in June. It fell <strong>24.2% in a single day</strong> and <strong>26.7% over the week</strong>, while the broader crypto market rose about 2% in the same window.</p> <p>The cause was not news. It was depth.</p> <ul> <li><strong>95.17% of all reported volume</strong> sat on <strong>one exchange called SafeTrade</strong>, which carries no CoinGecko trust score. A single PRL/USDT pair accounted for <strong>$738,399 of roughly $775,000</strong> traded in 24 hours.</li> <li>Both SafeTrade pairs reported <strong>$0.00 order book depth</strong>.</li> </ul> <p><em>An ordinary sell order moves a market like that by double digits. That is a structural fact about the token rather than a temporary condition.</em></p> <p>The supply picture amplifies it:</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Metric</th> <th>Value</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Market cap</strong></td> <td>$55.7 million</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Fully diluted valuation</strong></td> <td>$458.6 million</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Ratio</strong></td> <td>Over 8x</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Circulating supply</strong></td> <td>255 million of 2.1 billion, under <strong>13%</strong></td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>A token priced on one thin book, with 87% of supply still locked or unissued, has a wide range of plausible prices.</strong> Plan what you do with payouts accordingly, and do not treat a spot price as a reliable revenue estimate.</p> <h3 id="a-pool-was-hacked"> <a href="#a-pool-was-hacked" title="A Pool Was Hacked">A Pool Was Hacked</a> <a href="#a-pool-was-hacked" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="A Pool Was Hacked">#</a> </h3> <p>An issue opened on <strong>September 18, 2026</strong> reports that Pearl wallet 2.0.5 “still suspended sending and receiving after its pool hack from month ago.”</p> <p><strong>Read that twice, because it carries two facts.</strong> A Pearl pool was compromised around <strong>August 2026</strong>, and the official wallet responded by suspending transfers. The suspension was still in place a month later.</p> <p>The pool you choose holds your payout. Verify its incident history before pointing a rig at it.</p> <h3 id="the-project-website-is-unreachable"> <a href="#the-project-website-is-unreachable" title="The Project Website Is Unreachable">The Project Website Is Unreachable</a> <a href="#the-project-website-is-unreachable" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="The Project Website Is Unreachable">#</a> </h3> <p>At the time of writing, <strong>pearlresearch.ai does not reach a server.</strong> Every public resolver returns a null route, <code>0.0.0.0</code>, for the apex domain and for subdomains including <code>compute</code> and <code>explorer</code>. Domain registration reports <code>ACTIVE</code>, so this is a deliberate DNS state rather than an expiry.</p> <p><strong>Three links a mining guide would normally send you to are dead</strong>, including the block explorer. Mining Pool Stats still lists them, which is how readers end up chasing an address that never loads.</p> <p>Use <strong> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="prlscan.com"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://prlscan.com"> <a href="https://prlscan.com" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >prlscan.com</a> </span> </strong> for block exploration instead. I confirmed it returns a working page.</p> <h3 id="the-software-still-has-open-bugs"> <a href="#the-software-still-has-open-bugs" title="The Software Still Has Open Bugs">The Software Still Has Open Bugs</a> <a href="#the-software-still-has-open-bugs" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="The Software Still Has Open Bugs">#</a> </h3> <p>The public issue tracker shows unresolved problems as of late September 2026. Issue creation is restricted, so this is a partial view.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Issue</th> <th>Date</th> <th>What It Means</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Desktop wallet RPC code inactive</strong></td> <td>Sep 22</td> <td>The wallet cannot reach a node</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Testnet cannot sync from scratch</strong>, nodes wedge at height 36760</td> <td>Sep 22</td> <td>Sync logic has a blocking defect</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Wallet send and receive still suspended</strong> after the pool hack</td> <td>Sep 18</td> <td>Transfers are affected</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>macOS ARM64 release has an invalid code signature</strong></td> <td>Sep 17</td> <td>Will not run without bypassing Gatekeeper</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Prune mode drops certificates needed to verify headers</strong></td> <td>Aug 30</td> <td>A validation defect</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Node wedges indefinitely when no connected peer is a sync candidate</strong></td> <td>Aug 30</td> <td>Sync fragility</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>pearl-gemm fails on RTX 5070</strong>, hash kernels work but GEMM kernels fail</td> <td>Aug 31</td> <td>Newest consumer cards are unsupported</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><em>The RTX 5070 entry is the one to notice if you planned to buy a current card for this. The newest consumer architecture did not work with the official GEMM path.</em></p> <p><strong>What this adds up to:</strong> the mining software is actively maintained while the user-facing and market layers are the weak parts. SRBMiner shipped 3.6.9 with major efficiency gains the day before those wallet complaints landed.</p> <h2 id="is-the-chain-useful"> <a href="#is-the-chain-useful" title="Is the Chain Useful?">Is the Chain Useful?</a> <a href="#is-the-chain-useful" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Is the Chain Useful?">#</a> </h2> <p>This question deserves a careful answer, because “useful work” does double duty in most coverage. <strong>It describes a consensus mechanism and an economic claim, and those two things have sharply different answers.</strong></p> <h3 id="functionally-useful-partly"> <a href="#functionally-useful-partly" title="Functionally Useful: Partly">Functionally Useful: Partly</a> <a href="#functionally-useful-partly" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Functionally Useful: Partly">#</a> </h3> <p><strong>The chain runs. The surrounding product does not fully work.</strong></p> <p>What holds up:</p> <ul> <li><strong>Mainnet launched April 27, 2026</strong> and has produced blocks since.</li> <li><strong>The full stack ships and is real</strong>: a node, a wallet daemon, an SPV light client, a zero-knowledge proving system, and a GPU miner, all in one repository.</li> <li><strong>The plumbing is proven at the code level.</strong> The node, wallet, and light client fork from <strong>btcd</strong>, <strong>btcwallet</strong>, and <strong>neutrino</strong>, Bitcoin projects with years of adversarial testing behind them.</li> <li><strong>The codebase is a serious effort.</strong> 315 stars, 76 forks, more than 6,800 commits, and a public tracker where contributors file precise bug reports.</li> <li><strong>The mining side works.</strong> SRBMiner shipped 247 releases and optimized <code>pearlhash</code> repeatedly. Multiple pools run. Nockchain merge mining works.</li> </ul> <p>What does not:</p> <ul> <li><strong>Transfers are suspended in the official wallet</strong> following the pool hack.</li> <li><strong>The desktop wallet cannot reach a node</strong> as of late September, per its own tracker.</li> <li><strong>Sync logic has blocking defects</strong> on both testnet and mainnet paths.</li> <li><strong>The project website is unreachable.</strong></li> <li><strong>The newest consumer GPUs fail the GEMM path.</strong></li> </ul> <p><strong>The honest summary is that Pearl is functional at the protocol layer and unreliable at the product layer.</strong> For someone studying proof-of-useful-work, that is worth attention. For someone expecting to mine and get paid reliably, it is a warning.</p> <h3 id="technically-useful-the-mechanism-yes-the-marketplace-no"> <a href="#technically-useful-the-mechanism-yes-the-marketplace-no" title="Technically Useful: The Mechanism Yes, The Marketplace No">Technically Useful: The Mechanism Yes, The Marketplace No</a> <a href="#technically-useful-the-mechanism-yes-the-marketplace-no" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Technically Useful: The Mechanism Yes, The Marketplace No">#</a> </h3> <p>Here the honest answer splits in two, and conflating the halves is what most coverage gets wrong.</p> <p><strong>The mechanism is genuinely novel.</strong> Pearl’s NoisyGEMM routine runs noisy matrix multiplications on a GPU, hashes the result into a commitment, and wraps the work in a zero-knowledge proof so verification stays cheap. The construction rests on a real paper, “Proofs of Useful Work from Arbitrary Matrix Multiplication” by Komargodski, Schen, and Weinstein, which claims overhead of roughly <strong>1 + o(1)</strong> against a naive matrix multiply.</p> <p><strong>If the bound holds, the chain secures itself at almost no cost above the underlying compute.</strong> This is the thing previous PoUW attempts never managed. The math is not decorative.</p> <p><strong>The marketplace is not established.</strong> Hashrate Index described it directly: “today most of the useful work is inference nobody bought, which makes the bulk of current mining AI-shaped proof-of-work.” This is a fair summary. The compute is the right shape, and nobody is paying for most of it.</p> <p>The exception matters and it is real. Pearl landed an exclusive partnership with <strong>Together AI</strong>, which put a discounted Pearl-powered inference endpoint into production. This is the first customer, and it is why the project deserves more credit than the average AI-branded coin.</p> <p><strong>One customer is a proof of concept. It is not a market.</strong></p> <h3 id="practically-useful-for-now-with-a-closing-window"> <a href="#practically-useful-for-now-with-a-closing-window" title="Practically Useful: For Now, With a Closing Window">Practically Useful: For Now, With a Closing Window</a> <a href="#practically-useful-for-now-with-a-closing-window" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Practically Useful: For Now, With a Closing Window">#</a> </h3> <p>For a miner, the practical picture is mixed and time-limited.</p> <p><strong>Working in Pearl’s favour:</strong></p> <ul> <li>Existing GPUs earn something, including older cards, because the hardware profile is light</li> <li>Continuous miner efficiency improvements improve margin directly on hardware you already own</li> <li>Merge mining with Nockchain stacks a second revenue stream on the same hashrate</li> <li>Overhead near zero means the chain does not burn your electricity on pointless hashing</li> </ul> <p><strong>Working against it:</strong></p> <ul> <li><strong>The block reward declines by design.</strong> This is Bitcoin’s model, and emissions shrink whether or not the price rises.</li> <li><strong>Difficulty only goes up.</strong> Revenue per GPU has one direction available to it.</li> <li><strong>Liquidity is thin.</strong> Hashrate Index flags whether PRL earns liquidity beyond minor exchanges as a thing to track. Thin liquidity means wider spreads and worse realized prices.</li> <li><strong>The protocol upgrade.</strong> SRBMiner’s 3.6.8 release notes state a coming Pearl upgrade will make consumer-grade GPUs “pretty much useless.” Take it seriously. It comes from the developer who benefits from people continuing to mine.</li> </ul> <h2 id="the-verdict"> <a href="#the-verdict" title="The Verdict">The Verdict</a> <a href="#the-verdict" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="The Verdict">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Pearl is the most credible proof-of-useful-work implementation yet built, and it has not proven its work is useful in the economic sense.</strong></p> <p>Four claims, in order of confidence:</p> <ol> <li> <p><strong>The consensus mechanism works and the cryptographic claim is real.</strong> Pearl solved the hard technical problem, which was making PoUW cheap to verify. This is a genuine contribution regardless of what happens to the token.</p> </li> <li> <p><strong>The compute is a promise rather than a product.</strong> Producing inference is not the same as selling it, and today the paid share is one partnership against a network full of speculative hashrate. The flywheel is designed. It is not turning.</p> </li> <li> <p><strong>The window for consumer GPU mining is narrowing, and the protocol will close it.</strong> A falling reward, rising difficulty, a stated upgrade which removes consumer viability, and a softfork which already cut some miners by up to 87.5% add up to a time-boxed opportunity rather than an income stream.</p> </li> <li> <p><strong>The operational and market layers are the real risk, not the cryptography.</strong> A hacked pool, suspended wallet transfers, an unreachable website, unresolved sync defects, and 95% of volume sitting on one exchange with no order book depth are the things which decide whether mining pays. The protocol is the part that works.</p> </li> </ol> <p><em>The sharpest way to put it: Pearl solved the hard problem and has not yet solved the easy-sounding one. Making matrix multiplication provably useful is cryptography. Finding a buyer for the output is sales.</em></p> <p><strong>If you are here to mine, treat it as a short-horizon use of hardware you already own.</strong> Do not buy GPUs for Pearl. Do not build a rig on the assumption current numbers persist, because the emission schedule and the miner developer’s own release notes both say they will not.</p> <p><strong>If you are here to understand proof-of-useful-work, Pearl is the most important implementation to study right now.</strong> It is the first to reach real scale, which means the next two years of evidence will show whether “useful work” is a genuine primitive or a recurring failure with better cryptography.</p> <script type="application/ld+json"> { "@context": "https://schema.org/", "@type": "ImageObject", "contentUrl": "https:\/\/simeononsecurity.com\/pearl-prl-usefulness-assessment.webp", "caption": "Diagram assessing Pearl proof-of-useful-work across three axes, with functional maturity rated high, the technical mechanism rated strong while its paid marketplace is rated unproven, and practical mining viability rated time-limited", "license": "https://simeononsecurity.com/termsandconditions/", "acquireLicensePage": "https://simeononsecurity.com/contactus/", "creditText": "SimeonOnSecurity", "creator": { "@type": "Person", "name": "SimeonOnSecurity" }, "copyrightNotice": "SimeonOnSecurity", "associatedArticle": { "@type": "NewsArticle", "headline": "simeononsecurity", "url": "https:\/\/simeononsecurity.com\/", "datePublished": "2026-10-02 21:20:37.685427741 \u002b0000 UTC m=\u002b337.410153489", "author": { "@type": "Person", "name": "SimeonOnSecurity", "url": "https:\/\/simeononsecurity.com\/authors\/simeononsecurity" } } } </script> <center> <figure align="center" style="text-align: center; margin: 0 auto; max-width: 80%; max-height: 600px; min-width: 100px; min-height: 100px; height: auto; width: auto;" src="https://simeononsecurity.com/pearl-prl-usefulness-assessment.webp" alt="Diagram assessing Pearl proof-of-useful-work across three axes, with functional maturity rated high, the technical mechanism rated strong while its paid marketplace is rated unproven, and practical mining viability rated time-limited"loading="lazy" fetchpriority="low" itemprop="contentUrl" /> </figure> </center> <h2 id="key-takeaways"> <a href="#key-takeaways" title="Key Takeaways">Key Takeaways</a> <a href="#key-takeaways" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Key Takeaways">#</a> </h2> <ul> <li><strong>Pearl is a Bitcoin-derived L1 secured by proof-of-useful-work</strong>, where miners run noisy matrix multiplication instead of hashing. Mainnet launched <strong>April 27, 2026</strong>.</li> <li><strong>Mine it two ways</strong>: SRBMiner with <code>--algorithm pearlhash</code> against a pool, or Pearl’s own <code>vllm-miner</code> against a synced node.</li> <li><strong>Early profitability was a launch emission curve</strong>, not an AI demand story. Estimated RTX 5090 daily revenue roughly halved within weeks of the rush.</li> <li><strong>Miner efficiency releases partly offset the decline.</strong> Version 3.6.9 delivered the same or better hashrate at much lower power.</li> <li><strong>A rank-penalty softfork on August 6, 2026 cut effective hashrate by 50% to 87.5%</strong> for miners running above rank 128. Update your miner when network rules change.</li> <li><strong>The token trades one exchange deep.</strong> 95.17% of volume sat on SafeTrade with zero order book depth, and under 13% of supply circulates.</li> <li><strong>A pool was hacked around August 2026</strong>, and official wallet transfers were still suspended a month later.</li> <li><strong>The project website does not resolve.</strong> Use <code>prlscan.com</code> for block exploration instead.</li> <li><strong>Tune for efficiency, not clock speed.</strong> Pearl rewards memory efficiency, and underclocking memory cuts power more than it costs hashrate.</li> <li><strong>Use port 3360 on a single consumer GPU</strong>, and append <code>+NOCK_ADDRESS</code> to merge mine Nockchain.</li> <li><strong>Verify the MD5</strong> on any miner download before running it as root.</li> <li><strong>Mine with hardware you already own.</strong> The chain is functional at the protocol layer, unreliable at the product item.title: We Mapped 146,526 ‘Flock Cameras.’ 50,278 Were ClickShare Systems
item.category: "Security Research" , "Privacy Technology" , "Open Source Projects" , "Data Journalism" , "Counter Surveillance"
item.description: Our audit of Flock Finder found 50,278 Barco ClickShare devices and thousands of other false positives inside a 146,526-record camera map. Here is what failed, how we proved it, and what we changed.
item.content:encoded: <p><strong>We put 146,526 points on a surveillance-camera map. At least 50,278 of them were Barco ClickShare presentation systems. Conference-room hardware accounted for more than one-third of what our headline called “Cameras Mapped.”</strong></p> <p>This was our project, our data pipeline, and our mistake. Flock Finder queried WiGLE every day for MAC-address prefixes observed on Flock Safety cameras, published the results at full coordinate precision, and rendered them as equivalent pins. The records carried the word <code>suspected</code> in their metadata and the documentation mentioned false positives. The map and headline still communicated certainty.</p> <p>When we finally ran a frequency histogram over the SSID column, the dataset explained the failure in minutes. ClickShare was only the largest category. Another 6,099 records named themselves <code>SMARTGATE_*</code>; 3,801 began with the generic WiFi Direct prefix <code>DIRECT-</code>; 314 were the exact name <code>AndroidAP</code>; 138 said <code>Audi HUD</code>; 133 said <code>MAX-PRINTER</code>; and 30 contained another detector’s verdict string. In total, <strong>60,793 rows, or 41.5%, matched the original audit’s known-other naming rules.</strong></p> <p>We have now changed Flock Finder to publish evidence classes per record, exclude known-other hardware from the default map and headline, expose filters, flag records outside the primary market, and separate high-confidence prefixes from contract-manufacturer prefixes. This article documents the error, the evidence, and the limits that remain.</p> <hr> <h2 id="how-community-alpr-detection-works"> <a href="#how-community-alpr-detection-works" title="How Community ALPR Detection Works">How Community ALPR Detection Works</a> <a href="#how-community-alpr-detection-works" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="How Community ALPR Detection Works">#</a> </h2> <p>Community-built Flock detectors generally combine three kinds of wireless evidence:</p> <ol> <li><strong>WiFi MAC/OUI prefixes.</strong> The first bytes of a globally administered MAC address can identify the organization that received the address block.</li> <li><strong>WiFi behavior.</strong> An SSID, wildcard probe request, receiver address, channel pattern, or sequence of 802.11 information elements can narrow the device class.</li> <li><strong>Bluetooth evidence.</strong> Manufacturer IDs and service UUIDs can identify radios exposed by a particular product or firmware generation.</li> </ol> <p>OUI matching became common because it is cheap and passive. An inexpensive ESP32 can inspect nearby 802.11 frames without connecting to a network. A historical database such as <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="WiGLE"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://wigle.net/"> <a href="https://wigle.net/" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >WiGLE</a> </span> also lets a project search past observations without deploying its own scanners.</p> <p>The method moved through a community lineage: <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="DeFlock"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://deflock.org/"> <a href="https://deflock.org/" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >DeFlock</a> </span> mapping and local organizing; <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="colonelpanichacks/flock-you"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://github.com/colonelpanichacks/flock-you"> <a href="https://github.com/colonelpanichacks/flock-you" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >colonelpanichacks/flock-you</a> </span> ; forks and companion projects such as our own <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="flock-you-esp32"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://github.com/simeononsecurity/flock-you-esp32"> <a href="https://github.com/simeononsecurity/flock-you-esp32" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >flock-you-esp32</a> </span> ; and finally <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Flock Finder"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://github.com/simeononsecurity/flock-finder"> <a href="https://github.com/simeononsecurity/flock-finder" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Flock Finder</a> </span> , which applied the prefix list to WiGLE data at global scale.</p> <p>The original fieldwork deserves clear credit. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="@NitekryDPaul"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://github.com/NitekryDPaul"> <a href="https://github.com/NitekryDPaul" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >@NitekryDPaul</a> </span> observed 30 prefixes on real Flock equipment through promiscuous-mode research. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="DeFlockJoplin"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://github.com/DeflockJoplin/flock-you"> <a href="https://github.com/DeflockJoplin/flock-you" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >DeFlockJoplin</a> </span> contributed another during field testing. Those observations were legitimate. Our downstream error was treating <strong>“observed on a Flock camera” as if it meant “exclusive to Flock cameras.”</strong></p> <hr> <h2 id="the-structural-flaw-an-oui-is-a-supply-chain-fact"> <a href="#the-structural-flaw-an-oui-is-a-supply-chain-fact" title="The Structural Flaw: An OUI Is a Supply-Chain Fact">The Structural Flaw: An OUI Is a Supply-Chain Fact</a> <a href="#the-structural-flaw-an-oui-is-a-supply-chain-fact" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="The Structural Flaw: An OUI Is a Supply-Chain Fact">#</a> </h2> <p>The IEEE describes an OUI as a 24-bit identifier assigned to a vendor, manufacturer, or other organization. Combined with another 24 bits chosen by the assignee, it forms a MAC address. The <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="IEEE Registration Authority"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://standards.ieee.org/products-programs/regauth/"> <a href="https://standards.ieee.org/products-programs/regauth/" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >IEEE Registration Authority</a> </span> publishes the registry.</p> <p>That tells us who received an address block. It does not necessarily tell us which brand is printed on a finished product. Contract manufacturers build radio modules for many customers, and a single chip vendor can appear in cameras, projectors, printers, vehicles, and hobby boards.</p> <p>The registry assignments behind our list made the risk visible:</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Registrant</th> <th>Prefixes in the audited list</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td>Liteon Technology</td> <td><code>74:4C:A1</code>, <code>F4:6A:DD</code>, <code>9C:2F:9D</code>, <code>C0:35:32</code>, <code>E4:AA:EA</code>, <code>14:5A:FC</code>, and others</td> </tr> <tr> <td>Universal Global Scientific Industrial (USI)</td> <td><code>E0:4F:43</code>, <code>08:3A:88</code></td> </tr> <tr> <td>Espressif</td> <td><code>A4:CF:12</code>, <code>3C:71:BF</code></td> </tr> <tr> <td>Silicon Laboratories</td> <td><code>58:8E:81</code>, <code>90:35:EA</code>, <code>EC:1B:BD</code></td> </tr> <tr> <td>Flock Safety</td> <td><code>B4:1E:52</code></td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>The Espressif entries should have stopped us. Two prefixes in a supposed camera list belonged to the maker of one of the world’s most common embedded WiFi platforms, including the silicon used by many community detectors.</p> <p><code>B4:1E:52</code> is different because it is registered directly to Flock Safety. It had been added to the 38-prefix list at the audited commit, but <strong>had not yet been queried</strong>: <code>scan_stats.json</code> reported 31 queried prefixes. The same was true of six newly added battery-pack prefixes. The snapshot therefore provides no evidence about how common or rare Flock’s own prefix is, and we will not turn “not queried” into “zero results.”</p> <p>The current repository contains 39 prefixes after adding <code>E0:0A:F6</code> for parity with the detector firmware. Its retained scan summary still reports data for 31 prefixes, so the newer entries remain pending a completed recalculation rather than proven zero-result prefixes.</p> <hr> <h2 id="the-dataset-audited-itself"> <a href="#the-dataset-audited-itself" title="The Dataset Audited Itself">The Dataset Audited Itself</a> <a href="#the-dataset-audited-itself" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="The Dataset Audited Itself">#</a> </h2> <p>Every historical audit number below was regenerated from <code>data/flock_cameras.csv</code> at Flock Finder commit <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="5551829"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://github.com/simeononsecurity/flock-finder/tree/5551829"> <a href="https://github.com/simeononsecurity/flock-finder/tree/5551829" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" ><code>5551829</code></a> </span> with Python’s standard-library <code>csv</code> and <code>collections.Counter</code>. No new drive test was required. The names, geography, and prefix composition already contradicted the headline. Figures describing the corrected implementation come from the current repository’s retained <code>scan_stats.json</code> summary.</p> <h3 id="geography-was-an-early-warning"> <a href="#geography-was-an-early-warning" title="Geography Was an Early Warning">Geography Was an Early Warning</a> <a href="#geography-was-an-early-warning" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Geography Was an Early Warning">#</a> </h3> <p>Of 146,526 rows, 75,818 were in the United States, 70,674 were outside it, and 34 had no country value. Germany alone contributed 13,491 records, followed by Canada with 6,251, France with 5,839, Great Britain with 4,836, the Netherlands with 4,636, and Switzerland with 4,515.</p> <script type="application/ld+json"> { "@context": "https://schema.org/", "@type": "ImageObject", "contentUrl": "https:\/\/simeononsecurity.com\/flock-finder-us-non-us-split.webp", "caption": "Stacked bar showing 75,818 United States records, 70,674 records outside the United States, and 34 records with no country value", "license": "https://simeononsecurity.com/termsandconditions/", "acquireLicensePage": "https://simeononsecurity.com/contactus/", "creditText": "SimeonOnSecurity", "creator": { "@type": "Person", "name": "SimeonOnSecurity" }, "copyrightNotice": "SimeonOnSecurity", "associatedArticle": { "@type": "NewsArticle", "headline": "simeononsecurity", "url": "https:\/\/simeononsecurity.com\/", "datePublished": "2026-10-02 21:20:37.693260294 \u002b0000 UTC m=\u002b337.417986058", "author": { "@type": "Person", "name": "SimeonOnSecurity", "url": "https:\/\/simeononsecurity.com\/authors\/simeononsecurity" } } } </script> <center> <figure align="center" style="text-align: center; margin: 0 auto;" itemprop="caption description"> <p>The country histogram sums to 146,492 because 34 rows have a null country.</p> </figcaption> </figure> </center> <p>Geography is a screening signal, not proof. Flock describes its network as operating “nationwide” and says it connects customers across <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="49 U.S. states"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://www.flocksafety.com/flock-ecosystem"> <a href="https://www.flocksafety.com/flock-ecosystem" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >49 U.S. states</a> </span> . International expansion can also change the market boundary. We therefore flag out-of-market rows for review instead of deleting them or declaring every non-US record false.</p> <p>The conservative conclusion is enough: almost half the records occurred outside the project’s primary US market, so a worldwide OUI hit could not be treated as equally plausible without another signal.</p> <h3 id="more-than-60000-devices-named-themselves"> <a href="#more-than-60000-devices-named-themselves" title="More Than 60,000 Devices Named Themselves">More Than 60,000 Devices Named Themselves</a> <a href="#more-than-60000-devices-named-themselves" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="More Than 60,000 Devices Named Themselves">#</a> </h3> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>SSID family in the original audit</th> <th style="text-align: right">Records</th> <th style="text-align: right">Share</th> <th>What the name indicates</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td>Contains <code>ClickShare</code></td> <td style="text-align: right">0.2%</td> <td>Android hotspots</td> </tr> <tr> <td>Exact name <code>Audi HUD</code></td> <td style="text-align: right">138</td> <td style="text-align: right">0.1%</td> <td>Audi infotainment or <td><code>Flock ALPR [...]</code></td> <td style="text-align: right">30</td> <td style="text-align: right"><0.1%</td> <td>Another detector’s verdict stored as an SSID</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Combined original audit</strong></td> <td style="text-align: right"><strong>60,793</strong></td> <td style="text-align: right"><strong>41.5%</strong></td> <td>Identifiable as other hardware or detector output</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>Barco’s own support documentation says a ClickShare Base Unit’s default network name is <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="ClickShare-<serial base number>"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://www.barco.com/en/support/knowledge-base/2675-how-to-connect-to-your-clickshare-base-unit-wifi"> <a href="https://www.barco.com/en/support/knowledge-base/2675-how-to-connect-to-your-clickshare-base-unit-wifi" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" ><code>ClickShare-<serial base number></code></a> </span> . That gives us first-party confirmation of the product family without guessing from geography or vendor registration.</p> <p>The production classifier has since replaced those exact-name checks with case-insensitive regular expressions and includes ClickShare, SmartGate, WiFi Direct, AndroidAP, Audi HUD, MAX-PRINTER, and detector-output labels. On the same 146,526 rows, it catches 629 AndroidAP variants, 139 Audi HUD variants, and 134 MAX-PRINTER variants. The current repository therefore reports <strong>61,110 <code>identified_other</code> records</strong>, slightly more than the 60,793 found in the original audit.</p> <h3 id="the-confirming-signal-was-only-24"> <a href="#the-confirming-signal-was-only-24" title="The Confirming Signal Was Only 2.4%">The Confirming Signal Was Only 2.4%</a> <a href="#the-confirming-signal-was-only-24" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="The Confirming Signal Was Only 2.4%">#</a> </h3> <p>Only <strong>3,502 rows</strong> carried a genuine Flock-pattern SSID. Another 24,964 had no SSID at all. The remaining records either named other hardware or rested on an OUI plus an unclassified name.</p> <p>The 3,502 confirmed rows contained 161 genuine SSID variants: 3,342 instances of the bare name <code>Flock</code>, 157 one-off <code>Flock-XXXXXX</code> or <code>FLOCK-XXXXXX</code> provisioning names, and three other names containing <code>flock</code>. A previous README count of 166 variants included five distinct <code>Flock ALPR [...]</code> detector annotation strings. Those five are evidence of the detector, not the camera.</p> <script type="application/ld+json"> { "@context": "https://schema.org/", "@type": "ImageObject", "contentUrl": "https:\/\/simeononsecurity.com\/flock-finder-evidence-class-breakdown.webp", "caption": "A 100 percent stacked bar dividing 146,526 records into 3,502 SSID-confirmed, 57,267 named unclassified, 24,964 hidden OUI-only, 60,763 identified other, and 30 detector feedback records", "license": "https://simeononsecurity.com/termsandconditions/", "acquireLicensePage": "https://simeononsecurity.com/contactus/", "creditText": "SimeonOnSecurity", "creator": { "@type": "Person", "name": "SimeonOnSecurity" }, "copyrightNotice": "SimeonOnSecurity", "associatedArticle": { "@type": "NewsArticle", "headline": "simeononsecurity", "url": "https:\/\/simeononsecurity.com\/", "datePublished": "2026-10-02 21:20:37.693615653 \u002b0000 UTC m=\u002b337.418341418", "author": { "@type": "Person", "name": "SimeonOnSecurity", "url": "https:\/\/simeononsecurity.com\/authors\/simeononsecurity" } } } </script> <center> <figure align="center" style="text-align: center; margin: 0 auto;" itemprop="caption description"> <p>The old headline collapsed five materially different evidence classes into one count.</p> </figcaption> </figure> </center> <h3 id="prefix-quality-varied-dramatically"> <a href="#prefix-quality-varied-dramatically" title="Prefix Quality Varied Dramatically">Prefix Quality Varied Dramatically</a> <a href="#prefix-quality-varied-dramatically" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Prefix Quality Varied Dramatically">#</a> </h3> <p>The false-positive rate was not uniform. Some prefixes retained a useful Flock signal; others were dominated by named office or consumer devices.</p> <script type="application/ld+json"> { "@context": "https://schema.org/", "@type": "ImageObject", "contentUrl": "https:\/\/simeononsecurity.com\/flock-finder-per-oui-composition.webp", "caption": "Horizontal stacked bars for 31 OUI prefixes showing Flock SSIDs in green, known-other SSIDs in red, hidden SSIDs in light gray, and unclassified records in dark gray", "license": "https://simeononsecurity.com/termsandconditions/", "acquireLicensePage": "https://simeononsecurity.com/contactus/", "creditText": "SimeonOnSecurity", "creator": { "@type": "Person", "name": "SimeonOnSecurity" }, "copyrightNotice": "SimeonOnSecurity", "associatedArticle": { "@type": "NewsArticle", "headline": "simeononsecurity", "url": "https:\/\/simeononsecurity.com\/", "datePublished": "2026-10-02 21:20:37.69397955 \u002b0000 UTC m=\u002b337.418705295", "author": { "@type": "Person", "name": "SimeonOnSecurity", "url": "https:\/\/simeononsecurity.com\/authors\/simeononsecurity" } } } </script> <center> <figure align="center" style="text-align: center;
