Counts come from the 146,526-row audit snapshot.</p> </figcaption> </figure> </center> <p>Consider two prefixes that the old map labeled identically:</p> <ul> <li><code>70:C9:4E</code> had 495 rows: 133 Flock-pattern names and 29 known-other names.</li> <li><code>74:4C:A1</code> had 11,872 rows: 211 Flock-pattern names and 8,385 known-other names.</li> </ul> <script type="application/ld+json"> { "@context": "https://schema.org/", "@type": "ImageObject", "contentUrl": "https:\/\/simeononsecurity.com\/flock-finder-prefix-signal-contrast.webp", "caption": "Comparison of prefix 70 C9 4E with 26.9 percent Flock SSIDs and 5.9 percent known other against prefix 74 4C A1 with 1.8 percent Flock SSIDs and 70.6 percent known other", "license": "https://simeononsecurity.com/termsandconditions/", "acquireLicensePage": "https://simeononsecurity.com/contactus/", "creditText": "SimeonOnSecurity", "creator": { "@type": "Person", "name": "SimeonOnSecurity" }, "copyrightNotice": "SimeonOnSecurity", "associatedArticle": { "@type": "NewsArticle", "headline": "simeononsecurity", "url": "https:\/\/simeononsecurity.com\/", "datePublished": "2026-10-02 21:20:37.694354014 \u002b0000 UTC m=\u002b337.419079760", "author": { "@type": "Person", "name": "SimeonOnSecurity", "url": "https:\/\/simeononsecurity.com\/authors\/simeononsecurity" } } } </script> <center> <figure align="center" style="text-align: center; margin: 0 auto;" itemscope itemtype="http://schema.org/ImageObject"> <meta property="article:published_time" content="2026-10-02 21:20:37.694354014 +0000 UTC m=+337.419079760"> <meta property="article:author" content="SimeonOnSecurity"> <meta property="article:author:url" content="https://simeononsecurity.com/authors/simeononsecurity"> <meta property="og:license" content="https://simeononsecurity.com/termsandconditions/"> <meta property="og:see_also" content="https://simeononsecurity.com/contactus/"> <meta property="og:copyright" content="SimeonOnSecurity"> <img align="center" style="text-align: center; margin: 0 auto; max-width: 80%; max-height: 600px; min-width: 100px; min-height: 100px; height: auto; width: auto;" src="https://simeononsecurity.com/flock-finder-prefix-signal-contrast.webp" alt="Comparison of prefix 70 C9 4E with 26.9 percent Flock SSIDs and 5.9 percent known other against prefix 74 4C A1 with 1.8 percent Flock SSIDs and 70.6 percent known other"loading="lazy" fetchpriority="low" itemprop="contentUrl" /> <figcaption align="center" style="text-align: center; margin: 0 auto;" itemprop="caption description"> <p>One flat label concealed opposite signal-to-noise ratios.</p> </figcaption> </figure> </center> <p>The same pattern appears in the biggest rows: <code>F4:6A:DD</code> had 8,422 known-other names against 327 Flock names; <code>D0:39:57</code> had 8,270 against 473; and <code>E0:4F:43</code> included 6,238 known-other names against 66 Flock names. Prefix volume was not evidence quality.</p> <hr> <h2 id="the-feedback-loop-hidden-in-30-rows"> <a href="#the-feedback-loop-hidden-in-30-rows" title="The Feedback Loop Hidden in 30 Rows">The Feedback Loop Hidden in 30 Rows</a> <a href="#the-feedback-loop-hidden-in-30-rows" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="The Feedback Loop Hidden in 30 Rows">#</a> </h2> <p>Thirty records in Texas had SSIDs that were plainly another detector’s output:</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Detector label stored as SSID</th> <th style="text-align: right">Confidence written by that tool</th> <th style="text-align: right">Records</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><code>Flock ALPR [wifi_receiver_oui;low]</code></td> <td style="text-align: right">low</td> <td style="text-align: right">20</td> </tr> <tr> <td><code>Flock ALPR [wifi_oui_wildcard_probe;medium]</code></td> <td style="text-align: right">medium</td> <td style="text-align: right">4</td> </tr> <tr> <td><code>Flock ALPR [wifi_bssid_oui;low]</code></td> <td style="text-align: right">low</td> <td style="text-align: right">3</td> </tr> <tr> <td><code>Flock ALPR [flock_receiver_oui;low]</code></td> <td style="text-align: right">low</td> <td style="text-align: right">2</td> </tr> <tr> <td><code>Flock ALPR [wifi_hidden_ssid_oui;low]</code></td> <td style="text-align: right">low</td> <td style="text-align: right">1</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>Twenty-six of the 30 were labeled low confidence by the tool that created them. A WiGLE upload then stored the tool’s verdict in the SSID field. Our pipeline found the word <code>Flock</code> and could have treated that label as independent confirmation.</p> <p>Thirty rows are statistically small. The mechanism is consequential: tools that share a crowdsourced database can ingest one another’s output and launder a low-confidence guess into apparent corroboration. The correction deny-lists the entire <code>Flock ALPR [</code> pattern before checking for a confirming <code>flock</code> substring.</p> <hr> <h2 id="where-we-got-it-wrong"> <a href="#where-we-got-it-wrong" title="Where We Got It Wrong">Where We Got It Wrong</a> <a href="#where-we-got-it-wrong" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Where We Got It Wrong">#</a> </h2> <p>The README headline reported <strong>“Cameras Mapped | 146,526.”</strong> The map published full-precision coordinates and drew every result as the same kind of pin. It updated on a GitHub Actions schedule, giving a weak heuristic the appearance of a maintained inventory.</p> <p>We did include caveats. Every feature carried <code>match_confidence: "suspected"</code>. The README discussed ClickShare as a possible co-occupant, and the project maintained a separate candidate track for SSID discoveries. Those caveats did not govern the number, marker, or default view that readers actually saw.</p> <p>We hedged in prose and quantified in the headline. The map made the claim.</p> <p>The most avoidable part is that our <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="flock-you-esp32"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://github.com/simeononsecurity/flock-you-esp32"> <a href="https://github.com/simeononsecurity/flock-you-esp32" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >flock-you-esp32</a> </span> firmware already separated high-confidence identifiers from contract-manufacturer identifiers and scored weak evidence below the alert threshold. The concept existed in the same organization, but the mapping pipeline did not inherit it.</p> <p>We found the scale of the error by running a histogram on our own SSID column. It took minutes. We had been committing 146,526 rows of evidence against our presentation every day.</p> <hr> <h2 id="what-we-changed"> <a href="#what-we-changed" title="What We Changed">What We Changed</a> <a href="#what-we-changed" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="What We Changed">#</a> </h2> <p>The correction is implemented in Flock Finder’s data model and interface:</p> <ul> <li><strong>Per-record evidence:</strong> <code>ssid_confirmed</code>, <code>oui_high</code>, <code>oui_mfr</code>, or <code>identified_other</code>.</li> <li><strong>OUI tiers:</strong> prefixes are separated into field-observed high confidence and shared contract-manufacturer tiers.</li> <li><strong>Known-other exclusion:</strong> ClickShare, SmartGate, WiFi Direct, Android hotspot, Audi HUD, MAX-PRINTER, and detector-output SSIDs are excluded from the map and headline by default.</li> <li><strong>Visible uncertainty:</strong> marker colors, popups, counts, and filters expose the evidence class.</li> <li><strong>Market flagging:</strong> records outside the primary US market carry <code>out_of_market: true</code> and remain available for review.</li> <li><strong>A decomposed headline:</strong> 3,502 SSID-confirmed, 73,691 high-tier OUI suspected, 8,223 contract-manufacturer OUI suspected, and 61,110 identified as other.</li> </ul> <p>The corrected actionable headline is <strong>85,416</strong>, and that number still includes 81,914 unconfirmed OUI matches. It is a defensible accounting of what passed the current rules, not a verified camera inventory.</p> <p><code>identified_other</code> is also an operational classifier, not an oracle. ClickShare has strong first-party documentation behind its default SSID, while a broad pattern such as <code>DIRECT-</code> describes a WiFi Direct naming convention used by many product classes. Publishing the matching rule and <code>blocked_reason</code> field lets researchers audit those exclusions and revise them when evidence improves.</p> <h3 id="the-long-term-answer-is-firmware-fingerprinting"> <a href="#the-long-term-answer-is-firmware-fingerprinting" title="The Long-Term Answer Is Firmware Fingerprinting">The Long-Term Answer Is Firmware Fingerprinting</a> <a href="#the-long-term-answer-is-firmware-fingerprinting" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="The Long-Term Answer Is Firmware Fingerprinting">#</a> </h3> <p>OUI tiering limits damage but cannot make a shared manufacturer prefix product-specific. The stronger path is the ordered structure of 802.11 probe-request information elements. Upstream work documents this TLV signature:</p> <div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" style="color:#f8f8f2;background-color:#272822;-moz-tab-size:4;-o-tab-size:4;tab-size:4;-webkit-text-size-adjust:none;"><code class="language-text" data-lang="text"><span style="display:flex;"><span>2,12,127,221:506f9a16030103,45,191,221:0050f208000000 </span></span></code></pre></div><p>That sequence describes behavior of a particular firmware stack rather than ownership of a MAC block. Probe-request fingerprinting is an established device-identification technique; <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="published research on 802.11 MAC-layer fingerprinting"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://doi.org/10.1155/2017/6235484"> <a href="https://doi.org/10.1155/2017/6235484" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >published research on 802.11 MAC-layer fingerprinting</a> </span> shows that probe-request information elements can remain identifying when MAC addresses rotate. It also addresses the specific failure mode reported in <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="flock-you issue #43"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://github.com/colonelpanichacks/flock-you/issues/43"> <a href="https://github.com/colonelpanichacks/flock-you/issues/43" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >flock-you issue #43</a> </span> : <code>Flock Camera net.</code> appearing on sequential locally administered MAC addresses across 2.4 and 5 GHz.</p> <p>The signature still needs independent field validation across hardware and firmware versions, and malformed captures require defensive parsing. It is nevertheless the right direction. MAC randomization makes OUI-only matching a dead end on a timer.</p> <hr> <h2 id="why-this-matters-beyond-one-repository"> <a href="#why-this-matters-beyond-one-repository" title="Why This Matters Beyond One Repository">Why This Matters Beyond One Repository</a> <a href="#why-this-matters-beyond-one-repository" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Why This Matters Beyond One Repository">#</a> </h2> <p>People use surveillance maps to decide where they drive, park, report, research, and organize. A false pin redirects attention. Tens of thousands of false pins can discredit accurate observations beside them.</p> <p>There is also a credibility asymmetry. A vendor or critic needs one demonstrably false ClickShare pin to challenge the whole dataset. We supplied 50,278. Journalists and advocacy groups can repeat a clean headline faster than a later correction can follow it.</p> <p>Open-source transparency work earns trust through inspectable methods and visible uncertainty. Publishing the raw data helped expose our error, but raw access did not excuse the interface that overstated it. The correction belongs wherever a reader encounters the claim: field, filter, marker, legend, and headline.</p> <h3 id="a-request-to-every-flock-and-alpr-map"> <a href="#a-request-to-every-flock-and-alpr-map" title="A Request to Every Flock and ALPR Map">A Request to Every Flock and ALPR Map</a> <a href="#a-request-to-every-flock-and-alpr-map" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="A Request to Every Flock and ALPR Map">#</a> </h3> <p>Other Flock and ALPR mapping projects should audit their datasets too. This is an invitation to compare methods, not an allegation that every map inherited our mistake.</p> <p> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="WiGLE"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://www.wigle.net/stats/"> <a href="https://www.wigle.net/stats/" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >WiGLE</a> </span> is the broadest publicly accessible, globally searchable WiFi observation dataset we know of. That reach is exactly what made Flock Finder attractive: one API could turn a field-researched signature list into a worldwide map. It also made the error large enough to measure. A global database will return every unrelated product sharing a radio supplier’s address space, not only the product that motivated the query.</p> <p>Other maps use different evidence. Some rely on photographs and volunteer field observations; others import OpenStreetMap surveillance tags, public records, vendor disclosures, or data from another community project. Their totals are not directly comparable to our WiGLE results, and our 2.4% SSID-confirmed rate should not be projected onto a field-verified dataset. The common risk is that one project’s classification can flow into another project’s source data, then appear to be independent corroboration.</p> <p>Every public map should be able to answer a short audit:</p> <ol> <li><strong>What does one marker mean?</strong> A photographed device, a government record, an OUI match, a user report, or an import from another map?</li> <li><strong>How many records have direct product evidence?</strong> Publish counts by evidence class instead of one aggregate camera total.</li> <li><strong>Which sources are independent?</strong> Track provenance through imports so the same observation is not counted as multiple confirmations.</li> <li><strong>What contradicts the classification?</strong> Run frequency tables over SSIDs, vendors, countries, contributor labels, and every other categorical field.</li> <li><strong>How are uncertainty and disputes rendered?</strong> Put confidence and correction status in the marker, filters, exports, and headline.</li> <li><strong>Can another researcher reproduce the count?</strong> Publish the query, source snapshot, classification rules, and date.</li> </ol> <p>This audit does not make the Flock problem smaller. A network of ALPR cameras can still record travel, support searches across jurisdictions, and affect people who never consented to the collection. Accurate counts make that criticism harder to dismiss. If we are going to challenge surveillance systems, our maps need to distinguish what we observed, what we inferred, and what we confirmed.</p> <p>We made a well-informed mistake. The prefixes came from legitimate field research, the pipeline was reproducible, and the caveats were real. The inference still exceeded the evidence. Good intentions and good inputs do not remove the obligation to test what a system produces at scale.</p> <hr> <h2 id="reproduce-the-audit"> <a href="#reproduce-the-audit" title="Reproduce the Audit">Reproduce the Audit</a> <a href="#reproduce-the-audit" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Reproduce the Audit">#</a> </h2> <p>Check out commit <code>5551829</code>, then run the following from the repository root. It uses only Python’s standard library and prints the total, geography, common SSIDs, and selected named-device families.</p> <div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" style="color:#f8f8f2;background-color:#272822;-moz-tab-size:4;-o-tab-size:4;tab-size:4;-webkit-text-size-adjust:none;"><code class="language-bash" data-lang="bash"><span style="display:flex;"><span>git clone https://github.com/simeononsecurity/flock-finder.git </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>cd flock-finder </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>git checkout <span style="color:#ae81ff">5551829</span> </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>python3 - <span style="color:#e6db74"><<'PY' </span></span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span><span style="color:#e6db74">import csv </span></span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span><span style="color:#e6db74">from collections import Counter </span></span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span><span style="color:#e6db74"> </span></span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span><span style="color:#e6db74">with open("data/flock_cameras.csv", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f: </span></span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span><span style="color:#e6db74"> rows = list(csv.DictReader(f)) </span></span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span><span style="color:#e6db74"> </span></span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span><span style="color:#e6db74">ssids = Counter((row["ssid"] or "").strip() for row in rows) </span></span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span><span style="color:#e6db74">countries = Counter((row["country"] or "").strip() for row in rows) </span></span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span><span style="color:#e6db74"> </span></span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span><span style="color:#e6db74">families = { </span></span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span><span style="color:#e6db74"> "clickshare": lambda s: "clickshare" in s.lower(), </span></span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span><span style="color:#e6db74"> "smartgate": lambda s: s.lower().startswith("smartgate_"), </span></span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span><span style="color:#e6db74"> "direct": lambda s: s.lower().startswith("direct-"), </span></span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span><span style="color:#e6db74"> "androidap": lambda s: s.lower().startswith("androidap"), </span></span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span><span style="color:#e6db74"> "detector_output": lambda s: s.lower().startswith("flock alpr ["), </span></span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span><span style="color:#e6db74">} </span></span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span><span style="color:#e6db74"> </span></span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span><span style="color:#e6db74">print("rows", len(rows)) </span></span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span><span style="color:#e6db74">print("US", countries["US"]) </span></span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span><span style="color:#e6db74">print("non-US", sum(countries.values()) - countries["US"] - countries[""]) </span></span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span><span style="color:#e6db74">print("missing country", countries[""]) </span></span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span><span style="color:#e6db74">print("top SSIDs", ssids.most_common(20)) </span></span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span><span style="color:#e6db74">for name, matches in families.items(): </span></span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span><span style="color:#e6db74"> print(name, sum(matches(ssid) for ssid in ssids.elements())) </span></span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span><span style="color:#e6db74">PY</span> </span></span></code></pre></div><p>For the exact historical input, use the CSV from that commit rather than a current generated dataset. The project stopped committing the large CSV, GeoJSON, and per-OUI files after the audit because each scan rewrote hundreds of megabytes and had grown the repository substantially. Current generated data is restored from and published to the rolling <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="data-latest release"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://github.com/simeononsecurity/flock-finder/releases/tag/data-latest"> <a href="https://github.com/simeononsecurity/flock-finder/releases/tag/data-latest" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" ><code>data-latest</code> release</a> </span> ; the small <code>scan_stats.json</code> summary remains in Git. A missing generated file on the current branch therefore does not mean the historical evidence was deleted or that its count became zero.</p> <hr> <h2 id="the-lesson"> <a href="#the-lesson" title="The Lesson">The Lesson</a> <a href="#the-lesson" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="The Lesson">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>A heuristic labeled “suspected” in metadata but rendered as a confident pin on a map is a claim.</strong> The label has to live in the data model and the visualization, not only in documentation.</p> <p>The cheap check that would have caught this was a frequency histogram over every output field before publication. We had 146,526 rows of evidence against ourselves sitting in a CSV. We should have asked the dataset what it contained before telling readers what it meant.</p> Read More at https://simeononsecurity.com/

item.title: Sibling Sites - SimeonOnSecurity's Standalone Cybersecurity Tools
item.description: Every SimeonOnSecurity sibling site in one place. Seven standalone tools on their own subdomains, covering WiFi data maps, ALPR surveillance mapping, ESP32 counter-surveillance firmware, and resume optimization.
item.content:encoded: <p><strong>SimeonOnSecurity builds tools large enough to deserve their own web address.</strong> Seven standalone projects run on dedicated subdomains today. Each one does a single job, pulls its own data, and ships on its own schedule.</p> <p>This page collects all seven in one place so you know what exists, what each tool does, and where to find it. One more project, <strong>track-carrier-openroaming-support</strong>, publishes its results through a repository instead.</p> <p><em>Sibling sites are written in English only. They are not translated into the other site languages.</em></p> <script type="application/ld+json"> { "@context": "https://schema.org/", "@type": "ImageObject", "contentUrl": "https:\/\/simeononsecurity.com\/simeononsecurity-sibling-sites-subdomain-family.webp", "caption": "Illustration of the main SimeonOnSecurity site with its tool subdomains branching from it", "license": "https://simeononsecurity.com/termsandconditions/", "acquireLicensePage": "https://simeononsecurity.com/contactus/", "creditText": "SimeonOnSecurity", "creator": { "@type": "Person", "name": "SimeonOnSecurity" }, "copyrightNotice": "SimeonOnSecurity", "associatedArticle": { "@type": "NewsArticle", "headline": "simeononsecurity", "url": "https:\/\/simeononsecurity.com\/", "datePublished": "2026-10-02 21:20:37.700100561 \u002b0000 UTC m=\u002b337.424826326", "author": { "@type": "Person", "name": "SimeonOnSecurity", "url": "https:\/\/simeononsecurity.com\/authors\/simeononsecurity" } } } </script> <center> <figure align="center" style="text-align: center; margin: 0 auto;" itemscope itemtype="http://schema.org/ImageObject"> <meta property="article:published_time" content="2026-10-02 21:20:37.700100561 +0000 UTC m=+337.424826326"> <meta property="article:author" content="SimeonOnSecurity"> <meta property="article:author:url" content="https://simeononsecurity.com/authors/simeononsecurity"> <meta property="og:license" content="https://simeononsecurity.com/termsandconditions/"> <meta property="og:see_also" content="https://simeononsecurity.com/contactus/"> <meta property="og:copyright" content="SimeonOnSecurity"> <img align="center" style="text-align: center; margin: 0 auto; max-width: 80%; max-height: 600px; min-width: 100px; min-height: 100px; height: auto; width: auto;" src="https://simeononsecurity.com/simeononsecurity-sibling-sites-subdomain-family.webp" alt="Illustration of the main SimeonOnSecurity site with its tool subdomains branching from it"loading="lazy" fetchpriority="low" itemprop="contentUrl" /> <figcaption align="center" style="text-align: center; margin: 0 auto;" itemprop="caption description"> <p>Standalone tools, each on its own subdomain</p> </figcaption> </figure> </center> <h2 id="key-takeaways"> <a href="#key-takeaways" title="Key Takeaways">Key Takeaways</a> <a href="#key-takeaways" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Key Takeaways">#</a> </h2> <ul> <li><strong>Seven sibling sites</strong> run on dedicated <strong>simeononsecurity.com</strong> subdomains.</li> <li><strong>Three are passive data maps</strong> built from the WiGLE crowdsourced WiFi database.</li> <li><strong>Two are ESP32 firmware projects</strong> for detecting Flock Safety cameras in the field.</li> <li><strong>Offload Search</strong> rates one address at a time for carrier offload suitability.</li> <li><strong>ATS Resume Match</strong> scores and rewrites resumes for applicant tracking systems.</li> <li><strong>OpenRoaming carrier support</strong> is tracked in a repository, without a subdomain of its own.</li> <li>Every sibling site is <strong>open source</strong> and <strong>self-hostable</strong> unless noted.</li> </ul> <h2 id="sibling-sites-at-a-glance"> <a href="#sibling-sites-at-a-glance" title="Sibling Sites at a Glance">Sibling Sites at a Glance</a> <a href="#sibling-sites-at-a-glance" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Sibling Sites at a Glance">#</a> </h2> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Site</th> <th>What it does</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Helium Map"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://heliummap.simeononsecurity.com/"> <a href="https://heliummap.simeononsecurity.com/" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Helium Map</a> </span> </strong></td> <td>Maps Helium Mobile and Helium Free WiFi hotspots recorded by WiGLE</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Offload Search"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://offloadsearch.simeononsecurity.com/"> <a href="https://offloadsearch.simeononsecurity.com/" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Offload Search</a> </span> </strong></td> <td>Rates one address for carrier offload and nearby foot traffic</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="OpenRoaming Map"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://openroamingmap.simeononsecurity.com/"> <a href="https://openroamingmap.simeononsecurity.com/" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >OpenRoaming Map</a> </span> </strong></td> <td>Maps Hotspot 2.0, Passpoint, and OpenRoaming access points</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Flock Finder"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://flockfinder.simeononsecurity.com/"> <a href="https://flockfinder.simeononsecurity.com/" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Flock Finder</a> </span> </strong></td> <td>Maps suspected Flock Safety ALPR cameras by WiFi OUI fingerprint</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Eye Spy"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://eyespy.simeononsecurity.com/"> <a href="https://eyespy.simeononsecurity.com/" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Eye Spy</a> </span> </strong></td> <td>Flashes surveillance detection firmware onto an M5Stack Atom Lite</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Flock-You ESP32"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://flockyouesp32.simeononsecurity.com/"> <a href="https://flockyouesp32.simeononsecurity.com/" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Flock-You ESP32</a> </span> </strong></td> <td>Flashes Flock Safety camera detection firmware onto any ESP32 board</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="ATS Resume Match"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://atsresumeimprover.simeononsecurity.com/"> <a href="https://atsresumeimprover.simeononsecurity.com/" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >ATS Resume Match</a> </span> </strong></td> <td>Scores and rewrites a resume for applicant tracking systems</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <h2 id="what-counts-as-a-sibling-site"> <a href="#what-counts-as-a-sibling-site" title="What Counts as a Sibling Site">What Counts as a Sibling Site</a> <a href="#what-counts-as-a-sibling-site" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="What Counts as a Sibling Site">#</a> </h2> <p>A sibling site is a tool with a full application behind it. It has its own dataset, its own build pipeline, and its own subdomain.</p> <p>The single-page utilities on <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Tools"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/tools/"> <a href="/tools/" rel="follow me" >Tools</a> </span> (password checker, hash calculator, Base64 encoder, EXIF viewer, and the rest) stay on the main domain because they run entirely in the browser and need no backend.</p> <p>Sibling sites fall into three groups:</p> <p><strong>Passive data maps</strong> rebuilt from WiGLE records</p> <ul> <li><strong>Helium Map</strong></li> <li><strong>OpenRoaming Map</strong></li> <li><strong>Flock Finder</strong></li> </ul> <p><strong>Lookup and scoring tools</strong> driven by public APIs</p> <ul> <li><strong>Offload Search</strong></li> <li><strong>ATS Resume Match</strong></li> </ul> <p><strong>Device firmware</strong> with a browser flasher</p> <ul> <li><strong>Eye Spy</strong></li> <li><strong>Flock-You ESP32</strong></li> </ul> <p>The split matters for maintenance. Map projects depend on third-party data and break when an upstream API changes. Lookup tools depend on browser support. Firmware depends on hardware shipped to a reader.</p> <h2 id="helium-map"> <a href="#helium-map" title="Helium Map">Helium Map</a> <a href="#helium-map" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Helium Map">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Helium Map</strong> plots Helium Mobile and Helium Free WiFi network locations pulled from two sources: the WiGLE.net crowdsourced WiFi dataset and the Helium Blockchain Exporter API. The final published scan maps <strong>8,335 access points</strong>, and the repository also carries Helium-provided device status and subscriber growth tables.</p> <p>Markers carry the SSID, the RCOI, and the device category. Filter checkboxes hide categories you do not care about, and a search box matches SSIDs or RCOIs with an optional regular expression.</p> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <center> <meta itemprop="name" content="simeononsecurity"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://heliummap.simeononsecurity.com/"> <a href="https://heliummap.simeononsecurity.com/" title="simeononsecurity" target="_blank" class="markdown-btn" rel="noopener external" alt="simeononsecurity" target="_blank" > <button class="markdown-button"> Open Helium Map </button> </a> <p></p> </center> </span> <p><em>GitHub archived the upstream repository in April 2025, so treat this map as a dated snapshot rather than a live feed.</em></p> <h2 id="offload-search"> <a href="#offload-search" title="Offload Search">Offload Search</a> <a href="#offload-search" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Offload Search">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Offload Search</strong> answers one question: is this address a good spot for carrier offload?</p> <p>Type an address and the tool geocodes it, then returns the FCC Broadband Map for the area plus Google Maps, Foursquare, and Yelp links for checking nearby foot traffic. Nominatim reverse geocoding classifies the location as <strong>Business</strong>, <strong>Residential</strong>, or <strong>Other</strong> and estimates the odds a carrier accepts service there.</p> <p>An optional estimator turns a foot-traffic number into a rough offload figure using network averages. <em>Dwell time above the 5 to 30 minute average pushes the real number lower than the estimate.</em></p> <p>The tool runs in the browser, stores nothing, and needs no account. <strong>Run it before committing a venue to a hotspot or offload deployment.</strong></p> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <center> <meta itemprop="name" content="simeononsecurity"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://offloadsearch.simeononsecurity.com/"> <a href="https://offloadsearch.simeononsecurity.com/" title="simeononsecurity" target="_blank" class="markdown-btn" rel="noopener external" alt="simeononsecurity" target="_blank" > <button class="markdown-button"> Check an Address </button> </a> <p></p> </center> </span> <h2 id="openroaming-map"> <a href="#openroaming-map" title="OpenRoaming Map">OpenRoaming Map</a> <a href="#openroaming-map" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="OpenRoaming Map">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>OpenRoaming Map</strong> tracks <strong>Hotspot 2.0</strong>, <strong>Passpoint</strong>, and <strong>OpenRoaming</strong> access points recorded in the WiGLE dataset.</p> <p>The published map groups markers by operator, so OpenRoaming settled and unsettled RCOIs, Google Orion devices, IronWiFi devices, <strong>eduroam</strong>, <strong>cityroam</strong>, <strong>XNET</strong>, <strong>MetaBlox</strong>, <strong>Wayru</strong>, Helium deployments, and plain Hotspot 2.0 access points appear side by side. A daily GitHub Actions job fetches new records, rebuilds the map, and refreshes the README statistics, which list every unique RCOI with a count. The dataset resets each year and the previous year is archived. A companion Dune dashboard tracks the same network family.</p> <p><em>A yearly reset keeps the marker count readable instead of growing without limit.</em></p> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <center> <meta itemprop="name" content="simeononsecurity"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://openroamingmap.simeononsecurity.com/"> <a href="https://openroamingmap.simeononsecurity.com/" title="simeononsecurity" target="_blank" class="markdown-btn" rel="noopener external" alt="simeononsecurity" target="_blank" > <button class="markdown-button"> Open the OpenRoaming Map </button> </a> <p></p> </center> </span> <h2 id="flock-finder"> <a href="#flock-finder" title="Flock Finder">Flock Finder</a> <a href="#flock-finder" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Flock Finder">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Flock Finder</strong> maps suspected <strong>Flock Safety ALPR cameras</strong>. It queries WiGLE for networks matching the 31 known Flock Safety OUI (MAC address) prefixes gathered from public research, then plots each hit on a clustered Leaflet map. As of September 2026 the published map carries more than 146,000 suspected camera records across 138 countries.</p> <p>Every record shows the BSSID, SSID, OUI, channel, first-seen and last-seen dates, and a confidence label. A daily workflow re-scans at 06:00 UTC and keeps two years of data. The project also documents the SSID naming patterns seen in the wild, covering the bare <strong>Flock</strong> name, the <strong>Flock-XXXXXX</strong> provisioning format, and the <strong>Flock Camera net</strong> variant which no OUI lookup spots.</p> <blockquote> <p><strong>Warning: an OUI match is a heuristic, not proof of a camera.</strong> MAC prefixes get shared, reassigned, or spoofed, and WiGLE records arrive sporadically because Flock cameras wake only to upload. Treat the map as a lead, then confirm on site. The project maintains a full data policy, a data dictionary, and a corrections process.</p> </blockquote> <p>Detection hardware pairs with the map. <strong> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Flock-You ESP32"> <meta itemprop="url" content="#flock-you-esp32"> <a href="#flock-you-esp32" rel="follow me" >Flock-You ESP32</a> </span> </strong> below builds the same WiFi detection method onto a $5 board, and <strong> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="FlockYou detectors from STS Collective"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://stscollective.com/discount/SIMEONONSECURITY"> <a href="https://stscollective.com/discount/SIMEONONSECURITY" rel="nofollow noopener external sponsored" alt="Affiliate Link" target="_blank" >FlockYou detectors from STS Collective</a> </span> </strong> package it as a finished device with LED and audio alerts. Use code <strong>FLOCKFINDER</strong> for 20% off FlockYou hardware, or <strong>SIMEONONSECURITY</strong> for up to 20% off the full order.</p> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <center> <meta itemprop="name" content="simeononsecurity"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://flockfinder.simeononsecurity.com/"> <a href="https://flockfinder.simeononsecurity.com/" title="simeononsecurity" target="_blank" class="markdown-btn" rel="noopener external" alt="simeononsecurity" target="_blank" > <button class="markdown-button"> Open Flock Finder </button> </a> <p></p> </center> </span> <h2 id="eye-spy"> <a href="#eye-spy" title="Eye Spy">Eye Spy</a> <a href="#eye-spy" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Eye Spy">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Eye Spy</strong> is passive surveillance detection firmware for the <strong>M5Stack Atom Lite</strong> (ESP32-PICO-D4). It listens on BLE and WiFi for body cameras, ALPR systems, AirTags, personal trackers, drones, and hidden cameras, then scores what it hears.</p> <p>A single RGB LED reports the threat level: <strong>blue</strong> for startup, <strong>green</strong> for clear, <strong>yellow</strong> for caution, and <strong>red flashing</strong> for a likely recording or tracking device. The score drops one point every 60 seconds so stale hits fade.</p> <p>Scanning stays passive. The device sends no probe requests, so the equipment it hunts gets no hint the device exists. The sibling site hosts a web flasher plus a live dashboard, firmware installs over USB, and native unit tests cover the OUI and keyword tables without hardware on the bench. The Atom Lite is the primary target, and experimental builds exist for the LILYGO T-Dongle C5.</p> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <center> <meta itemprop="name" content="simeononsecurity"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://eyespy.simeononsecurity.com/"> <a href="https://eyespy.simeononsecurity.com/" title="simeononsecurity" target="_blank" class="markdown-btn" rel="noopener external" alt="simeononsecurity" target="_blank" > <button class="markdown-button"> Flash Eye Spy </button> </a> <p></p> </center> </span> <h2 id="flock-you-esp32"> <a href="#flock-you-esp32" title="Flock-You ESP32">Flock-You ESP32</a> <a href="#flock-you-esp32" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Flock-You ESP32">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Flock-You ESP32</strong> is a WiFi promiscuous-mode detector for Flock Safety surveillance cameras, ported to standard ESP32 hardware from <strong>colonelpanichacks/flock-you</strong>. A build starts at <strong>$5</strong> for an ESP32 DevKit and a USB cable, or $10 to $12 with a breadboard, a passive buzzer, and a 3D printed case.</p> <p>Every hit is scored from 0 to 100 across five techniques: WiFi promiscuous sniffing with three OUI confidence tiers, the wildcard probe signature, SSID pattern matching which catches <strong>Flock Camera net</strong> units on locally administered MACs, BLE cross-correlation, and multi-address matching on addr1, addr2, and addr3. Scores below 30 log quietly, scores from 30 to 59 read <strong>PROBABLE</strong>, and scores of 60 or higher trigger an alert.</p> <p>A buzzer plays the <strong>Super Mario Bros. World 1-2</strong> theme at startup, then two ascending beeps on each new detection. The bundled Flask dashboard tags hits with GPS and exports JSON, CSV, or KML for Google Earth. Boards include the ESP32 DevKit, M5Atom Lite, M5Atom Echo, M5Atom Voice, Atom VoiceS3R, and the LILYGO T-Dongle C5. 38 host-side Unity tests cover the detection tables without hardware on the bench.</p> <p><strong>Eye Spy and Flock-You ESP32 overlap by design.</strong> Eye Spy targets the M5Stack Atom Lite, watches a wider sensor list, and reports through one RGB score LED. Flock-You ESP32 runs on any ESP32 with 4MB of flash and carries the WiFi research behind the original Flock-You firmware.</p> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <center> <meta itemprop="name" content="simeononsecurity"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://flockyouesp32.simeononsecurity.com/"> <a href="https://flockyouesp32.simeononsecurity.com/" title="simeononsecurity" target="_blank" class="markdown-btn" rel="noopener external" alt="simeononsecurity" target="_blank" > <button class="markdown-button"> Flash Flock-You ESP32 </button> </a> <p></p> </center> </span> <h2 id="ats-resume-match"> <a href="#ats-resume-match" title="ATS Resume Match">ATS Resume Match</a> <a href="#ats-resume-match" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="ATS Resume Match">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>ATS Resume Match</strong> is a free, self-hostable resume optimizer. Parsing and scoring run in the browser, so the resume file stays on your machine unless you switch on an AI feature.</p> <p>It detects the resume type from seven profiles, reorders sections for the profile, scores the document across five dimensions, and shows the plain text an applicant tracking system reads. Keyword gap analysis compares the resume against a job post, the optimizer rewrites weak sections, and the cover letter generator applies a house style guide which strips em dashes, banned buzzwords, and passive voice.</p> <p>AI features work with OpenAI, Anthropic Claude, or a local Ollama model. Bring a key or run it offline. Export goes to PDF, DOCX, TXT, or Markdown, and the project ships a Dockerfile plus deploy targets for Vercel, Cloudflare Pages, and Netlify.</p> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <center> <meta itemprop="name" content="simeononsecurity"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://atsresumeimprover.simeononsecurity.com/"> <a href="https://atsresumeimprover.simeononsecurity.com/" title="simeononsecurity" target="_blank" class="markdown-btn" rel="noopener external" alt="simeononsecurity" target="_blank" > <button class="markdown-button"> Optimize Your Resume </button> </a> <p></p> </center> </span> <script type="application/ld+json"> { "@context": "https://schema.org/", "@type": "ImageObject", "contentUrl": "https:\/\/simeononsecurity.com\/passive-wifi-data-pipeline-to-map.webp", "caption": "Diagram showing WiGLE WiFi records flowing through a daily build job into an interactive map", "license": "https://simeononsecurity.com/termsandconditions/", "acquireLicensePage": "https://simeononsecurity.com/contactus/", "creditText": "SimeonOnSecurity", "creator": { "@type": "Person", "name": "SimeonOnSecurity" }, "copyrightNotice": "SimeonOnSecurity", "associatedArticle": { "@type": "NewsArticle", "headline": "simeononsecurity", "url": "https:\/\/simeononsecurity.com\/", "datePublished": "2026-10-02 21:20:37.702119211 \u002b0000 UTC m=\u002b337.426844955", "author": { "@type": "Person", "name": "SimeonOnSecurity", "url": "https:\/\/simeononsecurity.com\/authors\/simeononsecurity" } } } </script> <center> <figure align="center" style="text-align: center; margin: 0 auto;" itemscope itemtype="http://schema.org/ImageObject"> <meta property="article:published_time" content="2026-10-02 21:20:37.702119211 +0000 UTC m=+337.426844955"> <meta property="article:author" content="SimeonOnSecurity"> <meta property="article:author:url" content="https://simeononsecurity.com/authors/simeononsecurity"> <meta property="og:license" content="https://simeononsecurity.com/termsandconditions/"> <meta property="og:see_also" content="https://simeononsecurity.com/contactus/"> <meta property="og:copyright" content="SimeonOnSecurity"> <img align="center" style="text-align: center; margin: 0 auto; max-width: 80%; max-height: 600px; min-width: 100px; min-height: 100px; height: auto; width: auto;" src="https://simeononsecurity.com/passive-wifi-data-pipeline-to-map.webp" alt="Diagram showing WiGLE WiFi records flowing through a daily build job into an interactive map"loading="lazy" fetchpriority="low" itemprop="contentUrl" /> <figcaption align="center" style="text-align: center; margin: 0 auto;" itemprop="caption description"> <p>Records in, a daily job, a Leaflet map out</p> </figcaption> </figure> </center> <h2 id="related-research-projects"> <a href="#related-research-projects" title="Related Research Projects">Related Research Projects</a> <a href="#related-research-projects" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Related Research Projects">#</a> </h2> <p>Not every project needs its own address. When the output is a data table rather than an interactive map, the repository README does the job.</p> <h3 id="openroaming-carrier-support"> <a href="#openroaming-carrier-support" title="OpenRoaming Carrier Support">OpenRoaming Carrier Support</a> <a href="#openroaming-carrier-support" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="OpenRoaming Carrier Support">#</a> </h3> <p><strong>track-carrier-openroaming-support</strong> checks whether each mobile network operator supports OpenRoaming by running <strong>NAPTR</strong> and <strong>SRV</strong> lookups against every PLMNID (MCC and MNC pair) listed on mcc-mnc.com.</p> <p>The published result is blunt. <strong>0.20%</strong> of listed carriers answer the lookup. The README names each carrier which does, alongside its identity provider host and port, and adds a lookup table mapping public domains to their hosts, built from public certificates, public documentation, and authentication attempts. A GitHub Actions job re-runs the check each week and commits any change.</p> <p>The Wireless Broadband Alliance publishes a manual checker for these records at <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="wballiance.com/OR/Tools/realm-check.html"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://wballiance.com/OR/Tools/realm-check.html"> <a href="https://wballiance.com/OR/Tools/realm-check.html" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >wballiance.com/OR/Tools/realm-check.html</a> </span> .</p> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <center> <meta itemprop="name" content="simeononsecurity"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://github.com/simeononsecurity/track-carrier-openroaming-support"> <a href="https://github.com/simeononsecurity/track-carrier-openroaming-support" title="simeononsecurity" target="_blank" class="markdown-btn" rel="noopener external" alt="simeononsecurity" target="_blank" > <button class="markdown-button"> Read the Carrier Report </button> </a> <p></p> </center> </span> <h2 id="why-they-live-on-subdomains"> <a href="#why-they-live-on-subdomains" title="Why They Live on Subdomains">Why They Live on Subdomains</a> <a href="#why-they-live-on-subdomains" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Why They Live on Subdomains">#</a> </h2> <p>Isolation is the main reason. A sibling site fails alone. When a map workflow breaks, the main Hugo site keeps building and deploying.</p> <p>The other reasons hold up in practice:</p> <ul> <li><strong>Different stacks.</strong> The main site runs Hugo. The sibling sites run Python, Folium, Leaflet, React, and PlatformIO.</li> <li><strong>Different cadence.</strong> Maps rebuild every 24 hours. The main site deploys on content commits.</li> <li><strong>Different hosting rules.</strong> A subdomain gets its own cache rules, its own Cloudflare settings, and its own CORS policy.</li> <li><strong>Different failure modes.</strong> A 403 from an upstream API hits one tool, not the whole domain.</li> </ul> <p>The cost is duplication. Each project carries its own CI workflow, its own secrets, and its own data retention policy. Each one also needs a reader who remembers it exists, which is the job this page does.</p> <h2 id="next-steps"> <a href="#next-steps" title="Next Steps">Next Steps</a> <a href="#next-steps" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Next Steps">#</a> </h2> <ul> <li>Browse the <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="on-site tools"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/tools/"> <a href="/tools/" rel="follow me" >on-site tools</a> </span> for browser-only utilities.</li> <li>Read the <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="articles"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/articles/"> <a href="/articles/" rel="follow me" >articles</a> </span> for the research behind the maps.</li> <li>Practice with the <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="free certification practice tests"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/practice-tests/"> <a href="/practice-tests/" rel="follow me" >free certification practice tests</a> </span> .</li> <li>Follow the <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="guides"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/guides/"> <a href="/guides/" rel="follow me" >guides</a> </span> for build-along instructions.</li> </ul> Read More at https://simeononsecurity.com/

item.title: Which AI Models Can Run on a Raspberry Pi 4 or 5?
item.description: Use measured Raspberry Pi 4 and 5 results to choose local language models by memory, speed, and workload, from tiny LFM2.5 models to 3B and larger options.
item.content:encoded: <p>A Raspberry Pi can run a useful language model locally, but the model must fit the board’s memory and the response time your application can tolerate. A 2 GB Raspberry Pi 4 is best suited to models below about one billion parameters. An 8 GB Raspberry Pi 5 can run compact 1B–3B models comfortably and load some larger quantized models with substantial compromises.</p> <p>We benchmarked these models ourselves through Ollama on a <strong>2 GB Pi 4B</strong> and an <strong>8 GB Pi 5</strong>, both using microSD storage. The runs behind the tables used the same five short assistant prompts, system prompt, fixed seed, and 140-token output cap. We unloaded other models before each run and measured cold-load time, time to first visible token, total reply time, output speed, and peak resident memory. These were single-pass tests of a short-reply workload, so the results are sizing examples rather than universal speed or answer-quality rankings. The Pi 5’s <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Cortex-A76 CPU and available memory configurations"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://www.raspberrypi.com/products/raspberry-pi-5/"> <a href="https://www.raspberrypi.com/products/raspberry-pi-5/" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Cortex-A76 CPU and available memory configurations</a> </span> also differ materially from the Pi 4’s <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Cortex-A72 platform"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://pip-assets.raspberrypi.com/categories/545-raspberry-pi-4-model-b/documents/RP-008341-DS-1-raspberry-pi-4-datasheet.pdf"> <a href="https://pip-assets.raspberrypi.com/categories/545-raspberry-pi-4-model-b/documents/RP-008341-DS-1-raspberry-pi-4-datasheet.pdf" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Cortex-A72 platform</a> </span> .</p> <h2 id="the-model-types-that-make-sense"> <a href="#the-model-types-that-make-sense" title="The model types that make sense">The model types that make sense</a> <a href="#the-model-types-that-make-sense" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="The model types that make sense">#</a> </h2> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Kind of model</th> <th>Examples from the measurements</th> <th>Practical use</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td>Tiny text models, about 230M–600M parameters</td> <td>LFM2.5-230M, LFM2.5-350M, Qwen2.5-0.5B</td> <td>Short local commands, summaries, and constrained question answering; the best starting point for a 2 GB Pi 4</td> </tr> <tr> <td>Compact text models, about 1B–2B</td> <td>LFM2.5-1.2B, Qwen2.5-1.5B, Gemma 3 1B, MiniCPM5-1B</td> <td>More room for nuanced instructions on a Pi 5 or a higher-memory Pi 4, with slower replies than the tiniest models</td> </tr> <tr> <td>Quantized 3B–4B text models</td> <td>Qwen2.5-3B, Llama 3.2 3B, Gemma 3 4B</td> <td>More capable candidates for an 8 GB Pi 5 when a wait of several seconds per reply is acceptable</td> </tr> <tr> <td>Larger sparse or hybrid models</td> <td>LFM2.5 8B</td> <td>Technically runnable on the tested 8 GB Pi 5, but with a large memory footprint and long cold load</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>These are <strong>text-generation</strong> results. They do not establish performance for image generation, speech recognition, vision, or training. “Runs” also means more than fitting the model file on a card: the runtime, context cache, operating system, and other services need RAM. Quantization reduces the weight file size, but it can reduce answer quality, especially at extreme settings such as 1-bit weights.</p> <h3 id="what-our-numbers-measure"> <a href="#what-our-numbers-measure" title="What our numbers measure">What our numbers measure</a> <a href="#what-our-numbers-measure" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="What our numbers measure">#</a> </h3> <p>The benchmark sent short factual, procedural safety, retrieved-context, weather, and help prompts to Ollama’s chat API. Each model saw the same prompt set and seed. Before timing a model, we unloaded it so the next request would include a cold load; the reported <strong>wall time</strong> is the complete request, while <strong>tokens per second</strong> describes only output generation. We also recorded the first <em>visible</em> token, which matters when a model spends time reasoning before it answers.</p> <p>For memory, we sampled the Pi’s available RAM and swap alongside the resident memory of Ollama and its inference process during each request. The <strong>RSS</strong> figures below are process-resident memory, not the entire host’s memory demand. File-backed pages, the operating system, a browser, or another local service can still make a nominally fitting model swap. The tables use the original five-prompt, single-pass runs. We later extended the harness with a news prompt and reply-rule checks; those checks clarify what to look for, but they do not turn the earlier timings into six-prompt compliance results.</p> <p>Neither tokens per second nor parameter count is a quality score. A model can emit text quickly yet omit a requested source, exceed a word budget, or produce an unfinished sentence. We would compare models on the prompts we actually plan to send, then inspect their answers before choosing one for an application.</p> <h2 id="raspberry-pi-4-favor-the-smallest-models"> <a href="#raspberry-pi-4-favor-the-smallest-models" title="Raspberry Pi 4: favor the smallest models">Raspberry Pi 4: favor the smallest models</a> <a href="#raspberry-pi-4-favor-the-smallest-models" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Raspberry Pi 4: favor the smallest models">#</a> </h2> <p>The tested 2 GB Pi 4 had limited headroom. The smallest LFM2.5 models completed all five prompts, as did <code>qwen2.5:0.5b</code>. They are sensible choices for brief offline replies or a small local assistant.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Model</th> <th style="text-align: right">Model file</th> <th style="text-align: right">Measured output speed</th> <th style="text-align: right">Average reply time</th> <th>Observed memory or outcome</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td>LFM2.5-230M, imported GGUF</td> <td style="text-align: right">0.25 GB</td> <td style="text-align: right">12.8 tokens/s</td> <td style="text-align: right">7.2 s</td> <td>383 MB peak resident memory; 5/5 prompts</td> </tr> <tr> <td>LFM2.5-350M, imported GGUF</td> <td style="text-align: right">0.38 GB</td> <td style="text-align: right">8.6 tokens/s</td> <td style="text-align: right">8.6 s</td> <td>516 MB peak resident memory; 5/5 prompts</td> </tr> <tr> <td><code>qwen2.5:0.5b</code></td> <td style="text-align: right">0.40 GB</td> <td style="text-align: right">8.0 tokens/s</td> <td style="text-align: right">9.7 s</td> <td>5/5 prompts; available directly in Ollama</td> </tr> <tr> <td>MiniCPM5-1B, imported GGUF, reasoning off</td> <td style="text-align: right">0.69 GB</td> <td style="text-align: right">5.9 tokens/s</td> <td style="text-align: right">12.2 s</td> <td>883 MB peak resident memory; 5/5 prompts</td> </tr> <tr> <td>MiniCPM5-1B, imported GGUF, default reasoning</td> <td style="text-align: right">0.69 GB</td> <td style="text-align: right">5.7 tokens/s</td> <td style="text-align: right">33.3 s</td> <td>Only 1/5 prompts returned a useful visible reply</td> </tr> <tr> <td><code>qwen3:0.6b</code>, default reasoning</td> <td style="text-align: right">0.52 GB</td> <td style="text-align: right">6.4 tokens/s</td> <td style="text-align: right">40.4 s</td> <td>One empty reply; board rebooted</td> </tr> <tr> <td><code>granite4:350m</code></td> <td style="text-align: right">0.71 GB</td> <td style="text-align: right">4.6 tokens/s</td> <td style="text-align: right">15.5 s</td> <td>913 MB RSS, no swap or reboot; slow but stable</td> </tr> <tr> <td><code>gemma3:1b</code></td> <td style="text-align: right">0.82 GB</td> <td style="text-align: right">4.0 tokens/s</td> <td style="text-align: right">30.7 s</td> <td>Heavy swapping; board rebooted during testing</td> </tr> <tr> <td><code>qwen3.5:0.8b</code></td> <td style="text-align: right">1.04 GB</td> <td style="text-align: right">—</td> <td style="text-align: right">—</td> <td>Did not complete; board rebooted</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>The Pi 4 results are especially sensitive to the rest of the system. We observed board resets during larger-model tests, including a <code>qwen3.5:0.8b</code> run that never completed. That is evidence about our 2 GB setup, rather than a claim that every Pi 4 or every 1B model will reboot. A 4 GB or 8 GB Pi 4 has more memory, but its CPU will still make inference slower than on the tested Pi 5. We did not directly benchmark those Pi 4 memory variants.</p> <p>One early Pi 4 pass also appeared much worse than the final measurements: roughly 625 MB of staged GGUF files sat in a RAM-backed <code>/tmp</code>, leaving only about 500–600 MB free and pushing hundreds of megabytes into swap. After moving those files to persistent storage, the small-model results above gave a more useful picture of inference memory. On a 2 GB board, even the <em>location of a download</em> can distort a benchmark.</p> <p><strong>Recommendation:</strong> The imported LFM2.5-350M is our default for this 2 GB board. It remained stable at <strong>516 MB RSS</strong>, left about <strong>1 GB of RAM available</strong>, and passed <strong>5/6</strong> reply-rule checks in the Pi 4 compliance pass. It did miss source names in repeated Pi 5 testing, so applications that require attribution should check for it. Choose LFM2.5-230M when latency and memory headroom matter most: it was faster and lighter, but in one medical-context answer it garbled “nausea or vomiting” into “nausea/ventilator use.” That content error makes it a weaker default for safety or health replies despite its higher repeated mechanical compliance score. Choose <code>qwen2.5:0.5b</code> if you need a model from the <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Ollama registry"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://ollama.com/library/qwen2.5/tags"> <a href="https://ollama.com/library/qwen2.5/tags" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Ollama registry</a> </span> , while accounting for its weaker instruction compliance. <code>granite4:350m</code> stayed stable but took longer and used more memory; MiniCPM5-1B is viable only when the client disables reasoning. Avoid Gemma 3 1B and Qwen3.5 0.8B on this specific 2 GB setup because our runs triggered resets.</p> <h2 id="raspberry-pi-5-more-choice-with-a-speed-tradeoff"> <a href="#raspberry-pi-5-more-choice-with-a-speed-tradeoff" title="Raspberry Pi 5: more choice, with a speed tradeoff">Raspberry Pi 5: more choice, with a speed tradeoff</a> <a href="#raspberry-pi-5-more-choice-with-a-speed-tradeoff" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Raspberry Pi 5: more choice, with a speed tradeoff">#</a> </h2> <p>The 8 GB Pi 5 handled all <strong>25 models</strong> in our speed-and-memory benchmark. The table includes every run, including models we do not recommend for this short-reply workload. A dagger marks an imported GGUF. “Think off” records the setting used for the speed run; the separate compliance pass did not necessarily use that setting.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Model</th> <th style="text-align: right">File GB</th> <th style="text-align: right">Output tok/s</th> <th style="text-align: right">Reply s</th> <th style="text-align: right">Peak RSS MB</th> <th>Short-reply assessment</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><code>lfm2.5-230m</code> †</td> <td style="text-align: right">0.25</td> <td style="text-align: right">45.0</td> <td style="text-align: right">1.8</td> <td style="text-align: right">446</td> <td>Lowest latency; 78% repeated compliance</td> </tr> <tr> <td><code>bonsai-1.7b</code> †, Q1_0</td> <td style="text-align: right">0.25</td> <td style="text-align: right">15.3</td> <td style="text-align: right">8.2</td> <td style="text-align: right">871</td> <td>Skip: 1-bit weights and 3/6 single-pass compliance</td> </tr> <tr> <td><code>lfm2.5-350m</code> †</td> <td style="text-align: right">0.38</td> <td style="text-align: right">30.0</td> <td style="text-align: right">2.1</td> <td style="text-align: right">581</td> <td>Fast, but missed source citation in 5/18 repeats</td> </tr> <tr> <td><code>qwen2.5:0.5b</code></td> <td style="text-align: right">0.40</td> <td style="text-align: right">28.4</td> <td style="text-align: right">3.6</td> <td style="text-align: right">675</td> <td>Easy registry option; 34.4 s cold load and overlong answers</td> </tr> <tr> <td><code>gemma3n:e2b</code></td> <td style="text-align: right">5.62</td> <td style="text-align: right">6.1</td> <td style="text-align: right">25.9</td> <td style="text-align: right">5,261</td> <td>Skip: swap pressure alongside other Pi services</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>† Imported GGUF. Reply times and memory figures are from the five-prompt Pi 5 speed run; compliance figures come from separate six-prompt tests. A model without a compliance score was not shown to obey the reply rules.</p> <p>The small LFM2.5 models were the fastest <em>for this short-reply workload</em>. The 1.2B version offers a practical middle ground on the tested Pi 5. Gemma 3 1B is a registry-only alternative with better repeated reply-rule compliance than Qwen2.5 1.5B in our later tests. A 3B model may be worth the slower output for prompts that need more capacity, but these timings alone do not prove which model gives the best answers.</p> <p>Cold-load and first-token delays change the experience. LFM2.5-230M loaded in about <strong>0.21 seconds</strong> and produced a visible token in <strong>0.37 seconds</strong> on the Pi 5. Qwen2.5 1.5B took <strong>2.59 seconds</strong> to load and <strong>3.66 seconds</strong> to its first visible token; Qwen2.5 3B took <strong>5.60</strong> and <strong>7.97 seconds</strong>, respectively. For an occasional question, those delays may matter more than the output rate once generation begins. For a continuously loaded model, they matter less, but keeping a model resident consumes memory between requests.</p> <p>Other measured candidates illustrate why we do not rank by parameter count alone. With reasoning disabled, <code>qwen3:0.6b</code> reached <strong>23.0 tokens/s</strong> on the Pi 5 at <strong>1,069 MB RSS</strong>, while imported MiniCPM5-1B reached <strong>18.4 tokens/s</strong> at <strong>869 MB RSS</strong>. <code>granite4:350m</code> needed a <strong>0.71 GB</strong> download and generated <strong>12.1 tokens/s</strong>, despite its 350M label. Model packaging and architecture change the relationship between name, file size, memory, and speed.</p> <p>If your client can reliably send <code>think: false</code>, Qwen3 0.6B and MiniCPM5-1B are reasonable experiments when you want alternatives to LFM2.5. MiniCPM5-2B, Qwen3 1.7B, and Spark-X2.5 1.7B also ran on the Pi 5, but none offered a clear speed-and-memory advantage over our primary choices. The compliance test used default reasoning for MiniCPM5-1B and Spark-X2.5; its empty replies should not be presented as the outcome of their think-off speed runs. Conversely, a fast think-off timing does not establish that a bridge which omits that flag will receive a usable answer.</p> <p>If installation simplicity matters more than raw speed, Gemma 3 1B and Llama 3.2 1B are plausible registry choices on the 8 GB Pi 5. Gemma 3 1B followed the tested reply rules in <strong>15/18</strong> repeated replies. Llama 3.2 1B passed <strong>5/6</strong> in one pass, so its compliance estimate is less certain. Qwen2.5 1.5B loaded and answered faster than Gemma 3 1B in our timing run, but passed only <strong>4/6</strong> reply-rule checks in its single compliance pass. Choose between them using the requirement that matters to your own prompts.</p> <p>For occasional longer or harder text prompts, the quantized Qwen2.5 3B and Llama 3.2 3B are the 3B candidates with manageable memory use on our 8 GB Pi 5. We measured their speed and memory, and Qwen2.5 3B passed <strong>5/6</strong> in one compliance pass; we did not publish a comparable compliance run for Llama 3.2 3B. Their larger parameter counts are a reason to <em>test</em> them on tasks where smaller models fall short, not proof that they answered those tasks better. Granite 4 Micro and Micro-H, Qwen3.5 2B, Gemma 3 4B, Ling-3.0-tiny, and Gemma 3n E2B all fit or loaded in our Pi 5 trials, but offered less attractive latency, memory headroom, or reply reliability for this short-response application.</p> <p>The two Bonsai models demonstrate the cost of extreme quantization. Their Q1_0 files were strikingly small for 1.7B and 4B parameter names, yet the 1.7B model passed only <strong>3/6</strong> reply-rule checks. The 4B model passed a single six-prompt compliance pass, but took <strong>18.1 seconds</strong> per reply and has no repeated compliance confirmation. We would treat both as experiments rather than default recommendations, especially where answer quality matters.</p> <p>The 8B LFM2.5 result needs context: its hybrid design uses fewer active parameters per token, so its decode rate exceeded the measured 3B dense models. It still took <strong>34.4 seconds to load cold</strong> from microSD and used over <strong>5.3 GB resident memory</strong>. It is a demonstration of what fits, not a comfortable default for a Pi that also runs other services. The measured <code>gemma3n:e2b</code> similarly used about 5.3 GB resident memory and caused swapping alongside the other services on the test host.</p> <p>The LFM2.5 8B run also reached the full <strong>140-token cap</strong> instead of keeping its response brief. The 4B Gemma 3 run took <strong>14.3 seconds</strong> to its first token and <strong>30.3 seconds</strong> for the complete reply. Both can be loaded on this Pi 5, but neither behaved like a responsive small assistant in our tests. A tiny model with an appropriately short answer may serve a radio or command interface better than a larger model with a faster decode rate on paper.</p> <h2 id="memory-reasoning-and-model-format"> <a href="#memory-reasoning-and-model-format" title="Memory, reasoning, and model format">Memory, reasoning, and model format</a> <a href="#memory-reasoning-and-model-format" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Memory, reasoning, and model format">#</a> </h2> <p>A useful first estimate from our measurements is <strong>model download size × 1.4</strong> for resident inference memory. It is only a rule of thumb: context length, runtime settings, model architecture, and other processes can change the requirement. Check available memory while generating, keep only one model loaded on a small host, and leave room for the OS. A 4 GB board can reasonably start with the tiny or compact models, but our 4 GB recommendations are extrapolations rather than direct 4 GB tests.</p> <p>For example, a 0.73 GB LFM2.5-1.2B file corresponded to about <strong>967 MB RSS</strong> on the Pi 5, while the 0.99 GB Qwen2.5 1.5B file reached <strong>1,361 MB RSS</strong>. The rule works reasonably for those models, but it is not a hard limit. Plan for more than the measured model process if the Pi also runs an interface, search index, local library, or other background service. Watch swap use during a real request; a model that technically loads while constantly swapping is not a practical fit.</p> <p>Some models generate an internal reasoning block before their visible answer. In our tests, <code>qwen3:0.6b</code> on the 2 GB Pi 4 took much longer to produce visible text, and MiniCPM5-1B answered only one of five prompts with its default reasoning setting versus five of five with reasoning disabled. For a short response budget, set <code>think: false</code> in a compatible Ollama API request, or select a model that does not default to reasoning. This setting applies to supported models and clients; it is not a universal speed switch.</p> <p>The distinction matters because a token cap can include tokens spent on reasoning even when the user sees no answer. On the Pi 4, default-thinking <code>qwen3:0.6b</code> averaged <strong>40.4 seconds per request</strong>, and one prompt produced an empty visible reply. MiniCPM5-1B averaged <strong>33.3 seconds</strong> with its default setting versus <strong>12.2 seconds</strong> with reasoning disabled. We also disabled reasoning for the Pi 5 runs of Qwen3, Qwen3.5, MiniCPM5, Ling-3.0, and Spark-X2.5 where indicated in our records. Compare a model under the exact reasoning setting your client will use.</p> <h3 id="check-whether-the-reply-is-usable"> <a href="#check-whether-the-reply-is-usable" title="Check whether the reply is usable">Check whether the reply is usable</a> <a href="#check-whether-the-reply-is-usable" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Check whether the reply is usable">#</a> </h3> <p>For our short mesh-assistant workload, the response contract is as important as speed: at most <strong>90 words</strong>, no more than <strong>three bullets</strong>, plain text, a finished sentence, and use of supplied retrieval context with its source named. The bridge divides text into <strong>180-character chunks</strong>. A long answer occupies more radio airtime, even if the model generated it quickly.</p> <p>The later version of our benchmark checks for empty replies, a prompt-specific word limit, too many bullets, Markdown tables or code fences, an unfinished ending, missing terms from supplied context, and a missing source name. When we scored replies against the deployed assistant prompt, small models breached these rules regularly. The most consequential failures were <strong>empty replies</strong> when reasoning consumed the token budget, followed by answers that ignored retrieved context or omitted its source. Going over the word limit or using too many bullets still delivered visible text, but wasted airtime. These are mechanical checks, not a substitute for reading the answer: they cannot establish factual accuracy or whether safety advice is sound.</p> <h4 id="repeated-pi-5-compliance-results"> <a href="#repeated-pi-5-compliance-results" title="Repeated Pi 5 compliance results">Repeated Pi 5 compliance results</a> <a href="#repeated-pi-5-compliance-results" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Repeated Pi 5 compliance results">#</a> </h4> <p>We first ran six prompts once per model with a <strong>220-token cap</strong> and the deployed system prompt. Models that looked plausible were then tested twice more with a different seed, giving <strong>18 replies per model</strong>. A perfect single pass did not guarantee a perfect repeat. The repeated results below provide a firmer comparison for the short mesh replies we tested:</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Model</th> <th style="text-align: right">Replies that followed all checked rules</th> <th>Main observed failures</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td>Imported LFM2.5-1.2B</td> <td style="text-align: right">16/18 (89%)</td> <td>Two unfinished replies</td> </tr> <tr> <td><code>gemma3:1b</code></td> <td style="text-align: right">15/18 (83%)</td> <td>Three unfinished replies</td> </tr> <tr> <td>Imported LFM2.5-230M</td> <td style="text-align: right">14/18 (78%)</td> <td>Unfinished replies and missing source names</td> </tr> <tr> <td>Imported LFM2.5-350M</td> <td style="text-align: right">13/18 (72%)</td> <td>Missing source names</td> </tr> <tr> <td><code>qwen2.5:0.5b</code></td> <td style="text-align: right">11/18 (61%)</td> <td>Too many bullets, excess words, missing source names</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>On the <strong>2 GB Pi 4</strong>, the separate six-prompt compliance pass found <strong>5/6</strong> for LFM2.5-350M, <strong>4/6</strong> for LFM2.5-230M, and <strong>2/6</strong> for Qwen2.5-0.5B. MiniCPM5-1B improved from <strong>1/6</strong> with default reasoning to <strong>5/6</strong> with reasoning disabled. These Pi 4 scores are single-pass results, so we give more weight to the repeated Pi 5 results when discussing general instruction-following behavior, while using the Pi 4 runs to judge stability and speed on that board.</p> <p>The failures have different consequences. An <strong>empty</strong> reply gives the user nothing; an answer that ignores supplied material can be misleading. A missing source name prevents readers from checking attribution. Extra bullets or words mainly consume additional 180-character packets. An unfinished sentence may indicate truncation. The LFM2.5-230M medical-term error is a reminder that a reply can pass these mechanical checks and still be wrong. None of the five repeated candidates followed every rule in all 18 replies, so an application that requires a strict length or format should enforce it after generation as well and review high-stakes content separately.</p> <p>We also checked the actual bridge endpoint, Ollama’s OpenAI-compatible <code>/v1/chat/completions</code>, with retrieved WikiMed context. On the Pi 5, LFM2.5-1.2B returned a 28-word answer using six supplied terms; Qwen2.5-0.5B returned 38 words using seven. Both fit within two 180-character packets. That endpoint check confirms the imported LFM2.5 model works through the bridge’s request path, but one successful answer is not a reliability guarantee.</p> <p>Ollama publishes many ready-to-pull models, including <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Qwen2.5’s 0.5B, 1.5B, and 3B variants"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://ollama.com/library/qwen2.5/tags"> <a href="https://ollama.com/library/qwen2.5/tags" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Qwen2.5’s 0.5B, 1.5B, and 3B variants</a> </span> . We imported the small LFM2.5 models from <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Liquid AI’s GGUF releases"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://huggingface.co/LiquidAI/LFM2.5-350M-GGUF/tree/main"> <a href="https://huggingface.co/LiquidAI/LFM2.5-350M-GGUF/tree/main" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Liquid AI’s GGUF releases</a> </span> into Ollama. Check the exact tag or GGUF filename before downloading: model registries and repositories can change. Keep GGUF downloads on persistent storage; in our tests, staging files in a RAM-backed <code>/tmp</code> consumed scarce Pi 4 memory.</p> <h3 id="registry-tags-and-gguf-imports"> <a href="#registry-tags-and-gguf-imports" title="Registry tags and GGUF imports">Registry tags and GGUF imports</a> <a href="#registry-tags-and-gguf-imports" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Registry tags and GGUF imports">#</a> </h3> <p>An Ollama tag is the shortest path to a first test: pull the exact tag and run it. The small LFM2.5 models in our tables were <strong>GGUF imports</strong>, not tags named <code>lfm2.5-230m</code>, <code>lfm2.5-350m</code>, or <code>lfm2.5-1.2b</code> in Ollama’s public library. GGUF is a model-file format; names such as <code>Q8_0</code> and <code>Q4_K_M</code> identify quantization choices. The 230M and 350M LFM2.5 files we used were Q8_0, while the 1.2B file was Q4_K_M. Consequently, the same parameter count downloaded in another quantization may not have the same file size, memory use, or quality.</p> <p>To import the tested 350M variant, download its GGUF to a directory on persistent storage, create a Modelfile pointing to it, and let Ollama copy it into its model store:</p> <div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" style="color:#f8f8f2;background-color:#272822;-moz-tab-size:4;-o-tab-size:4;tab-size:4;-webkit-text-size-adjust:none;"><code class="language-bash" data-lang="bash"><span style="display:flex;"><span>mkdir -p <span style="color:#e6db74">"</span>$HOME<span style="color:#e6db74">/gguf"</span> </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>cd <span style="color:#e6db74">"</span>$HOME<span style="color:#e6db74">/gguf"</span> </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>curl -fL -C - --retry <span style="color:#ae81ff">5</span> --retry-all-errors -O <span style="color:#ae81ff">\ </span></span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> https://huggingface.co/LiquidAI/LFM2.5-350M-GGUF/resolve/main/LFM2.5-350M-Q8_0.gguf </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>printf <span style="color:#e6db74">'FROM %s/LFM2.5-350M-Q8_0.gguf\n'</span> <span style="color:#e6db74">"</span>$PWD<span style="color:#e6db74">"</span> > Modelfile-lfm2.5-350m </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>ollama create lfm2.5-350m -f Modelfile-lfm2.5-350m </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>ollama run lfm2.5-350m </span></span></code></pre></div><p>The import temporarily needs space for both the downloaded file and Ollama’s stored copy. We used resumable downloads because long GGUF transfers sometimes broke mid-file. Before importing a downloaded GGUF, compare its SHA-256 with the file hash published by its source; a partial transfer can otherwise look like a model problem.
