On our Pi setup, <code>/tmp</code> was RAM-backed, so staging a GGUF there reduced the memory available for inference.</p> <h2 id="a-practical-starting-point"> <a href="#a-practical-starting-point" title="A practical starting point">A practical starting point</a> <a href="#a-practical-starting-point" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="A practical starting point">#</a> </h2> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Hardware and goal</th> <th>First model to try</th> <th>Why</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td>2 GB Pi 4, default</td> <td>Imported LFM2.5-350M</td> <td>Stable at 516 MB RSS with about 1 GB available; selected after a medical-term error from 230M</td> </tr> <tr> <td>2 GB Pi 4, lowest latency</td> <td>Imported LFM2.5-230M</td> <td>383 MB RSS and 7.2-second average reply; verify content carefully, especially for health or safety questions</td> </tr> <tr> <td>2 GB Pi 4, registry-only</td> <td><code>qwen2.5:0.5b</code></td> <td>Direct Ollama pull and stable in our five-prompt Pi 4 run; 61% repeated compliance on the Pi 5</td> </tr> <tr> <td>4 GB Pi 4 or Pi 5</td> <td>Imported LFM2.5-1.2B, then test locally</td> <td>967 MB RSS and 89% repeated compliance on our 8 GB Pi 5; we did not benchmark 4 GB variants directly</td> </tr> <tr> <td>8 GB Pi 5, responsive assistant</td> <td>Imported LFM2.5-1.2B</td> <td>15.5 tokens/s, 4.7-second total reply, and the highest repeated compliance we measured</td> </tr> <tr> <td>8 GB Pi 5, registry-only setup</td> <td><code>gemma3:1b</code></td> <td>11.2 tokens/s, 1,262 MB RSS, and 83% repeated compliance</td> </tr> <tr> <td>8 GB Pi 5, try a larger text model</td> <td>Quantized Qwen2.5 3B or Llama 3.2 3B</td> <td>Both ran at about 5 tokens/s and used 2.4–2.8 GB RSS; Qwen2.5 3B passed 5/6 in a single compliance pass</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>These choices prioritize short, useful replies on a Pi that may also run other services. They are starting points rather than claims that one model is best at every task. In our single-pass Pi 5 compliance check, default-thinking <code>qwen3.5:0.8b</code> and Spark-X2.5 returned no compliant replies, while MiniCPM5-1B managed 1/6; a client that cannot disable their reasoning should avoid them for this short-reply workload. We would test the final model with the actual prompt, context length, concurrency, and response limit planned for deployment.</p> <p>For the registry model, after <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="installing Ollama for Linux"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://ollama.com/download/linux"> <a href="https://ollama.com/download/linux" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >installing Ollama for Linux</a> </span> , run:</p> <div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" style="color:#f8f8f2;background-color:#272822;-moz-tab-size:4;-o-tab-size:4;tab-size:4;-webkit-text-size-adjust:none;"><code class="language-bash" data-lang="bash"><span style="display:flex;"><span>ollama pull qwen2.5:0.5b </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>ollama run qwen2.5:0.5b </span></span></code></pre></div><p>Test with your own prompts, desired answer length, and other services running. Record both total reply time and memory use. That will tell you more about whether a model belongs on your Pi than its parameter count alone.</p> <p>On a memory-constrained node, keep an eye on swap while testing. If a larger model makes the board unresponsive, use a smaller model and set an Ollama service memory limit appropriate to that model so an oversized load fails instead of exhausting the host. A service cap is a safeguard, not a way to make an oversized model fit. The Pi 4 resets in our tests show why responsiveness and memory headroom belong in the selection criteria alongside tokens per second.</p> Read More at https://simeononsecurity.com/

item.title: Which Cybersecurity Career Fits You? 16 Starting Points, Many Paths
item.description: Explore a personality-themed video, multiple cybersecurity roles for each type, and practical exercises to compare career paths by their real work.
item.content:encoded: <p><strong>Cybersecurity is a collection of very different jobs.</strong> A security operations center (SOC) analyst investigates alerts, a security engineer builds controls, a privacy specialist works through data handling decisions, and a sales engineer explains technology to customers. Finding work you enjoy starts with understanding those daily tasks.</p> <p>The video below uses all 16 personality labels as a playful way to introduce these paths. Watch it, take the linked test if you want a starting point for reflection, and then use the role descriptions and small experiments in this article to see what actually holds your interest.</p> <p> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Watch the video on YouTube"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=FsplOmkbPI4"> <a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=FsplOmkbPI4" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Watch the video on YouTube</a> </span> .</p> <h2 id="take-the-personality-test"> <a href="#take-the-personality-test" title="Take the personality test">Take the personality test</a> <a href="#take-the-personality-test" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Take the personality test">#</a> </h2> <p>The video points viewers to the <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="free 16Personalities test"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://www.16personalities.com/free-personality-test"> <a href="https://www.16personalities.com/free-personality-test" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >free 16Personalities test</a> </span> . Its result can give you language for preferences such as structure, experimentation, collaboration, or independence. The publisher describes it as a starting point for self-reflection, not an employment screening tool or a way to assign someone a job. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="16Personalities’ own guidance"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://www.16personalities.com/for-ai"> <a href="https://www.16personalities.com/for-ai" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >16Personalities’ own guidance</a> </span> </p> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="simeononsecurity"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://www.16personalities.com/free-personality-test"> <a href="https://www.16personalities.com/free-personality-test" title="simeononsecurity" target="_blank" class="markdown-btn" rel="noopener external" alt="simeononsecurity" target="_blank" > <button class="markdown-button">Take the free 16Personalities test</button> </a> <p>The assessment opens on 16Personalities in a new tab. Use the result to generate career questions, not to rule out jobs.</p> </span> <h2 id="how-to-read-the-videos-16-pairings"> <a href="#how-to-read-the-videos-16-pairings" title="How to read the video’s 16 pairings">How to read the video’s 16 pairings</a> <a href="#how-to-read-the-videos-16-pairings" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="How to read the video’s 16 pairings">#</a> </h2> <p>The pairings below are <strong>the video’s examples</strong>, not hiring rules or evidence that a personality type predicts job performance. You can succeed in any of these roles regardless of your test result. Use the “try it” column to learn whether you like the work itself.</p> <script type="application/ld+json"> { "@context": "https://schema.org/", "@type": "ImageObject", "contentUrl": "https:\/\/simeononsecurity.com\/cybersecurity-role-families.svg", "caption": "Four career areas—defense and investigation, offensive research, governance and privacy, and engineering and response—surround a prompt to try the work", "license": "https://simeononsecurity.com/termsandconditions/", "acquireLicensePage": "https://simeononsecurity.com/contactus/", "creditText": "SimeonOnSecurity", "creator": { "@type": "Person", "name": "SimeonOnSecurity" }, "copyrightNotice": "SimeonOnSecurity", "associatedArticle": { "@type": "NewsArticle", "headline": "simeononsecurity", "url": "https:\/\/simeononsecurity.com\/", "datePublished": "2026-10-02 21:20:37.712261381 \u002b0000 UTC m=\u002b337.436987142", "author": { "@type": "Person", "name": "SimeonOnSecurity", "url": "https:\/\/simeononsecurity.com\/authors\/simeononsecurity" } } } </script> <center> <figure align="center" style="text-align: center; margin: 0 auto;" itemscope itemtype="http://schema.org/ImageObject"> <meta property="article:published_time" content="2026-10-02 21:20:37.712261381 +0000 UTC m=+337.436987142"> <meta property="article:author" content="SimeonOnSecurity"> <meta property="article:author:url" content="https://simeononsecurity.com/authors/simeononsecurity"> <meta property="og:license" content="https://simeononsecurity.com/termsandconditions/"> <meta property="og:see_also" content="https://simeononsecurity.com/contactus/"> <meta property="og:copyright" content="SimeonOnSecurity"> <img align="center" style="text-align: center; margin: 0 auto; max-width: 80%; max-height: 600px; min-width: 100px; min-height: 100px; height: auto; width: auto;" src="https://simeononsecurity.com/cybersecurity-role-families.svg" alt="Four career areas—defense and investigation, offensive research, governance and privacy, and engineering and response—surround a prompt to try the work"loading="lazy" fetchpriority="low" itemprop="contentUrl" /> <figcaption align="center" style="text-align: center; margin: 0 auto;" itemprop="caption description"> <p>Start with a kind of work that interests you, then test that interest with a realistic task.</p> </figcaption> </figure> </center> <h3 id="defense-and-investigation"> <a href="#defense-and-investigation" title="Defense and investigation">Defense and investigation</a> <a href="#defense-and-investigation" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Defense and investigation">#</a> </h3> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Video’s type and role</th> <th>What the work involves</th> <th>Try it before committing</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>ISFJ — SOC analyst</strong></td> <td>Triage alerts, investigate suspicious activity, document the result, and hand off incidents.</td> <td>Review a sample alert and write a short investigation note with evidence and next steps.</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>ISTJ — digital forensics or audit</strong></td> <td>Preserve evidence, build timelines, and check that findings can be reproduced.</td> <td>Build a timeline from a practice disk or log set and record where each artifact came from.</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>INFJ — threat intelligence analyst</strong></td> <td>Connect reports, indicators, and behavior into a picture defenders can act on.</td> <td>Read two public threat reports and write a one-page brief separating facts from hypotheses.</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <div class="personality-career-gallery" style="display:grid;grid-template-columns:repeat(auto-fit,minmax(180px,1fr));gap:1rem;margin:1.5rem 0;"> </div> <p>The common thread is careful interpretation. If you like following evidence and explaining what happened, investigate these roles even if your test returns a different type.</p> <h3 id="offensive-security-and-research"> <a href="#offensive-security-and-research" title="Offensive security and research">Offensive security and research</a> <a href="#offensive-security-and-research" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Offensive security and research">#</a> </h3> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Video’s type and role</th> <th>What the work involves</th> <th>Try it before committing</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>ENTP — penetration tester</strong></td> <td>Test systems within an agreed scope, validate findings, and explain how to fix them.</td> <td>Complete a legal training lab and write a clear finding with impact and remediation.</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>INTP — vulnerability researcher or reverse engineer</strong></td> <td>Examine software behavior and identify why a flaw exists.</td> <td>Analyze a deliberately vulnerable program and document the root cause.</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>ESFP — social engineering or physical assessment</strong></td> <td>Test human and physical controls under explicit authorization and communicate results tactfully.</td> <td>Design a tabletop exercise for an authorized team; assess the briefing and debriefing process.</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>ISFP — OSINT investigator</strong></td> <td>Gather and verify information from public sources while respecting privacy and scope.</td> <td>Investigate a fictional organization using public records and cite every claim.</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <div class="personality-career-gallery" style="display:grid;grid-template-columns:repeat(auto-fit,minmax(180px,1fr));gap:1rem;margin:1.5rem 0;"> </div> <p>Offensive jobs involve substantial reporting and scope discipline. Enjoying puzzles is a good reason to try a lab; professional work also requires restraint, permission, and a report someone can use.</p> <h3 id="governance-risk-and-privacy"> <a href="#governance-risk-and-privacy" title="Governance, risk, and privacy">Governance, risk, and privacy</a> <a href="#governance-risk-and-privacy" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Governance, risk, and privacy">#</a> </h3> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Video’s type and role</th> <th>What the work involves</th> <th>Try it before committing</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>ESTJ — GRC lead</strong></td> <td>Track risks, coordinate audits, and turn policy into repeatable decisions.</td> <td>Create a small risk register for a fictional service and explain how you ranked each risk.</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>ESFJ — third-party risk liaison</strong></td> <td>Gather vendor evidence and help business and security teams resolve gaps.</td> <td>Review a sample vendor questionnaire and write three useful follow-up questions.</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>INFP — privacy and data protection specialist</strong></td> <td>Examine how personal data is collected, used, retained, and shared.</td> <td>Draw a data-flow map for an imaginary app and identify where consent or retention needs review.</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <div class="personality-career-gallery" style="display:grid;grid-template-columns:repeat(auto-fit,minmax(180px,1fr));gap:1rem;margin:1.5rem 0;"> </div> <p>These roles have technical substance even when they do not spend the day in a terminal. They suit people who enjoy making decisions legible to others and working through tradeoffs across teams.</p> <h3 id="engineering-response-and-leadership"> <a href="#engineering-response-and-leadership" title="Engineering, response, and leadership">Engineering, response, and leadership</a> <a href="#engineering-response-and-leadership" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Engineering, response, and leadership">#</a> </h3> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Video’s type and role</th> <th>What the work involves</th> <th>Try it before committing</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>INTJ — security architect</strong></td> <td>Design controls and explain how systems fit together.</td> <td>Diagram a small application and propose three controls tied to specific risks.</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>ISTP — security engineer</strong></td> <td>Deploy, tune, and maintain security tools and infrastructure.</td> <td>Build a small lab control, test that it works, and document rollback steps.</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>ESTP — incident responder</strong></td> <td>Coordinate investigations and containment when events are time-sensitive.</td> <td>Run a tabletop incident and practice a concise status update.</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>ENTJ — CISO or security leader</strong></td> <td>Set priorities, manage budgets, and explain risk to executives.</td> <td>Draft a one-page plan that funds the highest-value controls within a fixed budget.</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>ENFJ — security awareness or human-risk lead</strong></td> <td>Teach practical habits and improve how people report suspicious activity.</td> <td>Turn one common phishing pattern into a brief training exercise and measure understanding.</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>ENFP — sales engineer or security evangelist</strong></td> <td>Demonstrate products, answer technical questions, and translate features into outcomes.</td> <td>Give a short demo of a security tool to someone without a security background.</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <div class="personality-career-gallery" style="display:grid;grid-template-columns:repeat(auto-fit,minmax(180px,1fr));gap:1rem;margin:1.5rem 0;"> </div> <p>The video uses memorable stereotypes to make the roles easy to recognize. Real teams need many working styles within each specialty: an incident responder may be quiet and methodical, while a security engineer may spend much of the week collaborating with people.</p> <h2 id="more-than-one-role-can-fit-each-type"> <a href="#more-than-one-role-can-fit-each-type" title="More than one role can fit each type">More than one role can fit each type</a> <a href="#more-than-one-role-can-fit-each-type" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="More than one role can fit each type">#</a> </h2> <p>The video’s match is one doorway into a specialty. The alternatives below are <strong>additional roles to explore</strong>, based on overlapping tasks and working preferences. They are not personality-test predictions. Pay attention to which activities appeal to you, even when the four-letter label beside them is not yours.</p> <h3 id="if-you-like-evidence-and-careful-analysis"> <a href="#if-you-like-evidence-and-careful-analysis" title="If you like evidence and careful analysis">If you like evidence and careful analysis</a> <a href="#if-you-like-evidence-and-careful-analysis" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="If you like evidence and careful analysis">#</a> </h3> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Type in the video</th> <th>Other roles to explore</th> <th>Why those roles may appeal</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>ISFJ</strong></td> <td>Identity and access management (IAM) analyst; vulnerability management analyst</td> <td>Both reward consistent follow-through, clear records, and closing the loop with system owners.</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>ISTJ</strong></td> <td>Security auditor; incident evidence coordinator</td> <td>Both depend on traceable evidence, repeatable procedures, and explaining what a record proves.</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>INFJ</strong></td> <td>Detection engineer; security research writer</td> <td>These turn patterns and adversary behavior into useful detections or understandable briefs. Detection engineering also requires substantial technical practice.</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>ISFP</strong></td> <td>Digital forensics analyst; privacy investigator</td> <td>These emphasize patient observation, source verification, and respect for the people affected by findings.</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>These roles differ in their outputs. An IAM analyst may resolve access requests and investigate exceptions every day. A detection engineer writes and tunes rules, then checks what they miss. A forensics analyst may spend hours verifying a timeline. Try producing each kind of artifact before choosing a course or certification around the title.</p> <h3 id="if-you-enjoy-experiments-and-breaking-down-systems"> <a href="#if-you-enjoy-experiments-and-breaking-down-systems" title="If you enjoy experiments and breaking down systems">If you enjoy experiments and breaking down systems</a> <a href="#if-you-enjoy-experiments-and-breaking-down-systems" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="If you enjoy experiments and breaking down systems">#</a> </h3> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Type in the video</th> <th>Other roles to explore</th> <th>Why those roles may appeal</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>ENTP</strong></td> <td>Application security consultant; purple team facilitator</td> <td>Both test assumptions, then work with defenders or developers to turn findings into improvements.</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>INTP</strong></td> <td>Malware analyst; application security engineer</td> <td>Both reward deep technical investigation and a clear explanation of why a system behaves as it does.</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>ISTP</strong></td> <td>Detection engineer; cloud security engineer</td> <td>Both involve building controls, testing them against real behavior, and fixing noisy or brittle configurations.</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>INTJ</strong></td> <td>Cloud security architect; threat modeling lead</td> <td>Both connect system design decisions to risks, controls, and long-term maintenance.</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>The most visible part of these jobs is often the least representative. A penetration test includes scoping and reporting. Reverse engineering includes notes that others can reproduce. Engineering includes maintenance and support after the exciting build. Ask yourself whether you would still want the role when those routine tasks fill half the week.</p> <h3 id="if-you-like-translating-risk-for-people"> <a href="#if-you-like-translating-risk-for-people" title="If you like translating risk for people">If you like translating risk for people</a> <a href="#if-you-like-translating-risk-for-people" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="If you like translating risk for people">#</a> </h3> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Type in the video</th> <th>Other roles to explore</th> <th>Why those roles may appeal</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>ESFP</strong></td> <td>Security awareness facilitator; customer security trainer</td> <td>Both use live communication and feedback to help people change behavior.</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>ESTJ</strong></td> <td>Security program manager; audit manager</td> <td>Both organize work across teams, make priorities explicit, and track whether commitments were completed.</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>ESFJ</strong></td> <td>Customer trust analyst; security awareness lead</td> <td>Both require patient follow-up and answers that make sense to people outside security.</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>INFP</strong></td> <td>Privacy analyst; human-centered security researcher</td> <td>Both examine the effect of security and data decisions on the people who use a system.</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>ENFJ</strong></td> <td>Security training manager; security program manager</td> <td>Both coordinate people, communicate clearly, and measure whether a program is useful.</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>ENFP</strong></td> <td>Security developer advocate; security trainer</td> <td>Both combine technical explanation, demos, and audience feedback.</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>Communication work is measurable work. A third-party risk analyst needs to decide whether vendor evidence answers a control question. An awareness lead needs to see whether reporting behavior improves. A sales engineer needs to handle a demo failure honestly and return with an answer. If you like people-focused work, sample those concrete deliverables rather than assuming the job is only meetings.</p> <h3 id="if-you-like-coordinating-decisions-under-pressure"> <a href="#if-you-like-coordinating-decisions-under-pressure" title="If you like coordinating decisions under pressure">If you like coordinating decisions under pressure</a> <a href="#if-you-like-coordinating-decisions-under-pressure" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="If you like coordinating decisions under pressure">#</a> </h3> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Type in the video</th> <th>Other roles to explore</th> <th>Why those roles may appeal</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>ESTP</strong></td> <td>SOC incident lead; crisis exercise facilitator</td> <td>Both involve triage, rapid communication, and keeping a team aligned as facts change.</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>ENTJ</strong></td> <td>Security program manager; GRC lead</td> <td>Both require setting priorities, negotiating resources, and being accountable for outcomes.</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>Incident response and executive leadership are not identical kinds of pressure. An incident lead works through incomplete evidence on a short clock; a program leader makes durable tradeoffs across budgets, people, and risk. If either appeals, practice both a 15-minute incident update and a one-page funding decision.</p> <h2 id="compare-the-work-environment-not-only-the-job-title"> <a href="#compare-the-work-environment-not-only-the-job-title" title="Compare the work environment, not only the job title">Compare the work environment, not only the job title</a> <a href="#compare-the-work-environment-not-only-the-job-title" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Compare the work environment, not only the job title">#</a> </h2> <h3 id="pace-and-interruption"> <a href="#pace-and-interruption" title="Pace and interruption">Pace and interruption</a> <a href="#pace-and-interruption" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Pace and interruption">#</a> </h3> <p>A SOC shift or incident-response rotation may interrupt planned work. Architecture, privacy, and research often allow longer blocks of focused analysis, though deadlines and incidents can still change the day. Ask practitioners what proportion of their week is scheduled versus reactive, and whether on-call work is part of the role.</p> <h3 id="deliverables-and-feedback"> <a href="#deliverables-and-feedback" title="Deliverables and feedback">Deliverables and feedback</a> <a href="#deliverables-and-feedback" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Deliverables and feedback">#</a> </h3> <p>Different specialties prove their value differently. Penetration testers produce findings and remediation discussions. Engineers produce working controls, runbooks, and fewer false alerts. GRC and privacy teams produce decisions and evidence that can withstand review. Choose a role whose ordinary output you would be willing to improve repeatedly.</p> <h3 id="entry-point-and-prerequisites"> <a href="#entry-point-and-prerequisites" title="Entry point and prerequisites">Entry point and prerequisites</a> <a href="#entry-point-and-prerequisites" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Entry point and prerequisites">#</a> </h3> <p>The video’s CISO and architect pairings are long-term directions for most newcomers. A first step toward architecture may be systems, networking, cloud, or security engineering. A route toward leadership may begin in operations, risk, project work, or another specialty where you learn to make and defend decisions. NIST’s <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="NICE Framework"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://www.nist.gov/itl/applied-cybersecurity/nice/nice-framework-resource-center/resources/occupations-jobs-and-work"> <a href="https://www.nist.gov/itl/applied-cybersecurity/nice/nice-framework-resource-center/resources/occupations-jobs-and-work" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >NICE Framework</a> </span> describes work roles through tasks, knowledge, and skills; use those descriptions to identify what you can practice next rather than treating a senior title as an entry-level target.</p> <h2 id="choose-by-tasks-not-four-letters"> <a href="#choose-by-tasks-not-four-letters" title="Choose by tasks, not four letters">Choose by tasks, not four letters</a> <a href="#choose-by-tasks-not-four-letters" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Choose by tasks, not four letters">#</a> </h2> <p>A useful next step is to pick <strong>two roles</strong> from different sections and run their small experiments. For each one, ask: Did I like the routine parts? Did I want to investigate further after the exercise ended? Could I tolerate the role’s communication demands and pace?</p> <script type="application/ld+json"> { "@context": "https://schema.org/", "@type": "ImageObject", "contentUrl": "https:\/\/simeononsecurity.com\/cybersecurity-career-exploration-loop.svg", "caption": "Four steps for exploring a cybersecurity career: notice preferences, try a realistic task, reflect on routine work, and check real role descriptions", "license": "https://simeononsecurity.com/termsandconditions/", "acquireLicensePage": "https://simeononsecurity.com/contactus/", "creditText": "SimeonOnSecurity", "creator": { "@type": "Person", "name": "SimeonOnSecurity" }, "copyrightNotice": "SimeonOnSecurity", "associatedArticle": { "@type": "NewsArticle", "headline": "simeononsecurity", "url": "https:\/\/simeononsecurity.com\/", "datePublished": "2026-10-02 21:20:37.713803628 \u002b0000 UTC m=\u002b337.438529386", "author": { "@type": "Person", "name": "SimeonOnSecurity", "url": "https:\/\/simeononsecurity.com\/authors\/simeononsecurity" } } } </script> <center> <figure align="center" style="text-align: center; margin: 0 auto;" itemscope itemtype="http://schema.org/ImageObject"> <meta property="article:published_time" content="2026-10-02 21:20:37.713803628 +0000 UTC m=+337.438529386"> <meta property="article:author" content="SimeonOnSecurity"> <meta property="article:author:url" content="https://simeononsecurity.com/authors/simeononsecurity"> <meta property="og:license" content="https://simeononsecurity.com/termsandconditions/"> <meta property="og:see_also" content="https://simeononsecurity.com/contactus/"> <meta property="og:copyright" content="SimeonOnSecurity"> <img align="center" style="text-align: center; margin: 0 auto; max-width: 80%; max-height: 600px; min-width: 100px; min-height: 100px; height: auto; width: auto;" src="https://simeononsecurity.com/cybersecurity-career-exploration-loop.svg" alt="Four steps for exploring a cybersecurity career: notice preferences, try a realistic task, reflect on routine work, and check real role descriptions"loading="lazy" fetchpriority="low" itemprop="contentUrl" /> <figcaption align="center" style="text-align: center; margin: 0 auto;" itemprop="caption description"> <p>Use a personality result to generate ideas, then validate them through practice and real job descriptions.</p> </figcaption> </figure> </center> <p>Then compare what you enjoyed with <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="NIST’s NICE Framework"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://www.nist.gov/itl/applied-cybersecurity/nice/nice-framework-resource-center/getting-started"> <a href="https://www.nist.gov/itl/applied-cybersecurity/nice/nice-framework-resource-center/getting-started" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >NIST’s NICE Framework</a> </span> , which describes cybersecurity work through tasks, knowledge, and skills. A work role is a grouping of responsibilities; actual job titles can combine several roles. A conversation with a practitioner or a realistic lab will tell you more than a personality label alone.</p> <p>If you’re new to the field, use the video and test to <strong>generate possibilities</strong>. Use the day-to-day work, your existing skills, and hands-on practice to choose where to invest your time.</p> Read More at https://simeononsecurity.com/

item.title: Docker in LXC on Proxmox: Reliability, Evidence, and VM Migration
item.description: Evaluate Docker inside Proxmox LXC with a documented AppArmor failure, a careful reading of a host-freeze report, diagnostic commands, and a VM migration plan.
item.content:encoded: <p><strong>Docker inside Linux Containers (LXC)</strong> trades some infrastructure overhead for more interactions between the application runtime and the Proxmox host. For Docker services your household depends on, a Debian <strong>virtual machine (VM)</strong> is a practical starting point because it separates the guest kernel and simplifies the environment you must reproduce during troubleshooting. This article examines the supplied video, checks its underlying incident report, and adds documented failures and a migration plan.</p> <h2 id="key-takeaways"> <a href="#key-takeaways" title="Key Takeaways">Key Takeaways</a> <a href="#key-takeaways" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Key Takeaways">#</a> </h2> <ul> <li><strong>Separate failure types:</strong> A Docker startup error, a stalled VM, and an unresponsive physical host require different investigations.</li> <li><strong>Evaluate the evidence:</strong> Stability after migration supports a recovery decision without proving the original cause.</li> <li><strong>Check current documentation:</strong> Native OCI image support and Docker nested inside LXC are different deployment paths.</li> <li><strong>Protect persistent data:</strong> Proxmox backups and Compose files do not automatically cover every application data location.</li> <li><strong>Test the recovery plan:</strong> Measure restoration, reboot behavior, and service availability before retiring the old deployment.</li> </ul> <h2 id="before-you-begin"> <a href="#before-you-begin" title="Before You Begin">Before You Begin</a> <a href="#before-you-begin" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Before You Begin">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Difficulty:</strong> Intermediate. <strong>Audience:</strong> Proxmox administrators choosing between nested Docker and Docker in a VM. You should recognize a Compose project, a container mount, and a Linux shell prompt before following the diagnostic examples.</p> <p><strong>Estimated effort:</strong> Allow 30–60 minutes for inventory and evidence collection. Migration time depends on database size, storage throughput, hardware access, and the outage window you choose. The examples below are documented procedures and illustrative reasoning, not benchmarks from a lab operated for this article.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Requirement</th> <th>Why it matters</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Host console access</strong></td> <td>Distinguishes network failure from a host-wide stall</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Current backups</strong></td> <td>Provides a recovery path before changing the deployment</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Container and VM IDs</strong></td> <td>Keeps host commands directed at the intended workload</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Application data inventory</strong></td> <td>Identifies volumes, bind mounts, databases, and external dependencies</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Separate test environment</strong></td> <td>Supports migration rehearsal without duplicate production writers</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <h2 id="watch-the-source-video"> <a href="#watch-the-source-video" title="Watch the Source Video">Watch the Source Video</a> <a href="#watch-the-source-video" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Watch the Source Video">#</a> </h2> <script> function loadLiteYouTubeScript() { if (document.querySelector('script[src^="/p/jsdelivr/npm/@justinribeiro/lite-youtube@1.5.0/lite-youtube.js"]')) { console.log('Lite YouTube script is already loaded.'); return; } var scriptTag = document.createElement('script'); scriptTag.src = '/p/jsdelivr/npm/@justinribeiro/lite-youtube@1.5.0/lite-youtube.js'; scriptTag.setAttribute('defer', ''); scriptTag.setAttribute('type', 'module'); scriptTag.setAttribute('fetchpriority', 'low'); document.body.appendChild(scriptTag); } document.addEventListener('DOMContentLoaded', function () { if (typeof yieldToMain === 'function') { yieldToMain(loadLiteYouTubeScript, "user-visible"); } else { loadLiteYouTubeScript(); } }); </script> <style scoped> .lite-youtube-fallback { aspect-ratio: 16 / 9; display: flex; justify-content: center; align-items: center; flex-direction: column; gap: 1em; padding: 1em; background-color: #000; color: #fff; text-decoration: none; } .lite-youtube-fallback::before { display: block; content: ''; border: solid transparent; border-width: 2em 0 2em 3em; border-left-color: red; } .lite-youtube-fallback:hover::before { border-left-color: #fff; } .lite-youtube-fallback:focus { outline: 2px solid red; } </style><div itemscope itemtype="http://schema.org/VideoObject http://schema.org/LearningResource" style="position: relative; padding-bottom: 56.25%; height: 0; overflow: hidden;"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Proxmox: The Hidden Danger of Running Docker Inside LXC"> <meta itemprop="description" content="An explainer about Docker nested inside Proxmox LXC, intermittent host freezes, and a migration to Debian virtual machines"> <meta itemprop="thumbnailUrl" content="https://img.youtube.com/vi/XyPBHhZg0Ok/maxresdefault.jpg"> <meta itemprop="contentUrl" content="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XyPBHhZg0Ok"> <meta itemprop="uploadDate" content="2026-09-15T17:00:09-07:00"> <meta itemprop="learningResourceType" content="Concept Overview"> <meta itemprop="educationalLevel" content="High school (US)"> <lite-youtube videoid="XyPBHhZg0Ok" videotitle="Proxmox: The Hidden Danger of Running Docker Inside LXC" videoplay="" nocookie posterloading="lazy" loading="lazy" params=""> <noscript> <a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XyPBHhZg0Ok" class="lite-youtube-fallback" style="position: absolute; top: 0; left: 0; width: 100%; height: 100%; border:0;" title="Proxmox: The Hidden Danger of Running Docker Inside LXC"> <span class="lyt-visually-hidden"></span> </a> </noscript> </lite-youtube> </div> <script type="application/ld+json"> { "@context": "https://schema.org", "@type": ["VideoObject", "LearningResource"], "name": "Proxmox: The Hidden Danger of Running Docker Inside LXC", "description": "An explainer about Docker nested inside Proxmox LXC, intermittent host freezes, and a migration to Debian virtual machines", "thumbnailUrl": ["https:\/\/img.youtube.com\/vi\/XyPBHhZg0Ok\/maxresdefault.jpg"], "contentUrl": "https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XyPBHhZg0Ok", "uploadDate": "2026-09-15T17:00:09-07:00", "learningResourceType": "Concept Overview", "educationalLevel": "High school (US)" } </script> <p><strong>Source video:</strong> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Proxmox: The Hidden Danger of Running Docker Inside LXC"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XyPBHhZg0Ok"> <a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XyPBHhZg0Ok" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Proxmox: The Hidden Danger of Running Docker Inside LXC</a> </span> , published September 15, 2026, by <em>Proxmox x Kubernetes x Homelab x Backup</em>. The central question is useful: how much operational uncertainty accompanies a resource-saving architecture?</p> <p><strong>Evidence boundary:</strong> The video narrates an incident and proposes lessons. The sections below distinguish the owner’s observations, documented software behavior, and recommendations derived from them.</p> <h2 id="what-the-incident-establishes"> <a href="#what-the-incident-establishes" title="What the Incident Establishes">What the Incident Establishes</a> <a href="#what-the-incident-establishes" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="What the Incident Establishes">#</a> </h2> <p>The original report describes an <strong>Intel Core i3-13100 and BIOSTAR H610MHP host</strong>. The owner reported intermittent freezes affecting management access and LXC services. A connected display stopped responding, although the report explicitly says syslog continued producing output. This is more specific than treating the event as entirely log-free. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Original Proxmox forum report"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://forum.proxmox.com/threads/pve-host-freezes-every-2-3-weeks.185009/"> <a href="https://forum.proxmox.com/threads/pve-host-freezes-every-2-3-weeks.185009/" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Original Proxmox forum report</a> </span> </p> <p>The owner later reported <strong>improvement after migration</strong>. In an August 3 follow-up, they described moving Docker workloads into Debian virtual machines and stopping the Docker-bearing LXCs. They reported no further freezes at the time of the update, while the video cites a 16-day stable period. Neither statement supplies a controlled reproduction or identifies a particular defective component. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Owner’s follow-up in the same thread"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://forum.proxmox.com/threads/pve-host-freezes-every-2-3-weeks.185009/"> <a href="https://forum.proxmox.com/threads/pve-host-freezes-every-2-3-weeks.185009/" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Owner’s follow-up in the same thread</a> </span> </p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Observation</th> <th>What it supports</th> <th>What it does not establish</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Long initial uptime</strong></td> <td>The earlier workload and software combination operated successfully</td> <td>Reliability after every later update</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Host and services stall</strong></td> <td>The outage extends beyond one application</td> <td>Docker as the root cause</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Migration precedes improvement</strong></td> <td>A useful operational workaround</td> <td>Which changed interaction removed the trigger</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Sixteen stable days</strong></td> <td>A bounded observation period</td> <td>Resolution of every two-to-three-week failure pattern</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>The <strong>observation period</strong> deserves scrutiny. Sixteen days falls inside a 14–21 day recurrence window. A longer observation period covering several former failure intervals, comparable workloads, and ordinary maintenance improves confidence, but still falls short of a controlled cause-and-effect demonstration.</p> <p><strong>Operational success and root-cause proof</strong> are separate outcomes. Restoring trusted household services is a valid reason to migrate. Describe the result as improved observed reliability until stronger evidence establishes the mechanism.</p> <h2 id="locate-the-kernel-boundary"> <a href="#locate-the-kernel-boundary" title="Locate the Kernel Boundary">Locate the Kernel Boundary</a> <a href="#locate-the-kernel-boundary" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Locate the Kernel Boundary">#</a> </h2> <div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" style="color:#f8f8f2;background-color:#272822;-moz-tab-size:4;-o-tab-size:4;tab-size:4;-webkit-text-size-adjust:none;"><code class="language-text" data-lang="text"><span style="display:flex;"><span>Docker inside LXC: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Application -> Docker runtime -> LXC namespaces and policy </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> -> Proxmox host kernel -> physical hardware </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Docker inside a VM: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Application -> Docker runtime -> guest Linux kernel </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> -> virtual hardware / KVM-QEMU </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> -> Proxmox host kernel -> physical hardware </span></span></code></pre></div><p><strong>LXC</strong> uses the host kernel. Namespaces, control groups, capabilities, seccomp, and security profiles restrict processes without supplying a separate kernel. Adding Docker inside LXC creates another container-management layer around workloads using the same underlying host kernel. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="LXC architecture and containment features"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://linuxcontainers.org/lxc/introduction/"> <a href="https://linuxcontainers.org/lxc/introduction/" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >LXC architecture and containment features</a> </span> </p> <p>A <strong>VM</strong> introduces a guest kernel. A guest kernel failure normally affects its VM, while Proxmox continues managing the other guests. The VM still depends on the physical host, hypervisor, storage, and networking. Hardware failure or a host-kernel defect remains a shared dependency.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Boundary</th> <th>Docker inside LXC</th> <th>Docker inside a VM</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Kernel used by applications</strong></td> <td>Proxmox host kernel</td> <td>Guest kernel</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Docker runtime environment</strong></td> <td>Constrained by the outer container’s policy</td> <td>Installed inside a conventional guest OS</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Guest kernel updates</strong></td> <td>Tied to the host kernel</td> <td>Managed inside the guest</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Physical host outage</strong></td> <td>Stops dependent workloads</td> <td>Stops dependent workloads</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>A VM limits <strong>some failure propagation</strong>, not all of it. An application process crash inside LXC does not automatically crash Proxmox. Likewise, putting every household service into one Docker VM still groups those services behind one guest operating system and one maintenance schedule.</p> <p>For the <strong>broader conceptual comparison</strong>, see <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Docker containers versus virtual machines"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/articles/docker-vs-vms/"> <a href="/articles/docker-vs-vms/" rel="follow me" >Docker containers versus virtual machines</a> </span> . Here, the decision concerns Docker’s placement within Proxmox and the resulting troubleshooting boundaries.</p> <h2 id="define-support-precisely"> <a href="#define-support-precisely" title="Define Support Precisely">Define Support Precisely</a> <a href="#define-support-precisely" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Define Support Precisely">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>“Unsupported”</strong> needs a named component and version. Distinguish vendor-recommended deployment, documented features, distribution maintenance, and a contractual support entitlement. A working nested stack does not prove all its combinations receive equal testing, while a recommendation for VMs does not mean maintainers refuse every nesting-related bug.</p> <p><strong>Current Proxmox documentation</strong> adds an important distinction. Its container-toolkit source describes <strong>Open Container Initiative (OCI)</strong> application-image support as a technology preview, with images converted into the LXC framework. It also recommends containers inside a QEMU VM for requirements emphasizing isolation and live migration. Importing an OCI image into this framework differs from installing Docker Engine and running Compose inside an LXC guest. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Proxmox container-toolkit documentation"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://github.com/proxmox/pve-docs/blob/master/pct.adoc"> <a href="https://github.com/proxmox/pve-docs/blob/master/pct.adoc" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Proxmox container-toolkit documentation</a> </span> </p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Deployment</th> <th>Question to verify</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Traditional LXC guest</strong></td> <td>Does its OS template and application fit the documented container restrictions?</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Docker nested in LXC</strong></td> <td>Which kernel, runtime, security-policy, and storage combinations have been tested?</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Native OCI image import</strong></td> <td>Does the installed Proxmox version provide the documented feature and required behavior?</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Docker inside Debian VM</strong></td> <td>Does the guest release meet Docker’s installation requirements?</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>Docker publishes a <strong>Debian installation path</strong>. Use its supported-release list and repository instructions for the guest. Record the versions you deploy rather than assuming an older tutorial remains accurate. This provides a documented installation baseline, not a guarantee of uptime or an automatic paid-support contract. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Docker Engine on Debian"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://docs.docker.com/engine/install/debian/"> <a href="https://docs.docker.com/engine/install/debian/" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Docker Engine on Debian</a> </span> </p> <h2 id="a-confirmed-nesting-failure"> <a href="#a-confirmed-nesting-failure" title="A Confirmed Nesting Failure">A Confirmed Nesting Failure</a> <a href="#a-confirmed-nesting-failure" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="A Confirmed Nesting Failure">#</a> </h2> <p>The <strong>2025 runc/AppArmor incompatibility</strong> is a verifiable example. The runc maintainers documented a failure involving descriptor reopening inside an outer container with an AppArmor profile. AppArmor misinterpreted an access under <strong><code>/proc/sys</code></strong> as an access under <strong><code>/sys</code></strong>, causing a policy denial. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="runc issue 4968"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://github.com/opencontainers/runc/issues/4968"> <a href="https://github.com/opencontainers/runc/issues/4968" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >runc issue 4968</a> </span> </p> <p>An <strong>affected startup</strong> reported this error fragment:</p> <div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" style="color:#f8f8f2;background-color:#272822;-moz-tab-size:4;-o-tab-size:4;tab-size:4;-webkit-text-size-adjust:none;"><code class="language-text" data-lang="text"><span style="display:flex;"><span>open sysctl net.ipv4.ip_unprivileged_port_start file: reopen fd 8: permission denied </span></span></code></pre></div><p>The recorded failure prevented <strong>container startup</strong>. It does not explain the forum owner’s host freezes. The issue records <strong><code>lxc-pve 6.0.5-2</code></strong> as a Proxmox fix for this specific problem, and the corresponding upstream LXC change merged on November 20, 2025. <em>Those are historical fix references, not a recommended package pin for a current installation.</em> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Maintainer’s fix summary"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://github.com/opencontainers/runc/issues/4968"> <a href="https://github.com/opencontainers/runc/issues/4968" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Maintainer’s fix summary</a> </span> , <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="merged LXC change"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://github.com/lxc/lxc/pull/4609"> <a href="https://github.com/lxc/lxc/pull/4609" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >merged LXC change</a> </span> </p> <p>The lesson is <strong>dependency coordination</strong>. A runtime security change interacted with the outer container’s policy, and the fix required work in another layer. Prefer the appropriate maintained package update for your release over permanently disabling AppArmor or retaining an old vulnerable runtime.</p> <blockquote> <p><strong>Key takeaway:</strong> This incident demonstrates a real nested-container compatibility problem and a real maintainer response. It establishes neither universal LXC instability nor the cause of a separate host lockup.</p> </blockquote> <h2 id="compare-the-real-costs"> <a href="#compare-the-real-costs" title="Compare the Real Costs">Compare the Real Costs</a> <a href="#compare-the-real-costs" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Compare the Real Costs">#</a> </h2> <p>Measure efficiency with your <strong>actual workload</strong>. Compare host memory pressure, CPU demand, storage latency, application response times, and recovery effort under equivalent conditions. Assigned VM RAM, guest free memory, and host resident memory represent different measurements.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Claimed saving</th> <th>Measurement to collect</th> <th>Additional cost to record</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Lower memory overhead</strong></td> <td>Host memory use and pressure during the same workload</td> <td>Time spent managing nested limits and diagnosing contention</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Faster deployment</strong></td> <td>Time to a working service with its data restored</td> <td>Time to rebuild after a failed update</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Simpler hardware sharing</strong></td> <td>Required devices, permissions, and successful application use</td> <td>Host-driver dependency and migration constraints</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Easier backups</strong></td> <td>A successful restore of all required data</td> <td>External mounts and application consistency</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>Docker documents <strong>unrestricted CPU and memory use</strong> by default unless constraints are applied. In an LXC deployment, the outer container adds its own limits. In a VM, the guest allocation adds another capacity boundary. A guest still needs capacity for its OS, Docker, caches, and peak application demand. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Docker resource constraints"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://docs.docker.com/engine/containers/resource_constraints/"> <a href="https://docs.docker.com/engine/containers/resource_constraints/" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Docker resource constraints</a> </span> </p> <p><strong>Hardware access</strong> is a workload requirement. Sharing a host graphics device with a container and assigning a PCI device to a VM involve different driver and isolation arrangements. List the exact device and application requirement before choosing. For example, a media workload requiring hardware decoding needs a successful decode test after migration, alongside ordinary HTTP health checks.</p> <p>Avoid <strong>universal overhead numbers</strong>. This article supplies no fixed RAM penalty or performance percentage because those figures require a controlled workload, configuration, and measurement method. Use an observed result from your own comparison in the decision record below.</p> <h2 id="collect-evidence-by-layer"> <a href="#collect-evidence-by-layer" title="Collect Evidence by Layer">Collect Evidence by Layer</a> <a href="#collect-evidence-by-layer" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Collect Evidence by Layer">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Begin on the Proxmox host</strong>, using an administrative shell. Replace <strong><code>101</code></strong> with the LXC ID under investigation:</p> <div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" style="color:#f8f8f2;background-color:#272822;-moz-tab-size:4;-o-tab-size:4;tab-size:4;-webkit-text-size-adjust:none;"><code class="language-bash" data-lang="bash"><span style="display:flex;"><span>pveversion -v </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>uname -r </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>pct config <span style="color:#ae81ff">101</span> </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>journalctl --list-boots </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>journalctl -k -b -1 --no-pager </span></span></code></pre></div><p><strong><code>pveversion -v</code></strong> records the installed Proxmox component versions. <strong><code>pct config</code></strong> records the outer container configuration. In <strong><code>journalctl</code></strong>, <strong><code>-k</code></strong> selects kernel messages, <strong><code>-b -1</code></strong> selects the previous boot, and <strong><code>--no-pager</code></strong> produces plain terminal output. Previous-boot messages require retained journal data. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Proxmox toolkit"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://github.com/proxmox/pve-docs/blob/master/pct.adoc"> <a href="https://github.com/proxmox/pve-docs/blob/master/pct.adoc" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Proxmox toolkit</a> </span> , <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="systemd journalctl reference"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://github.com/systemd/systemd/blob/main/man/journalctl.xml"> <a href="https://github.com/systemd/systemd/blob/main/man/journalctl.xml" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >systemd journalctl reference</a> </span> </p> <p><strong>Then inspect the Docker host</strong>, inside the LXC or VM running its daemon:</p> <div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" style="color:#f8f8f2;background-color:#272822;-moz-tab-size:4;-o-tab-size:4;tab-size:4;-webkit-text-size-adjust:none;"><code class="language-bash" data-lang="bash"><span style="display:flex;"><span>docker version </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>docker info </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>docker compose version </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>docker ps -a </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>docker stats --no-stream </span></span></code></pre></div><p>Record <strong>both environments</strong>. The container image tag alone omits Docker, containerd, runc, the host kernel, security policy, and storage backend. Save the incident time, recent updates, and whether the local host console responded. Redact credentials and private application details before publishing diagnostic material.</p> <p><strong>Inspect a specific workload</strong>, replacing <strong><code>app</code></strong> with its container name:</p> <div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" style="color:#f8f8f2;background-color:#272822;-moz-tab-size:4;-o-tab-size:4;tab-size:4;-webkit-text-size-adjust:none;"><code class="language-bash" data-lang="bash"><span style="display:flex;"><span>docker inspect --format <span style="color:#e6db74">'{{json .State}}'</span> app </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>docker inspect --format <span style="color:#e6db74">'{{.RestartCount}}'</span> app </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>docker inspect --format <span style="color:#e6db74">'{{json .Mounts}}'</span> app </span></span></code></pre></div><p><strong><code>docker inspect</code></strong> exposes state, restart count, and mount information for the named container. Treat a restart count as a clue to correlate with logs, not proof of a host-level defect. A recreated container also starts a new history. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Docker inspect reference"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://docs.docker.com/reference/cli/docker/inspect/"> <a href="https://docs.docker.com/reference/cli/docker/inspect/" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Docker inspect reference</a> </span> </p> <h2 id="distinguish-pressure-from-lockups"> <a href="#distinguish-pressure-from-lockups" title="Distinguish Pressure From Lockups">Distinguish Pressure From Lockups</a> <a href="#distinguish-pressure-from-lockups" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Distinguish Pressure From Lockups">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Capture Linux pressure information on the host</strong> while the problem develops:</p> <div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" style="color:#f8f8f2;background-color:#272822;-moz-tab-size:4;-o-tab-size:4;tab-size:4;-webkit-text-size-adjust:none;"><code class="language-bash" data-lang="bash"><span style="display:flex;"><span>cat /proc/pressure/cpu </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>cat /proc/pressure/memory </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>cat /proc/pressure/io </span></span></code></pre></div><p><strong>Pressure Stall Information</strong>, or PSI, reports time lost while tasks wait for resources. Its <strong><code>some</code></strong> and <strong><code>full</code></strong> fields describe different stall conditions, while <strong><code>avg10</code></strong>, <strong><code>avg60</code></strong>, and <strong><code>avg300</code></strong> summarize recent intervals. Memory pressure differs from memory occupancy: a large cache alone does not establish a shortage. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Linux PSI documentation"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://docs.kernel.org/accounting/psi.html"> <a href="https://docs.kernel.org/accounting/psi.html" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Linux PSI documentation</a> </span> </p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Evidence</th> <th>Useful interpretation</th> <th>Next check</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>One container repeatedly exits</strong></td> <td>Application or container-runtime failure</td> <td>Exit state, service logs, restart policy</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>SSH fails, console works</strong></td> <td>Network or management-path failure</td> <td>Link state, NIC driver, bridge, firewall</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Memory PSI rises under load</strong></td> <td>Tasks lose time to memory contention</td> <td>Limits, reclaim activity, OOM records, workload growth</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Storage requests stall</strong></td> <td>I/O dependency is delaying work</td> <td>Device health, storage logs, latency and queueing</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Watchdog reports a lockup</strong></td> <td>Kernel detector observed a defined stall condition</td> <td>Full trace, kernel version, reproducible trigger</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>No final log entry</strong></td> <td>Evidence collection ended before useful output arrived</td> <td>Persistent or external capture before recurrence</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>A <strong>Linux lockup report</strong> has a technical meaning. Kernel watchdogs distinguish soft and hard lockup conditions. A browser timing out does not establish either condition, and a missing watchdog report does not prove the host remained healthy. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Linux lockup-detector documentation"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://docs.kernel.org/admin-guide/lockup-watchdogs.html"> <a href="https://docs.kernel.org/admin-guide/lockup-watchdogs.html" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Linux lockup-detector documentation</a> </span> </p> <p><strong>Firmware and power-state changes</strong> are experiments. Record the previous setting, the reason for changing it, and the observation period. Disabling a CPU idle state changes power and thermal behavior, so a report involving another machine is insufficient evidence to prescribe the same setting universally.</p> <h2 id="preserve-useful-logs"> <a href="#preserve-useful-logs" title="Preserve Useful Logs">Preserve Useful Logs</a> <a href="#preserve-useful-logs" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Preserve Useful Logs">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Persistent journaling</strong> improves the chance of retaining evidence across a reboot. A journald configuration drop-in uses this setting:</p> <div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" style="color:#f8f8f2;background-color:#272822;-moz-tab-size:4;-o-tab-size:4;tab-size:4;-webkit-text-size-adjust:none;"><code class="language-ini" data-lang="ini"><span style="display:flex;"><span><span style="color:#66d9ef">[Journal]</span> </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span><span style="color:#a6e22e">Storage</span><span style="color:#f92672">=</span><span style="color:#e6db74">persistent</span> </span></span></code></pre></div><p><strong><code>Storage=persistent</code></strong> requests disk-backed journal storage when available. Configure retention limits and available disk capacity as part of the change, then verify earlier boots appear in <strong><code>journalctl --list-boots</code></strong>. Persistent logging still depends on the host completing writes before the failure. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="systemd journald configuration"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://github.com/systemd/systemd/blob/main/man/journald.conf.xml"> <a href="https://github.com/systemd/systemd/blob/main/man/journald.conf.xml" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >systemd journald configuration</a> </span> </p> <p><strong>External observation</strong> adds another perspective. Monitor the service from a different machine and record timestamps. A monitor running on the failing Proxmox host disappears during the same outage, reducing its value for distinguishing downtime from missing telemetry.</p> <p><strong>Illustrative test:</strong> Schedule a lightweight HTTP check from a separate system, then compare failures with host reachability and local-console behavior. An application timeout with a responsive host points to a different investigation than simultaneous application, management, and console failure. This is a diagnostic design, not an observed result from the source incident.</p> <h2 id="plan-a-controlled-migration"> <a href="#plan-a-controlled-migration" title="Plan a Controlled Migration">Plan a Controlled Migration</a> <a href="#plan-a-controlled-migration" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Plan a Controlled Migration">#</a> </h2> <p>Start with <strong>one low-risk Compose project</strong>. Prepare a Debian VM using a release listed in Docker’s installation documentation, establish backups, and configure resource allocations. Keep the original deployment available for rollback until the replacement passes its tests. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Docker’s Debian installation instructions"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://docs.docker.com/engine/install/debian/"> <a href="https://docs.docker.com/engine/install/debian/" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Docker’s Debian installation instructions</a> </span> </p> <p><strong>Inventory the Compose project</strong> from its working directory:</p> <div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" style="color:#f8f8f2;background-color:#272822;-moz-tab-size:4;-o-tab-size:4;tab-size:4;-webkit-text-size-adjust:none;"><code class="language-bash" data-lang="bash"><span style="display:flex;"><span>docker compose config --quiet </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>docker compose config --images </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>docker compose config --volumes </span></span></code></pre></div><p><strong><code>--quiet</code></strong> validates the configuration without printing it. <strong><code>--images</code></strong> lists referenced images, while <strong><code>--volumes</code></strong> lists named volumes. These commands do not export application data or provide a complete bind-mount inventory. Review the Compose file and each container’s mounts as well. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Docker Compose config reference"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://docs.docker.com/reference/cli/docker/compose/config/"> <a href="https://docs.docker.com/reference/cli/docker/compose/config/" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Docker Compose config reference</a> </span> </p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Data or dependency</th> <th>Migration action</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Compose definitions</strong></td> <td>Transfer project files and retain the tested configuration</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Secrets and environment</strong></td> <td>Recreate required values through the chosen secret-management process</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Named volumes</strong></td> <td>Back up and restore their contents with application-consistent procedures</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Bind-mounted paths</strong></td> <td>Transfer or reconnect the actual source data and verify ownership</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Databases</strong></td> <td>Use the database’s supported backup/restore or quiesced-copy procedure</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Devices and shares</strong></td> <td>Re-establish access and test application behavior</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Ports and DNS</strong></td> <td>Stage the replacement address and plan the cutover</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>Volumes</strong> outlive containers, but they do not migrate themselves. A Compose file names resources and defines services. Docker’s volume documentation describes separate backup and restore operations for persistent contents. Do not assume recreating the project restores its data. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Docker volume lifecycle and backups"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://docs.docker.com/engine/storage/volumes/"> <a href="https://docs.docker.com/engine/storage/volumes/" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Docker volume lifecycle and backups</a> </span> </p> <p>Check <strong>Proxmox backup coverage</strong> separately. Its backup documentation excludes device and bind-mount contents from container backups. A successful backup of an LXC root filesystem therefore does not establish protection for every directory exposed inside it. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Proxmox backup documentation"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://github.com/proxmox/pve-docs/blob/master/vzdump.adoc"> <a href="https://github.com/proxmox/pve-docs/blob/master/vzdump.adoc" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Proxmox backup documentation</a> </span> </p> <h3 id="check-storage-before-copying"> <a href="#check-storage-before-copying" title="Check Storage Before Copying">Check Storage Before Copying</a> <a href="#check-storage-before-copying" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Check Storage Before Copying">#</a> </h3> <p><strong>Inspect Docker’s actual storage configuration</strong> on each Docker host:</p> <div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" style="color:#f8f8f2;background-color:#272822;-moz-tab-size:4;-o-tab-size:4;tab-size:4;-webkit-text-size-adjust:none;"><code class="language-bash" data-lang="bash"><span style="display:flex;"><span>docker info </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>findmnt -T /var/lib/docker </span></span></code></pre></div><p><strong><code>findmnt</code></strong> identifies the filesystem containing the specified path. Replace <strong><code>/var/lib/docker</code></strong> if your daemon uses a different data root, and inspect containerd’s storage path when applicable. Docker documents a distinction between the containerd image store and classic storage drivers, with backend-specific requirements. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Docker storage-backend selection"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://docs.docker.com/engine/storage/drivers/select-storage-driver/"> <a href="https://docs.docker.com/engine/storage/drivers/select-storage-driver/" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Docker storage-backend selection</a> </span> </p> <p><strong>Recreate images and restore application data</strong> using the chosen backend’s documented procedures. Copying a live Docker data directory between different storage arrangements introduces additional assumptions about metadata, mount state, and consistency. It is a different operation from backing up a stopped application’s data volume.</p> <h3 id="cut-over-with-rollback"> <a href="#cut-over-with-rollback" title="Cut Over With Rollback">Cut Over With Rollback</a> <a href="#cut-over-with-rollback" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Cut Over With Rollback">#</a> </h3> <ol> <li><strong>Rehearse restoration</strong> in the VM using separate addresses and test data where appropriate.</li> <li><strong>Stop production writes</strong> during the agreed outage window and take the final consistent backup.</li> <li><strong>Restore and validate</strong> application data, permissions, credentials, and required hardware access.</li> <li><strong>Switch service routing</strong> after the replacement passes application-specific checks.</li> <li><strong>Keep the original stopped</strong> while retaining its configuration and recovery data.</li> <li><strong>Document rollback handling</strong> for data written after cutover before restarting the old system.</li> </ol> <p>Avoid <strong>two active writers</strong> against the same database storage. A rollback involving new production data requires a plan for preserving or intentionally discarding those writes. Merely restarting an old container does not reconcile two diverging data histories.</p> <h2 id="test-more-than-uptime"> <a href="#test-more-than-uptime" title="Test More Than Uptime">Test More Than Uptime</a> <a href="#test-more-than-uptime" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Test More Than Uptime">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Acceptance tests</strong> should follow the service’s purpose. A green container status establishes a running process. A usable service also requires its data, network access, dependencies, and recovery behavior.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Test</th> <th>Evidence to retain</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Application function</strong></td> <td>A successful real transaction, query, or media operation</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Data completeness</strong></td> <td>Expected records, files, permissions, and recent changes</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Guest reboot</strong></td> <td>Services return without manual repair</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Backup restoration</strong></td> <td>The restored copy completes the same functional check</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Representative load</strong></td> <td>Latency, CPU, memory pressure, and storage behavior</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Maintenance rehearsal</strong></td> <td>A tested update and a usable recovery procedure</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Longer observation</strong></td> <td>Availability records spanning several previous failure intervals</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>Worked decision:</strong> A camera service and an experimental downloader currently share one nested stack. Moving both into one VM improves kernel separation but preserves a shared guest-maintenance boundary. If camera availability is the priority, evaluate separate maintenance groups and resource limits, then test recording continuity during downloader updates.</p> <p><strong>Expected reasoning:</strong> The best placement follows the service dependency you need to isolate. Two VMs on one physical server still share its power, storage, and host kernel. If the requirement includes surviving the server’s outage, the design needs an additional independent system or an acceptable manual fallback.</p> <h2 id="create-your-decision-record"> <a href="#create-your-decision-record" title="Create Your Decision Record">Create Your Decision Record</a> <a href="#create-your-decision-record" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Create Your Decision Record">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Use measured evidence</strong> to choose a deployment and define when you will revisit it:</p> <div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" style="color:#f8f8f2;background-color:#272822;-moz-tab-size:4;-o-tab-size:4;tab-size:4;-webkit-text-size-adjust:none;"><code class="language-text" data-lang="text"><span style="display:flex;"><span>Service and household impact: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Current host / kernel / LXC / Docker versions: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Required GPU, device, and network access: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Measured memory, CPU, storage, and latency: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Known failure signature and recurrence interval: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Backup coverage and successful restore evidence: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Chosen deployment and reason: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Permitted outage window and recovery target: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Cutover and post-cutover data rollback procedure: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Acceptance tests and observation period: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Condition requiring another architecture review: </span></span></code></pre></div><p><strong>Choose LXC nesting deliberately</strong> when its benefits justify the integration work and you have tested the recovery path. Choose a VM when a conventional Docker guest environment and a separate guest kernel simplify the service’s operation. Neither decision substitutes for backups, monitoring, and host maintenance.</p> <h2 id="next-steps"> <a href="#next-steps" title="Next Steps">Next Steps</a> <a href="#next-steps" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Next Steps">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Inventory one service</strong> first. Identify its persistent data, physical dependencies, failure symptoms, and recovery target. Rehearse a restore before deciding whether a migration is necessary.</p> <p>For <strong>related work</strong>, use the <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Proxmox VE upgrade guide"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/articles/proxmox-ve-8-to-9-upgrade-guide/"> <a href="/articles/proxmox-ve-8-to-9-upgrade-guide/" rel="follow me" >Proxmox VE upgrade guide</a> </span> for upgrade planning and the <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Docker and Kubernetes security guide"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/articles/how-to-secure-your-docker-and-kubernetes-environment/"> <a href="/articles/how-to-secure-your-docker-and-kubernetes-environment/" rel="follow me" >Docker and Kubernetes security guide</a> </span> for workload hardening. Keep architecture selection, upgrade execution, and incident diagnosis as distinct decisions with their own evidence.</p> <h2 id="sources-and-evidence"> <a href="#sources-and-evidence" title="Sources and Evidence">Sources and Evidence</a> <a href="#sources-and-evidence" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Sources and Evidence">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Research checked:</strong> September 16, 2026.
